candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures reports of violent or high-risk student behavior and inadequate response: numerous circle reviews cite gang activity, 40+ fights, bathroom assaults, kill‑lists, wrongful arrests by police, sexual harassment, and persistent bullying left unaddressed (e.g., ‘Gang activity… you should not send your child’, ‘police … I got arrested … needed years of therapy’, ‘Children are being harassed and beat up in the bathrooms’). Square reviews refer to bullying and discipline issues less often and with far less systemic or violent detail, so posts with concrete safety crises belong here.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This grouping covers logistical, physical‑plant, and tech implementation problems: circle reviews repeatedly call out dysfunctional laptop/iPad programs, poor filtering, unresolved e‑book access, packed/absent buses, missed lunches, pest infestations, broken outlets, and overcrowded hallways (e.g., ‘laptops remain unused…can’t access my Chemistry book’, ‘busses are packed…not all students are receiving lunches’, ‘they cannot keep the building free of roaches’). Square reviews rarely document persistent infrastructure breakdowns, so items describing these concrete facility/tech/transport failures map here.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, tangibl: Use this bucket for descriptions of substantive program breadth and pathway offerings: many circle reviews enumerate vocational courses, award‑winning FFA/ag programs, senior internships that led to jobs, teacher‑adjunct dual‑enrollment and transferable college credits, strong music/theater achievements and state athletic championships (e.g., ‘12th grade project…helped him get a job’, ‘award winning Agriculture department’, ‘entered college with upwards of 40 College Credits’). Square reviews emphasize some extracurriculars but lack the same consistent, concrete program/pathway documentation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures governance and people‑management failures: circle reviews frequently recount front‑office rudeness, pass‑the‑buck between school and board, favoritism and confidentiality breaches, counselors unavailable or obstructive, politicized coach protection, and demands to pass failing students (e.g., ‘office is unorganized on purpose’, ‘Guidance did nothing to help any students but their favored few’, ‘they demand that we pass students who do not go to class’). Square reviews more often praise visible leadership and responsive staff, so accounts of sustained administrative unresponsiveness or favoritism belong here.
candidate_defs.square entries report worse core instruc: Assign reviews here that center on inadequate teaching and postsecondary readiness: square entries explicitly criticize failure to teach core academics, poor standardized‑test/Regents performance, declines in GPA after schedule changes, DIY or weak college counseling, and students needing remediation or summer school (e.g., ‘This school does not prepare kids for college at all’, ‘Regents test scores have been abysmal’, ‘the counseling needs to prep for college falls a bit short’). While circle reviews sometimes report mixed instructional quality, square reviews disproportionately describe systemic instructional and college‑prep shortfalls and belong in this bucket.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive on-: This bucket covers reviews that describe frequent fights, gang presence, chronic bullying/harassment (including racial/homophobic slurs and directives to self‑harm), and administrators who fail to effectively intervene — e.g., “Fights every day,” “Gangbangers…create problems,” “Students would tell me to self harm…Nothing was done,” and administrators saying “it is not bullying unless they physically hit you.” These items cluster around safety, student behavior, and staff non-response as recurring, school‑level problems in circle reviews compared with square reviews which report far fewer or more rapidly‑addressed incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a broader, concret: This bucket groups items documenting explicit programmatic offerings and measurable pathways — CTE/Tech centers, dual enrollment/Running Start, strong IB/arts/film/music programs, vocational auto tech, extensive clubs and field trips, and documented scholarship/competition outcomes (e.g., “dual enrollment with Wayne County Community College,” “Tech center…Nursing, EMT, Welding,” “annual film…Hamlet,” and seniors earning large scholarship totals). These reviews emphasize concrete curricular and extracurricular breadth and external partnerships that square entries often do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger persona: This bucket captures reports of teachers being regularly available (lunch/after school tutoring), small class sizes and principals/staff who know students by name, and multigenerational family loyalty or high parent/community day‑to‑day involvement (e.g., “teachers are in their classrooms at lunch and even stay after school to help,” “knew every child's name…250 something of them,” and “parents & community were always deeply involved”). These are relational, resource‑allocation and community features that make circle schools appear more family‑centric and personalized relative to square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This bucket groups complaints about leadership dishonesty, favoritism toward athletes/connected families, nepotistic hires, school‑board politics, and alleged cover‑ups or deliberate mismanagement (examples: “The administration lies…doesn't keep to their word,” “they only care if you are one of the richest people…or if they're in football,” “the comically inept school board,” “the staff is amazing…they do a very good job at covering up all the bad things they do”). These items point to governance and ethics failures being emphasized more in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational a: This bucket collects critiques centered on measurable academic shortcomings and operational breakdowns: weak AP/advanced coursework quality and college readiness (“Not a school that prepares students for collage!”, AP program is not good), high teacher turnover, misplaced registrations/credits and scheduling mistakes that force summer school, counselor overloads, and other day‑to‑day administrative/technology failures. These practical, outcome‑oriented problems are disproportionately reported in square entries versus circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, formal: These reviews emphasize concrete program infrastructure and measurable outcomes—AP/IB/dual-enrollment, CTE pathways, block schedules, college credits, high AP/ACT results and national recognition (e.g., AP scores, National Merit, scholarship totals)—claims that are frequent in circle but absent or far less concrete in square (examples: many AP/dual-enrollment classes, ‘excess of 40 hours of college credit,’ CTE pathways, block-schedule praise).
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher-qu: Circle reviewers repeatedly list diverse clubs, strong music/arts programs, an active student section and athletic successes (e.g., ‘one of the best bands,’ many clubs, spirit awards), while square reviews rarely document comparable extracurricular breadth or prominent arts/athletics achievements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety: Many circle reviews call out drugs, weapons, daily fights, sanctioned or tolerated bullying, metal-detector screening, and administrators failing to protect victims (e.g., students 'had to fight daily,' 'drugs are a horrible problem,' officers ignoring footage), a set of concrete safety failures and security gaps reported far more often in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers give specific operational problems (front office not answering phones, lost medical documents/grades, attendance office miscoding absences, IEP/504 failures, contradictory handbook applications, opaque or inflated grading practices), indicating systemic procedural and communication breakdowns that square reviews mention far less.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher disen: Square reviews more often describe teachers who don’t return calls/emails, are ‘clueless’ or ‘disengaged,’ inadequate remediation or targeted encouragement, and unmet IEP accommodations (e.g., teachers unresponsive to parent contact, failing to support struggling students), whereas circle reviews more frequently describe committed, credentialed or available teachers and targeted academic supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe, syste: These reviews describe frequent physical assaults, gang bullying, repeated fights, medical emergencies sent to ICU, sexual/violence incidents, and claims that school staff or leadership hid incidents or failed to report them (e.g., students sent to ICU, daily gang bullying, pupils stabbed with pencils, and assertions that the school 'covered it up'), while Square reviews lack or downplay these kinds of sustained safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, consis: Many Circle reviewers emphasize teachers who ‘go out of their way,’ routine tutoring/extra help, visible mentorship and counseling, and concrete outcomes (high scholarship totals, dual‑enrollment/AP success, college placements and vocational certifications), whereas Square reviews more often report uneven or absent one‑on‑one support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, fav: Circle reviews repeatedly allege family/name/employee-based advantages and athletic cronyism, plus discriminatory discipline and biased treatment (e.g., ‘if you don’t have the last name or money you are a nobody,’ athletic selections for staff relatives, unequal punishments, and race/sex‑based discipline complaints), problems that are not prominent in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: Circle contains many operational complaints about infrastructure and logistics (no A/C or broken elevators, overcrowded classes, lack of copies, bus and scheduling failures), recurring small fees/required fundraisers, meal‑service harm (children denied lunch), and late hires/poor staffing allocations—contrast Square, which rarely lists these specific operational failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader and more: Circle reviews frequently name structured pathways and high‑value programs—AP/IB/dual‑enrollment, explicit career pathways starting in 9th grade, strong vocational/shop and JROTC programs, band/athletic state championships, and certification programs—whereas Square reviews rarely enumerate comparable formal program breadth or high‑level extracurricular achievements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: This bucket captures reviewer claims about persistent, tangible threats to student safety and unmanaged student misconduct — e.g., repeated reports of "frequent fights," on-campus drug use and smell, gang references, single-day outbreaks ("17 fights in one day"), off-campus assault with concussion, and counselors shrugging off bullying. Items here describe active safety incidents and staff inaction or tolerance of dangerous behavior that reviewers contrast with square entries' far fewer or less severe safety allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: This groups claims about programmatic depth and postsecondary results — examples include many AP offerings, dual‑credit/college‑in‑the‑classroom courses, FAA Part 141 private pilot licensure, vocational/magnet industry certifications, Cambridge/Cambridge‑level classes, and concrete metrics (scholarship totals, National Merit finalists, college recruitment). These raw terms emphasize structural academic pathways and documented outcomes that circle reviewers report more often than square reviewers, who rarely cite such breadth or quantifiable college-prep credentials.
candidate_defs.circle entries document richer, higher‑p: This bucket covers claims about a wide variety of award-winning clubs, marching band success, mandatory/elite athletics, state championships, theater trips, ROTC and strong performing arts — and critiques that sports/band get prioritized above classroom learning (e.g., coaches intervening on grades). Circle reviewers repeatedly describe high participation, competitive wins, and institutional emphasis on extracurriculars, while square entries provide fewer high‑profile extracurricular achievements and less evidence of institutional prioritization.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater governance: This groups reviewer claims that problems stem from unresponsive principals, school boards, or district leadership — e.g., complaints being dismissed or reduced to 'annoyances,' a 'completely disconnected' school board, calls to file suit, and systemic inaction on parent concerns. These terms portray top‑level accountability, governance responsiveness, and policy-level failure as the primary problem in square reviews more often than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe facili: This bucket contains concrete operational/physical deficiencies reported by reviewers: extreme classroom heat/cold due to HVAC failure, lack of textbooks and basic supplies, overcrowded lunch periods and classrooms, leaking ceilings, broken cafeteria/inedible food complaints, and poor technology support. Circle reviewers raise these infrastructure and daily‑operations failures far more frequently than square reviewers, who emphasize other issues instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive, sp: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and high‑end outcomes at circle schools — AP/IB offerings, multiple career academies, dual enrollment, vocational/Ag/CTE tracks, internships, gold‑seal scholarships, state/national awards and documented alumni college placements (e.g., national rankings, full rides, band/mariachi acclaim) — whereas square entries rarely enumerate this depth of structured pathways or aggregate achievement evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews repeatedly document safety problems (chronic bullying, assaults, gang activity, riots/lockdowns, drug problems, weapons/threats) and examples of staff/administration failing to intervene or notify parents (e.g., ‘brutally attacked…no one helped,’ ‘los maestros…incapaz de mantener la seguridad,’ pepper‑spray/lockdown incidents), a pattern described far less often in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent fail: Circle reviewers provide repeated examples of inadequate or adversarial handling of IEPs/504s, poorly informed or unavailable counselors, denied therapies or services unless children are failing, and serious mental‑health harms (suicidal ideation), highlighting systemic gaps in individualized supports that square reviews do not commonly allege.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible, high: Many circle reviews emphasize consistently supportive, hands‑on teachers, named staff who go the extra mile, proactive parent‑teacher communication and online tools (PowerSchool/MySchoolBucks), parent involvement and material supports (coat closets), and administrators who are visible and personable — a pattern of relational investment described more often in circle than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit admi: Circle reviews frequently allege governance and leadership dysfunction — tenure‑driven power dynamics, favoritism toward athletes/teachers' children, accusations of grade changes or record manipulation, vindictive expulsions, rapid leadership churn, and authoritarian secretary/principal control — operational and policy failures that distinguish circle entries from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, deeper: These reviews repeatedly cite an extensive, organized set of in-school programs absent from square: award‑winning band/choir and theater rosters, multiple arts ensembles, many sports and championship teams, IB/AP pathways, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit courses, internships/CTE (e.g., CCAC classes, JROTC, welding/culinary), and magnet/school‑within‑a‑school tracks—claims square reviews do not substantively match (square mentions a handful of clubs or honors but not comparable depth or concrete program outcomes).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain explicit accounts of physical and sexual harassment, chronic bullying, drug use, gang activity, student assaults, and suicidality or psychiatric hospitalization (e.g., 'I was at the point of committing suicide... sexually harrassed and physically abused', 'students' suicides are largely ignored', 'drugs and sex'), while square reviews rarely allege sexual/physical abuse or suicidality and focus on less severe fights or search‑policy concerns.
candidate_defs.square entries depict greater instructio: Square reviewers more often describe teachers who 'don't teach', systemic gaps that force outside tutoring or relearning in college, and curricula that need parent/coach supplementation (e.g., 'With a little extra math and reading coaching outside the school', 'I was totally unprepared for college'), whereas many circle reviews emphasize in‑class rigor, AP/IB coursework, teacher availability, and measurable in‑school academic progress.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more entrenched so: Multiple circle accounts allege staff favoritism tied to athletes, donors, or family connections, longstanding nepotism and awards bias, and institutional discrimination or suppression of POC and LGBTQ+ expression (e.g., 'teachers sometimes hand out free passes to athletes', 'discriminate against POC and LGBTQ+ students', 'parents are notorious for running this school'), whereas square reviews more commonly assert inclusivity or do not allege systemic discrimination tied to family/money.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more active faci: Circle reviews frequently report ongoing or recent capital work and operational upgrades (full building renovations, newly opened high school building, air conditioning, new auditorium/gym/practice turf, one‑to‑one computing programs and technology rollouts, and explicit construction projects 'construction is done!'), while square reviews seldom cite comparable recent facility/tech investments and more often note unresolved resource or operational constraints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more violent safet: These reviews describe concrete safety threats and recurring non‑responses (gangs, shootings, bomb threats, multiple code‑reds, sexual‑assault token responses) and administrators who ignore or inadequately investigate bullying and anonymous complaints (e.g., “the violence…gangs are formed,” “administration does NOTHING unless the parent raises h$&* up,” “they just tell the victim to cope”). They group together accounts of students withdrawn for safety, prolonged absenteeism from fear, and unsafe lockdown/evacuation practices absent from square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more responsive: These reviews emphasize reachable, proactive leadership and staff practices—timely phone/email communication, active behavior monitoring/parental notification, enforced rules, accountable teachers, and competent college counseling (e.g., “No phone calls back” contrasts with square statements like “My son’s counselor has also been very supportive,” “teachers holding him accountable,” and “staff go out of their way to know the students”). They capture operational responsiveness and routine student supports that circle reviews often say are missing or inconsistent.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete, f: Many circle reviews enumerate specific programs and outcomes—STEM academies, IB/honors/AP lists, early‑college/dual‑credit, vocational shop/CTE pathways, capstones, and named college admits or 99% college placement—providing programmatic detail and quantifiable postsecondary evidence (e.g., “99‑100% college placement,” “earn an associate degree while in high school,” “AP Statistics, AP Calculus…,” partnerships with Cleveland Clinic). Square reviews rarely enumerate comparable formal pathways or sustained measurable placement stats.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more tangible reso: These reviews cite outdated textbooks, broken HVAC, missing lab/equipment, program cuts (music downsized), overcrowding, transportation problems, explicit payment‑linked bans on finals, tuition strain, and alleged donor/nepotism favoritism (e.g., ‘no air conditioning,’ ‘they started a tablet program’ vs. ‘Exams scheduled around tuition due dates…cannot take finals,’ ‘Chef…Board President has admitted the Chef is her live in boyfriend’). Square reviews rarely report the same breadth of infrastructure failures, tuition‑driven exclusions, or specific nepotistic misallocation claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries display stronger visible: Many circle reviews emphasize active parental volunteering, parent‑run fundraising, deep alumni ties, faith‑based or single‑sex mission identity, small‑town cohesion, and lively school traditions (homecoming cookouts, summer bridge, ‘felt like home’, ‘faith life outstanding’), portraying organized community investment and pride that square reviews do not consistently describe.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more visible, orga: This bucket groups contrasts where reviewers say circle schools have hands‑on principals/administrators, codified discipline systems, active communication and programmatic decisions (e.g., ‘the principal is on a first name basis…’, ‘system of demerits…4 demerits = 3 hour detention’, organized weekly newsletters), while square reviews more often describe administrative neglect, brushing off bullying, or being ‘terrible’/unresponsive; it captures concrete leadership actions, turnover, transparency, and policy use (e.g., nontransparent substance testing vs. administrators who back teachers).
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more consistent, i: This bucket captures cases where circle reviewers emphasize teacher dedication and hands‑on help (teachers who stay after to tutor, special‑education support, career/dual‑credit mentoring, ‘teachers take each child as if it was their very own’), whereas square reviews more often describe teacher favoritism, neglect, or uneven instruction; it covers classroom presence, long‑term teacher–student relationships, special‑education casework, and in‑class interventions.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups concrete safety and behavior differences: circle reviews list frequent fights, shootings/bomb threats, gang/drug activity, sexual misconduct allegations, and bullying leading to diagnosed depression or withdrawal, while square reviews typically describe isolated disrespect or less pervasive incidents; it indexes physical safety, supervision failures, and student‑on‑student harm.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more extensive, co: This bucket covers contrasts where square reviewers describe broad AP/accelerated offerings, STEM/IB/PLTW programs, high AP/SAT/college‑placement rates and formal university partnerships (e.g., ‘great AP classes’, ‘95% go on to college’, Sacred Heart partnership), whereas circle reviews more often highlight limited AP availability, rigid tracking, or mixed outcomes; it captures institutional program breadth, credentials, and measurable college/career pathways.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger extracurr: This bucket groups contrasts about extracurricular focus and resourcing: circle reviewers frequently report active athletics/traditions, donor/alumni influence in sports, program cuts or pay‑to‑play shifts, contested facility changes (labs torn down for weight rooms), and both visible tech programs and supply shortages, while square reviews either lack such broad extracurricular prominence or emphasize different resource problems; it captures allocation decisions, fees, facilities condition, and programmatic priorities (arts vs athletics).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more structured ad: This bucket groups raw terms where reviewers describe concrete curricular breadth and program structure at circle schools — e.g., multiple AP and IB offerings, named career academies (Biomedical, Technology, Skills Pathway), CTE/robotics awards, JROTC, dual‑enrollment and explicit college‑prep outcomes — contrasted with square reviews that lack or criticize such formalized advanced pathways.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more persistent: This bucket captures safety and discipline differences in which square reviews report ongoing peer violence, bullying, cutting/drug incidents, ignored assaults, and administrators who fail to intervene (e.g., fights, Nazi graffiti, unaddressed sexual threats), while circle reviews more often describe enforced anti‑bullying policies, active discipline, or absence of those persistent safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report materially better: This groups items where circle reviewers mention modern facilities and resources (new gym/college center, 3D printing/robotics labs, 1:1 laptops/iPads, award‑winning band, large clubs and program scale), whereas square reviews note aging/overcrowded buildings, shortages (textbooks, supplies), and far fewer named extracurricular resources.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, re: This bucket covers claims that circle schools provide prompt teacher/administrator communication, parent outreach, active principals working on turnaround initiatives, and documented improvement programs (AIMS, improved call systems), while square reviews repeatedly cite poor or delayed communication, unreturned calls, and leaders perceived as disengaged.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff favorit: This groups reviewer allegations about personnel practices at circle schools — coach bullying/favoritism, hiring relatives or unqualified staff, selective enforcement of rules, faculty theft or inappropriate behavior, and administration failing to hold staff accountable — contrasted with square reviews that more often praise steady, consistent staff or do not raise systemic favoritism/nepotism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete accounts of physical fights, daily/weekly bullying, assaults, sexualized vandalism, on‑campus overdoses, students leaving campus, stolen lunches, unlocked storage and supervision lapses (e.g., “kids walking away from campus…for 20 years,” “Bullying, weekly… By the second week there has been 20 people suspended,” “JV boys urinated in girls' locker room,” “a person… picked up from school…overdosed”). Square entries lack comparable reports and more often describe a safe or nurturing environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reports of unresponsive or abusive administrators, rapid leadership turnover, district neglect, opaque/biased discipline, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families, and alleged manipulation of enrollment/funding counts (examples: “Administration does not care,” “Revolving door on superintendents,” “They change dates on paper so they can count your child,” and “bias towards student athletes”). Square reviews do not make these systemic governance accusations and instead often praise administrative responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: This captures many concrete programmatic lists, facility descriptions and competitive outcomes in circle reviews—state championships, NJROTC awards and promotions, ‘HUGE theater,’ skate park, restaurant, extensive CTE/vocational offerings, and donor‑supported upgrades (e.g., “thriving JROTC…about 300 students,” “nearly 20 AP classes and take classes at 3 colleges,” “incredible options for… auto tech, carpentry”). Square entries mention extracurriculars but with less breadth, scale, or documented championships.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more polarized acade: This bucket captures the pattern that circle reviews more often report both high‑end offerings (AP/AVID/dual enrollment, extensive college counseling, honors pathways) and concrete academic problems in the same school—lack of AP‑qualified teachers, grade inflation, last‑minute grade changes, graduation delays, and claims of ‘no academic rigor’ or poor counseling (examples: “4 full time college counselors…visit 72 campuses,” alongside “Only 1‑2 teachers have the education required to teach AP…,” “delays in graduating due to mismanagement,” and “NO academic rigor”). Square reviews tend to present more consistent academic narratives without that same degree of internal contradiction.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistent,: This bucket groups square reviews that emphasize visible/practical administrative leadership, caring/dedicated teachers, effective parent communication and a generally safe, proud school culture (examples: “The Principal is absolutely wonderful,” “teachers are caring,” “Safe and positive environment,” and “I always feel like I can pick up the phone…”). These themes contrast with the many circle reports of administrative neglect, safety failures, and program variability.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive a: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete program structures and outcomes: circle reviewers cite heavy AP/IB/honors participation, Pre‑AP tracks, dual‑enrollment/college credit, mandated AP exam policies, high graduation/college‑bound rates (e.g., “11 AP courses,” “100% college bound,” “dual enrollment”), and explicit STEM/track organization — claims that square reviews largely do not make (square focuses more on vocational tracks or lacks advanced-program evidence).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety,: This groups descriptions of on‑campus danger and failures of protection: circle reviews document frequent physical fights, pervasive vaping/drug use, sexual‑misconduct criminal incidents and alleged cover‑ups, stalking with inadequate response, lockdowns during testing and other security breaches — specific safety failures rarely invoked in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff/adminis: This covers allegations about adults’ conduct and unequal treatment: circle reviewers accuse administrators and staff of rudeness, dishonesty, public humiliation, protecting favorites, athletic/wealth favoritism, nepotistic grading and enrollment manipulation, and bureaucratic gatekeeping of courses/supports (e.g., 'EVERYTHING IS FOOTBALL RELATED,' 'administrators lied,' 'if your child has the right last name they are almost guaranteed an A'), patterns not present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger parent: This bucket groups reviews highlighting active family involvement, bilingual/ESL parent outreach, PTA events, multigenerational alumni ties, faith‑based pastoral care and daily prayer, tight 'sisterhood' or small‑school pride, and community service/mission programs (e.g., Spanish‑language parental endorsements, named beloved teachers/principals, mission trips) — community/faith cohesion themes that square reviews rarely foreground.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete ope: This captures granular, actionable reporting on physical plant and money: circle reviewers list capital projects and new facilities, outdated textbooks or no hot water, metal detectors/cameras, classroom touchscreens, uniform/fee burdens, cafeteria problems, bussing to college, short block schedules, dorm supervision issues and funding levy failures — operational specifics that square reviews generally omit or do not detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket groups raw terms that describe on-campus fights, daily bullying/harassment, drug busts and hospitalization, firearms or violent assaults, pervasive racial/sexual harassment, widespread drinking/stealing, frequent security or police presence, and claims that administration fails to stop these incidents (examples: “two drug busts… one student going to the hospital,” “girls get punched in their faces by boys,” “There are fights almost daily,” and “vicious acts of physical violence go unchecked”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more stable, commi: This bucket captures contrasts where square reviews emphasize steady, communicative, and supportive leadership (board/principal involvement, clear administrative commitment) while circle reviews describe turnover, rude or vindictive administrators, misplaced priorities, lost records, nepotism, and opaque finances (examples: Square: “dedication of teachers and administration,” “the principal obviously cares”; Circle: “teachers stuck around for maybe 1 or 2 years,” “Lori Taylor is evil…”, “Where does the bingo money go?”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report a broader set of c: This bucket groups items naming discrete programmatic opportunities and pathways in circle reviews — Dual Enrollment, serious early‑college programs, NAF IT partnerships, shop/majors (dental assisting, graphic communications, fashion design), broad AP and vocational offerings, certifications and internships — whereas square reviews rarely enumerate this breadth (examples: “graduated with four college classes through Dual Enrollment,” “Dental Assisting shop,” “lots of classes to choose from,” vs. Square’s more limited program mentions).
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, hands‑on: This bucket covers claims that circle schools provide attentive teachers who 'go out of their way,' successful tutorial periods, long‑term advisors/counselors, high AP teacher preparation and remediation that improves struggling students, and concrete examples of staff accommodating special needs — contrasted with square reviews describing inexperienced teachers, poor classroom control, or little remediation (examples: “teachers really seem to care… will go out of their way,” “All students have the same advisor and counselor for all four years,” and “witnessed reading levels go from 3rd grade up to high school in a year”).
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete det: This bucket groups raw terms that enumerate physical‑plant conditions (pest infestations, AC only in offices, new stadiums, missing auditorium), scheduling/registration logistics (shortened passing periods, antiquated registration, lost transcripts), crowding/capacity limits, extra fees/fundraising pressure, and specific modernization or maintenance projects — details that square reviews seldom list (examples: “hallway be stuck in traffic,” “AC in administration office but not classrooms,” “waiting in line for hours to register… students not placed into needed classes,” “brand new state-of-the-art high school opening”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent physical fights, weapon/drug incidents, panic/suicide reports, smells of marijuana, repeated lockdowns and installation of metal detectors or bag checks (e.g., “metal detectors - don't knock it,” “fights almost on a daily,” “smell of marijuana coming from the bathrooms,” repeated lockdowns). They also document punitive/erratic discipline handling tied to those incidents (victims punished, cover‑ups), so a school that falls in this bucket is one where reviewers repeatedly cite concrete safety failures and compensating physical security infrastructure that Square reviewers do not.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent ad: Square reviews frequently highlight steady supervision, a safe/ordered environment, and concrete supports that prepare students for college (e.g., ‘There is no bullying… zero tolerance,’ ‘the new alternative education program…counselors and constant attention,’ ‘Pre & AP classes offered’ and direct counselor support), so a Square‑type school presents regular adult oversight, predictable disciplinary enforcement, and accessible, practical college-prep structures absent or weaker in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger evidence: Many Circle reviews point to small class sizes, conservatory/magnet identity, IB/advanced academies, dual‑enrollment or certificate academies, and concrete elite college matriculation claims (e.g., ‘top 20… Ivy admits,’ ‘several academies… FIU dual enrollment,’ ‘IB program…Stanford, Northwestern’). A Circle‑type school thus emphasizes selective or specialty curricular tracks and documented high‑tier postsecondary placement that Square entries generally do not assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers frequently allege nepotism, donor cliques, athlete favoritism, mandatory parent labor, administrative secrecy/cover‑ups, and board/union conflicts (e.g., ‘a small clique of administrators/teachers/well‑heeled donors runs the show,’ ‘football players get special privileges,’ ‘must work…or pay $800,’ ‘administration cares about ranking and covers up’). This bucket captures schools where governance and local politics—not only classroom practice—shape access, discipline, and resource allocation according to reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize tighter communi: Circle reviews repeatedly describe small‑town/family atmospheres, strong parent involvement, K–12 continuity, religious or magnet identity, selective admissions or long waiting lists, and financial sacrifice to attend (e.g., ‘small and friendly… like family,’ ‘5,000+ on the waiting list,’ ‘we paid double…worth it,’ ‘well‑rounded Christian Education’). Schools in this bucket are portrayed as cohesive, sought‑after, or identity-driven community institutions—features that Square reviews seldom emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more pervasive s: This bucket groups reviews that report grave on-campus safety and peer-abuse problems in the circle schools (e.g., racial slurs and lynching threats, repeated school‑shooting threats, students bringing guns, gang presence, rampant vaping/drugs, and chronic bullying) together with staff inaction; square entries, by contrast, rarely describe weapons/gangs or pervasive targeted harassment and often report managed security or isolated incidents. Examples: “called the N word multiple times and threatened to be lynched,” “over 40 school shooting threats…never punished,” “Bulliying runs rampant and unchecked,” versus square’s emphasis on controlled entries and active security teams.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reviews describing leadership problems at circle schools — principals who ignore parents, protect favored staff or families, manipulate student elections, threaten parents/legal pushback, or apply discipline inconsistently or punitively — whereas square reviews are more likely to describe approachable administrators or disciplined, systematized enforcement. Examples: “principal will back the faculty even when they are wrong,” “runs on nepotism & favoritism,” “principal ordered a revote of homecoming court,” contrasted with square’s statements that administrators are ‘approachable’ and security/discipline are priorities.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more extensive a: This bucket groups concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes emphasized in circle reviews — IB/AP breadth, dual enrollment, early‑college pathways, credit recovery, unique CTE shops and named academies, and cited college matriculation/credit — while square reviews more often lack these programmatic details or report limited AP breadth and low pass rates. Examples: “Dual Enrollment, National Honor Society, AP classes…earned college credit,” “Advanced Environmental Water Academy, automotive shop,” versus square’s notes of only 8 AP classes with a 9% pass rate.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: This bucket groups evidence that circle schools are described more often as providing one‑on‑one time, small class sizes, teachers who stay after school or dedicate extra time, and hands‑on instructional support, whereas square reviews more often describe apathetic or uneven teacher engagement and less routine personalized attention. Examples: “a lot of 1‑1 student to teacher time,” “teachers dedicate their own time to help students,” “small class sizes…teachers know their students well,” contrasted with square comments that many teachers are ‘here for a paycheck’ or less consistent.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight broader extracu: This bucket groups circle reviews that emphasize rich non‑academic supports and partnerships — award‑winning music and arts, orchestra partnerships (e.g., MYSO), expanding band programs, robust after‑school programs, parent education/ASL classes, campus clothing closets/bookstores, and scholarship/financial‑aid help — while square reviews rarely describe the same breadth of partnerships, family supports, or named arts collaborations. Examples: “The orchestra and music training has been unparalleled,” “parent education program provides ASL classes,” “free campus bookstore and clothing closet,” versus square’s lack of comparable community/arts program detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, cleare: This bucket captures cases where reviewers report concrete curricular structure and results at circle schools—tiered courses (general/ACP/honors, AP/IB, pre‑AP, ECE/college credit, CTE certification), specialty centers and credential pathways, and alumni/college-placement anecdotes (scholarships, UC/Harvard/elite placements) that square reviews lack or dispute. Examples: “different levels of classes…ECE and AP classes,” “CTE certified diploma,” and “Students here have gone to the best colleges in the state,” contrasted with square’s complaints about lacking rigor and reduced college encouragement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This groups descriptions of repeated student misconduct and harm (daily fights, truancy, robbery rumors, drug incidents, cluster suicides, pervasive bullying/racism) alongside accounts that administration either fails to intervene or enforces harsh/inconsistent punishments (collective punishments, punitive dean behavior). Examples: “Theres fights everyday…students smoke…and rumors that students get robbed,” “The number of suicides…absolutely shocking,” and “Punishments are harsh…and administration runs the school like a jail,” whereas square reviews do not provide comparable incident-level safety or mental‑health crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray more individualiz: This bucket covers reports of one‑on‑one teacher attention, low student/teacher ratios, formal academic support programs, on-site therapies, SAT/test prep, and counseling that reviewers describe at circle schools but not in square. Examples: “teachers work with him individually…one-on-one tutoring,” “speech therapy at school,” “Dr. Dunkley is even providing SAT prep classes,” and “low student/teacher ratio with an assistant available for one-on-one help,” contrasted with square’s lack of sustained in‑school remediation or therapy supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This captures allegations about leadership and district-level malpractice at circle schools—nepotistic hiring, cover‑ups, deleted negative reviews, botched credit/grade management, and explicit calls for administrator removal—issues square reviewers do not raise to the same degree. Examples: “most all employees and teachers are related,” “They have had many scandals…they have swept under the rug,” “they messed up all my credits,” and “take down negative reviews for their school on this site,” contrasted with square’s absence of comparable governance accusations.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete fa: This bucket groups mentions of tangible infrastructure and resourcing—new gyms/track, iPad rollouts (planned or chaotic), security camera installs, free buses, underfunded band vs expensive cosmetic spending, and parent-facing grade/attendance portals—that circle reviews often describe in concrete terms while square reviews rarely do. Examples: “handed out iPads…no plan,” “last year they put cameras everywhere,” “band program is shamefully underfunded,” and “You can opt to get school text messages…or use JupiterGrades,” whereas square lacks this level of operational/facility detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more s: Circle reviews repeatedly cite concrete advanced-academic programs and outcomes—AP/IB/Honors, dual‑enrollment, associate degrees, high ACT/test scores, broad scholarship and college-acceptance evidence (e.g., "helped her get a full ride," "graduated high school with associate degrees," "rated 13th in the state"). Square reviews rarely list institutional AP/dual programs or verifiable outcomes and more often warn students may be unready for college, so this bucket captures programmatic rigor and documented college/career results emphasized in circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, p: Square reviews more often describe teachers and counselors as professional, dedicated, and accountability‑focused (e.g., "teachers and guidance counselors are always there to support them," "so professional and dedicated"), whereas circle entries show far more variability—mixed praise but frequent accounts of favoritism, protected ineffective staff, or politicized staffing—so this bucket groups claims about overall staff professionalism and steady supportive accountability being stronger in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: Many circle reviews give concrete operational complaints—lost paperwork, transcript/credit errors, botched scheduling, failed 504/IEP accommodations, billing/exclusion incidents, and explicit budget-driven program cuts (e.g., "office constantly loses paperwork," "issues with their credits," "no money... youngest son didn't even have books"). Square reviews do not cluster around these programmatic/administrative breakdowns, so this bucket groups systemic process and recordkeeping failures attributed more to circle schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader, better: Circle reviews frequently enumerate rich EC offerings and investments—nationally competitive choir and band, multiple state‑level athletics accomplishments, vocational/shop certifications, large JROTC participation, active Parent Council/PTO, and 1:1 tech deployments (e.g., "huge choir...national honors," "Culinary...Electronics certification," "almost half of the school is in JROTC"). Square entries rarely document this depth or breadth of extracurricular/CTE programming or organized parent governance, so this bucket groups the programmatic and community resources emphasized by circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews contain stronger and repeated accounts of unaddressed bullying, drug/sexual behavior, racial harassment and even extremist student identities (e.g., "Non-white students get racist remarks... 'Neo Nazis'", "they have a drug problem... nothing we can do"), and describe administration as dismissive; while circle reviews include safety complaints as well, the pattern of normalized bigotry, substance issues, violent incidents, and explicit school inaction appears more prominent in square entries and is grouped here.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents, pervasive peer and cyber‑bullying, staff‑perpetrated misconduct or inaction (e.g., staff entering girls' restroom with no repercussions, coach accused of misogyny, frequent fights, drug/gang activity, police on campus), and failed interventions — patterns repeatedly attributed to the school in Circle but largely absent from Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: Circle reviews frequently name AP/IB/VPA/magnet/CTE programs, cite measurable gains or high ratings (A‑rated, improved test scores, specific ACT/GPA results, college acceptance stories), and describe formal college‑prep rules and outcomes, whereas Square reviews lack those concrete programmatic metrics or show declining advanced offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries show higher parent/commun: Circle reviewers repeatedly report active PTA, multi‑generational/alumni enrollment, parents relocating or building houses to enter the boundary, and community crisis support or organized parent advocacy — specific community involvement signals that Square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray more consistently: Many Circle reviews cite teacher caring, collaborative staff teamwork, and even name individual praised teachers and coaches (e.g., Mrs. Ivey, Coach Jones), plus examples of routine one‑on‑one help and proactive outreach; Square reviews instead contain more reports of disengaged, abusive, or favoritism‑prone staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader and bett: Circle reviews list extensive extracurricular breadth (marching band, theatre, FFA, sports, career academies), note thriving arts and music staffing, and cite concrete capital upgrades (new stadiums, turf, renovated libraries, classroom tech), while Square reviews do not present the same breadth or facility investment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: These reviews describe frequent fights, drug use/overdoses, hazing, teen pregnancy, routine bullying ignored by staff, and repeated bathroom closures for vaping (e.g., “every week there are at least 3 to 5 fights,” drug sweeps requiring two buses, a student overdosed in class, and “Bullying is a huge issue” left unaddressed). Falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on safety and widespread student-behavior problems that reviewers link to poor enforcement and learning disruption.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger/high‑ri: These entries name programmatic assets and outcomes—AP/IB/STEM tracks, dual‑credit/college courses on site, national competition finalists, large scholarship totals, and elite college matriculations (e.g., “Viator's AP track…STEM certified program,” “graduated from Pace with 36 college credits,” “Ivy League acceptances,” and “over $9 million in scholarships offered”). Content in this bucket foregrounds formal advanced coursework, dual‑credit mechanisms, competitive academic achievements, and quantifiable college preparation results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews accuse the board/leadership of opacity and incompetence, cite high principal/teacher turnover, budget cuts and program eliminations, facility decline or accreditation risk, and politicized funding priorities (e.g., “the school board seems to be clueless,” “lost more than half the staff,” “close to losing accreditation,” and “most of our funding goes to football”). Items in this bucket emphasize systemic leadership failures, contested budgeting, and governance problems as root causes of school decline.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent st: Square reviews repeatedly highlight accessible counselors, teacher outreach, coordinated parent‑teacher practices, and effective institutional responses (e.g., “The teachers always called or emailed to work on resolution,” “guidance department is always there for children,” and coordinated parent‑teacher conferences), portraying a school with formal support systems and reliable follow‑up. Texts in this bucket center operational competence in communication, counseling, and resolving student issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize faith/values‑or: These reviews stress religious/theology instruction, character formation, single‑sex or ROTC identity, heavy rules or military‑style discipline, and small classes/personalized teacher attention (e.g., “Christ centered…biblically-based education,” “ran like a military school,” and “Small class sizes…more one on one with students”). Content assigned here focuses on an explicit mission-driven culture (faith or character), stricter discipline doctrines, and/or organizational scale that enables individualized attention.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups raw terms describing concrete safety and peer‑misconduct problems that reviewers attribute to circle schools (e.g., repeated bullying, racial/ethnic harassment, antisemitic and anti‑LGBTQ hate crimes, gang activity, frequent fights requiring on‑campus police, teacher sexual offenses, and public sexual behavior). These items are about observable student safety incidents and hostile student culture rather than tone or opinion, and many circle reviews name bomb threats, lock‑downs, hate‑crimes, and administrators failing to stop repeated attacks—phenomena not reported in the square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: This bucket captures raw terms where circle schools are said to offer richer programmatic breadth—many AP/IB offerings, honors/debate/talented‑and‑gifted tracks, dedicated pathways (e.g., health/bio‑science, ROTC), strong marching band/theater/music programs, robotics, and formal external partnerships with colleges and hospitals. Review evidence includes explicit claims of 'myriad of AP offerings,' IB integration, health‑pathway partnerships (UCSD, SUNYAlbany), award‑winning band/arts, and structured study/tutoring supports, all of which are described more often for circle than square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a more small‑schoo: This bucket groups descriptions of small class sizes, teachers who collaborate and meet during lunch, individualized academic planning (iterative writing feedback, 1:1 help, study tables), strong alumni engagement and multi‑generation family attendance, and a hometown, 'everybody knows everybody' community—features reviewers repeatedly attribute to circle schools. These are concrete practices and social structures (class size, alumni involvement, individualized tutoring) that circle reviewers cite as distinguishing strengths not emphasized in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket groups explicit, material resource problems that reviewers tie to circle schools—no air conditioning with fainting/heat‑exhaustion incidents, dirty/disgusting bathrooms, overcrowded classrooms, chronic underfunding and lost staff due to budget strain, meal‑price/food quality complaints, and equipment/staffing shortages—contrasted with square reviews that describe 'incredible facilities' and better budgets. These are tangible facility/resourcing failures rather than abstract critiques of instruction.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more pro: This bucket collects raw terms where square schools are credited with effective leadership and community engagement—named devoted principals, administration praised for anti‑bullying intervention, high community turnout at events, professional handling of crises (COVID), and functioning guidance systems that help students graduate—features presented repeatedly in square reviews but largely absent or contradicted in circle reviews. These items refer to concrete leadership, discipline policy implementation, and community support practices that reviewers say materially distinguish square schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms where circle reviews describe concrete safety failures (daily/weekly fights, bomb threats, sexual harassment, gang activity, students punched, substance use, intrusive or negligent security, phone searches) that are reported as persistent and mishandled; Square reviews may mention isolated rude students or one assault but do not document the same scale or severity (examples: 'Fights every week', 'sexual assaults...not taken care of', 'bomb threats', 'students leaving campus unnoticed').
candidate_defs.circle entries document concrete college: This bucket captures circle reviews that cite specific, traceable college outcomes and programs (dual‑enrollment/early‑college associates degrees, students graduating with 40+ college credits, direct college admissions and scholarships, research programs, named college-credit partnerships), whereas square reviews lack comparable documented college‑credit pathways or measurable acceptance/outcome examples (examples: 'earned their associates degree', 'will graduate...with over 40 hours of college credit', 'direct admission into an architecture program and a scholarship').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staffing, hir: This bucket covers raw terms about teacher/coaching staffing dysfunction in circle reviews—misassigned teachers, coaches driving hires (hiring spouses), many inexperienced or underqualified teachers, high turnover, teachers 'phoning it in', and coach-dominant staffing—while Square typically describes uneven but less nepotistic staffing or focuses on isolated poor teachers rather than systematic misassignment (examples: 'hired a woman with a degree in music education to teach geometry', '95% of the teachers are coaches', 'losing 17 more teachers').
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight systemic favori: This bucket groups items where circle reviews describe concrete inequities—discipline favoritism, scholarships/awards tied to local clout, racial harassment and banners, socioeconomic and elitist cliques, inequitable athletic facilities for girls, mistreatment of students with disabilities, and tracked cohorts receiving unequal teachers—while square reviews do not show the same pervasive, structural exclusion (examples: 'they pick their favorite student and protect them', 'rich white kids...if you’re not white you’re going to struggle', 'female athletes share two locker rooms and have decaying practice areas').
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize coherent admini: This bucket groups raw terms where square reviews present a consistent improvement narrative and concrete operational supports—accessible principals, district/program turnarounds, tutoring before/after school, expanded programs, improved scheduling or facilities, and stable counselor/college‑prep assistance—whereas circle reviews more often describe fragmented or contested administrative responses and variable narratives (examples: 'Small district in the process of making an extraordinary turn around', 'tutoring is offered before & after school', 'principal has done a phenomenal job maintaining order and communicating with parents').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe ongoing daily threats to student safety—frequent fights, tolerated bullying (including teacher-on-student bullying), drug use, gang activity, and families withdrawing or relocating because of safety (e.g., 'about 15 fights this year', 'daily physically threatened', 'we had to pull our child out of the school'). In short, circle schools are characterized by pervasive peer violence and unaddressed victimization that reviewers tie to withdrawals and declining enrollment, a pattern absent or much reduced in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, measur: Circle reviews list concrete, high‑level academic offerings and outcomes—IB programs, extensive AP classes, dual‑credit partnerships, high ACT/college matriculation and scholarship examples (e.g., 'IB program is very challenging', 'national merit scholars every year', 'college credits from UConn/UNH', 'over 97% of Seniors went on to college'). These entries emphasize documented academic rigor and college-readiness metrics that square reviews generally do not provide or explicitly dispute.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader concrete: Circle reviewers repeatedly name tangible programs, facilities and supports—robotics labs and Macs, culinary and vocational classes, many clubs, modern classrooms/libraries, fundraising and booster involvement, and recent campus renovations (e.g., 'state of the art new campus', 'robotics...excellent Mac computers', 'more than 30 clubs'). This bucket captures claims of program breadth and facility investment that square reviews rarely enumerate.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics domin: Many circle reviews report athletics—especially football or basketball—being privileged culturally and financially, with special facilities/funding and selection biases toward travel‑team athletes (e.g., 'football is the sole focus... they have their own building', 'All money goes to sports', 'coaches favor travel-team experience'). These accounts frame sports as prioritized over academics or as producing favoritism, a theme distinct from the broader extracurricular/facilities bucket.
candidate_defs.square entries report more acute instruc: Square reviews frequently point to problems that directly reduce instructional quality and student support—chronic teacher absences, unqualified or unhelpful counselors, rude or non-teaching staff, leadership failures that disrupt programs and college guidance (e.g., 'WE DO NOT LEARN ANYTHING' due to teacher absences, 'guidance office offers no help in college preparation', 'unresponsive counselor', 'front desk never answers'). These are operational and personnel breakdowns reviewers tie to poor learning outcomes and unmet student needs, and they appear far more often in square entries than circle ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries report administrative mis: This bucket captures claims about leaders and governance actively mishandling records, covering up problems, showing nepotism/donor favoritism, retaliating against students/families, or behaving unprofessionally (e.g., lost credits/records, “GOOD OLE BOYS CLUB,” erased yearbook entries, plagiarism accusation, PR-directed fake reviews, punitive phone/device fines, and threats to revisit out‑of‑district enrollment). These are concrete governance/ethics failures rather than general complaints about responsiveness, and appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: This bucket groups mentions of institutional, curricular and program breadth: IB programs, many AP/Dual Credit offerings, Early College/Associates pathways, formal college partnerships/running-start, specialized magnet or regional recruitment, strong robotics/performing‑arts/STEM teams and named college matriculations or quantified test outcomes (e.g., IB diploma recipients, graduates attending Georgetown/Notre Dame/UCs, running start shuttles, Robotics praise). These concrete programmatic opportunities and documented postsecondary results are emphasized in circle entries more than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater teacher ac: This bucket covers descriptions of instructional access and individualized support such as small class sizes, teachers reserving before/after school time, one‑on‑one help, personalized learning communities, and adult staff acting as parental surrogates or mentors (e.g., 'teachers reserve time before and after school,' 'small class sizes allow personalized instruction,' 'faculty was like parents to me'). Circle reviewers more often report these hands‑on supports relative to square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and/or: This bucket includes concrete safety and behavior incidents and claims of institutional failure to resolve them—frequent physical fights, stabbings, gang pressure/recruitment, drugs/alcohol/weapons, sexual exploitation/assault allegations, high theft rates, police presence, and parents withdrawing children for safety reasons. Many circle reviews recount these severe incidents or unresolved bullying situations at greater frequency than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe operational, fac: This bucket captures recurring, concrete operational problems: chaotic scheduling and schedule changes, attendance/ tardy marking errors (bus delays marked tardy/absent), lost credits/recordkeeping errors, poor phone/parent communication, cafeteria/food service complaints, removed library books, maintenance and building‑quality complaints, and ineffective daily monitoring/security. These logistical and facilities failures — distinct from governance ethics or instructional quality — are described more often in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries have stronger advanced ac: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete, school‑level college-prep infrastructure (AICE/IB/AP, DE/dual enrollment, engineering or ACE academies, early‑college pathways) and cited metrics/outcomes (SAT averages, scholarship offers, Ivy/T20 admits). Examples: repeated Cambridge/AICE and IB mentions, ‘‘NRCA offers 14 AP classes… Over $28 million in scholarships,’’ engineering academy taught by industry professionals, and alumni reports of graduating with college credits or full tuition scholarships.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviews that describe frequent peer violence, bullying, sexual harassment/assault, gangs, weapons on campus, hazing, and administration ignoring or mishandling incidents (unsupervised assaults, inconsistent discipline, SRO/juvenile‑court complaints). Examples: ‘‘Fights break out constantly… concussion after an unsupervised hallway attack,’’ ‘‘white students using the n‑word… mocking transgender students,’’ and ‘‘kids with guns… they fight almost every day.’'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete admi: Reviews in this bucket recount tangible breakdowns in school operations and governance—lost transcripts, refusal to release records, transcript/report‑card holds for unpaid fees, chaotic scheduling, fundraising coercion, alleged financial mismanagement/corruption, mass staff turnover, and facility maintenance problems (leaking sinks, no A/C, pool issues, unsecured entrances). Examples: ‘‘Refusal to send transcripts… lost his records,’’ ‘‘holding report card until lunch debt is paid,’’ ‘‘Total inability to properly manage or spend money,’’ and ‘‘brand new $75M facility’’ (contrast instances of capital projects vs. mismanagement).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe higher teacher c: This bucket groups reviews that emphasize teacher-level strengths: highly credentialed or specialized staff (PhDs, college professors teaching classes), regular after‑school help, proactive counselors/guidance securing scholarships, and personalised teacher engagement. Examples: ‘‘worked with a Harvard valedictorian… Stanford PhD,’’ ‘‘they stay late and help any student,’’ and ‘‘Guidance Department secured enough scholarship money to pay for college; thanks to PBLHS.’'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: These reviews emphasize that circle schools offer wide, named pathways and postsecondary linkages (CTE/trades, SkillsUSA, ROTC, DECA, AVID, AP/IB, college center, pre-college classes with Hunter College, Mt. Sinai internships, engineering partnerships, CLEP/DANTES advice) while square reviews do not document the same breadth or concrete external partnerships.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain many concrete accounts of ongoing bullying, daily assaults, gang activity, drugs, weapons expulsions, on-campus sexual activity, bomb threats and students coming home with bruises, whereas square reviews do not describe this level or frequency of safety/criminal incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe unresponsive or absent administrators, grade/transcript mishandling, diploma withholding, punitive discipline without due process, nepotism/favoritism from office staff, and contested leadership turnover; square reviews lack this concentration of governance-level procedural failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more on‑site and: Many circle reviews note formal supports—CAP conflict resolution, clinical counselors, peer tutoring programs, monthly scholarship updates, remediation/colloquium blocks, on-site health clinics and structured exit interviews—that square reviews generally do not mention.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more polarized resou: Circle reviews frequently name sophisticated tech (1:1 iPads, Zoom/DTEN panels, laptops) and well‑funded pockets (broadcasting Macs, specialized labs) alongside serious facility neglect (rodents, roaches, mold, broken showers, lack of AC), and program funding imbalances (broadcasting well‑resourced while theater/mechanics underfunded), a contrast not present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, more nu: These reviews repeatedly name concrete programmatic pathways (AP/IB/MYP, Early College/dual enrollment, PLTW/engineering, vocational/CTE, honors/acceleration), cite AP/ACT metrics, college admissions and college‑level coursework, and programs like weekend AP workshops—while square reviews rarely list comparable programs or measurable outcomes. Examples: circle mentions 'Early College,' '54% 3.0+,' 'ACT 27,' 'AP exams/IB/PLTW,' and dual‑enrollment stories; square mainly references AP offerings or general college prep without the same program breadth or outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle reviews document concrete safety incidents and chronic behavioral problems—daily fights, vaping/drugs/alcohol culture, repeated bullying (including multi‑year and teacher‑perpetrated bullying), sexual‑harassment mishandling, lockdowns and security complaints—whereas square reviews either do not mention such severe incidents or describe far fewer/smaller behavior issues. Illustrative items: 'fights every single day,' 'lots of drugs,' 'lockdowns every other week,' 'multiple years of dropouts due to bullying,' and claims that administration ignored harassment.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more pronounced teac: Circle reviews often praise very caring, outreaching teachers, named graduation coaches, individualized remediation and sizable AP supports, but they also contain frequent reports of high teacher turnover, inexperienced hires, poor training (e.g., Autism, special‑ed gaps), and inconsistent instructional quality; square reviews present a more consistent picture of committed faculty with fewer extreme swings. Examples: 'teachers go above and beyond' vs 'TOO MUCH TEACHER TURNOVER…principal will hire and fire,' 'graduation coach' and 'procedural violations denying special ed' appear together in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: Numerous circle reviews allege systemic favoritism (alumni hiring, promotions of unqualified staff, athletics/activities spots reserved for insiders), selective admissions or expulsions, punitive district policies, operational failures (transcript/yearbook/meal account mishandling), threatened lawsuits, and calls for public investigation—whereas square reviews rarely raise patterns of nepotism or opaque governance. Representative claims: 'high percentage of staff that are alumni,' 'nepotism... pushed an unqualified administrator,' 'selective seats/committee reviews to bar students,' and 'no one returned calls about transcripts.'
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize richer extracur: Circle reviewers frequently list strong performing‑arts programs, large choirs/theatre, many clubs, intensive athletic cultures, recent capital investments or facilities, organized family rituals (orientation, Mass, lock‑ins), and near‑universal participation—while square reviews mention fewer arts or community rituals and focus more on academics or localized events. Examples: 'prestigious Cambridge IGSCE and performing arts,' 'multi‑million dollar football stadium,' 'almost entire student body participates,' and also critiques that 'sports are prioritized over academics' or that band practice interferes with class time.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe broader, more fo: These reviews repeatedly list concrete program breadth and structured offerings at circle schools—IB, JROTC, multiple APs, academies (business/health/film), vocational certifications (CPR, culinary/FFA), extensive clubs, robotics/drama, Chromebooks and mandatory help nights—whereas square reviews largely lack or downplay such formal program arrays (few/absent AP/IB, limited electives). Examples: circle mentions IB, JROTC, many APs and academy tracks, certifications and travel programs; square emphasizes an average campus with fewer advanced program listings.
candidate_defs.Circle entries document more concrete fa: Multiple circle reviews cite specific physical/operational breakdowns and sudden disruptions—moldy AC, trailers/pods, major overcrowding and traffic, one‑day bus service cut notices, bathrooms without locks, leaks/verm in the cafeteria—while square reviews generally report fewer detailed infrastructure failures and instead give more general environment comments. Examples: circle reports moldy AC and trailers, last‑minute bus cancellations, chronic leaks, and filthy cafeterias.
candidate_defs.Circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews frequently accuse school leadership or district governance of favoritism and cronyism (hiring relatives, discipline contingent on 'crony' status), board politics, refusal to act on parent safety requests, intimidation/shut‑downs of parents, and unanswered emails; square reviews do not make these concentrated governance/nepotism claims and often describe more collaborative or neutral administration. Examples: circle quotes about 'keeping everyone in the family', calls for hiring boards, and parents threatening public escalation when leaders ignore concerns.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive stu: A large set of circle reviews detail long‑running bullying from elementary through high school, teachers/staff failing to intervene (or encouraging bullying), retaliatory messages like 'snitches get stitches', unreported injuries and ineffective anti‑bullying protocols—square reviews rarely show this sustained pattern and sometimes report better handling or isolated incidents. Examples: circle accounts of K–12 bullying left unaddressed, students told not to report, and repeated failure to remediate aggressors.
candidate_defs.Square entries report weaker instruction: Square reviews commonly emphasize lack of academic challenge, weak math/science instruction, few honors/AP opportunities, poor standardized test/SAT signals and graduates needing remedial/foundation college courses, while circle reviews more often describe rigorous courses, advanced offerings, or measurable academic gains. Examples: square notes 'not pushed to be great', 'science dept isn't special', and graduates requiring foundation college classes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a private/paroch: These reviews repeatedly reference private‑school features — rising/steep tuition, scholarship/financial‑aid decisions, and faith‑based programming (daily chapel, Catholic/Jesuit identity, theology classes, explicit character formation and service requirements). Examples: many Circle comments cite 'steep tuition', 'tuition aide', scholarship favoritism, and 'Chapel services EVERYDAY' or 'make sure your son is catholic', distinguishing Circle as operating on a tuition/religious model that Square reviews do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a small‑school,: Circle reviewers frequently emphasize small enrollment, small class sizes, alumni continuity, senior→freshman mentoring and teachers who 'know students by name' and provide one‑on‑one help; they call the place 'like a family' and cite active alumni networks. Examples: 'classrooms are no more than 15 students', 'Teachers honestly care', 'MPS seniors take a serious mentoring role', and 'the alumni connections are very strong' — themes absent or weaker in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report higher prevalence: Many Circle reviews document frequent physical fights, gang/drug activity, theft, and targeted racial/sexual‑orientation harassment, describing an environment where 'the bully's run this school', 'kids are doing drugs in the bathroom', and 'I've seen kids get followed after school & beaten bloody.' These concrete safety/behavior incidents appear far more often in Circle than in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers commonly allege unresponsive administration, mismanaged budgets/layoffs, nepotism/favoritism, charter/leadership takeovers, and phone/notification breakdowns — e.g., 'They don’t answer phones', 'budgets cause teachers to be fired', 'Nepotism, Politics, and Cliques run this school', and 'slowly going down since the take over of charter usa.' Square reviews mention administration issues too but far less frequently and with different emphasis.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger program: Square reviews more often highlight sustained academic programs (IB/AP successes, dual‑enrollment, organized AP teachers), active arts and athletics departments, recent facility improvements and broad club offerings — e.g., 'IB program and AP classes... the arts department is amazing', 'the cafeteria looks so new... 2 new buildings', and 'lots to offer in education.' Those resource/structure themes are more characteristic of Square than Circle in these texts.

candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, concrete: Circle texts enumerate named programs and outcomes—IB designation, paid dual‑enrollment and on‑campus college credit, ROTC commissions, cosmetology licensure, strong shop/technical programs, extensive arts and band offerings, internships and scholarship totals—whereas Square mentions AP/electives more generically and lacks the same concrete program-level credentials and documented college/certification results.
