candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic instr: Square reviewers more often complain about low test scores, few AP courses, teachers who 'cruise' or are inexperienced, budget‑driven cuts to electives, and leadership inaction or indifference, whereas Circle reviews more frequently document concrete advanced programs, credentialing pathways, or specific remediation/dual‑enrollment interventions.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive,: This bucket captures concrete programmatic depth and built-in supports: circle reviews list large AP catalogs, STEM/CTE/magnet programs, dual‑credit hours, 1:1 online/Blazer Time/Power Hour tutoring, night/Saturday credit recovery and online‑paced options (examples: “over 25 AP courses, Duel Enrollment… STEM Academy,” “Blazer Time… Power Hour,” “over 40 hours of dual credit”), whereas square reviews generally mention fewer advanced pathways or only brief vocational affiliation.
candidate_defs.circle entries include more concrete fac: Circle reviews more often enumerate physical and tech resources or specific infrastructure problems — e.g., universal MacBook programs, new LEED/platinum buildings, state‑of‑the‑art labs, or conversely pests/no hot water/flooding and broken HVAC — (“Every student gets a Macbook,” “new edifice…platinum,” and “rats running around…no hot water”), while square reviews rarely provide comparable facility/tech specificity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews commonly describe committed faculty, low turnover, and accessible administrators (examples: “faculty is always striving for excellence,” “teachers are open and available,” “principal sets a tone of high achievement”), whereas circle reviews contain many counterexamples of unqualified hires, high turnover, administrator non‑responsiveness or favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: This bucket groups explicit safety and discipline breakdowns: circle reviewers recount gang activity, hospitalizing assaults, chronic bullying and staff inaction or inconsistent/punitive discipline (examples: “a haven for gang thugs,” “9 girls jump my daughter…the staff did nothing,” and “Persistently Dangerous Schools”), whereas square reviews rarely allege that level of violence or systemic non‑response.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger community/p: Circle reviews frequently document active parent/community oversight, multigenerational alumni pride, tuition/parent‑controlled governance and explicit school‑choice behaviors (examples: “I am an alumnus and parent…we have 2 granddaughters attending,” “The school is lottery based,” “private school so there is tuition”), while square reviews contain fewer such claims about parental control, multigenerational continuity, or formal selection/tuition dynamics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more peer-on-peer: This bucket captures raw terms that describe frequent and severe student-on-student harm and safety threats (physical fights, gang violence, daily hate speech, food fights, sexual assaults, pervasive vaping/substance use) reported in circle reviews but not in square; examples include 'Bullying is rampant', 'Gang violence ... Do not ever take your child here', 'Students use hate speech daily with no punishment', and allegations of 'Several sexual assaults within the school with no action.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This groups claims about leadership and school systems in circle reviews: administrators who ignore reports, cover up incidents, protect relatives, deflect complaints, charge families for services, and apply punitive or uneven discipline (victims punished, forced placements, invasive searches/drug tests); illustrative phrases include 'They cover up and hide student serious offenses', 'The district is more concerned with hiring teachers who are related', 'They will force your child out ... into alternative programs', and 'personal ipad was confiscated... eavesdropped on Instagram.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, formal: This bucket groups programmatic and outcome evidence in circle reviews: formal specialty programs and measurable college/career success (IB, Academic Center, AP/dual enrollment, honors/accelerated tracks, national-competitive teams, scholarships, high matriculation/dropout statistics); examples are 'IB Program For All', 'Junior and Senior High on one campus allowing AP in Junior High', 'national champions robotics team', 'over 95 percent proceed to college', and 'millions in scholarship money annually.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher incom: This bucket captures square reviews' recurrent claims about poor classroom practice and harmful staff behavior: teachers who 'do not care', use rote worksheets, are unable to teach required subjects, or act as bullies toward students; representative lines include 'Teachers do not care about the success of students... They are lazy', 'most teachers do not teach', and accounts of teachers bullying or being unqualified in subject matter.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This groups physical and logistical breakdowns reported in circle reviews: extreme overcrowding and mobile classrooms, no air conditioning or leaky roofs, broken computers/weak Wi‑Fi, reports of expired cafeteria food and lab safety hazards, and bus/transport problems; illustrative examples include 'no air conditioning... rooms in the 90's', 'mobile home classroom since the school is out of space', 'computers were ALWAYS broken', and 'extend the bus line ... to reach more deserving students.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews describe concrete, school-run academic pathways and measurable postsecondary results (AP/IB breadth, Early College/dual-enrollment totals, IB diplomas, high AP pass rates, ‘over 50 college credits offered’, 100% college-going claims, and elite matriculations to Yale/Columbia) that square reviews do not provide; examples include explicit scholarship pipelines, dual-credit totals, and alumni degree/scholarship outcomes used as evidence of school effectiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report institutionalized: Multiple circle reviews describe mandatory/regular worship and religion curriculum, school‑sanctioned prayer/clubs (chapel, Bible class, Christianity club replacing secular clubs), Catholic identity statements, and staff-led proselytizing in arts classes—concrete programmatic religiosity and disputes absent from square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray athletics-first c: Circle reviews repeatedly signal strong sports programs, mascot-centered school spirit, and explicit resource/staffing choices favoring athletics (e.g., full/overstated athletic hiring, complaints that ‘football gets all the attention,’ athletics crowding out academics, and many varsity teams), showing a tangible athletics-priority culture not present in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict a small, tight-kni: These entries emphasize small size/personalization, sustained family and alumni ties, active parent fundraising/foundations, 1:1 devices/individualized instruction, and frequent teacher mentorship or long-term staff continuity (parents/alumni endorsing the school across generations), concrete community features that contrast with square reviews' lack of multigenerational cohesion.
candidate_defs.square entries report leadership failure: Square reviews more often describe administrators who ignore complaints or prioritize image/athletics over student welfare, routine safety and supervision failures (bullying left unaddressed, fights, substance use), poor IEP/504 and special-education follow-through, and explicit recommendations to transfer away—concrete governance, safety, and accommodation breakdowns not emphasized in the circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger specializ: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete advanced‑academic offerings and outcomes in circle schools — AP/IB/honors tracks, dual‑credit and community‑college partnerships, magnet/selective admissions, conservatory and internship placements, and explicit alumni/university matriculation and scholarship wins (examples: ‘plenty of advanced classes’, ‘opportunity to take theoretical calculus at Stanford’, ‘massive scholarships…’, ‘offers more college dual‑credit hours’, and multiple alumni college success stories).
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more authoritari: This captures circle reviews that report strict, formal enforcement and added security measures — zero‑tolerance policies, suspensions for minor contact, increased security/police/PO presence, canine searches, tightened rules and digital filtering (examples: ‘zero tolerance policy… I always feel safe’, ‘not allowed to hug…suspension’, ‘there is more security’, ‘Go Guardian…you block everything’, and ‘they've made more rules…treat the kids like criminals’).
candidate_defs.Circle entries allege greater administra: These items document reviewers’ claims about leadership behavior and district governance at circle schools — protection of favored students, nepotistic/athletics‑driven funding, secretive firings, misallocated spending, targeted removals from programs, named calls for superintendent/board action, and frequent principal turnover (examples: ‘they protect each other’, ‘millions donated to football while teachers fired’, ‘they keep everything a secret…fired a great teacher’, and ‘6 or 7 different Principals in the last 5 years’).
candidate_defs.Square entries report more chronic under: This bucket groups square reviews describing persistent resource shortfalls and physical/instructional constraints — overcrowded classes and portable classrooms, antiquated hardware/software, lacking supplies and working infrastructure, poor cafeteria/lunch facilities and cutbacks to transportation or tech programs (examples: ‘45 students stuffed into a portable’, ‘desktops…majority software out of date’ in square, ‘not enough money for paper’, and ‘the school is run down and lacks even basic infrastructure’).
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive pee: These reviews describe student‑to‑student climate issues at circle schools — frequent fights, tolerated or staff‑enabled bullying, racialized discrimination, clique‑based teasing of lower‑income students, substance use and teen‑pregnancy concerns, social isolation of transfers and targeted harassment of special‑needs students (examples: ‘frequent fights during school’, ‘bullying is tolerated…by a few certain teachers’, ‘racism runs wild’, ‘alcohol and drugs are a real problem’, and ‘constant bullying…teachers would “address” the problems yet it never stopped”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reviews describing repeated peer violence, bullying (including death threats), gang‑related lockdowns, hazing, and administrators who ignore or mishandle reports (e.g., “too many instances of bullying to count,” “I got death threats…nothing was done,” “locked down…parents not informed,” “administration failed to inform the public”); it groups raw terms about pervasive unsafe behavior and ineffective discipline/communication by leadership.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more structured: Includes reviews that list concrete advanced offerings, outcomes and awards—AP/STEAM/dual‑enrollment/engineering tracks, award‑winning music/athletics, PSAT/AP successes and college scholarships (e.g., “all‑AP,” “dual credit classes available,” “state championships,” “accepted with Scholarships to Baylor”), i.e., explicit program breadth and documented postsecondary or competitive accomplishments that square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Groups items where reviewers note teachers going ‘above and beyond,’ consistent 1:1 attention, formal remediation hours, unpaid teacher study sessions, or iterative assessment practices (e.g., “9th hour” tutoring, teachers staying until 4–5pm, ‘taking time to explain things’ or allowing multiple retakes), contrasting with square reviews that emphasize less consistent or unavailable instructional help.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: This bucket covers concrete, facility‑level problems and operational policies called out in reviews—mold/worms in food, bed bugs, PCB contamination, unsanitary bathrooms, severe overcrowding/parking strain, contentious off‑campus lunch rules or broken drop‑off logistics (e.g., “mold in applesauce,” “PCBs…11,000 times limit,” “entire freshman class sits on gym floor”), distinguishing infrastructure/health failures from pedagogical or leadership topics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more institutional: Encompasses reports of biased or uneven rule enforcement (athletes/high achievers favored, white students let off more often), staff cliques/cronyism, punitive or arbitrary discipline, mishandled IEPs and special‑education record failures (e.g., “teachers pick favorites,” “only white kids let off,” “IEP staff won’t comply,” “teachers formed cliques ignoring new teachers”), i.e., structural inequity and unequal access to supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures raw items where reviewers say the school has pervasive peer-safety problems — e.g., “constant fighting,” metal detectors, knives/gun brought to school, near‑weekly LOCKDOWNs, widespread bullying and racial harassment, and mishandled student drug incidents — contrasted with square entries that emphasize a generally safe or stable environment and do not document repeated violent or drug-related episodes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This groups claims about leadership behavior and personnel practices: circle reviewers allege the principal/administration shield connected families and star athletes, fire or downgrade dissenting teachers, tolerate nepotism, refuse cooperation with law enforcement, and blame unions for inability to discipline — whereas square entries lack these allegations or instead describe engaged, accessible administrators.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, broader: This bucket covers concrete program and community infrastructure positives: many circle reviews list award‑winning arts, outstanding band/theatre/speech teams, nationally ranked athletics, numerous clubs (Robotics, Debate, Med Club), active alumni reunions and booster/parent fundraising (e.g., 'The Shark Fund' or national Sports Illustrated rankings), while square entries mention fewer or more modest extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit adva: Circle reviews frequently cite structured college‑prep programs and outcomes — IB/Pre‑AP/Early College, dual‑credit pathways, CUNY/Hunter tuition offers, high ACT/NI rates, National Merit candidates, and concrete college acceptances/scholarships — whereas square entries less often supply these named pathways or consistent, quantified postsecondary success metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: This bucket collects specific, operational complaints found predominantly in circle: teachers behind on PowerSchool/grade entry, 20‑year‑old textbooks, misconfigured MacBooks, no air conditioning/mold/pest/urine odors, overcrowding/address fraud, short lunches and long walks between buildings, and lost dual‑credit classes — issues square reviews rarely enumerate in this level of operational detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more severe safe: This bucket groups circle reviews that report concrete safety failures and frequent student-on-student harm—shootings, ambulance-level beatings, daily fights, widespread drug/alcohol use, threats, police involvement, and trauma-linked wellbeing problems—whereas square reviews lack or downplay such extreme incidents (e.g., circle: “One student was shot last year,” “Kids are high and drunk in school regularly,” PTSD tied to the school; square: “not very common” violence and a ‘safe’ feel).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete acad: This bucket captures circle reviews that enumerate programmatic options and outcomes (AP/honors, dual‑credit partnerships, Ivy Tech/college partnerships, CTE/CDL success, associate‑degree graduates, test-score/ACT data, documented college acceptances) while square reviews typically do not provide this level of concrete pathway/outcome detail (e.g., circle: “partnership with Ivy Tech,” “one of the highest ACT averages,” “many graduated with associate degrees”; square: no AP/dual‑credit/program metrics reported).
candidate_defs.circle entries reveal greater administra: This bucket groups circle accounts of leadership failures—unreturned parent requests, administrative placation of parents, favoritism, opaque image management, layoffs/turnover, district-level neglect or state‑takeover risk—that square reviews do not emphasize (e.g., circle: “principal is leaving… layoff notices,” “administration placates parents… will not address…,” “district superintendent has yet to return my requests”; square contains fewer or opposite claims about persistent administrative collapse).
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket captures square reviews that highlight consistent, accessible, mentoring teachers, helpful counselors, IB/AP guidance, routine after‑school tutoring and life‑mentorship—features presented as reliable supports that circle reviews generally lack or describe as uneven (e.g., square: “Saved my son… now at UNH,” “teachers are willing to help,” “guidance and counselors are top notch”; circle contains far more reports of inconsistent or indifferent instructional practice).
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse physical fac: This bucket covers circle descriptions of concrete facility and operational deficits—aging or filthy buildings, gym/roof closures, overcrowded cafeterias and buses, supply/technology shortages, outdated textbooks and broken lockers—while square reviews rarely raise such facility-level problems (e.g., circle: “nasty… haven’t cleaned since The Great Depression,” “lunch room line is horrible… buses crowded,” “lack of classroom technology”; square contains little or no comparable reporting).
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, more concr: These reviews describe explicit program breadth and outcomes (AP/Honors, IB, Dual Enrollment, specialized STEM electives like Organic Chemistry/Bio‑Chemistry, academies, large dual‑credit loads) and concrete college/scholarship results (full scholarships, Ivy/Top‑20 admits, millions in merit awards) that square entries do not; examples include claims of “40+ college level credits,” many AP/Dual Credit offerings, specialized academies, and named alumni college success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more hands‑on, per: Many circle reviews emphasize routine one‑on‑one teacher support, after‑school help, teachers knowing students by name, active PTA/parent programs and formal parent communication (weekly updates, recorded calls, admissions follow‑ups), in contrast to square’s weaker or inconsistent staff availability; examples include teachers 'stay after school,' 'one‑on‑one attention is great,' and named parent councils and outreach activities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive pee: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege student‑on‑student aggression, staff tolerance or participation in bullying, athletic and surname favoritism, nepotistic privileges, selective enforcement (lockouts, expulsions, severe uniform penalties) and harsh/punitive detention conditions — claims not present in square; examples include 'bullies receive little consequences,' 'athletes bribing teachers,' 'lockout for being one minute late,' and 'peanut butter sandwich detention.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: These items document systemic administration failures (zero/late communication, misplaced grades/transcripts, counselors that mismanage schedules or credits, chaotic bus/scheduling logistics, alleged misallocated spending, legal complaints and heavy‑handed oversight) that reviewers contrast with square’s more organized or differently‑problemed accounts; examples include 'The communication level is ZERO,' 'grades are submitted a week or more late,' 'bus schedules are a complete mess,' and 'multiple lawsuits from parents.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse special‑educ: Numerous circle reviews allege failed 504/IEP implementation, denial of medication or accommodations, disciplinary responses to disability symptoms, and administrators minimizing or mocking mental‑health crises — whereas square entries more often describe counseling support; examples include 'teachers do not accommodate 504 or special needs,' 'principal laughed in my face during a panic attack,' and special‑needs students put 'on a trial basis' or forced into summer classes.

candidate_defs.circle entries portray more consistent,: Circle contains multiple concrete examples of reliable parent portals, robo‑call/email reminders, responsive administrators, coordinated teacher/parent intervention meetings, and LMS/laptop rollouts (e.g., Genesisedu, Moodle, prompt teacher callbacks), while Square reviews repeatedly describe nonresponsive counselors, rude office staff, lost paperwork, and poor parent communication.
candidate_defs.square entries report more unresolved sa: Square reviews repeatedly document ongoing bullying, hallway intimidation, threats/bomb scares, staff intimidation and guidance counselors who 'were not very helpful,' and parents reporting that complaints produced no corrective action, whereas Circle contains fewer accounts of persistent unresolved safety crises of this kind.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more community eli: Circle reviewers frequently allege admission and discipline advantages for wealthy, legacy, or athlete families (e.g., 'zero standards for admission other than a parent's open checkbook,' 'Unless you have a certain name...,' and pay/parental control claims), a set of social‑access complaints that Square's reviews do not make.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, tracka: These reviews name concrete pathways and results (IB, dual-enrollment, AVID/college‑career centers, medical/technical magnets, documented college acceptances and scholarships) that tie school practice to postsecondary success (e.g., lists of alumni at UGA/Emory/GA Tech, '100% of IPoly seniors graduate and 98% go to college,' dual‑enrollment paid by the school, IB/AP exam participation), whereas square reviews rarely present that level of programmatic detail or alumni metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle reviews recount repeated bullying, fights, lockdowns, bomb threats, students leaving campus unsupervised, and administrators not addressing abuses (e.g., 'bullying is a constant,' 'bomb threats and lock downs we had weekly/monthly,' parents monitoring the parking lot), whereas square entries more often describe feeling safe or only isolated behavior problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more nepotism, fav: Circle reviewers repeatedly accuse leadership and staff of cronyism and protection of athletes/family members (e.g., 'Good ol boy politics,' 'principal shows favoritism toward family business owners,' 'the shining stars get away with it because teachers and coaches protect them'), describing systematic unequal enforcement of rules that square reviews do not report.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: Square reviewers frequently report reliably helpful teachers and counselors, active parent communication, coordinated supports, and fewer major misconduct reports (e.g., 'teachers were more than helpful,' 'students feel safe,' 'excellent college/career center'), portraying steadier everyday operations and student support than the more polarized accounts in circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: Circle reviews enumerate concrete logistical and infrastructure problems—no cafeteria, frozen classrooms, dilapidated buildings, lost report cards, frequent substitute coverage, inconsistent grading and scheduling, and parents receiving no responses—while square reviews contain far fewer or different operational complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete advanc: These reviews describe specific college‑prep and measurable academic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB/advanced classes, dual‑enrollment/college credit, National Merit/ SAT/ACT results, scholarship totals and named college placements) — e.g., Circle cites “consistently produces National Merit Scholars,” “85 seniors won $7.5 million,” “dual enrollment with Valencia… over a year of college completed,” and numerous AP/college‑credit anecdotes that Square does not provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize vocational/CTE: Many Circle reviews foreground trade and career programs, industry partnerships, certifications, and graduates’ career outcomes (CTE offerings in nursing/welding/teaching, OSHA/WorkKeys certification, associates degrees on graduation, vocational-to-career alumni stories), for example “CTE is offering many new programs” and students graduating with certifications or an Associate’s degree — topics Square rarely describes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: Circle contains repeated, concrete accounts of violence, shootings, drug dealing/use, gang problems, pervasive bullying/public sexual behavior and ineffective enforcement (administrators or security protecting gang members, police inaction, visible on‑campus drug deals), e.g. a reviewer saying counselors arrived only after a shooting, explicit drug‑and‑gang allegations, and staff dismissing bullying with 'kids will be kids.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviews more often accuse leadership of corrupt or dysfunctional governance — claims of administrators enriching themselves, corrupt budget allocation, nepotism/favoritism, mishandled refunds/fees, unilateral policy changes, harassment or threats toward parents, and formal complaints/state takeover warnings (e.g. filing complaints with the attorney general, allegations that 'administration and board members are becoming rich'), all of which Square does not emphasize.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, s: Square reviews more often describe dependable, proactive adults and school management — responsive principals, helpful guidance counselors, teacher mentorship/tutoring that prevented failures, and organized college advising (e.g. 'guidance counselors are good,' 'teachers and counselors were extremely helpful with college prep,' and anecdotes of staff averting a student’s dropout) — a pattern of reliable adult support less prominent in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger advance: These entries report concrete AP/honors/dual‑enrollment classes, rigorous grading/placement rules, high college matriculation and first‑choice acceptances, and specific college‑prep programs (e.g., AP classes, honors GPA thresholds, dual enrollment, documented scholarship totals and students entering college early), whereas square reviews lack comparable program detail or outcomes (examples: Circle: 'AP classes...my daughter will graduate with a BA...straight Bs won't get you on the honor roll'; Square: no detailed AP/college outcomes).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These entries describe repeated peer harassment, 'mean girl' culture, frequent fights, gang activity, property thefts, drug offers, and administrators/security failing to intervene (e.g., 'Bullying is a huge problem', 'Fights are common', 'clothes are stolen from the PE locker rooms'), while square entries rarely document comparable pervasive safety or daily disruption incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a small, personal: These entries emphasize small class sizes, teachers who stay after school as mentors, active PTSA/alumni traditions, and singular program strengths (marching band, drama, JROTC, mascot pride, or top athletics) — e.g., 'all the staff knows each girl by name', 'best band in the state', 'PTS O is AWESOME' — whereas square reviews do not consistently depict this combination of tight personalization plus marquee extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.circle entries report governance, policy: These entries allege systemic administrative problems such as rumor‑based expulsions, athletic favoritism, withheld records/grade manipulation, PTA lawsuits or bounced checks, nonenforcement of handbook rules, and district/board politicization (e.g., 'would rather believe rumors than investigate', 'PTA VIOLATED Chancellor Regs', 'teachers union worked hand‑in‑hand with administrators'), complaints that Square reviews do not predominantly make.
candidate_defs.circle entries detail facility, operatio: These entries provide concrete operational evidence about buildings, technology rollouts or decay, food quality, uniform expense burdens, free transportation, renovations or pest/shooting incidents, and budgeting decisions (examples: 'text books 10 years out of date', 'mice problem and had a shooting', 'uniforms are very expensive', 'new science wing'), whereas square entries tend not to present this level of day‑to‑day operational detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety failures—frequent fights, sexual assaults, student-on-staff threats, widespread drug/vaping use, high local suicide reports, lack of security guards, and bullying reports left uninvestigated (e.g., “teachers receive threats,” “sex in the parking lot,” “the bullying is beyond out of control,” “a police officer was injured”). Falling in this bucket means the school narrative centers on active safety and disorder problems that parents and reviewers say are inadequately remedied.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These items document operational and governance failures such as staff/legacy/donor favoritism, protected athletes, grade-alteration pressure, discipline quotas, administrators paying people to be silent, tithing/religious staffing rules, and allegations of legal/constitutional violations (e.g., “favoritism towards the employee’s children,” “teachers are resigning because they are being told to alter grades,” “secrets are kept,” “willfully violated the law”). Membership means reviews emphasize management malfeasance, selective enforcement, and governance secrecy as core problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: These reviews emphasize structured advanced pathways and quantifiable outcomes—full IB offerings, expanded AP/dual-credit options, dual-enrollment associate degrees, large scholarship totals and elite acceptances (e.g., “full IB Diploma program,” “3 graduates finished associate’s degrees,” “22 Million in scholarships,” “acceptances to Duke/Columbia/Yale”), framing the school as producing measurable college readiness and placements more often than Square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a performing-ar: Square reviews repeatedly foreground arts as the school’s defining extracurricular identity—strong theater, band, and performing-arts magnet programming and reputation—rather than athletics or vocational identity (e.g., “performing arts magnet identity,” “The art program is outstanding,” “band program is top notch”). candidate_defs.circle entries report more active indivi: These reviews highlight smaller class sizes, one-on-one teacher attention, structured in‑school academic supports (before/after/Zero-hour tutoring), vocational/shop and academy pathways (Agriculture, Engineering, Public Service, trades), strong parent/PTO engagement, and prompt teacher communication tools (e.g., “fewer kids in each class…more one on one attention,” “tutoring before school, after school, Zero hour,” “learned a trade,” “JupiterGrades.com and rapid teacher responses”). candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe concrete leadership failures (blaming bullied students, administrators who ‘harass teachers, students, parents,’ unreturned calls, fabricated data, forced good teachers out, opaque fees and bureaucratic barriers), e.g. “the principal literally told me that he thought my daughter 'asked for it'” and “the school will even fill out the application and pay the fee just to create the data!” — patterns absent or far weaker in square entries.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more severe studen: Multiple circle reviews recount daily physical altercations, police pepper‑spraying, pervasive racial slurs, and ongoing harassment that staff ignore — e.g. “EVERYDAY !” fights, “white kids pass around the n‑word,” and students with 'criminal records' — whereas square reviews rarely describe this level of violence or race‑based harassment.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe greater availabi: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite formal AP/IB offerings, concurrent/dual enrollment, extensive CTE/vocational programs, and specific alumni/employment outcomes — e.g. “Nearly 90%... take college classes... transferable credit,” “Great Honors/AP/Dual enrollment programs,” and named employer placements — resources and concrete college-credit pathways largely not reported in square entries.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more petty, incons: These accounts describe strict policing of minor infractions (ID/belt/dress-code detentions, ISS for small holes), selective enforcement and favoritism for athletes or vocal parents, and victims punished for responding to bullying — e.g. “If you have a dime size hole in your jeans, off to ISS” and “Rules seem to not apply to parents who speak out and students who play sports,” a pattern not emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries portray more consistent,: Square reviews more often present steady, positive evidence of academic preparation, teacher caring, safe culture, and clear college-prep signals (e.g. “Love this school,” “The teachers try very hard to reach the students,” consistent praise of outcomes), compared with circle’s highly polarized, contradictory accounts about the same school functions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more intensive col: These reviews emphasize IB/AP/honors breadth, heavy nightly homework and explicit college‑prep counseling and results (e.g., “IB classes,” “Lots of AP and honors,” heavy homework, National Merit scholars, ED acceptances to Duke, high ACT/scholarships), and also note both the stress of rigorous programs and concrete turnaround stories (failing→honor roll). candidate_defs.circle entries report greater facility &: Circle reviews repeatedly name superior or newly upgraded facilities, one‑to‑one device programs, extensive arts and athletics (state champs, award‑winning fine arts, turf fields, MacBook Pro distribution), and a wide roster of clubs and career internships, whereas square reviews lack comparable program/facility detail or document constrained offerings. candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger academi: These circle reviews repeatedly report higher curricular standards and concrete academic outcomes (rigorous college‑prep curriculum, AP/IB or magnet offerings, project‑based learning, dual‑credit, strong AP/IB/AP exam/ACT/SAT results, large scholarship totals and Ivy/Gates/elite college admits), e.g. claims of AP Calc pass, ‘DP sends students to IVY LEAGUE’, ‘$4M in scholarships’, and selective magnet status—features square reviews generally frame as limited or low‑expectation preparation.

candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews contain numerous policy/administration criticisms—allegations of nepotism, cover‑ups of staff–student relationships, book bans/censorship, strict/military or faith‑centered disciplinary regimes, cameras/uniform enforcement, hiring hand‑picked SROs, expulsions for sexual orientation, and grade/ enrollment manipulation to protect rankings—systemic governance and policy practices that square reviews rarely accuse at the same scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger special: This bucket captures reviews where circle schools list concrete advanced‑academic offerings and outcomes—IB programs, many AP/Honors classes, ACT prep, dual‑enrollment, and multi‑academy career tracks (e.g., “IB…earn college credit,” “ACT prep classes,” “13 academies specializing for student careers,” “abundance of advanced placement classes”). candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews describing concrete on‑site safety and behavior failures—fights, repeated physical assaults, gang/drug problems, bathroom harassment, bus incidents and reports that security/discipline 'won't catch them' or is 'laughable' (e.g., “fights everyday,” “rampant alcohol and drug problem,” “my boys were targeted in the bathroom,” “security seemed to be in place, but I don't think they worked very hard”). candidate_defs.circle entries have stronger and more vi: This bucket groups raw terms where circle reviews describe higher‑tier academic offerings and results (IB/AP breadth and quality, dual‑credit/AA and two‑diploma pathways, extensive STEM/career magnets, high ACT/SAT/test scores, named Ivy/military acceptances, alumni professional trajectories) while square reviews lack or criticize comparable advanced programming and college‑prep outcomes (e.g., circle: “IB program…best in the state,” “99+% college acceptance,” “AA degree with diploma”; square: “did not prepare me for college,” lacks AP/IB).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This captures claims about bullying, physical assaults/fights, gang activity, vaping/drugs/alcohol, thefts and threats, and schoolwide disorder that circle reviewers report more often (e.g., “fights every day,” “increase of vaping,” “gang territory,” “hit in the face with a book”) whereas square reviews rarely document recurring safety incidents at that level.

candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete fac: This bucket covers explicit, practical features and impacts—campus construction and new‑building plans, 1:1 devices and technology upgrades, overcrowding/parking, schedule/transportation changes, mandated parent volunteer/fundraising/tuition demands, sanitation problems, security camera/armed guard presence, attendance and lunch‑time policies—that circle reviewers often report in detail (e.g., “every student gets an iPad,” “overcrowded…not enough student parking,” “force parents to donate $150,” “bathrooms smell like fish”), while square entries include fewer of these concrete operational specifics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These entries emphasize formal advanced offerings (IB, AP, dual‑enrollment), measurable school improvement or high ratings (A/B jumps, top regional test scores, full‑ride scholarships), and an externally recognized college‑prep brand (examples: “The IB Program is exceptional,” “We went from being a B school to an A school,” “she will be attending OSU with a FULL ride”). candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reports of concrete safety problems (bullying, assaults, weapons/gun/shooting sightings, bomb threats, on-site drug offers, gang activity), plus accounts that staff or administrators ignored or inadequately responded (e.g., metal detectors/CPD presence cited, ‘offered drugs in restrooms,’ ‘bomb threats kept happening because response was slow,’ ‘bullied in front of admins who did nothing’). candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: This bucket groups governance-level problems: passive‑aggressive or incompetent principals and boards, nepotistic hiring/favoritism, public shaming, opaque/uncaring responses to parent complaints, and rigid or uneven discipline policies (e.g., ‘board are yes‑men,’ ‘administration sides with friends/upper‑class kids,’ ‘automatic 10 days for fighting,’ ‘shame/embarrass students’). candidate_defs.circle entries report higher teacher ins: This cluster covers teacher workforce and instructional practice: higher turnover/burnout, frequent teacher absences, disengaged or incompetent instruction, grade‑tampering or non‑grading, and staff rudeness/abuse (e.g., ‘many teachers leave or are driven out,’ ‘teachers don’t teach, just give packets,’ ‘hall monitors yell and curse at students’). candidate_defs.circle entries report more social‑cultur: Circle reviews repeatedly allege favoritism (donor/legacy/athlete protection), clique/brand‑based exclusion, bullying and targeted discrimination (transphobia, disability‑targeted bullying), plus on‑campus substance/weapon incidents and punitive or inconsistent discipline — social and behavior problems that circle reviewers emphasize more than square reviewers.

candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete criminal/safety problems (robberies, bomb threats, daily fights, student-on-student sexual misconduct, a 13‑year‑old beaten on the bus) and repeated accounts that staff or administrators failed to intervene ("police are there constantly", "the principal didn't want to deal with it", SRO/teacher on duty absent), patterns that appear far more often in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive s: Circle reviews repeatedly name IB/AP/dual‑credit, conservatory/arts, vocational certifications, intervention periods, after‑school tutoring and specific college acceptances/scholarships (e.g., 'IB classes available', 'dual credit', '26 and 32 hours of college credit', 'accepted to 13 universities'), signaling broader formal programs and one‑on‑one curricular adjustments that square reviews rarely mention.

candidate_defs.circle entries highlight broader, higher: This bucket groups programmatic extracurricular strengths and community investment: large marching-band participation, state athletic championships, successful drama/band teams, scholarship/tuition assistance, active alumni networks and volunteer logistics (e.g., “Big Red Marching Band—quarter of the student body…”, “athletic department often win the state championships”, “Thanks to the scholarship my son goes to this great school”). candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures reports of operational and leadership failures — late schedule/course changes, antiquated registration, ignored parental concerns, staff gossip/cliques, nepotism, image‑first responses, frequent leadership turnover and claims of intimidation (e.g., “they are very disorganized,” “staff had cliques,” “the administration looks the other way to avoid looking bad,” “they changed classes as late as November,” and “the one teacher that looked at helping him couldn't deal with lack of admin support and left”). candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger remedial: This bucket groups reviews emphasizing concrete support systems and positive student results — on‑site speech therapy and IEP supports, after‑school tutoring, responsive guidance/counseling, small class sizes, distributed MacBooks, and documented college acceptances/scholarships (e.g., “teachers hold extra tutoring sessions,” “He receives speech therapy… by senior year he graduated with a 3.8,” “students all receive MacBooks,” and “My son was accepted into every college he applied”). These claims contrast with square entries that more often report poor counseling, inadequate supports, or general academic failure.
candidate_defs.circle entries report athletics-centered: This bucket splits two related but distinct extracurricular patterns: many circle reviews complain that sports are institutionally prioritized at the expense of academics and that athletes receive preferential treatment (“sports program is the priority…as long as you're part of the football team, you can do whatever”), while other circle reviews celebrate broad, high-quality extracurriculars (strong band/dance/JROTC and many clubs). Both patterns — athletic prioritization/favoritism and a rich extracurricular ecosystem — appear far more often in circle entries than in square entries, which rarely report this combination of strong extracurricular breadth or explicit athlete favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive f: These reviews emphasize institution-level academic pathways and concrete outcomes—Early College/dual‑enrollment, AP/IB offerings, quantified metrics and university partnerships (e.g. “Early College High School…54% of the student body has a 3.0 or higher,” “students are now able to receive over 60 free college hours through Morehead State University,” and explicit AP/Dual Enrollment/IB examples). Content in this bucket signals organized, credentialed pathways and cited post‑secondary results rather than only anecdotal academic praise.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more substantial: These items highlight visible capital investment and school resources—new buildings/fields and 1:1 device programs and extensive clubs/teams (e.g. “gorgeous new baseball field…artificial turf football field,” “every student has a MacBook / laptop program,” and “13 different sports, and 19 different clubs” or award‑winning band/FFA). Such reviews foreground physical assets, technology deployments, travel and competitive extracurricular breadth as defining features.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket collects reports of acute safety and interpersonal harm: repeated bullying, racial/sexual orientation harassment, assaults, gangs, and sexual‑assault allegations (examples: “major issue with gang problems…The gangs run the town and the schools,” “bullying is rampant,” and explicit accounts of physical assault and sexual misconduct). Entries here focus on the prevalence, severity, and systemic nature of peer violence and hostile school climates.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe leadership and governance breakdowns—complaints that administrators and school boards ignore reports, fail to act on misconduct, manipulate outcomes, or tolerate problems (e.g. “I would tell teachers, principals, even the school board and no one would do anything,” “Multiple reports have been filed and no one has done a thing,” and administrators who ‘put on a show’). Content in this bucket emphasizes absent or ineffective institutional response and weak governance as the primary issue.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: These items focus on classroom practice and staff capacity problems—widespread claims of unmotivated or absent teachers, nontraditional/unqualified instructors, capricious grading, and low teacher morale (examples: “teachers are just unmotivated, bored, and frustrated,” “A lot of the teachers do not even show up,” and “Most teachers can't teach properly” vs. circle reports of proactive after‑school help or dedicated teachers). Reviews in this bucket center instructional quality and teacher workforce instability as the dominant concern.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger measur: These circle reviews foreground concrete, high‑end academic results and rigorous college-prep signaling (National Merit scholars, outstanding SAT/ACT/AP results, Ivy and selective college matriculations, long‑term salary/graduate outcomes and explicit claims of being a ‘college‑prep’ school), while square reviews lack comparable measurable outcomes and instead focus on curricular or support problems (examples: circle mentions ‘consistently produces National Merit Scholars,’ ‘graduates attend Harvard/Columbia,’ and concrete scholarship/SAT/ACT/college matriculation stories).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviewers more often describe recurring student‑behavior and safety problems — drugs, gangs, frequent physical fights, property theft, privacy violations, and police involvement — along with ineffective on‑the‑ground security, whereas square reviews rarely report sustained campus violence and instead emphasize other institutional faults (examples: ‘drugs were being sold right at the front door,’ ‘student fights almost daily,’ ‘clothes are stolen from PE locker rooms,’ and ‘police had to be involved’).
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger athleti: Many circle comments allege that athletics (especially football), boosters, or staff relatives receive outsized funding, social privilege, and grade leniency—plus explicit nepotism claims—while square reviews do not foreground this single‑sport/booster dominance (examples: ‘football is the sole focus…their own building,’ ‘football players are given free grades,’ ‘Chef paid $95K — board president’s live‑in boyfriend’ and ‘95% of the teachers are coaches’).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater administ: Circle reviews more frequently report leadership failures and uneven enforcement—unresponsive principals/counselors, ignored bullying reports, dereliction of duty, uncertified administrators, arbitrary rule application, and blame‑shifting—whereas square reviews more often describe engaged leadership or concrete remedial efforts (examples: ‘issues brought up to the principal and still nothing was done,’ ‘won’t return phone calls,’ ‘principal didn’t even have a certificate/license,’ and ‘administration has no control’).
candidate_defs.circle entries enumerate more concrete,: Circle reviews habitually list specific programs, pathway structures, and supports — Running Start, dual enrollment totals, trade shops, Rosetta Stone language offerings, virtual‑school accommodations for ADHD, Saturday Regents prep, scheduled in‑school tutoring, and strong music/arts — while square reviews generally offer fewer or vaguer programmatic details (examples: ‘over 50 college credits offered,’ ‘Lenape Technical School…allied health,’ ‘virtual school teachers go beyond their job to help him,’ and ‘Saturday Academy for Regents’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: These reviews describe concrete, repeated student-safety incidents and severe peer-on-peer harm in circle schools (e.g., weekly/monthly bomb threats and lockdowns, daily fights, gang involvement, students bringing weapons, sexual assaults, students forced to transfer because of bullying, and multiple reports of suicidal or PTSD-level impacts), while square reviews rarely document such pervasive violent or weaponized threats.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger teacher c: Square reviews repeatedly emphasize qualified, engaged teachers who return calls, give timely grades, offer daily progress updates, tutoring and accessible help, whereas circle reviews more often allege poor subject knowledge, ineffective substitutes, low expectations, chronic late grade posting, and higher turnover that undermines instructional continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger specializ: Circle reviewers cite detailed program breadth and accolades (award-winning robotics and agriculture, Allied Health and Culinary pathways, dual-enrollment/associate-degree outcomes, extensive AP/STEM honors, marching-band/state-sports success and named program awards), while square reviews lack or only generically reference such named, high‑impact programs and recognized student achievements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: Circle reviews contain numerous, specific facility and resourcing reports — both negative (filthy campuses, pest problems, overcrowded/cramped classrooms, out‑of‑date textbooks, underfunded arts/theater) and positive/capital changes (new campus, state‑of‑the‑art facility, upgraded fields) — and frequent notes about how funds are allocated (e.g., boosters/athletics favored, cosmetic spending), whereas square reviews rarely provide this concrete resource/facilities detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews document leadership problems such as hiding problems, favoritism toward donors/athletes or insider families, manipulating enrollment/selection, lost transcripts/administrative errors, counselors and principals not returning calls, mishandled crises and alleged cover‑ups (including dropped misconduct cases), while square reviews more often describe accessible or stable administration and do not catalogue the same pattern of systemic administrative failings.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger teacher: These reviews emphasize hands-on, named teachers, small‑school personalization, after‑school help, and counselors who proactively support students (e.g., “teachers ALWAYS go the extra mile,” “staff knows each student by name,” named staff praise and student recoveries), whereas square reviews more often report teachers as uncaring or inconsistently engaged. Content falls here when the distinguishing evidence is concrete teacher‑student relationships, individualized interventions, tutoring/office‑hour supports, or named mentoring staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These items document chronic peer‑behavior problems and safety incidents (bullying ignored by admin, ‘fights all the time’, drugs in bathrooms/buses, athlete‑clique ostracism, homophobic/racist slurs), whereas square reviews rarely describe such endemic student violence or substance culture. Put a review in this bucket when it centers on repeated physical threats, gang/drug activity, ongoing harassment, or systemic peer exclusion as defining school problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more failures, d: These differences point to IEP/ARD non‑compliance, years‑long delays to get official supports, lumping SPED students out of core classes, and inadequate remediation structures, while square reviews rarely allege systemic SPED breakdowns. Use this bucket for claims about special‑education non‑implementation, poor learning‑disability identification, missing accommodations, or sustained remediation failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight more administra: These reviews call out leadership churn, crony hiring, selective discipline (favoring athletes/white students), unresponsive or dismissive administrators, and politicized decision‑making, whereas square reviews tend not to foreground entrenched nepotism or selective enforcement. Place content here when the key distinguishing evidence concerns leadership behavior, governance problems, biased enforcement, or repeated principal/office failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries more frequently document: These notes cite dual‑enrollment, AP/Honors expansions, career academies, vocational certifications (aviation/CTC/skills pathways), and concrete outcome metrics or scholarship totals, while square reviews less often report such named pathway programs or credentialing opportunities. Assign a review to this bucket when it centers on program breadth/depth (AP/IB/dual enrollment, career academies, industry credentials) or concrete outcome measures tied to those programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger formal ad: These reviews describe concrete program offerings and outcomes in circle schools — AP/Pre‑AP, Dual Credit partnerships, vocational/CTE tracks (welding, medical, culinary), scholarship totals and documented college acceptances — e.g., “Dual Credit, AP courses,” “$2,000,000 in scholarship offers,” and students earning state/national CTE awards; square entries do not provide comparable, institutionally‑documented advanced pathways or measurable college/CTE results.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more staff profe: Circle reviewers raise repeated, specific allegations about staff wrongdoing and procedural failures — teacher‑student sexual relationships, anti‑LGBT/ racial bias, staff‑perpetrated bullying, SPED/504 failure and IEP noncompliance — (e.g. “multiple teachers... had relations with students,” “do not follow...504 plans,” “staff is very Anti‑Lgbt”), while square entries lack parallel claims of systemic staff misconduct or special‑education legal violations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance an: Circle texts frequently describe hostile or ineffective leadership, high principal/administrator turnover, unresponsive offices, opaque school‑board behavior and politicized community conflict — e.g., “no transparency... admin/board comprised of the same people,” “principal never returns calls,” and frequent leadership changes — whereas square reviews more often describe stable, visible principals or do not raise systemic governance crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews recount frequent physical fights, daily bullying, police on campus, bomb/shooting threats, drug problems and resultant student fear or emotional harm — examples include “Police are there almost every day,” “I've witnessed bullying at least once a day,” and “many endangerments dealing with shootings and bomb threats” — claims largely absent or explicitly denied in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews emphasize hands‑on counselor/staff support, an involved principal and concrete retention interventions (e.g., counselors and principals helping students catch up or arranging special pick‑ups to keep students enrolled), with statements like “amazing staff… devoted Principal,” and “guidance counselors... went above & beyond,” a pattern that contrasts with many circle reviews expressing staff unresponsiveness or administrative inaction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer academic pr: These reviews describe concrete advanced-academic offerings and downstream results not seen in square entries — e.g., IB and AP praise, on-site dual‑enrollment/early‑college pathways, students graduating with associate degrees, many scholarship awards, and alumni matriculation to selective universities (examples: “IB program… wonderful,” “graduate with your Associates,” “major college scholarships,” “enrolled at Cal Berkeley”). Falling into this bucket means the school narrative emphasizes structured college-prep pathways and documented postsecondary success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and more p: Circle reviews repeatedly list extensive clubs, performing-arts ensembles, and high-performing sports teams (marching band, theater, robotics, many clubs) and often note athletics’ cultural prominence or funding debates (examples: “athletics are all great… lots of clubs,” “more than one hundred state championships,” and complaints that football is over‑prioritized or funds are reallocated). Content in this bucket focuses on breadth/quality of out‑of‑class programs and the school’s sports/arts prominence or tensions between athletics and academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe smaller, close-k: Multiple circle reviews emphasize small classes, house/SLC structures, staff knowing students by name, visible administrators in classrooms, strong parent outreach, and one-on-one remediation (examples: “small and challenging… everyone knows everyone,” “teachers know all the students by name,” “deans... out all day talking to the student,” and individualized make-up work after illness). Items in this bucket signal that the school experience is organized around personalization and tight community ties.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more nepotism, fav: Several circle reviews make direct accusations of grade‑fixing, valedictorian favoritism, hiring family members, income- or race-based differential treatment, and opaque preferential enforcement (examples: “Do not even try to be considered for Valedictorian if you are not the son or daughter of a teacher,” “If your family's income is above average so is your child’s grades,” and reports of racial jokes tolerated). Content here centers on patterned unfairness in recognition, staffing, discipline, or resource allocation.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational/s: Square reviews more often document concrete safety incidents and imposed security measures (e.g., bomb threats, bathroom sign‑in), failures in counseling and IEP implementation, transcript/communication breakdowns, and claims that administration refuses responsibility or is unresponsive (examples: “two 'bomb threats',” “Guidance is inadequate,” “Didn’t provide any of the services in his IEP,” and “the counseling department is useless”). Materials falling in this bucket emphasize schoolwide operational breakdowns, safety events, and systemic service failures rather than program breadth or close-knit supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, concrete: These reviews frequently name specific advanced and career programs—IB and top-notch AP offerings, 'opportunity to take 40+ college credits,' dual/concurrent enrollment, JTED/CTE, woodshop/auto/AG, internships and workforce partnerships—whereas square reviews mention fewer or only isolated credit or dual‑enroll opportunities; examples include Circle’s lists of IB/AP/dual‑credit classes, vocational shops, CCAC courses and internships versus Square’s single dual‑enrollment mention.
candidate_defs.circle entries convey more concrete oper: Circle reviews include precise, verifiable details about the school—hours ('8:15-3:17pm'), named college matriculations, graduation counts/accreditation claims, energy/solar contracts, PCB contamination, and enrollment trends—while Square typically gives broader statements without these operational specifics; sample items: Circle’s college placement lists, PCB contamination report, energy contract and exact schedules versus Square’s lack of comparable measurable detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more c: Many Circle reviewers cite small class sizes, one‑on‑one attention, responsive teachers (quick email replies, after‑school help), individualized accommodations, music/coach mentoring, and counselors who secure scholarships, whereas Square reviews more often spotlight teacher apathy or uneven support; examples include Circle’s band teacher doing private lessons, counselors driving college admissions/scholarships, and repeated notes of personalized attention.
candidate_defs.square entries report more persistent sa: Square reviews more often emphasize daily safety threats, bullying left unaddressed, drug/deal/knife incidents, and a perception that administration blames students or ignores behavior—e.g., reports of a turned‑in knife, hallway drug deals, and administrators who 'won't address' a bully problem—whereas Circle reviews, while mixed, less frequently center the school narrative on unresolved violent/drug safety crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more bureaucratic/: Circle reviewers repeatedly document strict micromanaging rules/fees (dress‑code enforcement, yearly fees, charging parents for gym entry), accusations of favoritism toward athletes/staff kin, union protection and coverups, and administration prioritizing rankings/appearance over students—examples include forced fees to participate, claims that 'athletes can do no wrong,' named nepotism, and explicit statements that administrators 'cover up a lot just to make the school look good.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report pervasive student-: These reviews describe sustained peer violence and targeted abuse (e.g., “full of Bullies that pick on disabled or slower learning students,” “constant racism, sexism, and homophobia”) with repeated attempts to get help ignored or dismissed by school staff and deans (e.g., “Nothing was ever done…Conversations with teachers, the Principal and the Superintendent left the issues unresolved,” a dean who literally laughed). Falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on unsafe peer culture plus official nonresponse or inadequate anti-bullying protocol.
candidate_defs.circle entries document higher incidence: These reviews cite unethical or unprofessional staff behavior (coaches hiring spouses, teachers dating students, staff fistfights, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy families) and repeated mass layoffs or churn (e.g., “The new administration cleaned house…80% of the teachers were let go,” “teachers there only for the paycheck”), producing wide variability in instruction quality. Content in this bucket focuses on personnel ethics/selection problems and staffing instability rather than student programs or facilities.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize structured adva: Square reviews foreground formal college-preparatory architecture and credentials (AP Capstone, IB, many APs, dual-enrollment, industry certifications like cosmetology/robotics) and cite concrete outcomes (scholarships, college admit examples). Items in this bucket describe institutional programmatic rigor and explicit pathways to college or certification rather than vocational breadth or operational complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight broader hands-o: These comments catalogue a wide practical-program mix—WELDING, CULINARY, auto mechanics, JROTC, working on-site bank, community garden, state-champion gymnastics, many clubs and inclusive tryouts—and emphasize partnerships/internships and accessible ‘open to any kid’ extracurriculars. Belonging here means the school is portrayed as offering diverse, applied and extracurricular options and local partnerships rather than a narrow AP/IB focus.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: These reviews contain concrete complaints about building/health and logistical systems (mold, poor AC, trailers, broken Internet, missing buses, inedible food), plus punitive or coercive administrative practices (credits lost, transcripts withheld, suspensions for dress code, threats to withhold graduation items for unpaid fundraisers). Items in this bucket are about tangible operational breakdowns and heavy-handed or exclusionary enforcement practices rather than curriculum or staff professionalism alone.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more advanced ac: Circle reviews repeatedly list concrete programmatic offerings and measurable outcomes (AP and IB programs, college‑credit/A+ programs, named external partnerships and internships, vocational majors/shops, 1:1 tech, award‑winning band/athletics) and cite high scholarship totals and elite college placements; Square reviews do not provide the same density of partnerships, career majors, or aggregated postsecondary metrics. Falling in this bucket means the text emphasizes institutional breadth/depth of academic and career pathways and named outcomes (AP/IB, college credit, internships, vocational shops, marching band successes).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive and: Many Circle reviewers recount extreme safety and misconduct problems — gang activity, drug dealing, bomb/kill threats, sexual harassment/abuse, student suicides, unbroken-up assaults and life‑threatening staff injury — presented as school‑wide or recurring issues; Square reviews rarely report that level or scope of violent/sexual/drug‑related incidents. Items in this bucket center on concrete safety incidents, unaddressed bullying, substance/weapon exposure, and trauma linked to the school environment.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews include repeated accusations against leaders and school governance (metric‑gaming/clearing failing students, misrepresenting public image, misallocated maintenance spending, fraternization with students, political proselytizing, and district board blame), while Square reviews do not foreground these kinds of governance/manipulation claims. Content in this bucket focuses on concrete leadership/govt practices and abuses (data/metrics manipulation, favoritism, misused funds, administrative interference) rather than classroom or student behavior alone.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher apath: Square reviewers more often describe teachers as 'hit or miss,' 'there for a paycheck,' relying on substitutes, or failing to provide consistent extra help and instructional rigor, whereas Circle reviews frequently highlight caring, credentialed, and above‑and‑beyond teachers. Texts in this bucket emphasize pervasive instructional inconsistency, low teacher morale or disengagement, and classroom practices that undermine learning (substitutes, minimal instruction), presented as a dominant school problem.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent fa: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete process and legal complaints (504/IEP not implemented, procedural violations, parents forced to advocate, archaic special‑ed methods, or inconsistent accommodation follow‑through), whereas Square reviews rarely raise procedural special‑education failures. Items placed here report breakdowns in special‑education delivery, formal accommodation compliance, and the administrative communications required to secure those services.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student viole: These reviews describe concrete safety failures (e.g., “GANG ACTIVITY,” students being assaulted, on‑campus drug selling, fights where “staff did nothing,” and repeated reports of assaults or medical neglect) that square reviews do not raise; put simply, circle schools are characterized by reviewers calling out violent incidents, drug problems, and inadequate student supervision while square reviews lack those specific incident-level safety claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege governance failures—nepotistic spending and favoritism, refusal to provide transcripts, confidentiality breaches and a federal lawsuit, threats to involve law enforcement/SARB, cover‑ups, punitive removals tied to payments, and rude/unresponsive front offices—whereas square reviews rarely describe such systemic administrative abuse and cover‑ups.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more structured: Many circle reviews name extensive AP/honors offerings, 1:1 device and dual‑enrollment programs (students bused to community college, IGETC/Associate degree pathways), AVID, and concrete outcomes (major scholarship totals, college acceptances, US News recognition), while square reviews lack comparable descriptions of organized college-credit pathways and measurable postsecondary success.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, better-: Circle reviews list and praise many named activities (award‑winning band, choir, drama, AFJROTC, numerous clubs), describe accessible club/team participation and family/community fundraising to support programs, and cite state/national awards; square reviews tend to reference extracurriculars only generically or note limited offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: Circle reviewers frequently describe tutoring, zero‑hour help, onsite nurses/counselors, teachers who give extra time and close student bonds, and one‑on‑one support; in contrast square reviews repeatedly call out unhelpful or incompetent counselors, erratic grading, teachers surfing the internet or being unavailable, and a lack of reliable instructional support.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger and bro: These reviews highlight that circle schools more often report concrete advanced coursework, vocational pathways, and quantifiable college success — e.g., many AP/Honors/IB and Cambridge references, explicit CTE/health-technology/hospital partnerships, early-college practices, direct-admission and scholarship anecdotes, and cited scholarship totals/100% graduation claims — whereas square reviews more often note missing AP breadth, weak college counseling, or poor preparation without comparable programmatic evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism/favo: Circle reviewers frequently allege preferential treatment tied to athletics, alumni/teacher families, donor influence, or local‑born status and describe questionable admissions behavior (accepting anyone for funding, lowered eligibility thresholds, legacy hiring), e.g. claims that football players or cheerleaders get special treatment, teacher/coach relatives get advantages, and schools accept students to make up funding, complaints not mirrored in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews disproportionately describe staff hostility and instructional failures — teachers described as rude, disrespectful, bullying students, refusing help, regurgitating third‑party content, privacy breaches, and a lack of professional development — while circle reviews more often name caring, long‑tenured, or passionate teachers.
candidate_defs.square entries report more severe studen: Square reviewers more frequently document systemic safety problems and student misconduct (drugs, fights, violent threats, death threats, pervasive bullying, lack of supervision/security) and link these to poor learning environments, whereas circle reviews are more likely to report social inclusion, tolerant student climates, or active security measures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger parenta: Circle reviews often emphasize familylike community, high parental involvement, coordinated parent–teacher practices (regular joint conferences), 1:1 device/technology programs, individualized after‑school help, and proactive counselor/administrator communication — contrast to square reviews, which more frequently report poor parent communication, disengaged counselors, and fragmented outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger, struc: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete AP/ honors/dual-enrollment/STEM academies, clear college-counseling supports, quantifiable outcomes (SAT/ACT averages, scholarship totals, guaranteed funding) and students’ readiness for college — e.g., “over 25 AP courses, Dual Enrollment, new STEM Academy,” “Class of 2016 averaged 1124 on the SAT,” “helped her get a full ride to Univ of Alabama,” and “There is no doubt that the students are well-prepared for college.” These items stand apart from square reviews that lack schoolwide outcome claims or report weak college preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent sp: This bucket groups reports of concrete special-education breakdowns in the building and district: long delays to placement, teachers unfamiliar with IEPs, expired accommodations, and repeated non‑implementation (e.g., “one teacher had no idea what an IEP was,” “went two years without testing,” “504 Plan… never happened,” and “services…aren’t nearly as implemented and encouraged”). These operational special‑needs failures are described far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket covers reviews alleging repeated or extreme safety problems and adult inaction: sustained physical harassment and assaults, gang or police presence, bomb threats, allegations of principal verbal abuse, and claims that teachers/administrators fail to stop bullies (e.g., “threw me into a trash can…no one did anything,” “police are there constantly, bomb threats,” “the principal screamed at kids,” and “the bullies here run the school and the teachers and principal will not do anything”). These are school-safety/response failures that contrast with square reviews that rarely describe sustained physical victimization or chronic nonresponse.
candidate_defs.circle entries report explicit faith-bas: This bucket captures concrete religious mission and routine faith practices or single-sex instruction: daily prayer and monthly liturgies, Jesuit/Catholic identity, Christian character education, and all‑girls/all‑boys program structures (e.g., “You pray every morning…a liturgy every month,” “follows Catholic teaching…foundation of spiritual education,” and “all-girl…Without the stress of male students she is very focused academically”). These institutional faith/single-sex features appear much more often in circle reviews than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics/arts: This bucket includes reviews that describe a sports- or flagship-arts‑dominated culture (marching band or athletics singled out as a flagship), audition/tryout selection, boosters, resource imbalances favoring athletics, and coach/AD protection or nepotistic favoritism (e.g., “the marching band is amazing…one of the top in our state,” “sports program dominates…non-athletic things have to fund themselves,” “not anyone can just come in…you have to try out,” and “kids who have been here their whole life…get to play more”). These programmatic and resource-allocation patterns are a distinct extracurricular/funding theme not captured by the academic, safety, special‑ed, or religious buckets.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ad: These entries emphasize formal, structured academic offerings and quantifiable college success — e.g., repeated mentions of AP/IB programs, dual‑enrollment and block schedules, ACT prep clubs, earnable college credits, IB test/score reporting, and alumni Ivy League/college matriculation anecdotes — whereas square entries rarely name such programmatic infrastructure or concrete outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: Square entries disproportionately describe threats to student safety and heavy-handed security/discipline (fights, drug concerns, campus police intimidation, students antagonized by SROs, reports of unsafe/violent incidents), while circle entries more often assert fewer or more managed violence/safety problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse physical fac: Circle reviewers supply numerous facility-level complaints (rats/roaches/centipedes, sewage‑pond portable units, mold/leaking sinks, rotten food, packed hallways and 35‑student classes, locked/unlocked door problems), indicating chronic building/sanitation and overcrowding issues not described in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger day‑to‑: Circle entries repeatedly cite teachers staying after school, phone/one‑on‑one help, dedicated high‑quality teachers and concrete student turnarounds (improved grades, top‑of‑class, scholarship/college placements), whereas square entries more often report instructional gaps, unhelpful teachers, or lack of consistent, individualized classroom support.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviews contain many concrete governance complaints — unreturned principal emails, policy-driven or district blame-shifting, conflicts of interest (administrators who coach), favoritism toward athletes/donors, alleged racist/nepotistic practices, financial misallocation and board escalation — depicting systemic managerial dysfunction more often than square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: These reviews cluster reports that circle schools offer and credibly show rigorous curricula and results (AP/ Cambridge/dual‑enrollment, rising test scores, scholarships, explicit college‑prep claims). Examples: 'Each year test scores have improved… #1 & #2 in LBUSD API scores', 'nearly 20 AP classes… take classes at 3 colleges', 'Massive scholarships are awarded…' versus square reviews that emphasize being unprepared for college or missing AP offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report smaller school siz: Many circle reviews describe intimate, small‑school scale and personal familiarity (teachers know students by name, multi‑generation alumni, family atmosphere, low student:teacher ratios) that contrast with square reviews emphasizing large, crowded campuses and students feeling lost.
