Examples: 'around 500 children', 'The faculty know you by name', 'My husband and myself graduated… my son just started', versus square's 'It's a small school' contradictions and overcrowding complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: A recurring pattern in circle reviews is concrete safety and peer‑violence incidents—bullying left unaddressed, lock‑downs, gang activity, shootings and targeted intimidation—descriptions largely absent from square. Examples: 'The bulling here is real and they do nothing to help', 'bomb threats', 'There was a gang related shooting outside of the school', and allegations of vandalism/intimidation of coaches.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize district/fiscal: Square reviews more often attribute problems to budget and district decisions—discontinued programs, teacher cuts, understaffing, and fiscal constraints tied to falling academic quality—whereas circle reviews less frequently blame district funding. Examples: 'discontinued many programs, cut classes, cut teachers', 'The district has declined in quality', and 'Teachers honestly are working under horrible conditions regarding pay and no contract.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more organized p: Circle reviews frequently list concrete in‑school supports and specialty programs—strong special‑education programming or remediation, Saturday schools, Writing Centers, JROTC/FFA, tech centers and dual‑enrollment partnerships, and broad extracurricular/competitive teams—features square reviews rarely enumerate. Examples: 'special education program... above any expectations', 'dual enrollment with Wayne County Community College', 'lots of clubs, Marching Band, competitive band, theatre and the fishing team' versus square's lack of comparable program detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: This bucket groups circle reports that list concrete programmatic college-prep offerings and outcomes (AP/IB classes, specialized academies, dual-enrollment/early‑college pathways, SAT/ACT prep) and explicit score/placement improvements — e.g., mentions of AP American History and IB Diploma, academies that count as college credit, Toledo Early College/associate-degree pathways, free summer ACT prep, Cleveland Clinic fellowships, and claims that “test scores have blossomed” or students matriculating to Ivy/medical programs — features not present in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a stronger athleti: This bucket captures circle claims that sports and event culture are institutionally prominent or prioritized over academics — e.g., "All money goes to sports," football glorification, athlete recruitment/scholarships, state championships and highly energized fan sections, cheer/pep culture, and extensive named extracurricular rosters — patterns Square reviews do not attribute to their schools or that Square frames as secondary.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive disc: This bucket groups circle accounts of no‑warning zero‑tolerance discipline, routine suspensions that harm learning, coercive/nontransparent drug testing, principals handling incidents "in house" or covering up, administrative bullying/harassment, and centralized punitive decision‑making (e.g., "Suspension is the ONLY form of dicipline," nonrandom substance testing, "administration harasses teachers, students, parents"), contrasts that Square reviews generally do not make.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater failures: This bucket groups circle reports of systemic neglect or harm to students with disabilities and mental‑health needs — e.g., IEPs not followed or students removed because of an IEP, special‑education classrooms isolated from activities, "no effective support for learning disabilities," counselors who "didn’t help," students asked to withdraw for mental‑health reasons, and documented physical assault of a student with special needs — issues Square reviews rarely report.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistentl: This bucket captures Square reviewers’ frequent claims of committed, high‑quality instruction, supportive faculty and counselors, and responsive communication (e.g., "The commitment of faculty and staff is tremendous," "teachers go above and beyond," counselors described as "amazing," and praise for administrative responsiveness), contrasting with many Circle reports that detail instructional neglect, unresponsive administrators, or inconsistent teacher quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger advance: These entries describe concrete, school-run academic offerings and outcomes that outpace square: named AP courses and IB tracks, honors/AP-heavy schedules, explicit college‑matriculation stats and counseling infrastructure, heavy homework expectations and rigorous coursework (e.g., AP Calculus/Statistics, IB encouragement, ‘99% go on to college’, extended AP credit and ACT success). They also call out organized academic supports (tutoring, college guidance) and one‑to‑one device programs that enable continuity of learning, which square reviews typically lack or criticize as weak.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, award‑win: These entries name extensive extracurricular ecosystems (30+ clubs, award‑winning drama, competitive music, national FFA/Beta competitions, debate, service programs) and documented athletic championships/coaching cultures, while also often noting staff favoritism for athletes and clique-driven recognition (e.g., state titles, ‘exceptional drama program’, but ‘teachers/coaches protect shining stars’). Square entries rarely list comparable breadth or documented championships and more often emphasize limited extracurricular options or problematic athletic leadership without championship evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger local com: These entries describe active parental attendance at events, formal parent communication systems and coordinators, small enrollment or tight neighborhood continuity, multigenerational loyalty, and a ‘family’ or college‑like campus feel (e.g., strong parent fundraising/donations, power‑school access, small class sizes, lifelong local ties). Square entries, by contrast, typically lack such sustained community involvement or emphasize larger, more anonymous school scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These entries allege concrete governance problems — corrupt or misallocated budgets, levy/levy‑defeat rationales tied to mismanagement, suppressing public forums, firing dissenting teachers, residency/fiscal conflicts, and poor district responsiveness to complaints — describing structural leadership failures distinct from everyday classroom issues (e.g., ‘budget allocation system is very corrupt,’ principals who retaliate or hide, and spending on cosmetic projects instead of safety). Square reviews typically criticize leadership competence or priorities but do not make the same cluster of fiscal-corruption and reprisals allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These entries document specific and extreme safety incidents and supervisory breakdowns — shootings, repeated beatings, death threats, on‑campus drug selling and intoxication, sexual harassment, daily food fights, pervasive bullying and targeted abuse of special‑needs students, and failures or inconsistent enforcement by staff — often paired with ineffective or punitive disciplinary responses (e.g., isolation to independent study, suspensions used to remove problems). Square entries rarely present this level or frequency of violent/safety incidents and instead focus on other operational or cultural problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, measur: These reviews emphasize concrete academic rigor and pathways (AP/AICE/IB, dual‑credit, AFROTC, academies), heavy homework expectations, published test scores, scholarship totals and named alumni college placements—e.g., “½ hour per class per night,” “Students have earned over 3 million dollars in scholarships,” “abundance of AP and dual credit classes” and multiple claims of full‑ride/IVY matriculation—whereas square reviews mostly lack such program detail or measurable outcome evidence and often portray academics as only average.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews describe recurring fights, gang presence, weapon incidents, sustained bullying, and claims staff/administration fail to intervene (e.g., “lots of Bullying, fights,” “When a student brings a gun to school… administration 'plays it off',” and “they wont do anything about bullying unless your parents are well known”), while square reviews either omit pervasive safety failures or report fewer/isolated behavioral incidents and quicker resolutions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviews supply concrete operational and governance complaints—sudden bus service cuts, leaked GPAs, exam/schedule mismanagement, calls for impartial board investigations, and claims that administration 'could not care less'—for example: “letter one day before school…ten students can no longer ride the bus,” “recent leak of all student GPAs,” and demands to place the superintendent on leave; square reviews rarely document such systemic operational failures and more often describe accessible or improving administration.
candidate_defs.circle entries document larger teacher‑l: These items emphasize substitute‑heavy classes, teachers accused of false grading or public shaming, coaches assigned to teach with poor instruction, high turnover and targeted forcing‑out of strong teachers, and preferential grading for athletes—e.g., “teachers will give students good grades if they are in the football team,” “Most of her classes have substitutes,” and “false record of assignments”—while square reviews more often report stable, accessible or uniformly caring teachers without the same level of misconduct or favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize tight local com: Circle reviews frequently frame the school as a small, family‑like, faith‑integrated or community‑anchored institution (denominational instruction, weekly chapels, multigenerational enrollment, alumni loyalty, parents encouraged to volunteer, and inclusive opportunities because of small size)—for example: “God is at the center,” “I graduated… I have 3 children enrolled,” and “Due to the smaller student numbers… there are so many more opportunities”—whereas square reviews rarely describe religious mission, deep alumni continuity, or that same small‑school, community‑participation dynamic.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: This bucket groups differences where reviewers of the circle-school describe safety crises (multiple fights, gang presence, widespread drug use, lockdowns, students seen using drugs) and a prominent law‑enforcement/ SRO presence, while square reviewers report few or no comparable safety incidents; examples include ‘First 3 months at least 12 fights broke out,’ ‘the drug use is extremely big here,’ and a PSAT lockdown versus square’s absence of fights or gang reports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger/high‑prof: Contains claims that the circle-school foregrounds high‑visibility programs (top‑ranked athletics, JROTC, conservatory arts, Broadway teachers, multi‑million dollar stadiums, international trips, private lessons and frequent productions), whereas square reviews either omit or downplay such flagship extracurricular breadth; illustrative lines: ‘fantastic sports program (top 25 in the country by Sports Illustrated)’, ‘conservatory-style arts tracks’, and ‘Congrats to all on a great show today!!!’.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete academ: Groups instances where circle reviewers cite AP/IB offerings, dual enrollment, accreditation/distinctions, specific test scores, high college matriculation/graduation statistics and alumni success (e.g., ‘IB Diploma/Certificate’, ‘99+% college acceptance rate’, ‘full 6 years accreditation’), while square reviews generally lack such measurable outcome claims or program-level evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more nepotism, fav: This bucket captures circle reviews that accuse the school/district of entrenched family hiring, favoritism in discipline/opportunities, named administrators behaving vindictively or unprofessionally, alleged PR manipulation, and repeated principal/staff turnover (e.g., ‘Nepotism, Politics, and Cliques run this school,’ ‘Lori Taylor is evil…’, ‘many of our teachers now are substitutes; at least three principals in five years’), while square reviews do not center these systemic personal‑favor issues to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent te: This bucket collects differences where square reviewers emphasize reliable teacher outreach, in‑class attentiveness, extra‑help availability (after‑school tutoring, caring counselors), and day‑to‑day responsiveness, whereas circle reviews more often describe uneven or absent routine classroom support; examples include square statements like ‘Teachers truly care…they get back to you within a couple hours’ and circle contrasts where ‘if you are failing…that teacher will not help you.’
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, formal: These reviews emphasize concrete advanced‑academic pathways (AP/honors, dual‑enrollment, Middle College, AA/college credit completion, specialized academies) and tied outcomes (high ACT/SAT averages, top‑tier college acceptances)—e.g., “seniors…going to Brown, Northwestern, Yale,” “students graduate with AA degree,” and “all AP class options” — claims that Square’s reviews do not match.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pervasive i: Square reviews more often attribute weak school quality to classroom instruction and teacher capacity—comments like “teachers don’t teach,” “terrible teachers,” VCR‑based classes, and “does not prepare kids for college at all”—painting systemic instructional and curriculum failures not emphasized in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete safety and criminality reports—ongoing fights, gang affiliation, visible drug use, vandalism, probationers on campus, and pervasive bullying (e.g., “constant danger,” “threatened… affiliated in the crip gang,” “bullying is everywhere”)—claims that Square’s entries largely lack or report as less frequent.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight a broader, more: Circle reviewers repeatedly praise or document expansive extracurricular assets and community/faith culture—nationally prominent music programs and multiple athletic championships, JR‑ROTC/faith retreats, vocational pathways, donor‑driven facility projects, and a tight small‑town ‘families first’ ethos—where Square is more likely to report narrower offerings, stigma around participation, or a single dominant program (e.g., football).
candidate_defs.circle entries show more polarized and i: Circle reviews contain contradictory administrative narratives (named beloved principals/counselors alongside claims of high‑paid ineffective superintendents, turnover, nepotism, uneven discipline, and poor parent communication), e.g. “the principal was always walking the halls” vs “administration is constantly changing” and “preferential treatment” or “Board refuses to act,” a pattern of governance volatility and polarization not observed as often in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: Many circle reviews recount sustained safety problems ("bullied constantly everyday," "bad drug problem," explicit racial/transphobic threats, "belt fights on the bus") and describe administrators/staff who "do nothing about bullying" or ignore complaints; square reviews rarely allege systemic safety failures and sometimes praise counselors or orderly environments, so this bucket groups raw terms about student safety incidents, harassment types, and administrative non‑response to those incidents (metal detectors, severe bullying narratives, and unaddressed mental‑health harms).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more formal spec: Numerous circle items list organized advanced programs and credentials (Cambridge/AICE, AP, CTE certifications, magnet tracks, dual enrollment) and concrete alumni/college outcomes (Ivy acceptances, full scholarships, alumni career trajectories), whereas square reviews rarely name those formal pathways; this bucket captures program structure, credentialing, dual‑credit pathways, and measurable postsecondary results described by reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics as an: Circle reviewers repeatedly assert that "athletics absolutely drive the school," cite double standards for athletes, sports‑focused admissions/legacy preferences, no‑cut policies, new stadium investments, and social deference to athletes, while square reviews mention sports without portraying them as dominant; this bucket groups claims about resource/prioritization choices, athlete preferential treatment, and admissions tied to athletics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews contain repeated complaints about administrators not acting on complaints, unanswered emails, tenure or hiring practices that shield ineffective teachers, and weak district/board oversight (e.g., 'administration chooses to do nothing because he/she is tenured,' 'No one returns your emails'), whereas circle reviews more often describe active principals or recent leadership hires; this bucket captures governance, accountability, and communication failures attributed to school leadership or boards.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more small‑schoo: Many circle items highlight tight communities, teachers/principals who "know students by name," required teacher help nights, named roles (graduation coach), organized parent anti‑bullying groups, and strong alumni networks that support students, while square reviews more often report larger impersonal scale or uneven teacher availability; this bucket groups concrete practices that produce individualized attention, mentorship, formal tutoring or counseling supports, and parent/alumni engagement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, formal a: These reviews describe concrete programs and outcomes: AP/IB/Honors tracks, dual‑credit/college‑in‑the‑schools offerings, documented scholarship and ACT success, college partnerships/seminars, and students entering college with credits—e.g., “Honors, AP, and IB classes,” “over forty college credits…entering college as a sophomore,” and Bucknell‑hosted engineering seminars—features that Square reviews rarely list and sometimes explicitly contrast with students being unprepared for college.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: This bucket covers claims of wide activity catalogs, strong arts/athletics, facility renovations, school‑scale programs and community financial backing—examples include long club lists (Robotics, Mock Trial, band of 300), state/national marching band wins, newly renovated athletic facilities, community fundraising to 'save the school,' and paid dual‑credit tuition—resources and alumni/parent support that Square reviews generally do not document.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These items document physical fights, pervasive bullying, racism/sexism/homophobia, sexual harassment, hazing, student‑on‑student and staff‑on‑student abuse, on‑campus drug incidents, and related long‑term harm (e.g., antidepressants, transfers), e.g. “there are fights all the time,” “Racism is the norm,” staff grabbing students/causing bruises, and alleged drug distribution—problems Square reviews seldom raise or report with the same severity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report systemic governanc: This grouping captures allegations about hiring favoritism and unqualified promotions, high principal/coach turnover, opaque or absent communication with families, punitive enforcement or authoritarian leadership, and board insularity—examples include nepotistic promotions from counselor→principal, “You WILL NEVER get anyone to answer” calls, accusations that 'leadership is about who you know,' and ‘administration focused on making this school a prison compound.’
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: These reviews emphasize inconsistent or poor classroom instruction, widespread teacher apathy or uncertified instructors, lack of tutoring/academic follow‑through, failures in college‑readiness and guidance, and students graduating unprepared—illustrated by comments like “Depending on the teacher, you can either have a great year, or a horrible one,” uncertified remediation teachers, guidance that 'doesn't help them figure out what they want to do,' and claims that students 'are not prepared for college.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: This bucket captures many Circle reviews that describe riots, frequent fights, assaults requiring ambulances, lock‑downs, gangs, widespread drug use, high pregnancy rates, and ‘bullying is rampant’ narratives (e.g., reports of fights, pepper‑spray hallways, ambulance calls, and pervasive drug pressure), contrasts with Square reviews that do not describe these chronic safety/drug/violence problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete, i: Many Circle reviews list concrete interventions (IEP/ADHD accommodations, one‑on‑one meetings, morning/evening tutoring, SAT prep, teachers available at lunch/after school), special‑education/autism supports, middle‑school pipelines and dual‑enrollment/college credit programs or documented college matriculation—features Square reviews rarely provide with the same specificity.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This groups Circle reports of systemic problems like administrators who ‘sweep accusations under the rug,’ nepotistic favoritism (teacher/athlete/parent perks), formal barring/expulsion for poor grades, manipulated student elections, and calls for school‑board reevaluation, in contrast to Square reviews which criticize leadership decline or discipline in milder, non‑systemic terms but do not allege cover‑ups or entrenched cronyism.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger surveil: Circle reviews frequently mention formalized monitoring and punitive regimes—mandatory/random drug testing, heavy computer/email monitoring, rigid uniform and device bans, demerit suspension policies and blanket punishments—while Square reviews lack comparable descriptions of systematic surveillance or such consistently punitive enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent in: Square reviews commonly describe steady leadership or turnaround, accessible/responsive teachers and counselors, competitive athletics/rivalries, tangible facility upgrades (new auditorium, turf), and clear alumni college/scholarship successes—patterns presented far more consistently in Square than in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, concrete: This bucket captures reviews that describe explicit, school-run academic rigor and credentialing (large AP/IB offerings, routine in-school ACT/PSAT prep, dual-enrollment/college-credit courses, documented National Merit/college matriculation outcomes). Examples: circle reviewers cite “my kids are in all‑AP,” “IB is the district‑unique pathway,” “daily ACT practice,” “20 hours of college credit,” and high rates of college matriculation — patterns absent or criticized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Includes accounts of frequent physical fights, severe harassment (including self‑harm directives), visible substance abuse, gang/weaponized assaults, and claims that staff or coaches ignored or minimized incidents. Representative evidence: circle reviewers note “fights break out constantly,” “students told me to self harm… nothing was done,” “alcohol and drugs are a real problem,” and coaches/admin who ‘smirked’ or ‘led team out before medics arrived,’ contrasts with square’s relative lack of such severe safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic staf: This bucket covers reports of entrenched favoritism (donor cliques, family-name protection for team selection), nepotism, tenure-protected complacency, staff racism/sexism, bribery/collusion allegations, and leadership that sidelines parent/student concerns. Illustrative lines: circle reviewers allege “a small clique…runs the show,” “teachers are tenured and unconcerned,” “teachers racist against Hispanics,” and “principal takes teachers’ side,” framing governance and equity problems not asserted to the same degree in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: This groups descriptions of distinct non-core academic assets — conservatory-level arts, award‑winning band/choir/theatre, aquatics centers and pools, strong FFA/agriculture, vocational internships/certifications and high‑level athletic facilities — that reviewers say the school offers. Examples: circle cites “one‑of‑a‑kind arts conservatory,” “aquatic center,” “medical assistant certification,” “state‑of‑the‑art technology and auditorium,” and well‑funded arts, whereas square reviews rarely document comparable specialized program breadth/resources.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: This bucket captures reviews emphasizing active PTAs/booster clubs, formal parent outreach (coffee with admin, president meets parents), small classes, long staff tenure, close teacher access, Freshman transition programs and cohesive school pride or family atmosphere. Examples: circle reviewers praise “PTSA and booster club really care,” “smaller class sizes…get to know the teachers,” “Freshman Academy prepared me,” and long‑term community ties — contrasted with square’s more fragmented parental complaints and weaker descriptions of schoolwide cohesion.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe repeated peer-on-peer abuse and targeted discrimination (e.g., 'N word at least 3 times a week', 'tons of bullying', 'mean girl behavior') and allege staff/administrators often ignore, minimize, or retaliate against reporters ('administration was not much help', 'they did NOTHING', 'they let the kid know you told on him'). Clustered examples include racialized discipline, witnessed bullying in front of adults, threats after reporting, and calls for school closure for safety reasons.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: These reviews document logistics and governance breakdowns: lost transcripts and withheld records, billing disputes and even lawsuits, graduation cap/ diploma mishandling, counselor scheduling errors and advice that harms students, slow/nonexistent responses to parent requests, and pandemic-era operational failures ('lost his records', 'billing lawsuit', 'I placed a request for my transcript... still haven't heard', 'district handling of the pandemic has been laughable').
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger instituti: Square reviews more often name structured academic pathways and external partnerships (college credit/dual‑enrollment, AP/IB readiness, college relationships) and cite concrete outcomes ('fantastic school in terms of academics', 'working relationship with the two colleges', dual‑credit/IB pathways) indicating an institutional emphasis on advanced coursework and college preparation that circle reviews less consistently assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater institutio: Many circle reviews allege top‑down resource and cultural bias toward sports—especially football—including statements that 'all money goes to football', preferential treatment or grade leniency for athletes ('giving football players passing grades'), and surname/family-based advantages ('unless you have a certain last name forget getting any help'), framing athletics as prioritized over academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small-sch: These reviews emphasize small classes, close teacher–student relationships, active mentorship and outreach, structured transition/family programs, visible traditions and parent fundraising ('small class size allows each student to be known', 'teachers go above and beyond', 'Open House twice a year', 'PARENTS CLUB is INCREDIBLE')—portraying a tightly knit, personalized school community that square reviews describe far less often.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: This bucket captures reports of concrete safety and conduct problems (assaults, daily harassment, fights, pervasive bullying, drugs, guns) combined with claims that staff or administration either ignore victims, punish victims, or enforce discipline unevenly; examples include "My child was assaulted IN FRONT OF THE 'SECURITY' GUARD... the guard and principal refused to hold the other student accountable," "bullying non-stop and not a thing was done about it," "we saw security take a gun out of a locker," and allegations that victims are punished while perpetrators are not. Entries in this bucket describe real incidents, on-campus/off-campus drug activity, visible weapons or gang-like behavior, and inconsistent or ineffective protective interventions (e.g., police involvement but school inaction, cameras installed yet bullying unaddressed).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: This bucket groups concrete programmatic offerings and documented outcomes—AP/IB, CTE and trades, dual enrollment/college credits, mandatory JROTC or 9th-grade CTE exposure, extensive extracurricular options (band, robotics, clubs), competitive athletics/band achievements, night/Saturday credit recovery—and cited college/scholarship results. Representative examples: "The IB Program and the AP classes offered are excellent... best IB Program in the state," "my son is learning a trade... co-op opportunities," "graduated with 36 college credits," "3-time national championship winning band," and multiple scholarship/elite-college acceptances (Harvard, Gates, Belmont).
candidate_defs.circle entries record more administrativ: This bucket covers accusations that hiring/retention are driven by relationships or internal politics ("Good Ol' Boy system," nepotism), that certain staff (coaches, athletes, families) receive special treatment, and that administrators protect poor performers or retaliate against parents; examples: "a majority of the staff is relative to others," "coaches can do what they want," "teachers sometimes hand out free passes to athletes," and claims tenure/political shields keep ineffective staff in place. Entries here focus on structural personnel practices, opaque hiring/firing, favoritism in discipline or program access, and calls for staff accountability or removal.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more instructional: This bucket groups concrete classroom- and assessment-level failings: claims of systemic grade inflation and tolerated cheating ("Blatant cheating is allowed... cell phones used during tests"), teaching narrowly to standardized tests with pay incentives, untrained or inexperienced instructors ("new teachers out of college who don't know anything," "teacher googling experiments"), and highly inconsistent rigor/homework expectations. It includes both complaints that standards are artificially low (allowing students to pass) and that instruction is uneven or unprepared, with examples like "Grades at Steinbrenner are inflated..." and "Teachers are not effective on the high school level."
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This bucket captures concrete, actionable operational deficits: recurring facility problems (no A/C, sewage smells, mold, disgusting bathrooms, mice), broken or inconsistent communications/attendance systems (lost doctor notes, SchoolMax reliance), chaotic device rollouts, insufficient counseling or special-ed follow-through (unavailable counselors, program cuts), overcrowding/class-size complaints, and funding/classroom shortages. Example snippets: "There is a SEWAGE smell... mold in the music building," "The counselor has been less than helpful... why have a website if you're not going to keep it updated," "they gave iPads with no plan," and "we face shortfalls in funding... need two more classrooms."
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more abundant an: These reviews repeatedly name AP/honors/dual‑credit, early‑college pathways, integrated ACT prep, high SAT/ACT scores and concrete scholarship/college acceptances (e.g., 'AP, accelerated, and dual credit', 'I got a 32 ACT', 'full ride' and 'earned 26–32 college hours'), while square entries mention general course variety but lack comparable lists of advanced tracks or quantified college outcomes.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more frequent and: Many circle reviews document daily fights, in‑class drug use, sexual harassment, death threats and bullying targeted at protected groups — often adding that staff ignored or mishandled reports ('FIGHTS daily', 'did drugs in class', 'staff did NOTHING', 'death threats'), whereas square reviews raise fewer or more isolated safety incidents and more often describe administrative attention to safety.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more small‑school,: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe teachers going above and beyond (staying after school, one‑on‑one help, 'Power Hour' or breakfasts in class) and life‑changing special‑education support ('teachers will meet with him whenever', 'saved their lives'), while square entries less frequently depict this level of individualized, consistent teacher/special‑needs intervention.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pronounced so: Circle comments frequently call out entrenched cliques, wealth/status or athletic favoritism, religious/community exclusion (e.g., 'If you don’t have lots of money... you will not fit', 'Menonite' exclusion), and selective or nepotistic team/admissions behaviors, while square reviews emphasize broader diversity and inclusivity or do not emphasize these exclusionary mechanisms.
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more visible, st: Square reviews more often highlight an involved principal and strong counseling or administrative accommodation (e.g., 'principal was willing to help so my oldest could graduate', 'School counselors are top notch!') and mention formal supports that help graduation or career pathways, whereas circle reviews more often describe administrative invisibility, broken follow‑through, or favoritism in enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures descriptions of routine fights, widespread bullying, on-campus substance use, teen pregnancy, gang/robbery incidents, locked restrooms/denied lunches, frequent in-school phone searches, and students allowed to walk off campus — often with claims that discipline is ineffective or mishandled (e.g., “Bullying is a huge problem,” “Kids are high and drunk in school regularly,” “There were a few fights... we are not allowed to use the restroom during instructional times”). These are concrete safety/behavior incidents and front-line disciplinary practices that circle reviewers report far more often than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket covers concrete program and outcome claims such as extensive AP/IB offerings, freshman engineering, high AP/IB participation, explicit test scores and college admits (e.g., “took many AP classes and scored a 34 on his ACT,” “accepted to Ivy league”), high college-matriculation rates and scholarship totals, and explicit statements of college readiness — features circle reviewers cite more frequently than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater parental/c: This groups real-world community dynamics described by reviewers: multi-child/K–12 enrollment continuity, active PTO/Parent Council work, visible parental volunteers, local pride and retention (“proud mother of three... my youngest are still attending”), bilingual parent concerns, and repeated endorsements or parental recommendations — concrete signs of stronger parent/community engagement and retention reported in circle reviews versus square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures systemic governance and personnel issues: allegations of hiring uncredentialed or problematic teachers, high leadership turnover, arbitrary firings, nepotism and favoritism in discipline/scholarships, administrative secrecy, union/board collusion, and calls for investigations or governance takeover (e.g., “they hire uncredentialed former students,” “fired a great teacher just because they didn't like him,” “the corruption and flaws outweigh the progression”). These are governance/staffing practices and misconduct allegations that circle reviewers report much more often than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader extracur: This bucket collects concrete descriptions of program breadth and priorities: large theatrical/music programs, state-championship athletics, extensive FFA/vocational offerings, community internships, JROTC and many clubs, plus explicit complaints that athletics sometimes get prioritized or funded at the expense of academics (e.g., “they spend millions on athletics but still don't win,” “convert the school into an athletic complex… give little funding to AP program”). Circle reviewers describe larger/more varied extracurricular and vocational activity and related resource-allocation debates far more than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These entries describe concrete, institution-level academic offerings and outcomes—AP and IB course growth, large AP catalogs, dual‑enrollment/running‑start and early‑college credit, career/technical academies, high AP pass/ACT scores, and named college matriculations—whereas square reviews rarely cite comparable program breadth or measurable outcomes (examples: “running start…graduate from high school and college at the same time,” “about 20 AP classes,” “near‑perfect ACT 35,” and detailed college acceptances vs. square’s lack of outcome metrics).
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: Circle reviews repeatedly name extensive non‑academic programs and how money/priority is directed to them—arts majors, commercial art/architectural drafting, nationally ranked marching band, 13 career academies, booster support and athletics breadth—while square reviews do not document comparable program variety; this bucket also captures claims about how funds/facilities are allocated (e.g., athletics grants vs. underfunded arts) such as “the athletic department got $250K for new bleachers while jazz band equipment was deemed a ‘splurge’.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more visible, en: Many circle reviews report administrators who are accessible, newly placed by the district, or actively trying to turn the school around (principal who 'knows all the students', district‑installed principal, ‘new administration is a positive improvement’), whereas square reviews more often emphasize unresponsive or ineffective administration without the same cluster of visible improvement actions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups reports of pervasive peer misconduct and safety failures—chronic bullying ignored by staff, in‑class fights and student‑run disorder, theft from lockers/backpacks, widespread drug use, hazing, and claims that security/discipline are ineffective or unevenly enforced—whereas square reviews provide fewer examples of these systemic safety failures (examples: 'rampant, constant and pervasive bullying', 'drivers hopping curbs at speed', 'theft is a major issue', 'SEVERE drug problem').
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater gaps and f: Circle reviews more often describe concrete breakdowns in supports (IEP mishandling, special education intake failures, unqualified/absent counselors, lost attendance/doctor notes, transfer credit problems, poor identification of learning differences), while square reviews seldom provide comparable, detailed accounts of those systemic support failures (examples: 'IEP area handled very poorly', 'counselor ignored my daughter and lost her doctor's note', 'transfer of credits problems').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket captures concrete safety and behavior failures described in reviews: circle entries repeatedly allege daily fights, gang activity, rampant vaping/drug use, sexual assault/harassment, and bullying that staff/administration tolerate or ignore (examples: “Fights on campus almost daily… Vaping is rampant,” “Bullying was out of control,” “Sexual assault & harassment was more common…”). By contrast square entries rarely describe such systemic safety breakdowns and often note discipline is addressed or is a lesser concern.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket groups school-level academic strength signals: square entries emphasize AP/IB/honors availability, measurable test results and college placements (e.g., “AP offerings good…students have gone to MIT, Duke, Yale,” “CCRPI score up by over 10 points”), while many circle entries explicitly warn of poor college prep, low proficiency, or lack of AP offerings (e.g., “Students are not well prepared for college,” “less than 50% proficient”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more specialized v: This bucket covers concrete program and facility offerings: circle reviews list magnet majors and career academies, strong CTE/vocational certificates, many clubs/arts and athletic championships, internship/senior projects, and tangible investments like 1:1 iPads, new stadiums, labs and tech pushes (examples: “Advanced Technologies Academy…majors like Engineering,” “every student gets an ipad,” “award winning Math program,” “commercial baking…certification courses”). Square reviews lack or mention fewer of these specific specialized program/facility claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects concrete operational and governance failures: circle reviewers cite lost transcripts, repeatedly changed schedules, unresponsive principals/secretaries, inspection-driven performative fixes, accusations of nepotism/board politicization and profiteering (examples: “They 'lost' my transcript,” “schedule was changed 4 different times,” “blatant nepotism, palm greasing,” “administration and board members are becoming rich at families expense”). Square entries generally report more organized communication and fewer governance-corruption allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger small‑: This bucket groups cultural/community features beyond programs: circle reviews frequently describe deep local pride, multi‑generation enrollment, faith-based mission and spiritual programming, high parental/alumni involvement and game-day fan support (examples: “small town atmosphere…multiple generations,” “faith oriented mission,” “when it's game time…the whole town comes”). Square entries portray less of this tight familial/faith culture or emphasize different community dynamics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader/higher‑per: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and measurable outcomes at circle schools — e.g., extensive AP/honors and CTE offerings, off‑campus college credit, rising API/CST/ACT scores, scholarships and alumni university placements (Harvard, UW‑Madison), and awards for improved freshman on‑track rates — whereas square reviews more often highlight systemic academic failure or limited AP access.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews repeatedly praise teachers and counselors as passionate, well‑educated, and helpful with college prep (examples: 'incredible — so passionate, well‑educated, caring', 'college prep was excellent'), while circle reviews more often contain claims of pervasive teacher disengagement, slow grading, refusal to accept make‑up work, or scarce caring teachers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent admi: Many circle reviews document concrete logistical failures — misplaced IDs, tuition/billing mistakes, scheduling/placement errors, nonresponsive email communication, rude receptionists, and other procedural mishaps — contrasting with square reviews that rarely list that cluster of distinct operational errors.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: Square reviews contain repeated accounts of unresolved bullying, homophobic/racial mockery, ongoing fights, drug problems and students 'getting away with it' or administrators not adequately addressing sexual harassment, whereas circle reviews are more likely to describe either safer day‑to‑day environments or administrative intervention (or different safety patterns).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize community, miss: Circle reviews frequently foreground local identity and institutional mission — small student‑to‑teacher ratios, faith‑based or single‑gender missions, heavy parental/alumni booster engagement, material supports, and standout programs (mariachi, JROTC, FFA, robust clubs and arts) — while square reviews focus more on internal programmatic issues and less on that tight‑knit community/mission profile.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: These entries emphasize formal advanced pathways (AP, IB, academies), dual-enrollment/college-credit opportunities, and concrete college/scholarship outcomes (e.g., “more than twenty AP and honors courses,” “junior/senior campus allowing AP in junior high,” “class of 2013…over $9,000,000 in scholarships,” and claims of 98–100% college-going). By contrast square entries lack broad AP/IB depth or report poor preparation and lower test/scholarship outcomes, so content in this bucket signals that the school provides extensive, high‑level academic pathways and measurable postsecondary success relative to square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more accessible, i: These entries describe routine one‑on‑one attention and wraparound supports (teachers available before/after school, morning labs, dozens of teachers opening rooms for tutoring, counselors coordinating supports), and better parent outreach (frequent emails/calls); e.g., “teachers have always made themselves available…before school, after school,” “lab in the morning…,” and “administrators, teachers and counselors who really go out of their way to CARE.” Square entries more often describe unresponsiveness, poor teacher follow‑through, and lack of help, so inclusion here means the reviews portray consistently reachable, individualized staff support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Entries in this bucket document leadership instability, nepotism, alleged cover‑ups, punitive coercion of staff/parents, and broken promises (e.g., multiple principals in short time, “they hire coaches…based on who they know,” “administration lies,” requests to remove specific vice principals, and reports that complaints are 'swept under the rug'). Square entries rarely make these governance/cover‑up claims; content placed here signals systemic management problems and politicized or dishonest decision‑making rather than isolated instructional critiques.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent seve: These entries recount recurring violent disruptions, weapons/drug incidents, sexual assaults, and heavy security measures (daily/weekly fights, knives/drugs on campus, metal detectors, monthly lockdowns), e.g., “fights all of the time!”, “students bringing knives drugs,” and “we have to go through the metal detectors every morning.” Circle entries more often describe feeling safe or isolated incidents; membership in this bucket means reviewers portray ongoing, acute student-safety crises and consequential security protocols that square emphasizes more than circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater facilities: This bucket groups claims of superior or expanding physical assets and program resources—award‑winning drama/choir, new medical labs, green/sustainable buildings, 1:1 laptop programs, abroad trips, strong extracurricular menus—and notes funding mechanisms (tuition, parent fundraising) that support them (e.g., “1st green school,” “added school buses…new medical lab,” “drama trips to Broadway,” and “parents pay $7,000+ / fundraising relays”). Square entries more often describe resource scarcity, overcrowding, or supply shortfalls, so inclusion here signals a resource‑rich/expanded extracurricular environment tied to different funding than square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger and mor: Circle reviews repeatedly name specific, high‑level programs and measurable outcomes (AP/IB, STEM academy, dual‑enrollment, vocational trades, ROTC, clear scholarship totals and college matriculation) and document scheduled academic supports tied to college/career (buses to college fairs, laptop programs, resource centers). Square reviews rarely list that programmatic detail or quantified outcomes, instead offering only general remarks about academics or a few AP classes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain many concrete safety incidents and negative student behaviors—drug busts and hospitalizations, stabbings and expulsions for weapons, repeated violent fights, student‑on‑student sexual misconduct, targeted hate crimes, and sexualized vandalism of girls’ locker rooms—whereas square reviews do not offer comparable accounts of such severe or recurrent safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries discuss student support s: Circle reviewers provide detailed operational descriptions of counseling and special‑needs services (overloaded counselors, missed counseling appointments, 504/IEP mishandling, loss of school psychologist) and also cite concrete supports (math/English resource centers, scheduled tutoring days, college‑prep logistics); square reviews rarely discuss these support‑service operations in such depth.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege greater administra: Circle reviews more often accuse leaders of protecting insiders or athletes, failing to report or covering up staff misconduct (sexual relationships with students), breaking trust (nepotism, scapegoating, threatening CPS), and chronic turnover or school‑board interference, whereas square reviews seldom present this pattern of governance opacity or alleged malfeasance.
candidate_defs.circle entries include more concrete fac: Circle reviewers frequently describe tangible building and operational conditions—central air vs broken AC during tests, recent renovations or new science wings, mold or mice, bus/tardy policies, changes to school hours, withheld report cards for unpaid lunch debt—while square reviews rarely provide the same level of concrete facility/operational reporting.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete, recurring safety incidents inside and around the school—explicit gang affiliation, daily physical fights, drug use, theft, bomb-threats and even allegations of predators—e.g. “My son was bullied by gang members EVERY DAY,” “more like a combat zone,” “majority of the students here are gang affiliated,” and reports of theft and bomb threats; square entries by contrast either deny pervasive violence or describe only occasional incidents and situational fear (e.g. “there are fights but none violent” or isolated monthly incidents).
candidate_defs.circle entries present more concrete aca: These reviews cite measurable academic outcomes and named program structures—SAT/ACT averages, percent enrolling in postsecondary education, AP/IB course lists, state-recognition and National‑level matriculation—e.g. “Check their school profile…SAT/ACT scores,” “All students take the ACT…97% enter post‑secondary,” and repeated IB/AP references; square entries typically praise teachers or describe honors tracks but lack comparable objective performance data or program-level outcome statistics.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher-: These reviews enumerate extensive programs and capital investments—state‑winning athletic teams, acclaimed marching band, vocational academies/industry certifications, 1:1 device rollouts and new/LEED buildings—e.g. “state‑winning teams,” “band…one of the best,” “STA students are all issued laptops,” and “new LEED‑platinum facility,” whereas square reviews rarely list comparable breadth/depth of program offerings or recent capital upgrades.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: These reviews describe operational and governance problems—nepotistic hires, award/recognition bias toward teachers’ children, athletic favoritism, arbitrary/harsh discipline, suppression of dissent and secrecy—e.g. “more than 90 percent [Student of the Year winners] are teacher’s children,” “17+ teachers left…because of the nepotism,” “if you play football you can do anything,” and “principle makes up ridiculous rules daily,” while square entries seldom level the same systemic favoritism/nepotism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, in: These reviews document routine teacher outreach, after‑school tutoring/study tables, small-class relationships, proactive counselors and explicit special‑needs or inclusion programs—e.g. “Some teachers will stay after school…they give extra credit,” “they provide after school study table and one‑on‑one tutoring,” “twice as many programs for aiding students with learning disabilities,” and “teacher parent communication has always been timely”; square entries more often describe uneven teacher availability, poor counseling, or lack of structured remediation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe, recur: This bucket captures reports of concrete safety crises in circle schools — shootings at games, bomb and shootout threats, gang fights, frequent physical assaults, fire‑alarm pulling, students threatening or attacking teachers, and allegations of administration protecting perpetrators (e.g., assistant principals ignoring gang activity or alleged cover‑ups of sexual misconduct). These are recurring, operational safety failures described in multiple circle reviews and are not present (or are much less frequent) in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more formalized: This groups circle reviews that list concrete programmatic capacity: branded Scholars/STEM pathways, multi‑year arts magnets with professional instruction, many APs/dual‑enrollment offerings, dedicated college‑counseling staff (e.g., 4 full‑time counselors, campus visits), academy/career pathways, structured grade‑recovery (8th‑period/Friday), and 1:1 tech rollouts. These are specific institutional programs and supports consistently described as present at circle schools but missing or less developed in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more administrat: This bucket covers square reviews that emphasize office apathy, admission/application nonresponse, parents being treated as outsiders or shut down, politicized district/board dysfunction, and leaders who deflect responsibility (e.g., 'the office does not care' or 'superintendent doesn't respond'). These are managerial and communication failures between school leadership and families that appear more often in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger small‑: This groups circle reviews describing tight-knit, small‑school culture, multi‑year parent volunteers and foundations soliciting donations, engaged/principal‑level visibility, robust alumni networks, local volunteer partnerships (e.g., Master Gardener garden), and parents shaping residential choices to preserve bus routes — concrete community‑integration features that square reviews do not report as frequently.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: This bucket includes square reviews describing teachers unwilling/unable to teach, lack of differentiation or response to struggling classes, poor guidance/counseling, students graduating unprepared for college, and systemic lack of remediation or academic support. These are classroom‑level and student‑outcome deficiencies emphasized in square entries versus the comparatively stronger instructional/support evidence described in many circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report abundant concrete: This bucket groups reviews that list named, operational programs and measurable outcomes at the school — e.g., dual‑enrollment/AA pathways, 40+ hours of college credit, IT certifications, Biomedical/Law/performing‑arts magnets, CTE tracks, auditioned arts ensembles, and concrete AP pass‑rate claims — all described in specific programmatic terms that Square reviews rarely cite.
candidate_defs.square entries report widespread teacher: Reviews in this bucket describe classroom‑level failures: teachers who ‘don’t teach,’ ‘barely engage,’ are abusive or unprofessional, favor students, mishandle testing, or otherwise produce inconsistent instruction and low rigor (examples: 'terribly horrible Algebra teacher,' named ineffective teachers, AP teachers not preparing students), complaints that are far more prominent in Square than Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict a small, family‑li: This bucket captures reports of tight community ties and personalization — small class sizes, staff knowing students by name, ‘like a family’ language, extraordinary parental involvement, lifelong alumni networks, and active parent onboarding or close teacher–family oversight — characteristics repeatedly emphasized in Circle but not in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege systemic administr: Grouped here are reviews that point to district/board level problems (superintendent resignations, ‘very corrupt’ district, board rubber‑stamping, alleged law/policy violations, resource misallocation, cover‑ups, threats to sue), describing governance and administration as the primary institutional breakdown rather than isolated teacher issues; these governance‑level allegations are concentrated in Circle.
candidate_defs.square entries highlight established ins: This bucket contains reviews emphasizing formal, reputation‑level strengths — structured IB/AP/honors tracks, high ACT/college‑placement metrics, named prestigious outcomes (e.g., full‑ride to Stanford, national merit), and a programmatic reputation for college readiness and academic prestige — themes more characteristic of Square reviews than Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: These reviews highlight concrete, school‑level offerings and outcomes that signal advanced academic capacity (AP/IB/biomedical tracks, dual‑credit/running‑start partnerships, PhD‑led summer research, specialized magnet/STEM/CTE certifications) whereas square reviews largely omit or downplay such program depth; examples include circle mentions of ‘variety of AP classes,’ ‘IB program,’ ‘dual credit classes through CMC and CU,’ and ‘Science Summer Camps with PhDs.’
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics/band: Circle reviews repeatedly describe mandatory sports, high‑level athletic/band success, institutional prioritization of athletes, and even abusive coaching or athletic favoritism (e.g., ‘numerous state titles,’ ‘mandatory sports after‑school,’ ‘the football program gets all the attention,’ and complaints that ‘football players get out of trouble easier’), while square reviews do not portray this systematic athlete‑first prioritization.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: Many circle reviews recount concrete safety problems and unresolved harm — fights, stabbings, drugs, sustained peer or staff bullying, misgendering/transphobia, and allegations of inadequate response to sexual assault or threats — for example ‘I got shanked at this school,’ ‘bullying is tolerated,’ and ‘students doing drugs,’ whereas square entries rarely document such widespread safety or violence claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: Circle reviews contain multiple operational and governance complaints such as nonresponsive principals, arbitrary punishments, selective policy enforcement, nepotistic hiring, transcript/scheduling/registration errors, withheld records or refunds, and fundraising/alumni solicitation concerns (e.g., ‘principal is very rude and does not return phone calls,’ ‘transcript doesn’t show passed class,’ and ‘they would have withheld his records’), while square reviews provide fewer or different administration‑failure narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray stronger small‑sc: These reviews emphasize one‑on‑one teacher availability, low class sizes, advisory/after‑school tutoring mandates, community internships/volunteer placements, formal ELL or alternative‑education links, on‑campus clinics and active PTA/alumni engagement (examples: ‘students are known by name,’ ‘teachers required to stay for tutoring until 3:15,’ ‘internships at Botanical Garden/Civil Court House,’ and ‘separate ELL program’), whereas square reviews less often describe consistent, structured personalized supports or tight community embedding.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, broader, a: These reviews describe concrete program breadth and success—named IB/AP programs, dual‑enrollment and college partnerships, robust music/performing ensembles, vocational programs (culinary, culinary chefs named), robotics, FFA, and measurable outcomes (100% graduation, Ivy/UC acceptances, students entering UNC/Cornell)—claims that the square reviews do not make or that square characterizes as limited elective/AP offerings. Examples: circle cites IB/AP/dual credit, culinary and robotics programs and explicit college acceptances; square mostly lacks such program detail or reports few electives.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete safety incidents—daily fights, thefts, gang‑related bullying, drug use and overdoses, clusters of suicides and clinical depression, racial harassment and sexualized peer culture—whereas square entries rarely report such pervasive violence or clinical mental‑health harms. Illustrative items: circle mentions 'many frightening instances of drug use, gang‑related bullying, daily fights,' an overdose picked up from school, and a cluster of suicides.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: These items cite administrators as unresponsive, punitive, power‑hungry or opaque (lost credits, expulsions later overturned, data manipulation, refusal to answer parents, misappropriated county money, opaque budgeting, punitive mass detentions, problematic out‑of‑district enforcement), plus calls for governance fixes or school closure—claims that square reviews do not make. Examples: circle accuses principals of refusing phone calls, altering data, expelling students then reversing decisions, and links problems to district mismanagement or budget shortfalls.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize smaller class s: Circle reviews repeatedly describe small graduating cohorts and K–12 intimacy, easy parent‑teacher communication (PowerSchool, MySchoolBucks, prompt emails), regular before/after‑school tutoring, dedicated counselors and named supportive teachers, and strong multigenerational community pride—features square reviews generally do not emphasize. Examples: circle notes 'class size about 15,' teachers who 'know all the students,' daily grade portals, active parental participation, and targeted counseling programs.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews contain repeated classroom‑level accusations—most teachers 'do not teach,' instructors who cannot deliver subject matter, teachers acting like bullies or withholding help, and students left to teach themselves—claims that are more prominent in square than in the circle set. Examples: square statements include 'most teachers do not teach,' 'teacher could not speak the foreign language she was teaching,' and parents reporting staff who 'act like bullies.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: These reviews document concrete safety incidents (frequent fights, gang activity, robberies, hospitalizing assaults, on-campus smoking/substance use) and allege the school or leaders deny or fail to address them (e.g., “A LOT of fights… gang activity,” “ends up in the hospital… nobody helps,” “school refuses to address recent Bully issues!”). This bucket captures reports of unsafe student behavior plus explicit claims that administration tolerates or ignores those threats to student safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader,: These reviews describe high-profile extracurricular strengths and external partnerships — state championships and perennial athletic success, nationally/internationally competitive choirs and theater, expansive club lists, internships/fellowships/dual‑credit partnerships, and specialized vocational shops (e.g., Advanced Environmental Water Academy, automotive shop) — often framed as signature assets (e.g., “record 8 State Championships,” “huge choir… wins top honors,” “intern program at the Franklin Institute”). This bucket groups programmatic, competitive, and experiential offerings that reviewers highlight as distinctive school-level opportunities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These comments point to leadership and governance problems—persistent nonresponse to parents, rude front-office staff, political favoritism and hiring bias, budget/curriculum oversight gaps, high turnover, improper employment verification, and allegations of institutionalized favoritism or retribution (e.g., “They won't return my phone calls,” “Very political… favored for sports,” “no oversight of the budget or curriculum,” “forced resignations”). This bucket is about systemic managerial/governance breakdowns rather than classroom instruction or isolated discipline incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more proactive col: These reviews emphasize concrete college-prep infrastructure and counselor involvement — accessible guidance for ACT/FAFSA/scholarships, an organized IB program, measurable college‑readiness outcomes, and explicit counselor-driven testing/registration support (e.g., “School counselors keep you on path for success… assist with ACT, FAFSA,” “My son is in its IB program and learned a lot”). This bucket groups evidence of institutional, counselor-led supports and formal advanced-academic pathways that reviewers attribute to better postsecondary preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more teacher staff: These reviews describe structural teacher problems (severe understaffing, teachers carrying 6–7 classes per day, teachers reassigned to security/substitute duties), inconsistent or disengaged instruction (boring/fluff classes, inexperienced AP teachers), and teacher misconduct or favoritism/humiliation (public rudeness, boundary breaches, revenge-motivated behavior) — e.g., “severely understaffed… teachers asked to give up prep time,” “teachers are hit or miss… some fantastic, some so bad,” “if a teacher does not like you they will be rude to you in public.” This bucket focuses on classroom staffing, workload, pedagogical quality, and teacher–student boundary issues rather than schoolwide governance or extracurricular offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize religious/spiri: These reviews describe explicit faith structures and spiritual outcomes (masses, Kairos retreats, theology expectations, claims of spiritual growth) that are repeatedly foregrounded as part of the school experience (e.g., “strong, faith‑filled community,” “If you aren’t ‘strong catholic’ the theology classes are hard,” “I have not only grown academically, but spiritually as well”), whereas square reviews contain no comparable faith‑based programming or spiritual outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report named, structured: Circle reviews list concrete programs (IB/AP academies, AVID/PUENTE/Upward Bound/dual enrollment, engineering/health academies, magnet programs) and cite outcome metrics (AP pass rates, college acceptances, graduation/college‑enrollment claims), e.g. “IB and AP program,” “Only 17%... pass AP tests,” and “My daughter has been accepted to her top 3 colleges,” while square reviews rarely provide the same breadth of named pathways or school‑level outcome data.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger individ: Many circle reviews emphasize small class sizes, teachers who go above and beyond, scheduled academic supports, and routine after‑school tutoring (e.g., “Teachers are always ready and willing to help,” “colloquium classes… extra support,” “teachers volunteer on weekends”), whereas square reviews more often discuss general program offerings or isolated teacher helpfulness rather than pervasive, structured individualized support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report nepotism, socioeco: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege biased treatment and resource capture—nepotism, donor/wealth influence, preferential treatment for varsity athletes, and athletics receiving disproportionate funding (e.g., “a lot of nepotism,” “they only want parental involvement from parents who are wealthy,” “varsity players get special treatment… funds them more than any other club”), claims that square reviews do not make with the same frequency or specificity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent in: Square reviews commonly describe reliable leadership, effective problem resolution, and a safer, more orderly climate (e.g., “excellent problem resolution systems,” “Safe environment,” “principal… deals aggressively with any negative situations”), contrasting with many circle reviews that recount inconsistent support, pervasive bullying/violence, and unresolved administrative inaction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These entries emphasize concrete program breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, specialized STEM electives, dual‑enrollment/college credits, internships and vocational tracks) and cite high selective‑college matriculation and measurable results (e.g., 21 college credits at graduation, Ivy/Tier‑1 admits), while square entries lack systematic evidence of those programmatic offerings or outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety,: This groups reports of fights, gang activity, weapons/police involvement, drug/vaping problems, repeated thefts, chronic truancy/roaming halls, overcrowding/mobile classrooms and facility failures (no AC/heat collapses) — problems described as occurring on campus and producing immediate physical/psychological harm, which square entries do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive ind: These entries describe small class sizes, high teacher accessibility (email/phone/open tutorials), after‑school tutoring, targeted interventions for struggling or bullied students, and counseling/mentorship success stories (IEP support successes, students ‘saved’ from dropping out), whereas square entries tend not to describe that consistent, school‑provided individualized outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: This bucket captures complaints about principals abusing power, alleged nepotism, rude or unhelpful registration/office staff, refusal to discipline staff/students, and claims that responsiveness or athletic/club access depends on wealth/connections or residence — governance and equity failures highlighted in circle entries but largely absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive cla: Square entries repeatedly call out teachers not teaching (reading from books, poor lesson quality), failed curricula or assessment practices, teacher immaturity/unprofessional acts, and systematic instructional neglect — substantive classroom‑level failures that square reviewers emphasize more than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety problems inside and around campus (gang formation, frequent fights, lockdowns, off‑campus assaults causing concussion/brain bleed, rampant drugs/alcohol/vaping, regular thefts and truancy) that square reviews do not. Example evidence: “there are fights almost daily,” “the violence… gangs are formed,” “lockdowns every other week,” and an off‑campus assault that caused a concussion and brain bleed.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, concret: These reviews enumerate structured college‑prep and enrichment offerings and named program outcomes (IB, AP, dual enrollment with paid tuition, early college/NAF partnerships, award‑winning arts, nationally ranked teams, flipped‑classroom recognition) whereas square reviews rarely list comparable program breadth. Examples include: “IB Diploma Programme, dual credit, AP…”, “tuition is paid by the school” for concurrent enrollment, “award‑winning newspaper, Gay‑Straight Alliance, Robotics,” and national media coverage for a flipped model.
candidate_defs.circle entries surface special‑education: Many circle reviews make detailed claims about special‑education practice—successful mainstreaming, formal 504 compliance, but also understaffing, withheld IEP information, class removal of special‑needs programming, and recommendations to hire outside counselors—topics square reviews rarely mention. Illustrative lines: “My son has an IEP and Conrad has helped him mainstream,” contrasted with “they honestly don't care… 3 'co‑Ed' teachers for 9th–11th,” and “withholding of information…and deceptive practices in my son’s IEP.”
candidate_defs.circle entries raise governance, enrollm: These reviews call out higher‑level policy and fiscal drivers that shape school condition—school board/principal decline, favoritism tied to donations, boundary exceptions and out‑of‑district enrollment for money, budget cuts leaving facilities deteriorated, and alleged deceptive rebranding—while square reviews seldom discuss these system‑level causes. Examples: “the School Board and principal have begun destroying everything good,” “pander[ing] to the rich families for donations,” “40+% of students from out of district for the money,” and “Failure to pass school budgets leaves the facility in deteriorating condition.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe more active, res: Square reviews more often report principals and teachers who intervene, effective anti‑bully policy or expulsions, accessible guidance/counseling, and a protective family‑style environment—concrete managerial responses that circle reviews usually lack or contradict. Examples: “The Principal is awesome… makes sure that the students are safe,” “guidance department is always there for children,” “effective anti‑bully policy,” and administrators who removed ineffective teachers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and pe: These texts contain far more concrete accounts of violence, drugs, sexual harassment/assaults, gang activity, routine fights, thefts, loitering/unauthorized visitors, ineffective camera/security follow‑up, and campus drug/smoking incidents (e.g., “Fights everyday,” “Lots of drugs,” “Several sexual assaults…with no action,” “bookbag and leather jacket was stolen…camera saw nothing”), whereas square entries rarely describe such systemic safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete ad: Many circle reviews enumerate formal programs and hard metrics — AP participation and national rankings, dual‑enrollment and large transferable college credit totals, CUNY/Hunter pathways, ACT/Scholarship scores, National Merit and honors outcomes (e.g., “entered college with upwards of 40 College Credits,” “Both my kids got above a 31 on the ACT”), while square entries emphasize program changes (IB/standards) or give fewer concrete college‑readiness metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries include more specific acc: Circle texts repeatedly reference IEP/504 processes, outside medical specialists recommending accommodations, counselor responsiveness or failure, diagnosed depression/anxiety tied to bullying, and even clinical advice to withdraw (e.g., “diagnosed with depression and having to be removed,” “specialist and neurologist stated this was necessary,” “psychiatrist…child should no longer attend”), whereas square entries rarely supply this level of concrete special‑education or mental‑health detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive ext: Circle reviews frequently list structured non‑academic offerings and pathways — performing arts support, VPA/IB/magnet academies, Career‑Tech shops, internships with radio/news stations, broad clubs and no‑cut athletics (e.g., “AOC…internships with professional radio stations,” “incredible options…auto tech, carpentry”), while square entries seldom enumerate comparable breadth of arts/CTE/magnet programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit pare: Circle texts contain many allegations and examples of wealthy or connected parents shaping opportunities, donor/nepotistic favoritism, out‑of‑zone athlete advantages, disappearance of student dues, district debt or rejected alumni funds, problematic transportation and opaque communications (e.g., “wealthy and connected parents make sure their kids get everything,” “money paid by students for 'dues' vanishes,” “out of zone kids play on the sports teams”), whereas square entries provide far fewer concrete claims of community capture or financial/operational malfeasance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more advanced acad: These reviews repeatedly name rigorous offerings and concrete outcomes—AP/IB/Cambridge tracks, dual‑credit/college‑in‑the‑classroom, specialized academies (engineering/performing arts), technical centers, high ACT/AP/scholarship figures and alumni admissions—whereas square reviews lack comparable program depth or measurable college metrics (examples: 'college credit from Eastern and Central Washington,' 'ACT 27,' '4 ED into Cornell').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute physica: Circle reviews include explicit, incident‑level safety and health problems—guns/weapons on campus, on‑site drug dealing and overdoses, frequent fights, thefts, expired milk, mice/rodent and pest infestations, and unsanitary facilities—claims that are largely absent from square entries (examples: 'kids who are dealing drugs and overdosing,' 'milks are usually expired,' 'rats and cockroaches').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism/weal: Many circle reviewers allege that opportunities and discipline hinge on family ties, local insider status, or athletic/wealth clout—'good school if you're rich… or very good in sports,' parent‑pressure influencing outcomes, athletics funding prioritized and non‑football programs cut—while square reviews do not emphasize entrenched local favoritism (examples: 'they give preference to kids who grew up here,' 'sports get all the money').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff qualifi: Circle accounts more often allege uncertified or incompetent teachers, widespread unprofessional behavior (gossip, cell‑phone use, lying to parents), teacher bullying/retaliation and high turnover—claims not commonly made in square reviews (examples: 'uncertified teachers... teachers lie to a parent's face... take complaints out on your student!').
