candidate_defs.circle entries report more active, forma: Circle reviews describe concrete administrative policies and day‑to‑day operations—metal‑detector/phone‑scan security, aggressive fundraising drives, schedule structure (many half‑days, seven classes, block‑scheduling debates), explicit policy changes, and on‑site supports (therapists, tutoring, counselors, college information)—whereas square reviews tend to offer broader critiques of culture or staff without as many specific operational or programmatic actions (examples: 'scanner school… public safety takes phones,' 'administration aggressive about contacting parents for fundraising,' 'in‑school therapists and tutoring programs').
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger teacher: Circle reviews frequently highlight in-class teacher dedication, mentoring, and close student support — e.g., “teachers care… willing to go the extra mile,” teachers who ‘help the best they can,’ and statements that teachers ‘work with student and parent to be successful’ — whereas Square reviews more often document disengaged, inconsistent, or absent instruction and high teacher turnover. This bucket captures reports about instructional practice, teacher qualifications/attendance, outreach to families, and individualized student support (examples: named supportive teachers, parent–teacher collaboration, versus Square’s ‘teachers cruise on the internet’ and variable/apathy claims).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle contains many allegations about administration and governance problems — e.g., ‘principal is uninvolved and will NOT return parents’ phone calls,’ ‘horrendous nepotism… one family runs the place,’ refusal to send transcripts and hanging up on callers, hidden athletic handbooks, and claims that administration ‘makes most decisions’ without parent voice — while Square reviews tend to describe more responsive, organized leadership. This bucket groups reports about school leadership behavior, board/decisionmaking transparency, favoritism/nepotism, complaint processes, policy enforcement, and personnel changes (examples: refusal to act on bullying, opaque discipline policies, or board-driven budgeting vs Square’s praise for principals and organized admin).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: Many Circle reviews explicitly list and praise concrete programs and recent facility/ capital investment — e.g., ‘fantastic music program,’ marching band state championships, new Fine Arts Center, strong agricultural/vocational tracks, and requests for new instruments/uniforms — while Square reviews more often note program cuts, poor lunch/bathroom facilities, and requests for modest funding. This bucket covers tangible offerings and building/equipment investments (program breadth/quality, facility renovations, instrumentation, staged capital projects, and stated resource needs).
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger measura: Circle reviews frequently cite concrete academic metrics and pathways — AP/IB/Dual Enrollment classes with 5s, top SAT/ACT placement, 100% graduation claims, U.S. News recognition, large scholarship totals and first‑choice acceptances — whereas Square reviews emphasize weak AP pass rates, declining scores, teacher shortages, or nonselective placement concerns. This bucket captures reports about course rigor, availability of advanced tracks, statewide/national rankings, graduation and college‑placement statistics, and discernible outcome evidence (e.g., ‘percentage of alums who graduate college is triple the national average’ versus Square’s lack of comparable metrics).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize local community: Circle reviews more often foreground small‑town or faith‑based identity, close alumni ties, active parent organizing/PTA efforts, parental satisfaction or multi‑child endorsements, and demographic homogeneity or community pride (examples: ‘safe community… hometown feel,’ ‘treated like family,’ alumni reunions, and tuition-as-investment statements), while Square reviews report more families withdrawing, contested residency/tax tensions, or less cohesive local pride. This bucket groups community‑level attributes around social cohesion, parental activism/withdrawal, religious mission, alumni continuity, and demographic/contextual descriptions of the school’s surroundings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more serious safet: These reviews describe concrete safety events and security practices—e.g., a firearm on campus, regular K‑9 searches and random police sweeps, lockdowns, expulsions, and even law‑enforcement home visits for attendance—that square entries do not recount; falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on criminalized incidents and heavy security enforcement rather than routine classroom safety concerns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more pervasive s: Many circle reviews call out systematic insider advantage and staff wrongdoing—’A LOT of favoritism,’ coaches/athletes protected, teachers talking badly about students, staff physically touching students, and explicit anti‑LGBT/POC discrimination—so content in this bucket documents interpersonal staff abuse, preferential treatment tied to family/athletic connections, or discriminatory punishment.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize formal advanced: Circle reviews frequently cite structured, credentialed programs and results—IB/full‑diploma programs, AP/dual‑enrollment classes, scholarships, strong ACT/SAT/AP results, and alumni college matriculation—so texts in this bucket focus on formal advanced coursework, dual credit, and concrete postsecondary outcomes as defining school features.
candidate_defs.circle entries report explicit administr: These items highlight institutional rules and enforcement practices—automatic fight suspensions, a 12‑week graduation eligibility rule, dress‑code prioritization over instruction, discouraged formal referrals, arbitrary ISS/OSS application, and inconsistent policy enforcement—so belonging here means the review emphasizes how written rules or ad hoc administrative choices (and their uneven application) shape student experience.
candidate_defs.circle entries foreground tangible commu: Reviews in this bucket focus on community ties and material context—active PTOs and multigenerational alumni, faith-based programming and weekly Mass, small‑school family atmosphere or community relocation to attend, plus concrete notes on facilities/technology or operations (1:1 laptops, turf fields, overcrowding, broken computers, late buses, sanitation or funding allocations)—i.e., the school is defined by its community identity and physical/resource realities rather than only by abstract program descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: These reviews describe frequent peer violence and targeted abuse (homophobia, racism, cyber‑bullying, special‑needs harassment, daily fights and gang presence) and say reporting or anti‑bullying programs are ineffective or expose victims (examples: “Homophobia and Racism is common,” “Fights everyday,” “cyber‑bullying is a problem,” and “when it was reported they... expect you to name names”). Square reviews lack these sustained claims of targeted harassment or systemic anti‑bullying failure.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Many circle reviews allege district/board coverups, repeated renewal of ineffective administrators, nepotistic hiring, punitive or opaque discipline policies, and front‑office unresponsiveness (examples: “School board covers for their colleagues. GOOD OLE BOYS CLUB,” “superintendent is out of touch,” and “Absolutely horrid communication coming from the office staff”). Square entries do not make comparable claims about systemic board or principal‑level corruption or chronic parent communication breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete an: Circle reviews enumerate specific programs and outcomes—IB/AP/Dual Credit, CTE pathways, project‑based learning, documented college acceptances, arts majors and industry partnerships, and named research/college credit programs (e.g., SUNY research, St. John's College Advantage, Broadway instructors, state championships)—whereas square reviews rarely list this depth of concrete programmatic or college‑credit detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray higher teacher co: Circle reviewers repeatedly report dedicated, high‑qualification teachers, scheduled in‑school help times and robust out‑of‑class support, small or reasonable class sizes, and strong teacher‑student relationships (examples: “Dedicated teaching staff,” “Every Monday and Thursday... 20 minute break for students to get help,” and “More than 80% of their teaching staff have a Masters”). Square reviews tend to emphasize uneven or ineffective instruction and weaker teacher responsiveness instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater capital in: Circle reviews frequently mention new or renovated buildings, upgraded athletic and arts facilities, first‑rate auditoriums, issued iPads/laptops, and visible infrastructure projects (examples: “new beautiful state of the art facility,” “Students in 9th and tenth grade get an Apple computer,” and multiple renovation/field improvements). Square reviews, by contrast, focus more on underinvestment, maintenance issues, or make no comparable claims of recent major capital upgrades.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader formal aca: This bucket captures concrete programmatic scope and outcomes (AP/IB/honors, dual‑enrollment, ROTC, career academies, associate‑degree graduates and named college matriculations) that appear much more often in circle reviews—examples include repeated mentions of AP/honors loads, dual‑enrollment and associate‑degree outcomes, ROTC/magnet/medical academies, and explicit college-readiness metrics—while square reviews typically lack these sustained, school‑level program descriptions or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This groups claims about governance and operations: circle reviews frequently name lost transcripts and records, unresponsive principals and counselors, opaque fundraising/bingo money, misallocated capital vs. staff spending, tolerated nepotism/cronyism and ad‑hoc policy enforcement, whereas square reviews rarely raise those specific administrative transparency, recordkeeping, or nepotism problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket covers repeated, concrete safety and climate failures in circle reviews—daily non‑physical bullying left unaddressed, fights/drug incidents/vaping/overdoses, bomb threats and slow responses, clique/exclusionary cultures, and allegations of racial bias or punitive discipline—whereas square reviews more often omit or minimize pervasive safety/discipline crises.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: This bucket groups teacher‑level instructional and professional attributes that are emphasized more in square reviews (dedicated, accessible teachers, smaller classes, tutoring/Saturday school, counselor help) contrasted with circle reviews' frequent reports of absent/neglectful instruction, high turnover, inexperienced or unprofessional teachers, and mid‑term departures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer facilitie: This captures concrete physical and extracurricular resource signals found more often in circle reviews—recent renovations, pervasive classroom technology, large endowments/alumni funding, standout arts/band/theater programs and state athletic championships, boarding/dorm facilities or FFA success, and explicit high parental/enrollment demand—features that square reviews seldom document.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete pr: These reviews give concrete, program-level evidence (named AP/STEM teachers; 1:1 laptops; new wellness center; sustained band/ROTC excellence; vocational/shop and senior‑project pathways) and measurable student outcomes (full scholarships, 100% college‑bound claims, alumni college success) that square reviews do not provide. Example items: 'new funding that has brought in a wellness center,' 'At Freedom every student gets a laptop,' 'I was blessed to receive the Arrupe Jesuit Full Collegiate Scholarship,' and repeated praise of AP/honors and band programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe, speci: These reviews document concrete safety incidents and allegations and often claim counseling or administration failed to remediate them (e.g., sexual assaults, physical assaults on teachers/students, repeated threats, and counselors who 'shrug it off'), whereas square reviews rarely describe this cluster of severe safety failures. Example items: 'many sexual assaults at this school that is not taken care of,' 'From 2017-2019 there has been numerous safety threats,' and 'There is a lot of bullying though, and the counselors seem to shrug it off.'
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more favoritism, n: These reviews accuse school actors of privileging insiders—by admissions, athletics, grade changes, or scholarships—and describe nepotistic hiring and resource skewing, claims that are largely absent from square reviews. Example items: 'under the "Who You Know Policy" for the intake process,' 'parents who give the most or the alumni families are the ones who get catered to,' 'scholarships go to well connected rich insiders,' and staff-parent conflicts of interest.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive sta: Square reviews more often describe systemic instructional problems (lazy/unhelpful staff, students unprepared for college, poor teacher quality) and lack of student supports (insufficient counseling/mental‑health services, reactive rather than preventative responses), in contrast to circle reviews that more often document concrete supports or stronger instructional programs. Example items: 'absolutely no support for students with mental health issues,' 'Kids are not prepared for college,' 'staff is lazy and rude,' and 'Our counseling is awful… Students begged for a mental health counselor.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger organiz: These reviews repeatedly note structured parent and alumni involvement (active alumni association, Band of Brothers mentoring, class advisors and committee leadership, frequent volunteerism) and tie those networks to student supports—features square reviews rarely emphasize. Example items: 'The Alumni Association is stronger and more involved than most universities,' 'The Band of Brothers process... assigning every incoming student a mentor,' and 'I was very involved with my kids... being a Class Advisor and part of a few Committees.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent unaddressed bullying, daily fights, bathroom assaults, on‑campus drug/alcohol/vaping use, hate‑symbol vandalism, and sexual harassment (e.g., “40+ fights last year,” “Drugs in this school huge issue!!!!”, “swastikas carved on the desks”, and reports of bathroom beatings), whereas square entries do not contain the same breadth or frequency of these safety and substance allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviews repeatedly accuse leaders and nonteaching staff of active wrongdoing or bias—grade tampering, covering up incidents, nepotism, preferential treatment of athletes/wealthy students, staff bullying and discriminatory rules about grooming or LGBT students, and removing negative reviews—claims that are generally absent or far less frequent in the square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete adv: Many circle reviews include numeric program evidence and measured outcomes (AP/IB course counts and pass‑rate critiques, college placement/sholarship figures, documented college credit or early admission, Blue Ribbon recognition and quantified enrollment figures like 'With over 25 AP courses' or '99‑100% college placement'), while square reviews typically lack that level of concrete program/outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more tangible faci: Circle reviewers note specific physical and operational deficits—overcrowded classes (e.g., class sizes jumping to ~40), missing stall doors and insufficient cafeteria seating, obsolete textbooks/computers, locked restrooms, accessibility problems, late buses and other service failures—problems that square reviews do not emphasize to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger locali: Circle reviews more often describe a tight, multigenerational, faith‑oriented or neighborhood community with active parental/alumni involvement, families relocating to attend, long‑term retention and granular local pride (e.g., 'very close knit community', alumni returning, 'built our home in the Lone Peak boundaries', explicit Christian identity), whereas square reviews rarely foreground that same depth of local family/alumni culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers of circle schools recount concrete safety failures (bomb threats, sexual harassment, explicit violent bullying, drug use/arrests, gun/shooting signs) and examples of adults/agencies worsening or ignoring problems (bus driver/passive staff, police directing a harmed student away from a counselor, counselors siding with aggressors, self‑harm handled by a 'sign a contract'). These are explicit behavioral/safety incidents and documented non‑responses that distinguish circle reviews from square ones that rarely report comparable severe safety events.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater athletics/: This bucket captures reviewers who describe athletics- or extracurricular-dominated cultures, state‑level team success, broad activity breadth (band, theater, many clubs), booster/town support, and visible capital/facility upgrades (new fields, pools, media/math buildings, smart‑classroom tech)—e.g. 'BEST TEAMS IN THE STATE!!!', strong music program and new facilities, lacrosse field and pool—which contrast with square reviews that do not foreground that scale of athletics/extracurricular prominence.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: This bucket groups raw items alleging problematic leadership practices at circle schools—nepotistic hiring and protectionism, tenure limiting accountability, favoritism in athletics or grading, corrupt evaluation practices, rigid policy‑first discipline (zero tolerance or petty enforcement), and broken promises or refused remedies (refused class moves, unfulfilled interventions) —distinct from square reviews that lack these specific corruption/favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ad: This bucket covers circle reviews that name specific college‑prep structures and outcomes (multiple APs, 10 APs taken with 31 college credits, Running Start/Sno‑Isle/dual‑enrollment partnerships, Early College programs, very low dropout and high matriculation rates, explicit dual‑credit agreements) — reporting tangible course pathways and measurable postsecondary results that square reviews often do not provide.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: This bucket groups raw items where square reviewers emphasize steady adult support and outreach—helpful/knowledgeable guidance counselors, caring and motivating teachers, responsive principals (regular emails, phone calls, online grade access like Pinnacle), and effective parent‑school communication—contrasting with circle reviews that more often report teacher neglect, inconsistency, or broken follow‑through.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent physical fights, gangs, assaults, daily bullying, racial slurs and unchecked violent behavior with staff failing to act (e.g., “kids are getting assaulted every single day,” “vicious acts of physical violence go unchecked,” “there's gangs, and fights,” “WAY TO MUCH BULLYING…”), whereas square reviews contain few or no comparable accounts of ongoing physical safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete, f: Many circle reviews enumerate structured offerings and tracked outcomes — IB/AP access, medical/vocational magnets, robotics/STEM teams, scholarship/graduation metrics and college matriculation examples (e.g., “IB Program,” “AP/Honors…98% matriculate,” “nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships,” “I am attending Stanford now”), while square reviews rarely provide the same level of named programs or documented outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers allege nepotism and preferential treatment (e.g., “it’s all about who you are and who your dad is,” athletes protected), political protection of coaches, punitive/deferential discipline (dean retaliation, inconsistent suspensions), administrators weaponizing parent conversations or silencing dissent — claims that appear far less or not at all in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: Circle reviews emphasize large spectator sports culture, competitive/award-winning teams and a wide extracurricular menu (e.g., “football is big…thousands show up,” “Soccer regional champs…Baseball winning regionals,” “award winning band, chorus, robotics, plethora of clubs”), whereas square reviews seldom describe that same scale or breadth of extracurricular/athletic prominence.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger arts/musi: Square reviews more often highlight exceptional arts and music programs, supportive counselors/principals and alumni/community pride (e.g., “The Arts and Music programs are second to none,” “a really supportive principal,” alumni saying students thrive in college), patterns that are emphasized more in square than in the circle sample.
candidate_defs.Circle entries emphasize a faith-based p: These reviews describe explicit Catholic/religious instruction, tuition-based enrollment, and faith-integrated formation as central features (e.g., “I love the religion history…,” “sending our daughter to a Catholic high school,” “monthly tuition is reasonable”), whereas square reviews describe a public/ISD context and do not frame the school around tuition or religious curriculum.
candidate_defs.Circle entries foreground school culture: Circle reviews repeatedly cite mascots, school chants/traditions, robust arts opportunities, and multi-generation/familial belonging—examples include ‘Solid as a Rock’, numerous arts- and theatre-success anecdotes, and ‘if you say you are from Edgewood, they immediately begin to treat you like family’—while square reviews mention theatre or boosters only incidentally and lack this woven cultural identity.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe organized turnar: Circle reviews name schoolwide improvement programs and tracked progress (e.g., ‘turnaround school for two years and it is making great progress’), provide specific student turnaround anecdotes and college-readiness outcomes (‘failed every class… now I'm passing every class’; ‘well prepared for his college experience’), and depict consistently caring teachers, whereas square reviews lack descriptions of organized improvement efforts and report mixed or inconsistent staff support.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more exclusionary: Several circle reviews allege nepotistic/clique behavior and socioeconomic stratification ('If your parents are not part of a certain social circle…', 'you're either rich, religious, or you're nobody') and link bullying to dropout risk, while square reviews do not report these patterns of social exclusion or wealth-based status systems.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more problematic f: Circle reviews call out intrusive or harmful administrative communications—specifically an automated/robotic call system that repeatedly contacts households and emergency contacts—an operational family-engagement complaint not present in square reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report broader, higher‑pe: These Circle reviews repeatedly name award‑winning arts, band and athletic teams, magnet/CTE/robotics programs, large club rosters, and concrete alumni placements (e.g., band >300 members, award‑winning robotics, students admitted to Ivy/boarding schools, millions in scholarship offers), whereas Square reviews rarely list comparable program breadth, awards, or long‑term placement evidence.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe sharper within‑s: Circle reviewers frequently report program‑track neglect, cliques, nepotism/family favoritism, and extreme divergence of student outcomes (some thriving in elite tracks while others feel excluded or traumatized), e.g., law‑magnet students treated as second‑class, athletic favoritism, and new‑student exclusion—patterns not emphasized in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries document more concrete ac: Circle texts give specific, operational supports such as free summer ACT prep, universal after‑school help hours, vocational/technical training, dual‑credit/AP inventories, and credit‑recovery/alternative‑school routes (students graduating early or remediating), whereas Square reviews lack comparable, named support programs or structured pathways.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more concrete admi: Circle reviews contain detailed accounts of administrative rules and actions (closed campus, 4x4 block schedule, expulsion threats, conditional admissions), hiring bias or religious‑priority claims, principal misconduct/retaliation, formal complaints and state findings, and legal actions to secure services—specific operational and governance practices less frequently described in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more frequent acco: Square reviews more often sound the alarm about fights, drug/theft/safety fears, sink‑or‑swim cultures with poor instruction, and urgent parent warnings to avoid or leave the school (e.g., 'DO ANYTHING TO AVOID THIS TERRIBLE INSTITUTION', students frightened to attend, parents relocating), a pattern of immediate safety and systemic failure emphasized more in Square than in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews highlight concrete curricula and outcomes at circle schools: AP/IB/honors expansion, longstanding dual‑credit agreements (e.g., 40+ dual‑credit hours with tuition paid), organized ACT prep, and alumni reporting college credits (e.g., 21 college credits on graduation) or superior college readiness. Put simply, circle reviews repeatedly point to formal advanced-course pathways and trackable postsecondary success (high AP scores, college placements, counselor‑led college support) that square reviews do not match.
candidate_defs.circle entries show broader, better‑fund: Circle reviews enumerate a wide, well‑resourced extracurricular ecosystem—award‑winning music and theater, many named sports teams (cross country, track, basketball, football), inclusive open‑access clubs, state championships and visible school spirit—whereas square reviews mention only a few activities or highlight exclusivity. This bucket captures systematic breadth and competitive recognition (well‑funded arts/library, team trophies, widespread student participation) as a distinguishing, material feature of circle schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries reflect more active paren: Multiple circle reviews report strong, organized parent clubs, engaged alumni networks that aid students, close K–12 continuity and ‘family’ atmospheres, plus explicit religious programming (weekly chapels, Bible as a subject), or private‑school style admissions/tuition practices. These concrete community, volunteer, alumni and faith structures—and parents’ willingness to sacrifice (long commutes, turning down moves)—are recurring operational realities in circle schools that square reviews generally lack.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic stude: Square reviews disproportionately describe persistent multi‑year bullying (student‑on‑student and sometimes staff‑perpetrated), fights requiring police, drug incidents, and reviewers’ sense that administrators ‘sit back and watch’ or fail to intervene. This bucket groups material safety/discipline failures and the tangible absence of effective adult intervention as a defining condition of square schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete op: Circle reviews contain many specific operational breakdowns—lost transcripts, guidance counselors misplacing records or missing appointments, confusing block/six‑block schedules, bus/attendance chaos, tenure‑protected underperformance, favoritism/nepotism, and allegations of administration prioritizing image or secrecy—that materially affect students’ progression. These repeated, actionable governance and staffing problems (distinct from general morale or tone) are more frequently and specifically reported in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe recurring physical fights, pervasive bullying, gang activity, off-campus assaults (including concussion/brain-bleed cases), routine substance use/vaping, videos/viral reputation damage, and regular disruption (e.g., “at least 2 fights a month,” “3–5 fights every week,” “Gang violence… Do not ever take your child here”), phenomena that Square reviews rarely claim and instead emphasize relative safety and fewer violent incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews repeatedly allege principals and boards that ignore parent complaints, refuse paperwork or homeschool transcripts, share private files, resist escalation to the board, and run ‘good‑ol’ boy’ hiring/board entrenchment (examples: principal 'will NOT return parents' phone calls', superintendent 'refused to give me transcript', 'admin/board is comprised of the same people'), while Square reviews more often describe visible, engaged principals and transparent turnaround efforts.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staffing inst: Multiple Circle reports name uncertified or out‑of‑field teachers, high turnover, frequent subs/absences, teacher bullying or misconduct (even physical restraint), and favoritism toward athletes or staff relatives ('teachers play favorites', 'most teachers were uncertified', 'they have a turnover of high school teachers'), whereas Square reviews tend to praise committed, certified teachers and stable staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more structured co: Circle reviews frequently list concrete programs and outcomes—dual‑enrollment totals, associate-degree pathways, PhD-led summer research, medical/CTE magnets, internships and industry partnerships, articulated credits (e.g., 'over 50 college credits offered', 'student earned an associates degree', 'PhD to student ratio of 3:20')—claims that Square reviews rarely offer and instead focus on different program mixes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent fr: Square reviews more consistently describe accessible teachers and counselors, clear parent communication, structured after‑school help and honors/AP/arts breadth (examples: 'Teachers are amazing... help when needed', 'School counselors are top notch', 'multiple band and orchestra levels', many AP classes), presenting a safer, better‑resourced everyday instructional environment than most Circle accounts.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, more num: These reviews repeatedly cite program-level offerings and measurable postsecondary gains at circle schools — e.g., IB, AP, dual‑enrollment, free CUNY tuition paths, adjunct‑taught courses, large transferable credit totals and documented college acceptances — whereas square reviews rarely name such pathways or concrete college-credit outcomes and instead offer only general statements about college prep.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Many circle reviews document ongoing fights, weapons, sexual harassment, gangs, bomb threats, systemic bullying and claims that reports are ignored or swept under the rug; square reviews rarely describe these severe safety incidents and instead focus on other problems or isolated behavioral issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: Circle reviewers frequently list award‑winning bands, state‑level athletics, booster involvement, well‑developed vocational/culinary programs and coordinated coach support, while square reviews mention fewer organized, award‑winning extracurriculars and often note program decline or limited offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stricter, more p: Circle reviews repeatedly describe zero‑tolerance rules, punitive demerit systems with no appeals, strict dress/uniform enforcement, denial of basic needs (bathroom access) and frequent minor punishments, whereas square reviews more often describe inconsistent or weak discipline rather than highly formalized punitive regimes.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistentl: Square reviews more often praise accessible teachers, committed administration, timely feedback and strong counseling support, while many circle reviews document administrative instability, turnover, unresponsiveness, favoritism/cronyism, and failures in parent communication or procedural supports (504/IEP, attendance, records).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more specialized a: These reviews describe abundant, named academic tracks and activities (IB, AP, dual‑enrollment/Running Start, AVID, ROTC, biomedical programs, auditioned arts, strong music/orchestra/choir, many clubs and sports) and tie them to concrete outcomes (scholarships, National Merit, Ivy/Selective matriculation, associate degrees). Example evidence: multiple Circle notes of 'IB program,' 'both received major college scholarships,' '100% four‑year college matriculation,' and 'dual enrollment/associate degree' claims — patterns largely absent or unquantified in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews allege frequent on‑campus fights, police presence, drug use/selling, homophobia/racism/sexism, chronic bullying, and claims that administrators 'let bullying and assault slide' or advise victims to 'deal with it.' Illustrative items include 'police are there almost every day,' 'kids coming to school drunk and high and selling drugs,' and 'they WILL NOT help… teach the victim to deal,' which are far more prominent in Circle reviews than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: These reviews document concrete failures of school operations and infrastructure — overcrowded buses and lunchrooms, portable classrooms, missed buses, missing yearbooks/transcripts, broken HVAC and lab hazards, chaotic graduations, and onerous or opaque fees. Representative examples: 'packed buses…get home at 3:30,' 'yearbook you won't get it until the next year,' 'no working AC…rooms reach 95°F,' and detailed lists of mandatory fees — issues repeatedly reported in Circle but not in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more favoritism, c: These reviews call out staff/administrative favoritism (favorites among teachers and admins), parent‑employment advantage, cronyism in student elections, and athletic bias (coaching favoritism, girls’ programs neglected, coaches advantaging athletes for scholarships). Example evidence includes 'assistant principal picks favorites,' 'only way to get child ahead is if parent works there,' 'revote ordered to favor football players,' and repeated calls to 'find a new football coach' — social‑access problems concentrated in Circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe substantially st: These circle reviews list concrete, organized college‑level and career pathways (AP and IB programs, Dual Credit, early‑college/college partnerships, extensive CTE/vocational tracks, industry certifications, measurable college matriculation examples) that square reviews generally lack or dispute (square often notes limited AP/dual options or poor college readiness). Examples: circle lists AP/IB, dual‑enrollment, SUNY/Bucknell partnerships, trades (welding, autobody), and high college placement evidence vs. square’s claims of no AP/IB or weak college prep.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent, p: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe teachers who mentor, provide after‑school help, rapid teacher–parent contact, small‑class individualized placements, and accessible counselors, whereas square reviews more often report teacher disengagement or limited communication. Illustrative evidence: circle mentions instantaneous teacher communication, named teachers doing college outreach, frequent parental access to staff and extensive after‑school help; square more often notes teachers 'hand out paperwork' or fail to respond.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviews contain many concrete allegations of problematic administrative practices—frequent turnover and mass firings, unresponsive or authoritarian office behavior, selective enforcement/nepotism, pushing students through graduation for money, refusal to provide transcripts/records, and grade/credit manipulation—while square reviews seldom describe these systemic administrative failings. Examples include claims of repeated end‑of‑year staff layoffs, refusal to send transcripts, administrators enforcing policies inconsistently, and accusations of manipulating credits to fit district ratings.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews more often describe gangs, daily fights, theft, bomb/gun incidents, widespread bullying, anti‑LGBTQ and racial harassment, teen pregnancy/vulnerabilities and serious threats, whereas square reviews rarely document comparable pervasive safety or identity‑based victimization. Representative items: circle mentions gangs/violence, death threats, frequent fights, anti‑gay culture and systemic racial harassment, and increases in vaping and theft.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize greater extracu: Circle reviewers frequently report a wide array of extracurriculars (strong sports, award‑winning band/cheer, extensive clubs, parent‑run programs, PTSA activism), long family enrollment traditions, and parents volunteering to run programs, whereas square reviews generally do not portray this same breadth or deep multigenerational community engagement. Examples: circle cites state championships, numerous clubs and mission trips, active PTSO/parent volunteers, and multi‑generation alumni attendance, contrasted with square’s narrower extracurricular mentions.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more formalized: These reviews emphasize concrete programmatic rigor — IB programs, numerous AP/honors classes, formal dual‑credit/dual‑enrollment partnerships (e.g., Ivy Tech), transferable college credit and cited alumni college placements and test‑score metrics — whereas square reviews lack such documented advanced‑course pipelines or measurable post‑secondary outcomes (examples: circle mentions IB, AP, dual enrollment and scholarship/college success; square contains no dual‑credit/IB references).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews recount on‑campus drug offers (even in bathrooms), gang presence or shootings, repeated lockdowns, widespread bullying/hazing and students dropping out as a result, often paired with claims that those incidents go unhandled; square reviews include fewer or no comparable accounts of gang/drug incidents and less evidence of unresolved, systemic student violence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviewers frequently document principals/offices who are unreachable or dismissive, punitive policies tied to tuition or missed donations, lost paperwork/attendance/grade errors, residency/fraud complaints and contested district funding priorities (e.g., money funneled to football), while square reviews are less likely to allege this mix of administrative neglect, punitive financial discipline, and record mismanagement.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher incom: Square reviews more often allege unqualified or uncertified teachers, pervasive instructional neglect (movies in class, lack of remediation), large numbers of ineffective staff or substitutes, and students graduating underprepared — in contrast to circle reviews that more frequently describe engaged, credentialed, and student‑supportive teachers.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger commun: Circle reviews highlight active parent and booster involvement, close‑knit/alumnae networks, faith or mission‑based programming, abundant extracurricular arts/STEM facilities (planetarium/observatory, camps, arts dominance), small‑school personalization and visible community pride, whereas square reviews rarely foreground cohesive alumni/parent networks, faith identity, or the same level of specialized campus resources.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, mat: These reviews describe tangible campus and material problems (broken toilets, no air conditioning, filthy restrooms, underfunded arts/library/technology, outdated labs, cafeterias not operating) and funding/classroom shortfalls; examples include “toilets are broken…school is run down with no air,” “Resources for art class are limited to $1.50 per student,” and appeals for more classrooms and fundraising—issues that appear far more often in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger/ broader: Circle reviews frequently name AP/dual‑enrollment, 1:1 device rollouts, conservatory arts, vocational/CTE tracks, block/accelerated schedules and concrete scholarship/college placements (full rides, students attending Harvard/OSU, 26–32 college credits), e.g. “AP classes while in Junior High…dual enrollment,” “Carnegie Hall-worthy music ensembles,” and multiple scholarship claims—program breadth and measurable college outcomes are emphasized more in circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews recount physical violence, gang affiliation, daily fights, pervasive bullying, roaming/skipping, teen pregnancy and security lapses (metal detectors/cameras mentioned but security ineffective), such as “fights every day,” “threatened by students affiliated in the crip gang,” and “half the girls are pregnant,” which are much more prominent in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege nepotistic hiring, staff/administrator misconduct (physical grabbing, boundary violations, misogynistic behavior), unequal enforcement favoring athletes, uncertified principals and top‑down or dictatorial leadership, e.g. “they clearly keep everyman in the family,” “a teacher actually grabbed her,” and “principal didn’t even have his principal’s certificate,” patterns that contrast with square’s fewer governance/favoritism accusations.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, s: Square reviews more often describe accessible guidance/counseling, structured college counseling and working remediation (tutoring, counselor availability), while circle contains many complaints about inadequate college counseling, IEP mishandling, unreliable counselors and slow/ineffective grade/communication processes—examples include square’s “very good counseling department” versus circle’s “There is no staff to help with anything college related” and “Does not follow through with IEPs.”
candidate_defs.circle entries have stronger college‑pre: These reviews describe circle schools as academically rigorous and outcome‑oriented (claims like “prepares students for ANY school,” expanded AP/IB offerings, AP/IB diploma evidence, college‑credit partnerships with UNH/UConn/UHart, Lone Star/Exemplary awards, and concrete alumni/college matriculation anecdotes), whereas square reviews emphasize uneven academics, students pushed out, and fewer concrete college‑outcome examples. Falling into this bucket means reviewers point to higher standards, AP/IB/dual‑enrollment access, measurable test/college success, or explicit claims of superior college readiness in circle but not in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Many circle reviews highlight small class sizes, low student‑teacher ratios, same advisor for four years, teachers who know students by name, strong parent volunteer networks and cohesive ‘family’ communities, while square reviews more often describe large classes, parents needing to fight for fixes, and weaker routine parent‑school cohesion. Content in this bucket centers on sustained one‑on‑one support, advisory continuity, tight community oversight, and explicit examples of local parent involvement reported in circle but not square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Circle reviews frequently allege acute safety and behavioral crises (metal detectors and daily bag checks, frequent lockdowns, robberies, high local suicide rates, repeated physical assaults and bullying, drugs/vaping acknowledged by administration, drug testing and court referrals, and reports of staff‑orchestrated bullying) whereas square reviews rarely detail such acute safety incidents. Items in this bucket are concrete operational or disciplinary crises and legal/punitive escalations that reviewers tie to student safety and wellbeing in circle more than in square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive sta: Square reviews recurrently call out teacher indifference or ‘paycheck’ mentality, inconsistent or poor instructional quality, administrators who are unresponsive or persecuting students, lost paperwork, and governance problems (leadership ghosting, failure to discipline, systemic mismanagement), whereas circle reviews more often describe dedicated teachers or clearer administrative responsiveness. This bucket groups allegations of staffing apathy, high turnover, unequal discipline, nepotism/favoritism, and failures of school governance that are reported more by square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete pr: Circle reviews supply many specifics about programs and facilities—career/technical shops and articulations, medical/magnet programs, named college partnerships and dual‑enrollment, security cameras, first‑rate auditoriums, issued iPads/laptops, renovations, and also explicit budget choices or cuts (flat‑screen TVs, cuts to tech/arts) — while square reviews rarely list that level of concrete program/facility detail. Content in this bucket is about tangible institutional offerings, infrastructure, technology rollouts, and explicit funding or reallocation decisions that reviewers document more in circle than in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe facili: These reviews describe concrete infrastructure and sanitary failures (no air conditioning with students fainting, mice/centipedes/mold, broken faucets, filthy buildings), large capacity overruns and packed lunches (e.g., '2,200 kids in a school that is supposed to only hold 1,500', 'lunch periods are horrible packed'), and neighborhood safety spillovers — contrasts that square entries instead describe renovated, modern, or well‑maintained facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more explicit ad: Many circle reviews list named tracks/programs and outcome metrics (AP/STEM offerings, 'SEA DISC'/'TEAM'/'magnet program', 'dual‑credit/two diplomas', AP pass rates, '22 Million' scholarship totals, and placement at top universities), whereas square reviews rarely provide this same level of structured, measurable college‑prep program detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize extracurricular: Circle reviewers repeatedly tie school identity and social status to activities (strong choir/band, celebrated ROTC/JROTC and football, statewide athletic recognition) and describe exclusionary social hierarchies based on program membership ('Unless you are in Rotc/Jrotc or football, you are nothing'), while square reviews mention extracurriculars more generically or with less status‑based social stratification.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle contains frequent, concrete complaints about leadership and governance — 'administration has made working…unbearable', lost records, threats to call the AG, inconsistent/over‑punitive discipline (automatic suspensions, restricted bathrooms), and staff favoritism/nepotism — in contrast to square entries that more often describe responsive administrators or single isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more organized wra: Circle reviews commonly note explicit support programs and pathways (enrichment centers, praised counseling/IEP services, robust CTE/vocational shops, senior capstones, career academies, measurable CTE awards and dual‑credit opportunities), indicating institutional investment in social supports and alternative postsecondary pathways that square reviews largely do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete accounts of on‑campus danger and peer-on-peer harm that appear disproportionately in circle reviews (e.g., “fights all the time,” weekly bomb‑threats/lockdowns, multiple suicides, on‑campus assaults, drug busts, pervasive bullying and intolerance, racial slurs heard by adults). Inclusion means the review documents repeated safety incidents, physical violence, or enduring unaddressed bullying as a central operational problem rather than a one‑off complaint.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more named speci: This groups circle reviews that enumerate concrete programs and outcomes (IB/STEM academies, AP/STEM tracks, JROTC, dual‑enrollment, recording studio, explicit AP pass‑rate or ACT/SAT metrics, career pathways, alumni college acceptances and scholarships). A review falls here when it reports formal, school‑level programs or quantifiable outcomes (e.g., ‘only 17% pass AP tests’, ‘the only IB in the district’, ‘full scholarship to Howard’) rather than only general statements about quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more resource, fun: This bucket collects circle reports of constrained or mismanaged resources and resulting operational deficits: tuition hikes, forced fundraising/parent donation expectations, pocketed funds allegations, cuts to aides/programs, overcrowding, flooding/mold/poor HVAC, gross bathrooms, and reliance on local levies. Inclusion requires mention of concrete fiscal/physical resource shortfalls or funding practices that materially affect programs or daily operations.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger local/: This groups circle reviews that foreground a school’s small‑town or religious identity, multi‑generational ties, and social hierarchy—e.g., explicit Catholic/all‑boys identity, ‘‘we bleed green/Go Aggies’’, successive family graduates, visible wealth/status signalling, surname‑based favoritism, and exclusion of newcomers. Reviews belong here when they center community identity, faith mission, legacy ties, or social/parental status as defining the school culture and admission/social dynamics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staffing inst: This bucket groups square reviews that focus on personnel and day‑to‑day operational breakdowns: high substitute usage and turnover, teachers described as hostile/incompetent, counselors unhelpful, micromanaging or exclusionary administrators, inconsistent discipline or parental removal incidents. Inclusion requires the review to emphasize unstable or ineffective staffing and school operations (instructional quality, counseling, scheduling, notification systems) as the dominant problem.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures accounts of physical violence, gang activity, riots/lockdowns, on‑campus substance use, sexual harassment, bus assaults, and repeated bullying that reviewers say is ignored or enabled by staff (e.g., “a riot broke out…pepper‑sprayed…numerous fights,” “Alcohol and other substances are taken into and used at school,” “Some of the staff even bully students…they will look the other way,” and multiple reports of repeated bullying left unaddressed). Content in this bucket describes direct, repeated safety threats or staff complicity in student harm rather than isolated misbehavior.
candidate_defs.square entries report more AP/honors/qua: This bucket groups reports that emphasize formal advanced academic pathways, exam performance, and explicit numeric outcomes (e.g., AP scores, graduation rates, ACT averages) — for example Square’s references to strong AP offerings and top AP scores and Circle’s lack of AP data contrasted with Square’s AP/college matriculation claims. Items here are concrete descriptions of honors/AP rigor, measurable test results, and documented college‑preparation achievements (e.g., 'AP Calculus classes…almost the entire class scored 5s,' 'graduation rate is 80%' appears on the other side as a missing feature).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more vocational,: This bucket covers reviews reporting robust career/technical programming, on‑campus college courses, concurrent enrollment, industry certifications, ROTC/CTE shops, and systematic 1:1 technology (e.g., 'nursing, cosmetology, welding, A/V,' 'concurrently enrolled in college, which the school is paying for,' 'provides 1:1 technology to every single student,' 'technology school offering certifications'). These items emphasize applied pathways and credentialing rather than traditional AP/honors routes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: This bucket includes descriptions of unresponsive or retaliatory principals, micromanagement, favoritism/political patronage, alleged cover‑ups, PTA absence or disempowerment, and questionable governance influence (e.g., 'He will use parents private conversation with him against your children,' 'Very political…favored for sports,' 'They also take down negative reviews,' and allegations of religious/congregational control). Content here focuses on leadership, governance, transparency, and accountability failures rather than classroom instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational a: This bucket captures concrete, recurring operational problems and budget/resource shifts such as sudden bus cuts and overcrowded buses, food service strikes, program downsizing or reallocation (e.g., chemistry labs torn down for a weight room), fundraising dependency, abrupt schedule/policy changes, and facility turnover or renovation claims (e.g., 'letter one day before school…ten students can no longer ride the bus,' 'music program down sized due to budget cuts,' 'they spend all their income on marketing'). These items describe unstable day‑to‑day operations and visible reallocations that affect access and program continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more structured ad: These reviews describe concrete, institutionalized academic pathways in circle schools — AP/Honors offerings, dual‑enrollment and college‑credit programs, named magnet tracks and hands‑on vocational programs (auto tech, culinary, biomedical/Allied Health magnet, TRANSTEM/industry academies). Example evidence: multiple circle reviewers cite dual enrollment/college credits, AP/Honors classes, and explicit magnet/vocational offerings, whereas square reviews rarely mention dual credit, detailed magnet tracks, or robust career‑tech provision.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger teacher m: Circle reviewers more often describe caring, highly accessible teachers, formal tutoring/peer‑tutoring and mentoring programs, active alumni/parent involvement, and productive parent–teacher communication (examples: formal peer tutoring program, LINK/freshman mentoring, teachers staying after until 4–5pm, active parent foundations), while square reviews describe weaker or more uneven teacher responsiveness and less sustained parent/community support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: Circle reviews include repeated first‑hand accounts of serious on‑campus safety problems — daily gang bullying, multiple witnessed fights, students bringing drugs, bomb/shooting threats and routine police/security presence — whereas square reviews more often report only minor scuffles or no major violent incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, inc: Circle reviewers frequently cite strict or punitive enforcement (zero‑tolerance suspensions, credit denial, expulsions), inconsistent or preferential discipline (favoritism toward athletes/families, nepotism, collective punishments), and failures on administrative obligations (IEP/504 noncompliance, lost records), describing an enforcement culture that can be both harsh and uneven; square reviews tend not to emphasize this combination of punitive policy plus favoritism to the same degree.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic under: Square reviews more often point to systemic resource problems — overcrowded classes and students 'falling through the cracks,' rundown buildings and broken infrastructure, insufficient textbooks/equipment, low funding and staffing shortages — while many circle reviews instead highlight smaller class sizes, recent facility investment, or better resourcing and technology.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more formal advanc: These reviews emphasize concrete program offerings and outcome metrics (AP/AICE/IB, CTE academies, dual‑enrollment with community college, summer/school credit recovery and stated ACT/college‑readiness scores) and name alumni successes; examples include circle notes of Valencia community college credits, AICE/Cambridge praise, ‘extremely high college and career readiness score,’ and alumni admitted to selective colleges — features that square reviews rarely cite or quantify.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more consistent, p: These reviews name individual teachers, describe routine after‑school/morning labs, mentoring programs, sustained teacher continuity, alumni/ former‑staff return, and family‑like culture (e.g., Link Crew, named beloved teachers, teachers helping at lunch or running clubs), whereas square reviews focus less on named personal bonds and more on variable or impersonal staff behavior.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more student safet: These reviews recount concrete negative student behaviors and safety events — drug use, regular fights, sexual‑assault arrests, bomb threats, students slammed during sports, and quantified student departures — often coupled with claims that administration failed to stop or adequately address them, a pattern largely absent from square reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: These accounts allege protectionism (pay/admissions favoritism, preserving certain teachers or athletes), manipulation of enrollment/funding counts, administrators threatening parents (calling law enforcement or SARB), and punitive or inconsistent discipline (moving students to alternative schools, blanket punishments), distinguishing them from square reviews which rarely allege systemic corruption or deliberate favoritism.
candidate_defs.Square entries report more operational s: Square reviews more often call out capacity shortfalls, overloaded classes, substitute/teacher‑vacancy problems, disorganized front‑office operations, and facility maintenance/food or sanitation complaints — concrete resource and management failures that reviewers tie to weaker instruction and student experience, a cluster less prominent in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures reviews where circle schools are portrayed as having coherent advanced‑academics (AP, IB, honors, dual‑enrollment, vocational pathways), explicit college‑prep systems, and concrete alumni outcomes (acceptances to elite schools, large scholarship totals, high pass rates); examples include claims like “The AP program is excellent,” “IB integration…,” “100% graduation rate,” and reports of millions in merit scholarships and specific college placements, contrasted with square entries that lack sustained program detail or measurable alumni outcomes.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report broader, higher‑qu: This groups entries emphasizing rich, varied student life at circle schools — thriving band/choir/theatre, state/national competitive achievements, many sports, multiple theatres/gyms/auditorium, ASB traditions and large‑scale spirit events — e.g., “marching band… placed nationally,” “three theatre spaces, two gyms, a 640‑seat auditorium,” versus square entries which are often silent or report limited extracurricular strength.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers systemic governance and personnel issues described in circle reviews: allegations of scandals or cover‑ups, arrogant or inaccessible principals, favoritism toward athletes/wealthy parents, mishandling of transfers/credits, failures to implement IEPs/FAPE, and routine non‑responsiveness to parents (e.g., “they have had many scandals… swept under the rug,” “office won't do anything unless you harass them,” and claims of biased discipline).
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more facility, res: Reviews in this bucket document concrete physical and operational problems at circle schools — mold/roaches, no air conditioning, leaking ceilings, chronic overcrowding, missing lunches, fragmented online assignment systems, and unsafe busing/weather policies — e.g., “buildings have mold and roaches,” “over half of the students don't get a lunch,” and calls for a new high school, while square entries more often mention new construction or do not report these deficits.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more frequent stud: This groups accounts of persistent student‑behavior and climate problems at circle schools: daily fights, ignored bullying, exclusionary cliques and athletic dominance, overly punitive or inconsistently enforced discipline (including problematic zero‑tolerance use), and emotional neglect incidents (e.g., “people pick physical fights everyday,” “staff doesn’t deal with bullying,” “suspend these children for anything”), compared with square entries which typically do not document this same level of recurrent safety/peer‑climate breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures concrete incident reports and safety failures appearing disproportionately in circle reviews — e.g., repeated fights (“every other day there is a fight”), on‑campus drug dealing and repetitive drug use, explicit death/threat claims (“I had my life threatened”), car break‑ins, student‑on‑student sexual misconduct, and a reported tobacco/food safety crisis. Items here are about actual safety/crime events and their handling, not tone or sentiment.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, concre: This bucket groups circle reviews that list specific high‑level academic programs and measurable outcomes — e.g., named AP/STEM teachers and organized AP instruction, Dual Enrollment credits, large scholarship/award wins (Gates, Ohio State Scholar), Ivy/elite acceptances and Intel/competition finalists — presenting tangible program breadth and documented postsecondary success absent or unsubstantiated in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize small‑school pe: This captures circle descriptions of intimate scale and active community supports tied to outcomes — e.g., 'one big family' culture, small class sizes and teachers knowing students by name, extensive parent volunteering/PTSA programs, multi‑generation alumni loyalty, and community partnerships (volunteer gardens, feeder rebuilding), which contrast with square reviews that lack those sustained, organized family/alumni participation claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege systemic favoritis: This bucket groups structural equity complaints concentrated in circle reviews — examples include staff/alumni cliques and 'good‑ol‑boy' hiring, preferential treatment of student‑athletes, 'family name' immunity from consequences, cover‑ups by upper admin, and disciplinary double‑standards — i.e., institutionalized favoritism rather than isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: This bucket collects square reviewers' recurring operational and instructional deficits — complaints about many young/inexperienced or unlicensed teachers, weak teaching of study skills, limited course/arts offerings, declining enrollment or mismatched staffing, and special‑education shortcomings — concrete, programmatic, and staffing issues that undermine instruction more often in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more pervasive b: These reviews report concrete safety problems (fights, gang activity, knives/weapons, hospitalizing assaults, on-campus smoking/drug use, metal detectors) and repeatedly allege that administrators minimize or sweep bullying/assaults under the rug; examples include 'constant fighting, and putting up metal detectors,' 'Drugs are running rampant and they try to keep it quiet,' and 'Most accusations are swept under the rug so administrators don't come under fire.'
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete specia: Many Circle reviews list specific, structured programs and outcomes—IB diplomas and guaranteed scholarships, aviation/FAA Part 141 pilot licensure, ROTC/JROTC, career‑technical pathways and academies, AP breadth, dual‑enrollment/college credits and external rankings or scholarships—e.g. 'the IB program... guaranteed the Bright future scholarship,' 'nation's only high school where a student can earn a FAR, Part 141 Private Pilot's license,' and 'students earning over 19 credits of college credits through AP Classes.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain direct allegations of punitive governance and politicized leadership—firing dissenting teachers, nepotism/favoritism tied to donors or church/staff families, systematic suppression of complaints, and leadership resignations—for example, 'Principal fired all the teachers who raised concerns,' 'district suffers from cronyism,' and 'Most accusations are swept under the rug.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more individuali: A large subset of Circle reviews highlight small classes, one‑on‑one teacher attention, active college counseling, hands‑on remediation and high parental/fundraising involvement—statements such as 'The teachers are one on one with the students,' 'The college readiness and counseling program warrants an additional star,' and 'Fathers and mothers clubs are VERY active in fundraising' illustrate this pattern.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic resou: Square reviews more often single out budget-driven harms—cuts to Calculus/AP and advanced classes, staff attrition, overcrowded classrooms, threatened loss of federal funding, and administrators running the school like a business—for example, 'they cut Calculus, AP Probability and Statistics...,' 'class sizes approaching 30,' and 'close to losing federal funding.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic bull: These reviews describe recurrent peer and adult bullying, cyber‑harassment, hate‑crimes and even physical abuse (e.g., “Adults are the worst bullies,” “I was hate crimed multiple times,” video‑documented assault with an alleged principal cover‑up) and frequent on‑campus fights and PTSD reports, together with administrators who ‘did nothing’ or dismissed complaints — contrasts with square entries that emphasize safety, counseling intervention and few serious incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger AP/honors: Many circle reviews name concrete advanced offerings and outcomes — numerous AP/honors classes, career academies with gold‑seal scholarships, vocational arts (culinary, broadcast, fashion), and alumni matriculation to selective universities (UGA, Emory, GA Tech, Ivy admits, ‘100% college bound’) — while square reviews rarely cite comparable program breadth, scholarships or specific college matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews repeatedly highlight teachers and administrators who ‘get to know each child,’ proactive guidance and retention efforts (e.g., counselors who ‘went above and beyond,’ drop‑out prevention intervention, administrators who arranged transportation to ensure graduation), in contrast to circle reports that more often describe dismissive leadership and poor parent‑school communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational/r: Circle reviews document staffing shortages, frequent teacher absenteeism/layoffs, program and teacher cuts, funding shortfalls, overcrowded cafeterias/short lunches, pest/maintenance issues and lost student records (e.g., ‘teachers were often absent,’ ‘110% over capacity,’ ‘rat in the cafeteria,’ ‘we don’t have a lot of money’), whereas square entries rarely describe this cluster of logistic and resourcing breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, par: Circle reviewers allege family‑staff hiring networks, donation‑influenced disciplinary reversals, athlete favoritism and unequal rule enforcement, plus gaming of grades/assessments (e.g., ‘most all employees and teachers are related,’ expelled student reinstated after alumni donations, ‘EVERYTHING IS FOOTBALL RELATED!’, ‘pre‑tests taken repeatedly’ and grade inflation), claims not made in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive bul: This bucket groups reviews describing repeated student‑on‑student bullying, sexual assault reports, racial and LGBTQ+ harassment, theft, serious injuries, threats (shootings/bomb threats), and patterns of staff inaction or victim‑blaming (e.g., 'Bullying is tolerated…administration does nothing,' 'Sexual assault, bullying, and racial bias are rampant,' 'I had to leave…because of the constant bullying,' 'Theft is a major issue') — contrasts with square entries which rarely report systemic sexual/racial abuse or staff‑enabled harassment.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, explic: This bucket captures reviews emphasizing faith integration, Christian/Catholic formation, prayer in school life, single‑sex identity and ‘brotherhood,’ and doctrinal discipline or intolerance (e.g., 'biblical truths and Christian character integrated into ALL aspects,' 'all‑boys…man for others…Jesuit tradition,' 'Leviticus 20:13 in its honor code,' 'teachers…consistently pray over their students'), a programmatic emphasis absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust advanc: This groups mentions of concrete AP/AICE/honors offerings, documented AP placement and graduation/college‑ready statistics, counselor‑driven scholarship access and elite matriculation anecdotes (e.g., 'put my child in AP classes...91% graduation rate,' 'colleges they go onto include MIT, Penn,' 'qualified for the Hope Scholarship… I have them to thank for it,' 'alum became a posse scholar and attends Middlebury'), whereas square reviews more often describe general academic decline or lack of measurable elite outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: This bucket groups reviews noting one‑on‑one teacher time, proactive registration counseling, required/expected parental service, municipal responsiveness, relocation to enroll, and named engaged principals/counselors (e.g., 'a lot of 1-1 student to teacher time,' 'personal, one‑on‑one counseling when registering,' 'we moved here specifically for Timpview,' 'Dr. Dunkley…providing SAT prep classes'), in contrast to square entries which emphasize harder‑to‑reach staff or impersonal administrative problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an athletics‑do: This bucket groups reviews that report sports as a primary institutional priority, athlete preferential treatment, funding skewed to athletics, and simultaneously enumerate broad extracurricular offerings (band, arts, FFA, JROTC, clubs) — examples include 'Football is a huge money maker,' 'athletes get preferential treatment,' 'everything revolves around athletics,' alongside 'arts, drama, music, debate…' and 'almost half of the school is in JROTC'; square entries do not present the same combination of athlete privilege plus broad program inventory.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: These reviews contain repeated concrete safety events and security practices (e.g., two recent drug busts with hospitalization, students bringing a gun, monthly drug-dog/lockdown procedures, frequent fights, hazing, vaping everywhere, social-media glorification of fights) while square reviews rarely describe on-campus violence, lockdowns, or drug enforcement actions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly name governance and operational problems—rude or combative assistant principals, administrators who lie or ignore complaints, board-level religious/nepotistic control, scapegoating, frequent principal/staff turnover, and poor complaint resolution—whereas square reviews tend to describe leadership problems more mildly or focus on different issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: Many circle reviews list named advanced offerings and measurable outcomes (numerous AP and Dual Credit classes, STEAM shift, ECE/dual enrollment, health-technology/hospital partnerships, magnet strands, explicit college acceptances/scholarship claims), while square reviews seldom enumerate comparable structured advanced or magnet programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report wider, better-docu: Circle reviews often enumerate rich extracurricular ecosystems—top-ranked marching band, fully funded arts and athletics, international travel, service trips, many named clubs, leadership/TA roles, and claims that funding supports these programs—whereas square reviews either mention fewer arts/media offerings or focus primarily on athletics with less breadth.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete, op: Circle reviewers give specific accounts of remediation and supports (before/after-school tutoring, free dual‑credit, strong counselors, summer-bridge programs) as well as procedural failures (IEP/504 noncompliance, lost credits, inconsistent counselor availability), while square reviews less often include this level of concrete, student‑level program and compliance detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe facili: These reviews call out concrete building- and service-level failures — roaches, sewage smells, leaking sinks, no hot water or air conditioning, disgusting bathrooms, expired/contaminated food, and aging/obsolete textbooks/computers — details absent or far less frequent in square (examples: 'so many roaches', 'no hot water', 'food is expired', 'textbooks are so old').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews describe daily fights, vaping/drugs, racial harassment, sexual misconduct allegations, severe bullying that caused anxiety/medication or transfers, and staff/administration failing to intervene or even enabling perpetrators (examples: 'fights every single day', '9 girls jump my daughter…the staff did nothing', 'caused her a lot of anxiety…had to go on meds').
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight stronger extrac: Circle reviewers repeatedly emphasize high-performing sports, band/choir/drama achievements, state championships, mascot-driven spirit, multi‑generation alumni engagement and calls to recruit alumni back — concrete program success and community pride that square reviews rarely match (examples: 'more than one hundred state championships', 'Choir and Drama programs are AMAZING', 'I’m proud to be an eagle').
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, f: Square reviews more often point to structured rigour and empirical outcomes (IB/AP programs, high ACT/other test scores, scholarship numbers, IB/college‑prep reputations) as the school's defining strengths, whereas circle reviews are more mixed on these metrics (examples in square: 'IB program...one of the highest testing scores', in contrast to circle's mixed classroom-quality reports).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain repeated, concrete governance complaints (named superintendents to be fired, unpaid/undelivered extracurricular fees, grade changes, refusal to respond to parents, frequent principal/administrator turnover and hiring/firing controversies) that portray systemic mismanagement absent or less explicit in square (examples: 'Superintendent...should be fired', 'band dues...never used', 'administrative communication is absolutely terrible').
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This bucket captures cases where circle reviews report concrete college‑prep programming and outcomes (AP/IB, honors, dual‑enrollment, named external partnerships, internships, students earning college credits or full rides) and classroom rigor (challenging coursework, high standards) that square reviews do not; examples include circle mentions of dual enrollment with Hunter College, IB/AP pathways, 36 college credits at graduation, and ‘better prepared for college’ statements versus square claims of being unprepared for college and low‑intensity classes.  Content belongs here when the school’s academic breadth, external partnerships, and measurable college outcomes are emphasized as contrasts to square’s weaker programing or results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a small‑town/close: This bucket groups circle reviews that describe small‑school intimacy, town traditions, high extracurricular participation/variety (marching band, drama trips, many clubs, robotics, strong arts), and widespread friendly support from teachers, custodial and office staff; illustrative items are ‘small and friendly,’ high marching‑band participation, lists of community events (Pumpkin walk, Albion Fair), and praise for front‑office/cafeteria staff.  Use this label when reviewers emphasize cohesive community ties, strong after‑school offerings, and easily reachable staff as distinguishing features not present in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe explicit faith‑b: This bucket covers circle reviews that report religion integrated into daily schooling (teacher prayer, Bible‑centered curricula, required religious conformity, warnings that disagreeing with Bible principles will cause problems), e.g., statements that the school ‘teaches about God,’ daily prayer by teachers, and ‘Christ‑centered education.’  Flag content here when the school’s religious programming, expectations of religious conformity, or faith‑driven discipline are salient differentiators versus square.
candidate_defs.circle entries document administrative f: This bucket collects circle accounts alleging systemic governance problems tied to favoritism: district hiring of relatives, small cliques of donors/administrators running decisions, protection of athletes/’good old boy’ students (teachers punished for grading them down), covert information sharing, or punitive/secret readmission rules — e.g., claims of district nepotism, donor cliques, and contracts not renewed after disciplining favored pupils.  Use this when reviews point to structural governance bias, insider protection, or opaque administrative control as a defining school characteristic distinct from square.
