candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: This bucket contains square reviews that describe low teacher engagement or poor instruction (teachers ‘don’t teach’, grade inflation or easy work), leaders who ignore parent concerns, and acute safety problems — bullying enabled by staff, racial harassment, repeated fights, drugs/coach misconduct, and families leaving or switching schools because of academics or safety; examples include ‘teachers don’t care,’ administrators who ‘enable bullying,’ reports of racist language, and families withdrawing to cyber/private schools.  Assign content here when the dominant differentiator is operational failures in instruction, leadership responsiveness, or student safety described more often in square than circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups items where circle reviewers describe concrete, repeated safety incidents and student misconduct (fights, gang lockdowns, weapons, widespread vaping/drugs/alcohol, sexual exploitation) that are absent or minimized in square reviews (e.g., “Constant fights… locked down,” “kids vape everywhere,” “brass knuckles beating,” “rampant alcohol and drug problem” vs. square’s lack of gang/drug/shooting claims). Membership means the school narrative emphasizes actual on-campus threats to student physical safety and pervasive substance use rather than only isolated discipline complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, tracka: This bucket covers concrete programmatic evidence in circle reviews—AP/dual‑enrollment counts and outcomes, CTE certification pathways, measurable college matriculation/graduation statistics, alumni professional trajectories, and formal college partnerships (e.g., “100% graduate/98% go to college,” multiple dual‑credit/CTE pathways, named alumni MDs and graduate degrees, ‘11 AP classes’ and Gateway partnerships) —whereas square reviews rarely provide comparable, measurable postsecondary evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader and hig: This bucket gathers references to abundant or flagship extracurriculars in circle reviews—award‑winning bands, auditioned arts schools, statewide athletic championships, dozens of clubs, intense practice schedules and community fan culture (e.g., “best band in the state,” ‘‘admissions by audition to 2 art forms,’’ ‘won 2 State Titles,’ ‘more than 30 clubs,’ heavy after‑school practice demands’) —contrasting with square entries that either omit such depth or describe more limited programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This bucket groups concrete governance and logistical failures circle reviewers report: unresponsive front offices, separate/overstaffed attendance offices, months‑long teacher vacancies, failing metal detectors, bus no‑shows, standards‑based grading upheavals, and deteriorating facilities (e.g., “front office…never checked on her,” “no teacher for Biology for 3 months,” “metal detectors…don’t work,” “facility is falling apart”), whereas square reviews more often describe functioning parent portals, organized improvement projects, or do not report such systemic operational collapse.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater staff-dr: This bucket captures reviewer reports that staff or leadership impose ideological/religious requirements (mandatory church membership and tithing, Bible class), push political views, or practice favoritism/nepotism and unprofessional behavior—public humiliation, cursing at students, protecting ‘good old boy/girl’ offenders, and letting athletes buy favoritism (e.g., “teachers required to attend Trinity church (10% tithing),” “teachers impose political agenda,” “they will lie to your face,” “preferential treatment for athletes/local kids”)—features described in circle but not in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups raw terms describing active administrative problems in circle schools—e.g., claims that leaders ‘hide problems,’ ‘show favoritism,’ ‘hold transcripts hostage,’ ‘censor the newspaper,’ or tell students they are ‘just seeking attention’—contrasted with square reviews that more often describe reachable or attentive administrators and district‑level neglect rather than deliberate concealment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This groups passages where circle reviewers recount concrete safety failures (fights, students ‘stabbed with pencils,’ drugs/tobacco on buses), systemic bullying, race‑ and disability‑based exclusion or fear (‘never met a person of color that fully feels safe’), restraints/code greens for special‑needs students, and gang involvement—situations square entries rarely describe at the same level of severity.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater variabil: This bucket covers teacher‑level operational issues emphasized in circle reviews—routine worksheet/rote instruction, teachers not showing up, disrespectful staff, poor substitutes and burnout—often alongside a small number of named, exemplary teachers; square entries tend to report fewer systemic classroom‑practice failures or present them as more isolated incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ac: This groups claims that circle schools offer named, tangible programs and supports—Saturday tutoring, dual enrollment, growing AP/honors/STEM offerings, CTE pathways, scholarship/work‑study communication and explicit college admission outcomes (early admission, well‑prepared graduates)—whereas square reviews give fewer concrete program examples and more generalized complaints about academic failure.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict stronger localized: This bucket captures circle statements about intense local loyalty and parental activism (parents relocating or buying homes to attend, parent‑run programs, alumni support), strong school spirit and athletics/arts centrality, and also parent/booster exclusion or clique behavior; square entries rarely present that same mix of mobilized community support or demand.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety incidents and failed protections (e.g., 'My son was targeted and bullied for two weeks and they never did anything about it', 'a haven for gang thugs', 'smoking in bathrooms', calls for drug prevention, and 'armed San Jose Police constantly patrolling the school') and document staff blaming victims or token responses to assault/suicide threats—patterns largely absent from the square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive a: Many circle reviews enumerate program breadth and outcomes—'offers many APs, as well as honor courses', 'dual credit enrollment', 'excellence medical academy', 'Their JROTC program is top notch', 'students have earned over 3 million dollars in scholarships', and first‑choice university acceptances—whereas square reviews less often report this constellation of advanced/dual‑credit and career pathway evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, fav: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege family‑ties and favoritism in staffing and discipline ('the schools staff is mostly related', 'preferential treatment to students whose parents do more for the teacher', 'a lot of nepotism among the educators/administrators'), plus claims of administrative politics and cover‑ups (dropped sexual‑relationship cases, accusations of bullying by administration), complaints that square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater variabil: Circle reviews contain many operational criticisms—high teacher turnover ('About 16 or more teachers left last year'), inconsistent course delivery across sections, slow or subjective grading ('Most of the teachers take a long time handing assignments back'; 'teachers always give you zeros if you don't understand something'), administrative test/logistics failures ('missed SAT deadline because the school failed to notify students'), and both permissive and punitive grading/attendance practices—issues that are less frequently described in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries depict more consistent st: Square reviews more often describe caring, stable adults and responsive leadership ('the best teachers... truly dedicated faculty and staff', 'The administration and Board seem to be sensitive to the community needs', 'My son is in its IB program and leant a lot'), along with organized parental/community partnership and formal student supports—qualities that contrast with the problems emphasized in many circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports of widespread physical fights, targeted and identity‑based bullying, gang affiliation, drug selling/use, security‑staff misconduct, and allegations that school leaders decline to intervene (e.g., 'Fights everyday,' 'Gang affiliation,' 'Bullying is a major issue... They do not take bullying seriously,' 'the VP doesn't follow thru,' 'students sell drugs'), which appear repeatedly in circle reviews but are described as isolated or absent in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more diversified: Circle reviews frequently list named programs, block/4‑day schedules, AP/IB/academy offerings, CTE/vocational pathways, dual‑enrollment/Running Start and concrete credit/college outcomes (e.g., 'Skills Pathway certificate,' 'over 40 hours of college credit,' 'ranked 155 in the nation,' 'college credits transferred to Rutgers'), while square reviews generally lack these specific programmatic or measurable post‑secondary claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more claims of s: Many circle items allege patterned unequal treatment—athletes or donor/legacy families receiving preferential admissions, financial aid, discipline protection, or hiring/promotion through nepotism (examples: 'the rich run the school... athletes... get a free education,' 'if you are the child of an alum... you get the best treatment,' 'nepotism... pushed one administrator with no teaching experience'), whereas square reviews do not advance sustained claims of institutional favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete oper: Circle reviewers repeatedly document day‑to‑day infrastructure and logistics problems—overcrowded lunches/buses, dirty restrooms, missing facilities (no cafeteria/track), failing HVAC/textbooks, and technology/internet shortages (e.g., 'ONLY GET one slice of pizza,' 'buses are crowded... well over capacity,' 'no air conditioning or heat,' 'our computers years old'), complaints that are rarely raised in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more detailed indi: Circle entries provide granular accounts of one‑on‑one supports (teachers staying after school, proactive guidance counselors) alongside explicit failures in special‑education accommodations, IEP/504 noncompliance, counseling breakdowns, and scheduling/counseling collapse (examples: 'teachers stay after school...','She lets me know what i need to do to graduate,' versus 'they don't follow IEP'S AND 504'S,' 'guidance office shut down for a week,' 'counseling is awful... only got one because... a kid shot up the place'), while square reviews mention guidance or IEP issues far less concretely.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize advanced academ: These reviews repeatedly name concrete programs and outcomes—AP/IB breadth, many AP classes and National Merit finalists, formal dual‑enrollment/early‑college and associate‑degree pathways, career/technical shops (Dental Assisting, Graphic Communications, renewable energy, High Tech Academy), strong guidance counseling, and reported elite college acceptances—which together portray substantive academic/credential pathways and college preparedness that Square reviews rarely document (examples: ‘third most dual enrollment courses,’ ‘graduate with an Associates Degree,’ ‘tons of AP classes and many National Merit Finalists’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe overcr: Many Circle reviews describe tangible infrastructure and logistics problems—extreme overcrowding and mobile classrooms, HVAC failures (no A/C or heat), roaches and gas‑pipe issues, missing supplies, bus‑fleet and transportation breakdowns, lost schedules/enrollment errors, and rude/inefficient front‑office service—issues Square reviews do not raise (examples: ‘4,000 students… mobile home classroom,’ ‘lack air conditioning… class sizes too large,’ ‘attendance showed my kid unverified absent but we had dr. notes they lost’).
candidate_defs.circle entries document more bullying, f: Circle reviewers report repeated student‑on‑student violence and harassment plus administration and staff responses that worsen harm—numerous fights and gang history, bullying that led to suicidal ideation and psychiatric care, staff privacy violations (confiscated iPad, eavesdropping on social media, staff entering restrooms), forced drug tests and expulsions, and claims that administrators protect bullies or ignore complaints—whereas Square reviews lack this cluster of safety failures (examples: ‘40+ fights last year,’ ‘she now is suicidal… responsible students have not been properly dealt with,’ ‘discipline manager… gone into the girls restroom’).
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more nepotism, fav: Circle reviews frequently attribute problems to biased personnel and governance—charges of hiring/selection based on family ties, favoritism toward athletes (grades, disciplinary leniency, funding), ‘good ol boy’ politics on school boards, unqualified principals, and fabricated or politicized accountability data—patterns Square reviewers do not report (examples: ‘they take care of their own children… coaches or alumni,’ ‘school board is rife with politics and over paid bureaucrats,’ ‘teachers will give students good grades if they are in the football team’).
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize safer, small‑to: Square reviews more often depict a school as safe, community‑oriented, and strong in performing arts and supportive services—statements about a ‘safe’ environment, caring and responsive teachers/counselors, thriving band/theater programs and arts magnet identity, and family‑style cohesion—features that Circle reviews either do not emphasize or counter with complaints (examples from Square: ‘Safe… like a family,’ ‘theater teacher Bruce Taws,’ ‘DA’s music program is unique,’ ‘counselors were great to help my son navigate scholarships’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more unmanaged stu: This bucket captures reports of concrete on-campus safety breakdowns and lack of adult supervision in Circle reviews (fights, police arrests/injuries, students roaming off campus, stalking incidents, repeated safety threats, students allowed to leave campus, thefts and pregnancy increases) that Square reviews do not describe or describe as far less frequent (examples: “From 2017–2019 there has been numerous safety threats,” “kids wandering the halls evading adults,” “a police officer was injured and arrests were made”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, aut: This bucket groups Circle claims about harsh or arbitrary discipline, expulsions/denials of reenrollment, strict phone/uniform/pass rules, dress‑code suspensions, and racially or preferentially unequal enforcement and nepotistic protections—plus staff participation in or protection of bullying—whereas Square lacks these charges (examples: “Freedom of speech is not allowed…Get arrested,” “Get an F more than twice…you get kicked out,” and “discipline is not equal…exceptions made for certain people,” alongside allegations of racial bias and staff‑protected cliques).
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger parent/co: This bucket covers Circle descriptions of active parent groups, multigenerational alumni ties, visible leadership and welcoming community identity, frequent parent‑school contact, and alumni outcomes—positive community forces that Square reviews generally do not describe (examples: “My husband and myself graduated…my son just started,” “the parent groups…we as parents have felt so welcomed,” and “Best HS Alumni Association in the country”).
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic inst: This bucket isolates Square reviewers’ recurring claims that instruction and academic support are uneven or absent—large class sizes, teachers who 'don’t teach,' poor college preparation, unhelpful counselors, and students feeling like 'a number'—claims more prevalent in Square than in Circle (examples: “classes were 30+ to a room,” “they simply read out of a book…they do not actually teach anything,” and “the faculty never addressed my problems”).
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete ope: This bucket groups Circle reviews that enumerate concrete administrative logistics and program facts—facility renovations or HVAC failures, Chromebook rollouts, detailed fee/waiver practices, staffing allocation choices, quantified dual‑enrollment credits, JROTC/ROTC and career program listings, and named awards—details rarely present in Square (examples: “renovated all school facilities in 2018,” “every student issued a new Chromebook,” “over 60 free college hours through Morehead State,” and specific fee‑waiver practices).
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger specializ: These reviews describe concrete academic infrastructure and outcomes (AP/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment/early‑college, high graduation and scholarship figures, district/state growth metrics and longstanding accreditation) that square reviews typically lack; examples include “AP programs... more students are succeeding on the AP exams,” “one of the few schools... offer the International Baccalaureate,” “over 95% of the students proceed to college,” and “free college credits while in high school.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety proble: Many circle reviews recount pervasive peer violence, death threats, physical bullying, frequent fights, visible off‑campus drug dealing, and extreme disciplinary tactics (e.g., students locked in rooms with police) along with administrators failing to intervene — in contrast to square reviews which more often describe a safer, monitored environment; illustrative quotes: “received serious DEATH threats from varsity football players,” “the school is not safe at all... juvenile jail,” and “locks kids in room with police when they don’t get what they want.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report worse administrati: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe unreturned calls, counselors who 'don’t seem to care,' front‑office staff who 'rarely answer the phones,' board/district mismanagement, and explicit calls for external/state review or board reevaluation, whereas square reviews more often describe visible, responsive administrators and effective counselor support; examples include “counselors never gave my student the time of day,” “No phone calls back from Principal,” and “PA department of education needs to review... the administration.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher unpro: Square reviews uniquely emphasize staff misconduct and immaturity (teachers laughing during student harassment, staff appearing unprofessional or retaliatory, accusations like 'teachers are more immature than the students'), including explicit claims of staff‑instigated bullying or retaliation that circle reviews do not foreground; representative lines: “a teacher laughing as an autistic girl was bullied,” “Teachers are too busy having affairs... making fun of students on Facebook,” and “they take it out on the student.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: Circle reviews commonly list extensive, organized extracurricular offerings (marching band and arts honors, JROTC, strong athletics, robotics, vocational/shop programs, business/community partners), facility investments and facility upkeep (AstroTurf, updated tech, bonds), and concrete scheduling/after‑school tutoring, while square reviews rarely detail comparable program breadth or external partnerships; examples: “marching band has won many STATE competitions,” “vocational classes offered while still being able to complete college prep,” “free after‑school tutoring Tues/Thurs 3–4PM,” and “Astro Turf on its baseball fields.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive, un: These reviews describe frequent fights, assaults (bathroom and after‑school beatings), bullying and hate speech that administrators often ignore or unevenly punish—e.g., claims that students are 'harassed and beat up in the bathrooms,' 'administration does not deal with dangerous students,' or that victims are disciplined while aggressors are not—whereas square entries do not report the same scale of unaddressed physical violence or systemic disciplinary collapse.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger formal co: Many circle reviews cite concrete advanced offerings and outcomes—AP/IB programs, PLTW/dual‑enrollment, high ACT/SAT scores, scholarships, AA degrees and named college acceptances or 100% passing cohorts—(e.g., 'IB Diploma', 'scored a 34 on his ACT', 'dual enrollment paid by the school'), while square reviews lack comparable, consistent evidence of schoolwide advanced-program breadth or measurable college-placement metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistently: Numerous circle reviews highlight staff who provide one‑on‑one help, proactive tutoring, accommodating guidance counselors, and family‑like care (e.g., 'teachers are always willing to help', 'guidance was very accommodating', 'treated like family'), whereas square reviews more often document overwhelmed, unresponsive, or disengaged teachers and counselors.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviewers frequently allege nontransparent policies and decisions—nepotistic hires, favoritism in discipline and athletics, withheld camera footage, coercive substance‑testing, budget misallocation and heated local election battles (e.g., 'principal won't allow you to see camera footage', 'coaches hand‑pick players from social circles', 'budget allocation system is very corrupt')—while square reviews focus less on such opaque governance or community political conflict.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: Circle reviews more often describe abundant clubs, strong band/arts and athletics, new buildings or up‑to‑date tech (iPads, Mac labs, 3D printers), and formal performing arts/athletic achievements (e.g., 'one of the top 5 band programs', 'new high school building opened', 'many clubs and state champs'), whereas square entries tend to report fewer electives, reduced extracurricular breadth, or lack comparable facility/technology detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report administrative mal: These reviews describe concrete governance failures inside the building — e.g., grade‑alteration pressure and teacher resignations, discipline‑quota directives to stop writing kids up, lost transcripts, deceptive IEP withholding, nepotism and placating parents to avoid punishment — patterns repeatedly asserted in circle reviews but not in square ones (examples: “stop writing kids up because we had already met our quota,” “teachers are resigning because they are being told to alter grades,” “they will lose transcripts,” “administrators cover up a lot just to make the school look good”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Circle reviewers document high‑frequency, high‑severity student misconduct and safety failures inside the school — daily/weekly physical fights, groping in crowded halls, robbery/threats, widespread bullying ignored by staff, and prevalent drug use — along with staff nonresponse (e.g., “girls getting groped in packed hallways,” “the fights are almost every day,” “weed is super popular,” “my daughter got jumped and all they said was sorry”), whereas square reviews rarely report this scale of threat.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe athletics‑center: Circle reviews repeatedly point to athletics as a dominant institutional priority (new turf/football/baseball facilities, donor‑driven resource flows, all money goes to sports) and to preferential treatment for athletes (playing time, softer discipline, grade leniency tied to donations), e.g., “the first 3 things you'll see driving onto campus are a gorgeous new baseball field…a turf football field,” “all money goes to sports,” and “students of families that donate to the school are not being punished for bad behavior,” while square reviews emphasize other programs (music, IB) and do not foreground athletic favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader formal adv: Many circle reviews list concrete program offerings and outcomes — honors/AP/IB classes, dual‑enrollment, block scheduling, certified vocational programs, paid work‑study and documented AP/college acceptances (Stanford, Binghamton, college scholarships) — e.g., “Honors, AP, and IB classes,” “paid work study…money goes to tuition,” and “students passing AP exams and going to Stanford to local community colleges,” claims that appear far more often in circle entries than in square ones.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: Square reviews more often describe sustained teacher competence, parent communication, and staff who go beyond (named great teachers, counselors who communicate frequently, alumni who credit teachers for college prep), plus fewer reports of chronic turnover or widespread incompetence; examples include “Outstanding teachers that care about their students,” “Mr. Heathcock… communicates with parents almost daily,” and student success stories tied to teacher support, which contrast with circle claims of higher turnover and pervasive ineffective instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: These entries emphasize specific curricular offerings and quantifiable postsecondary results (AP/IB listings, dual‑enrollment/College‑of‑Campus programs, scholarship totals, National Merit, documented college degrees) and describe heavier academic rigor/homework; examples include detailed AP course lists, $7.5M class scholarship totals, 1:1 laptop/iPad programs, and PBL/STEM/college‑credit pathways that square entries do not document.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures concrete safety/fear incidents and systemic supervision failures reported in circle entries — daily fights, students beaten bloody, weapon displays/pulled gun, regular code‑red lockdowns, student drug use, police on campus weekly and students fleeing school — issues that square entries typically do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger persona: Circle reviewers frequently report individualized teacher support, creative accommodations (IEP/504/ADHD), responsive counselors, small class sizes/known‑by‑name culture, active PTSA and community/church partnership, and localized admissions touches (handwritten invites), contrasts that square entries lack or describe less often.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more insider favor: This bucket groups claims that access and benefits depend on connections or status — 'who you know' admissions, multi‑generational/local preference, athletes and vocal parents getting special treatment, club/team favoritism, and peer socioeconomic policing — patterns circle reviewers call out far more than square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviews repeatedly document dysfunctional leadership and operations — named principal/superintendent critiques, unreturned calls, record manipulation allegations, opaque budgeting, failed bond/funding, inconsistent scheduling/discipline, phone/PA system failures, slow/unequal tech rollouts and facility maintenance problems — problems square entries mention far less or not at all.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust curric: These reviews describe concrete, organized academic and enrichment offerings (IB, many AP/Honors, dual‑enrollment/AA completion, industry certifications, vocational tracks) plus high‑level extracurriculars (nationally ranked band/orchestra, ROTC, successful sports, alumni career networking) and named awards/college placements—examples include IB status, students graduating with AA degrees, Stanford/UC links, national ensemble competitions, and school improvement/Blue‑Ribbon awards that Square reviews do not mention.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more instructional: These reviews allege poor day‑to‑day teaching practices and outcomes—teachers handing out irrelevant worksheets, students slipping from A/B to D/F, grade inflation, insufficient homework, unmet mentor/tutoring promises, and widespread claims that teachers ‘don’t know how to teach’ or are unresponsive—complaints that Square’s reviews counter with stronger claims about effective instruction and college preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Multiple Circle reviews document frequent physical fights, bullying (including homophobic/racist slurs tolerated by staff), weapons expulsions, police/security actions that worsened situations, and long‑term mental‑health impacts or transfers for safety reasons—patterns Square reviews largely do not report or report as less severe.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege two‑tier enforcement, family‑name/insider protection, coaches/boosters receiving special treatment or suspected theft, administrators erasing yearbook entries or threatening punitive measures (CPS, fees), and explicit claims that athletics or elite donors drive decisions—administrative favoritism and retaliation themes absent or far weaker in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational/r: These reviews cite concrete facility and service deficits—class sizes of 30–43, underfunded arts and labs requiring out‑of‑pocket costs, bed‑bug reports, inadequate lunch service, bus stop/transportation failures, missing textbooks/technology portal problems, and chronic scheduling/registration or communication breakdowns—problems Square reviews generally do not raise or raise less often.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures reports of concrete on-campus danger in circle reviews — fights and gang activity, weapons and stabbings, drug use, chronic bullying and cyber‑harassment, and repeated threats to student safety (e.g., “fights at least once a week,” “students brought guns…were not expelled,” “i got shanked at this school,” “The bullying is out of control”). These are distinct, operational safety failures (incidents and exposures) rather than merely complaints about climate or discipline procedure.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: This groups circle comments that enumerate formal AP/Pre‑AP/Early College/dual‑credit offerings, high AP/ACT/SAT outcomes, direct top‑college matriculation, and distinctive CTE offerings (e.g., Advanced Environmental Water Academy, automotive shop, associate‑degree pathways, quantifiable AP/college-credit successes and alumni outcomes). These are school-structure/program claims about curriculum breadth, credentialing and measurable postsecondary results rather than anecdotal teacher quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader, award‑: Circle reviews frequently list many clubs (GSA, Asian Club, Drama, etc.), high‑profile arts and band achievements, competitive athletics/FFA/Mock Trial successes, travel trips, and strong school pride/alumni ties (e.g., marching band trophies, band trips to New York, state athletic qualifiers), marking organized, visible extracurricular strength and communal identity distinct from academics or admin issues.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: This bucket collects square reviewers’ repeated claims about low instructional skill, teachers who 'do not teach,' unprofessional or bully‑like teacher conduct, poor classroom control, uncertified or underqualified teachers, and AP teachers who fail to prepare students — operational problems centered on day‑to‑day teaching practice and classroom management (e.g., 'most teachers do not teach,' 'teachers themselves act like bullies,' 'could not speak the foreign language she was teaching').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers circle statements about administrations mishandling discipline (cover‑ups, in‑house handling), failing counselors/transcript and college-office breakdowns, ignored confidentiality/ legal compliance, inconsistent/unwritten policy enforcement, emergency/parent‑communication failures, overcrowding/parking and chronic supply or facility deterioration (e.g., 'Confidentiality laws are largely ignored,' 'transcript never sent,' 'parking is a nightmare,' 'voicemail always full'). These are operational, compliance, and resource-allocation failures distinct from teacher practice or extracurricular strength.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: These reviews describe concrete safety problems inside the building (daily fights, bomb threats, vandalism, police presence), chronic bullying and racism, pervasive vaping/drug problems, and repeated privacy/sexual misconduct incidents (e.g., JV boys urinating in girls’ locker room) — all reported much more often in circle than in square, which generally reports few or no bullying/safety crises and in some cases explicitly says bullying is rare.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: Many circle reviews cite multiple AP/IB/Cambridge courses, honors placement, entrance-percentile thresholds, national academic competitions, alumni admission to elite colleges, and formal dual-credit arrangements, or explicitly call the school 'rigorous' and selective; square reviews rarely reference such concentrated advanced-course infrastructure or elite college-placement examples.
candidate_defs.circle entries document richer extracurr: Circle reviewers repeatedly note broad arts and music excellence, marching-band and orchestral partnerships, large FFA/agriculture programs, modern tech (3D printing labs, telescopes, robotics), planned renovations, and extensive extracurricular clubs, whereas square reviews more often describe limited electives, fewer extracurricular opportunities, and lower-tech facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete admi: Circle reviews contain many specific complaints about scheduling/transcript errors, lost IDs, late buses, denied advanced-credit requests, punitive grading/makeup denials, uneven discipline (victims punished, athletes favored), opaque front‑office behavior and bureaucratic obstacles, while square reviews typically describe clearer admin communication or do not enumerate these operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger inclusive: Square reviews more often describe accessible, dedicated teachers, effective counselor/parent communication, inclusive supports (neurodiversity, welcome for diverse students), community investment and stable zoned‑school continuity, contrasting with many circle reviews that emphasize exclusivity, cliquishness, or fractured administrative relationships.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete curricular breadth and outcomes at circle schools — explicit AP/IB/gifted offerings, Mandarin/innovative electives, dual‑enrollment/STEM academies, high standardized scores, near‑100% college matriculation, named scholarship winners and alumni professional outcomes (e.g., “over 25 AP courses,” “IB curriculum…preparation for…selective colleges,” “100% of my graduating class went on to college,” “Bill Gates Millennium Scholarship”). Falling in this bucket means the school is reported to have formal advanced tracks, routine college counseling, and documented external performance metrics that square reviews do not assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Many circle reviews allege governance and operational breakdowns at the district/school level — stolen or mishandled records, administrators who 'flat lied', nepotistic hiring tied to coaches, corruption and palm‑greasing, counselors who never return messages, and calls for board intervention or closure (e.g., 'they even flat lied… kept my student active in their system,' 'blatant nepotism, palm greasing,' 'The counselor has not returned any messages in 9 months'). Items in this bucket describe systemic leadership or bureaucratic failures (not just single‑teacher issues) that impede student placement, discipline follow‑through, or parental communication.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more pervasive s: These square reviews report frequent, serious safety/discipline incidents — recurring fights, on‑campus drug activity, gang behavior, probation officers or probationers attending classes, and a sense that misbehavior is unchecked or unevenly enforced (examples: 'Huge Drug problem at this school!', 'There Is a Huge Drug problem', 'probationers with the PO on site', 'students are constantly in fights'). Content in this bucket signals a school environment where student misconduct and inadequate or biased disciplinary enforcement are the primary operational concerns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive, we: Circle reviews frequently enumerate many funded clubs/teams, robust music/arts programs, well‑maintained or newly built facilities, endowments/alumni support, and one‑to‑one device programs (examples: 'outstanding music program', 'huge endowment… outstanding facilities', 'tablet program… every student carries a tablet', '25 AP courses, new STEM Academy, College and Career Access Center'). Belonging here means the school is portrayed as resourced for diverse extracurriculars and capital projects in ways square reviews don’t claim.
candidate_defs.square entries describe weaker classroom: Square reviews more often report poor or inconsistent instruction, frequent teacher absences or mid‑year resignations, unstable staffing (classes without teachers), and failures to provide extra help or accommodations (e.g., 'WE DO NOT LEARN ANYTHING… teachers are absent', 'Halfway through the year about 3 teachers resigned', 'I needed extra help and never got it' attributed to square). Items in this bucket indicate operational classroom problems — staffing instability and low instructional follow‑through — that reduce day‑to‑day student learning and support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews emphasize concrete academic offerings and outcomes: multiple circle comments list 20 AP classes, IB/DE/dual‑enrollment and Cambridge/CLEP credit, named scholarship pipelines, higher standardized test performance and explicit college matriculation successes (e.g., 'Test scores consistently higher than state averages', 'prepared for college', 'many AP courses available'). Falling into this bucket means the school narrative centers on institutional academic pathways, credits, and measurable post‑secondary results that square reviews do not claim.
candidate_defs.square entries report systemic instructi: Square reviews repeatedly characterize classroom instruction and grading as undermining learning—claims include 'School is not teaching at State Standards', 'every assignment/test is only worth 1% of their grade', busywork, unacceptable pacing, and students left unprepared for college—concrete, schoolwide academic-process criticisms not present in the circle set. Content falls here when reviewers describe curriculum/assessment/grade‑policy or statewide accountability failures as core problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety,: Many circle reviews document high‑severity incidents and health/facility harms—examples include allegations a teacher assaulted a student, a student bringing a gun, past sexual‑assault cases left unaddressed, swastikas carved on desks, routine locker thefts and locked bathrooms causing UTIs—claims about immediate physical safety or hygiene that square reviews generally do not make. Use this bucket for reviews that focus on concrete, high‑risk safety incidents or facility/health failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff and adm: Square reviews frequently call out rude or arrogant teachers and front‑office staff, unresponsive counselors, administrators who ignore parents, favoritism or selective enforcement, and families who removed children for safety—specific governance and interpersonal failures (e.g., 'If you want a call back you might as well forget it', 'we withdrew our daughter due to bullying') that distinguish the square set. Put content here when the primary critique is staff/leadership behavior, selective enforcement, or punitive/retaliatory responses driving family exits.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader extracur: Circle reviews enumerate wide program breadth—state championships, thriving marching band and arts magnet programs, vocational/agricultural offerings, career academies, an on‑site working bank—and also raise disputes about resource shifts (e.g., athletics prioritized over arts). Reviews belong in this bucket when they foreground concrete non‑academic programming, vocational/arts magnets, and how resources are allocated across those programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and pe: These reviews document concrete safety failures and student misbehavior in circle schools (fights, weapons, severe drug problems, hazing, physical assaults, students sent to ICU, pervasive bullying and cover‑ups) that square reviews do not (e.g., 'too much fights and kids bring weapons to school,' 'SEVERE drug problem…faculty and administration choose to ignore,' 'Bullying is TERRIBLE…child came home crying every day').
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: Circle reviews list specific programmatic breadth and college‑prep pathways (AP/dual‑enrollment, early‑college, NAF/academy partnerships, strong band/choral programs, scholarship/ACT outcomes, college centers) with actionable detail, whereas square reviews are more generic about programs (examples: 'AP classes and dual enrollment…enter college as a sophomore,' 'fantastic music program,' 'Massive scholarships are awarded').
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic fail: Circle reviews repeatedly describe inadequate remediation, ignored IEPs/504s, missed accommodations, and counselors who do not follow up (e.g., 'IEP was overlooked and not being followed,' 'neither the teachers nor the guidance counselor knows how to deal with kids that do not understand,' 'counselors take over a week to reply'), problems not reported in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries indicate stronger, more v: Many circle reviews emphasize an engaged, personal school culture—accessible principals, teachers who know students by name, small enrollment/family atmosphere, active alumni and parent networks, and targeted roles like a 'Graduation Coach' (examples: 'the principal knows just about everyone's name,' 'small student body so it has a family atmosphere,' 'parents have been totally active'), whereas square reviews lack these consistent claims of intimate, hands‑on leadership.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: Circle reviews more often allege bureaucratic/operational breakdowns (lost test/grade records, registration failures, outdated textbooks, broken technology), contested governance/admissions or tuition/ROI concerns, and staffing instability (examples: 'losing needed testing scores,' '5 attempts to register my child,' 'tuition is far too high for the quality of education,' 'faculty are pretty much in and out every year'), themes that square reviews generally do not raise.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reports of frequent lockdowns, fights, on-campus drug use and smell, gang activity, physical assault, pervasive peer bullying, homophobic/racist slurs, and ongoing threats—e.g., claims of 'lockdowns every other week,' 'Drugs in this school huge issue!!!!', 'girls get punched in their faces,' and 'At least half of the kids are homophobic and racist'—whereas square entries either minimize violence or frame incidents as episodic and emphasize student supports and safety enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more authoritari: This bucket groups concrete operational and governance problems: allegations of nepotism and 'good ole boys' cover-ups, withholding records/tuition refunds, punitive dress and discipline policies, K9 searches and heavy police presence, selective enforcement, surveillance/camera misuse, and board-level mismanagement (e.g., 'withheld his records until payment', 'School board covers for their colleagues', 'the principal loves to tell you what he sees on his video cameras'), contrasted with square entries that focus more on administrative neglect or bad communication rather than systematic cover-ups or coercive surveillance.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: This bucket captures specific programmatic behaviors that support individual students: teachers staying after to help, regular proactive calls/emails to parents, counselors who actively plan courses and help college planning, one-on-one tutoring and remediation, and visible parent volunteer/fundraising engagement (e.g., 'All the teachers are nice and are willing to stay after', 'The school counselors are great with helping students decide on classes', 'they frequently call and check up on my kids'), while square reviews mention teacher support less often or describe more mixed/inconsistent teacher responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, longer-run: This bucket groups evidence of deep extracurricular ecosystems and signature programs—national-champion robotics, extensive band/marching traditions, JROTC/drill teams, FFA, vocational/agricultural facilities, and many named clubs/sports with strong community pride (e.g., '13 different sports, and 19 different clubs', 'one band, one family', 'national champions robotics team')—whereas square entries tend to mention fewer specific high‑level competitive traditions and emphasize more limited after-school supports or general activities.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize measurable acad: This bucket groups square reviews that foreground standardized-test performance, IB/AP program structure, alumni college success and state metrics (e.g., 'MCAS scores are also higher than the average scores in the state', 'IB diplomas and strong alumni outcomes', 'Baldwin students score consistently well on AP tests'), contrasted with many circle entries that either highlight variable/unaccredited outcomes, remediation populations, or lack consistent aggregate outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more abundant extr: These circle reviews repeatedly describe concrete program breadth and campus assets (e.g., strong band/choir/music recognition, arts conservatory production demands, JROTC, Ag departments, engineering/public‑service academies, internships, study‑travel, 1:1 computing, auditoriums/gyms/greenhouses, after‑school clubs and robust athletics) that square reviews do not; examples include “one of the best music programs,” named Ag teachers, numerous out‑of‑country trips, and extensive lists of clubs and facilities, whereas square lacks comparable listings of institutional resources or organized program breadth.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger academic: Many circle reviews emphasize high‑level coursework and demonstrable postsecondary outcomes—AP/IB classes, dual‑credit with a nearby community college, high SAT/ACT averages and multi‑million dollar scholarship totals, and alumni claiming college preparedness (e.g., skipping college English or earning large merit scholarships)—whereas square reviews more often describe weak college prep or remediation needs and do not provide the same aggregate metrics or sustained AP/IB/dual‑enrollment evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent safe: Circle entries contain multiple concrete reports of student violence, unresolved bullying, thefts, gang/drug problems, pest infestations and unsanitary bathrooms (e.g., 'stabbing last year,' 'snitches get stitches,' 'water never has soap,' 'roaches and mice,' 'no cameras/guards'), while square entries rarely document this cluster of physical‑safety, hygiene, or serious violent‑incident failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, exc: Circle reviews more often allege explicit punitive or gatekeeping practices and governance problems—public shaming by leadership, withholding exams or diplomas for late payments or fundraising shortfalls, refusing program access or recognition, coercive testing/denied religious exemptions, nepotism and board politics—whereas square reviews do not commonly cite these kinds of deliberate exclusionary or payment‑linked administrative actions.
candidate_defs.square entries report more operational/a: Square reviews disproportionately describe chronic operational failures and frontline instructional problems—e.g., grades not entered/PowerSchool not updated, counselors and teachers not returning calls, teacher apathy or rushed instruction, inconsistent/subjective grading and teaching to the lowest common denominator—whereas circle reviews more often describe active teacher supports, prompt tutoring, or coherent administrative responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer programmati: These reviews emphasize concrete, school-run programs and outcomes — e.g., extensive AP/IB/dual‑enrollment success and students entering college with credits, nationally competitive arts/choir, strong band/music, robust athletics and championship records, vocational/FFA/agriculture and JROTC pathways — while Square reviews lack comparable program depth or documented college‑credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Circle reviews contain repeated accounts of daily bullying, gang activity, constant fighting, police/pepper‑spray responses, physical assaults on vulnerable students and claims that administration fails to intervene, whereas Square rarely describes pervasive or violent safety problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers describe favoritism/nepotism (pet students, grade bias), coercive practices (threats of expulsion, withholding graduation items tied to fundraising), suppression of negative reviews, inconsistent or manipulative discipline (boot‑camp rooms, silent punishment), and district/board dysfunction — a cluster of governance and punitive-administration problems not present in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive tea: Many Circle accounts highlight teachers who give daily progress updates, stay after school, provide one‑on‑one catch‑up tutoring, small class attention, effective IEP mainstreaming, and measurable student improvement, while Square reviews more often describe missed outreach and students ‘falling through the cracks.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger local com: Circle reviews repeatedly note small/family‑like school cultures, multigenerational pride, intense parent volunteerism and neighborhood selection to follow bus routes, selective/admissions cues, and explicit religious/faith‑based policies or moral contracts — community identity and faith-based governance that Square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket groups raw terms describing recurring fights, gang activity, weapons, visible drug/tobacco use, pervasive bullying, and on‑campus safety threats in circle reviews (e.g., “fights all the time,” “they have kids with guns...,” “lot of drugs, fights,” “tobacco can be smelt through the school”), contrasted with square reviews that rarely describe daily violence or weapons and instead emphasize supportive staff and safety.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: This captures claims of unresponsive or rude office staff, leadership turnover, broken policy enforcement (’Zero Tolerance’ not enforced), confidentiality breaches, PTA/financial irregularities, and calls for firings in circle reviews (examples: “Our board does nothing,” “no attendance is recorded,” “confidentiality… forced me to tell,” “bounced checks… lawsuit”), whereas square reviews more often praise administrative responsiveness or do not report such systemic governance failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete pr: Includes circle reports that name specific, functioning programs, certifications, and campus amenities—IB/AP/college‑credit programs, vocational shops and licensure, strong athletics and arts teams, new construction and campus facilities, and explicit graduation/college‑placement claims (e.g., “St. John’s College Advantage program,” “cosmetology state exam,” “new addition... Library, Gym,” “ASA... leading... graduation and college enrollment”), while square reviews tend to make vaguer claims about academics or note facility decline without naming many concrete programs or credentials.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater teacher st: This bucket groups frontline classroom and personnel claims in circle reviews—high teacher turnover, inexperienced hires, teachers perceived as paycheck‑driven or unprofessional, favoritism toward athletes/affluent families, phone use/poor classroom management, and absenteeism shifting work to parents (e.g., “new teacher every year,” “sit on their phones,” “favoritism,” “Teachers take MANY half days off”), contrasted with square reviews which more often describe consistently dedicated or supportive teachers and less pervasive turnover.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more explicit, co: Circle reviews repeatedly name IEP failures, special‑ed mismanagement, disputed medical accommodations, active or absent guidance counselors, and on‑site clinical/tutoring programs (examples: “don't follow IEPs,” “we pay... private therapist that comes to school,” “CAP provides conflict resolution, clinical counselors,” “Guidance Counselors are very active”), whereas square reviews rarely raise detailed special‑education/IEP disputes or the same level of counselor/program specificity.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe substantially br: These reviews report concrete program depth (AP/IB, large dual‑enrollment/college‑credit pipelines, IB diplomas) and quantified outcomes (students with 40–50+ college credits, high ACT/ scholarship totals, Ivy/competitive college admits) that circle schools foreground but square reviews largely omit or treat only anecdotally (examples: “opportunity to take 40+ college credits,” “IB program is exceptional,” “$9 million in scholarships,” versus Square’s lack of school‑level matriculation stats).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: Many circle reviews describe daily bullying/fights, gang activity, drug dealing/overdoses, sexual staff misconduct, school resource officer and juvenile‑justice complaints and explicit charges that the school ‘refuses to address’ these problems — a pattern of serious safety incidents and inadequate administrative response that Square reviews do not replicate (examples: “GANG ACTIVITY,” “kids dealing drugs and overdosing,” “teacher arrested for sex with a student,” “recent Bully issues that the school refuses to address!”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more inconsistent: Reviewers of circle schools repeatedly recount IEP/504 implementation failures, denied accommodations, missing ESL supports, counselor breakdowns or the need to hire outside advocates, and harmful handling of behavior‑label placements — issues that appear far more often in circle entries than in square entries (examples: “no ESL programs,” “Transition Planning Meeting…has yet to take place,” “happy to take money from a scholarship… but miserable when they have to accommodate them”).
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater internal con: Circle reviews frequently contain both strong evidence of committed, mentoring teachers and professional development (named inspiring teachers, after‑school help, teacher PD) and simultaneous reports of abusive, neglectful, or absent staff (yelling, hostility, chronic substitutes, grading failures), indicating wide within‑school variability not seen in the more uniformly characterized Square reviews (examples: “teachers actually do teach…teachers yell and scream,” “many teachers are brilliant…and the rest are the exact opposite”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more community/adm: These reviews describe systemic governance issues — favouring locals or athletes, denominational hiring bias, accusations of mismanaged funds, opaque communication, politicized transfers, and faith‑centered daily practices that exclude non‑adherents — patterns of community polarization and administrative partiality that distinguish circle entries from the generally less‑politicized, more administratively stable Square accounts (examples: “The Administration has favorites…Athletes are given a golden ticket,” “school tends to favor members of Church of Christ,” “funds are mismanaged,” “communication with parents is nil”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: These circle reviews contain concrete, serious safety incidents and ongoing behavior problems (overdoses and drug use, guns found in lockers, frequent/graphic fights, sexual assault, death threats, food fights, theft/vandalism) and also describe staff inaction on bullying—examples include a student picked up for an overdose, reports that a gun was removed from a locker, and multiple accounts of repeated physical assaults—none of which appear with the same frequency or severity in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete, spe: Circle reviewers frequently name on-site dual‑enrollment/early‑college programs, industry certifications, AP/advanced course results, explicit scholarship and college‑matriculation rates, and 1:1 device programs (MacBooks/iPads/interactive boards), often citing numeric outcomes (e.g., 99%+ college acceptance, specific AP/ACT scores, ‘graduate with an associate degree’), whereas square reviews rarely provide these program specifics or measurable performance data.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more athletics/par: Circle reviews repeatedly allege an athletic-first culture and explicit favoritism—athletes or wealthy/connected parents receive different rules or protection, employee children get reserved perks, and booster influence shapes decisions (examples: 'different set of rules for students who participate in the big sports,' 'teacher's children win awards', 'student can only excel if your parents are in the right clique'), claims that are far less present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational n: Circle reviewers document concrete administrative and operational breakdowns—nonresponse to emails, poor recordkeeping, vacant/temporary principals, budget mismanagement, opaque fundraising, pest/maintenance problems, heating/AC failures and building deterioration—alongside examples of poor scheduling and mismanaged course tracks, while square entries contain fewer of these specific operational failure anecdotes.
candidate_defs.circle entries are more internally polar: Many circle reviews juxtapose high praise for teacher commitment, strong arts/athletics or successful alumni with simultaneous severe complaints about leadership, safety, or policy (e.g., 'teachers really care' next to 'administration disregards students' or 'great arts program' alongside reports of drug problems), producing pronounced contradictory accounts within the same school that square reviews present far less often.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete, hig: These reviews list specific programs, named coaches/teachers, competitive outcomes and programmatic variety (e.g., “Amazing FFA Chapter,” “marching band is the best,” engineering program students built a plane, DECA, extensive UIL and travel trips), while square reviews rarely enumerate that many distinct, high‑performing activities or program details.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Multiple circle reviews describe explicit safety crises and staff/administration failing to act — e.g., “the drug use is extremely big here,” gang affiliations and students who ‘were stabbed,’ staff protecting gang members, predators alleged, and victims disciplined — a set of concrete safety/discipline claims not present in the square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Circle reviewers frequently cite low student‑teacher ratios, ongoing teacher outreach (teachers staying late, unpaid tutoring), dual‑credit/AP credit accumulation and concrete college matriculation stories (e.g., ‘10 AP courses, went to college with 31 credits’, scholarship facilitation), whereas square reviews provide less evidence of sustained, individualized academic/counseling interventions.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete fa: Circle reviews contain many specific facility and tech notes — from universal Macbooks/tablets and smartboards to new stadiums, solar panel projects, or negative details like mold, trailers, and AC issues — while square reviews make few comparable concrete claims about device programs or named capital projects.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent vi: Square reviewers repeatedly describe administrators and teachers as proactive and caring (visible principals, teachers who ‘reach out,’ organized scheduling/policies that reduce cliques or improve safety), portraying steady leadership and systematic adult support that circle reviews either do not report or contrast with accounts of administrative unresponsiveness and turnover.
candidate_defs.circle entries report chronic underfundi: This bucket groups reviews that describe tangible resource shortfalls and budget-driven decisions at the school: repeated budget cuts, underfunded arts/band programs, missing textbooks, facility disrepair, eliminated busing, high activity/registration/uniform fees, and problematic tech rollouts (e.g., “band program is shamefully underfunded,” “I paid $500 on registration day!!!,” “we've gone through multiple budget cuts,” “most kids not have books”). Square entries make few or no such claims about chronic underfunding or repeated service reductions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety, bully: This bucket captures concrete accounts of student misconduct and failures of protection/discipline: frequent fights, in-class drug use and solicitation, gang activity, racial slurs/Nazi-costume tolerance, pervasive bullying (including retaliation when reported), teacher absenteeism and classroom abandonment, and security that is visible but circumvented (e.g., “kids literally did drugs in class,” “Gang activity… you should not send your child,” “When a child speaks out it just makes things worse,” and “hundreds of cameras… faculty members fail to catch troublemakers”). Square reviews, by contrast, more often describe effective security, fewer fights, or less pervasive bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger instituti: This bucket groups reviews that describe stable academic rigor and demonstrable outcomes at the school: national or county rankings, high ACT/SAT performance, consistent AP/IB/Early College offerings and dual-enrollment metrics, steady honors/AP enrollment and college placements, and long-tenured, well‑regarded teachers (e.g., “nationally ranked… my children have all scored >34 on ACT,” “Early College… 54% of student body has a 3.0 or higher,” and “staff and administration that has been there for years”). These institutional prestige claims and consistent teacher-quality reports appear far more in square entries than in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report systemic favoritis: This bucket groups reviews alleging unequal treatment tied to family connections, donations, staff relationships, or internal politics that influence student opportunities and discipline (e.g., “If you are employed by the school, donate money or work on the board then your child(ren) will be treated great,” “last names and money matter most,” and “you have to play politics to get anywhere”). Square entries rarely make such claims about nepotism or donor-based advantages.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict strong community/p: This bucket captures concrete community-level patterns and identity-driven school models: high parental fundraising/volunteerism, families relocating or choosing the school, small-town/close-knit/house or SLC structures, faith-based or culturally targeted missions (e.g., ASL/Deaf culture, single‑gender academies), and organized alumni/parent involvement (“parents volunteer via The Shark Fund,” “I moved so my child could go to this school,” “located on the grounds of the St. Andrew Abbey,” “small learning community houses”). Square entries seldom emphasize these strong, mission- or choice-driven community behaviors.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive saf: This bucket groups raw items where reviewers of the circle schools describe systemic safety problems and weak or inconsistent on-site enforcement—e.g., “Cyber bullying is an all time high,” “There is a huge drug problem,” multiple accounts of sexual harassment/assault, repeated fights, and criticisms like “where was the school police?” and unlocked/locked-bathroom or unsupervised hall complaints. It captures concrete incidents, security staffing problems, and recurring student-misconduct claims that reviewers tie to inadequate response or policy enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a broader, more: This bucket groups raw items naming programmatic offerings and pathways: circle reviews enumerate internships, fellowships, IB/AP clusters, CTE/trades, JROTC/AFJROTC, robotics, DECA/FBLA, film/media electives, and award-winning fine arts and varsity sports, often with examples of how those programs lead to jobs or college credit. It captures content about program variety, articulated career tracks, and tangible extracurricular/facility strengths that circle reviewers describe in detail (e.g., internship-to-job senior projects, award-winning band, many vocational shops).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible, site: This bucket captures mentions of engaged principals, named administrators taking corrective action, concentrated campus improvements and new construction—e.g., “under the leadership of Principal Tony Ratliff… finds a solution right away,” plus repeated lists of new libraries, stadiums, field houses, CTE buildings and renovated classrooms. These are concrete, campus-level operational changes and leadership visibility that circle reviewers link to improved culture or discipline.
candidate_defs.square entries report more district-leve: This bucket groups items where reviewers point to higher-level governance failures rather than only school-site problems—examples include allegations that “the district has regressed,” favoritism and political hiring, district indifference to parent complaints, and cost-saving deflections that deny student services. These comments focus on board/district decisionmaking, resource allocation, and systemic favoritism or political interference as the primary cause of school failures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic staff: This bucket covers recurring claims that square schools suffer from low teacher accountability and uneven instructional practice—e.g., teachers ‘‘give up’’, ‘‘just show up for the paycheck’’, counselors ‘‘have no clue’’, arbitrary grading, and poor homework communication. It groups operational classroom- and staffing-level failures (teacher apathy, erratic grading, weak counseling) that reviewers tie directly to student support breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, more fo: These reviews describe concrete curricular pathways (abundant AP/Honors and IB programs, dual‑enrollment/college credits, CTE/vocational tracks, technical-center offerings, and conservatory-style arts training) and cite measurable outcomes (high test/AP performance, college acceptances, dual‑credit sophomore entry). Example evidence: multiple Circle notes of 'lots of APs', 'IB curriculum', 'career pathway for every student', 'dual enrollment/40+ credits' versus Square's lack of comparable inventories of formal advanced/CTE options.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These reviews cite physical and operational deficits—aging buildings, leaks and rain damage, pest infestations (roaches/mice/bats), broken facilities/technology, dirty cafeterias/food‑poisoning reports, overcrowded classrooms, long commutes and insufficient supplies—often linking them to program cuts or safety risk. Example evidence: Circle items referencing 'oldest school of the county', 'constant leaks, heat outages', 'No supplies! No books! Computers don't work!' contrast with Square reviews that rarely describe such chronic infrastructure failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews recount repeated physical assaults, sexual harassment, gang- and drug-related incidents, vaping/substance use, severe public harassment at events, and complaints that discipline is lax or inconsistently applied (e.g., minor suspensions, victim isolation). Example evidence: Circle statements include 'beaten up four times', 'sexually harassed and no authority did anything', 'vapes are the craze', and 'bullying is highly overlooked', while Square contains few comparable documented violent/safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews allege staff and leadership misconduct (rude front-office, threats/physical misconduct by staff, retaliation against advocates), systematic favoritism (athletic/socioeconomic/staff‑children bias), political hiring and broken governance (revolving door, board ignoring parents), and poor complaint follow‑through. Example evidence: Circle claims like 'favoritism is a huge thing', 'administration is immoral', 'run off over half the teachers in three years', and 'they will not investigate anonymous reports' are common compared to fewer or opposite claims in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe a stronger small: These reviews emphasize smaller class sizes or lower student‑to‑teacher ratios, teachers 'going above and beyond', extensive extracurricular breadth (band, theater, dozens of clubs, ROTC, student enterprises), robust arts programs and frequent local events, plus multigenerational alumni engagement and school pride. Example evidence: Circle reports 'teachers know our names', 'over 100 clubs', 'theatre program is amazing', and 'many generations of family attended', whereas Square reviews less often depict such pervasive community cohesion or alumni continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more polarized, cont: Circle reviews frequently contain starkly opposing firsthand accounts about the same school—high praise and glowing alumni outcomes alongside accusations of systemic failure—(e.g., “The staff and teachers are simply the best” vs “THIS SCHOOL IS TERRIBLE!!!”, or one reviewer listing elite college admits while another claims 85% fail), producing internal inconsistency that Square lacks, where reviews present a single, consistent alumni-success or single-problem narrative.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: Circle content repeatedly catalogs wide program breadth and community supports—marching band, robotics, many clubs, no‑cut sports, internships, Dual Enrollment/college credits, active alumni mentorship and state athletic championships—whereas Square mentions far fewer extracurriculars and less alumni/community engagement (Square typically highlights one or two programs rather than a broad ecosystem).
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Circle reviews contain many concrete operational failures and politics—lost transcripts, withheld records, mysterious fines, inability to get transfers, principals who don’t return calls, allegations administration protects poor teachers or tampers grades, and calls for governance takeover—while Square reviews rarely describe such pervasive mismanagement or deliberate protectionism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: Circle contains numerous specific safety and behavior problems—weapons, on‑campus drug distribution and vaping, repeated bullying, lockdowns, frequent fights, students withdrawing for safety reasons, and claims that discipline is lenient for athletes or inconsistently enforced—whereas Square generally reports fewer or milder disciplinary incidents and quicker staff intervention.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more consistent,: Square reviews emphasize a stable, teacher-focused environment and uniform academic framing (e.g., supportive/welcoming teachers, AP rigor framed positively as college preparation, consistent alumni-success messaging or a clear community‑college pathway) with fewer contradictions or extreme operational failures than Circle, which oscillates between strong academic outcomes and numerous countervailing problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, formal a: These reviews emphasize institutional academic pathways and outcomes—IB/AP/Honors, dual enrollment/Running Start, college matriculation and test‑score evidence—(e.g., “The IB program is exceptional,” “offers various AP and Dual Enrollment programs,” “students scored in the 99th percentile,” “All 250 students continued their education in college”). They capture program structure and measurable postsecondary success more often than square entries, which give fewer concrete advanced‑program descriptions or consistent college‑outcome claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer arts, music: Circle reviews repeatedly call out extensive fine‑arts infrastructure and public showcases—conservatory/arts focus, ‘amazing Music and arts program,’ frequent concerts, exhibitions and award‑winning drama and music—(e.g., “entertained often by concerts and exhibits,” “one‑of‑a‑kind arts program,” “arts programs are phenomenal”), whereas square entries seldom describe that depth of arts programming or regular public performances.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray a tighter small‑s: Many circle reviews describe small class sizes, teachers who ‘become family,’ strong PTSA/parent involvement, multigenerational alumni loyalty and individualized staff support (e.g., “teachers and staff often becomes...a family,” “I graduated... I will try to send my two boys there,” “outstanding parent involvement”), presenting sustained community continuity and personal teacher investment more than square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Numerous circle reviews document chronic safety and behavior breakdowns and poor follow‑through—frequent fights (even ‘17 fights in one day’), vandalism, on‑campus drug sightings, and reports that bullying and incidents went unaddressed (e.g., ‘bullying is out of control,’ ‘they turned a blind eye,’ ‘students break school properties’), a pattern far more prominent in circle than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews more often flag leadership/office hostility, poor parent communication, chronic staff departures and bureaucratic gatekeeping—(e.g., “No one pays the slightest bit of attention to parents,” “the admin staff are a joke,” “staff leaves yearly,” “They won't be calling you until it's a huge problem”), indicating administrative unresponsiveness and personnel instability more frequently than circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete violent and safety failures (physical fights, assaults that caused concussions, sexual-assault allegations, teen pregnancies, property crimes) and repeated bullying/discrimination (racism, transphobia, homophobic monitoring) that staff or administration failed to remediate — e.g., an unsupervised hallway assault that left a freshman concussed, multiple accounts of unhandled bullying and alleged sexual assaults, and claims that teachers ‘bat an eye’ at racist/homophobic behavior. Falling in this bucket means the school narrative centers on student‑on‑student harm and systemic failure to protect and follow up rather than isolated discipline problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Many circle reviews call out leadership churn and poor governance (multiple principals/superintendents in a few years), unilateral policy changes (extended days without vote), nepotism in special-ed leadership, suppression of public forums, and district indifference or coverups — e.g., administrators ‘turn the other way,’ ‘sweep issues under the rug,’ or live outside the community. Content in this bucket focuses on unstable or politicized leadership, weak accountability, and obstructed complaint/feedback channels rather than primarily classroom or student-behavior issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater availabi: These reviews list concrete programmatic offerings and outcomes (AP/IB courses, dual‑enrollment with a university, AVID college-prep, freshman engineering, vocational/engineering magnets, college tours/scholarships) and cite measurable results (graduation rates, alumni at selective universities). Items in this bucket emphasize explicit curricular pathways, partnerships, and documented college/career placement rather than only anecdotal claims about rigor or general academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, routine: Numerous circle reviews emphasize small class sizes, teachers who provide 1:1 tutoring before/after school, teachers knowing students by name, and staff opening rooms for supervised study and mentorship (example: teachers coming in early for individual tutoring and assistants providing one‑on‑one help). A review falls here if it highlights consistent, concrete instructional supports and teacher availability (including special‑needs patience) as a dominant on‑the‑ground characteristic.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible extra: Circle reviews frequently catalog wide extracurricular ecosystems (robotics, debate, marching band, strong sports records), active PTO/boosters enabling programs, prominent athletics culture (athlete worship, scheduling priorities), concrete facilities investment or renovation plans, and also recurrent cash burdens on families (tuition, mandatory fees, fundraising). Content matched to this bucket centers on how resources are allocated and manifested through extracurricular offerings, booster/parent action, athletic prominence, capital projects, and the direct financial cost to families.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more frequent an: This bucket captures concrete reports of repeated physical fights, pervasive bullying, on-campus drug dealing and smoking, bomb threats/lockdowns, and even alleged sexual assaults with staff inaction — e.g., “there are mostly fights in the school and outside,” “Several sexual assaults within the school with no action,” “groups of kids... smoking,” and claims that police are rarely called — patterns that appear in many Circle reviews but are largely absent or far less severe in Square.
