candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: This groups instances where reviewers name explicit programmatic options and outcome metrics — honors/AP and Middle College/dual‑credit classes, named CTE programs, awards and rising CCRPI/API scores, and claims of school‑of‑choice demand — e.g., “offers honors and AP... double‑credit courses affiliated with cochise college,” “new CTE area,” and “CCRPI score up by over 10 points,” which occur more often in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries show more concrete eviden: This bucket includes accounts of small class sizes, teachers going ‘the extra mile,’ teacher‑initiated outreach, coordinated multi‑teacher intervention meetings with parents, Blazer/extra‑help time, and teachers spending personal funds — e.g., “every teacher invests in the lives of my children,” “they called a meeting with all his teacher and my husband and I,” and “principals who spend out‑of‑pocket money for the school” — which are prominent in Circle but less present in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This covers allegations about school/district leaders and boards — claims that the board ‘allows the district to break laws,’ hiring and program decisions based on who you know, favoritism toward wealthy parents or athletes, administrators who won’t return calls or retaliate against complainants — e.g., “If you are a parent with deep pockets they will do anything for you,” “principal refuses to cooperate,” and calls for investigations or leadership change, which are concentrated in Circle compared with Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete campus: This bucket groups tangible, place‑level and community descriptors (campus acreage, recent construction/bond projects, libraries/technology/equipment, named arts/FFA/athletic programs, boarding/residential structures, and explicit faith identity) — e.g., “70 acre suburban campus,” “library... like stepping into Hogwarts,” “award winning Agriculture department,” “just passed a building bond,” and repeated references to Bible/chapel/Catholic identity — features more frequently and specifically documented in Circle than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger specializ: These reviews describe concrete program depth (AP/IB/AICE/dual‑enrollment, honors, career academies) and quantified outcomes—excess college credit, scholarships, national awards, and students entering college with credits—whereas square reviews give only mixed or program‑specific success; examples include claims of 'students walked into college with 12 credit hours,' 'AP classes can't be beat,' and named IB/AVID/engineering pathways in circle entries versus Square's weaker, anecdotal college‑prep comments.
candidate_defs.circle entries report a broader, deeper: Circle reviews enumerate many clubs, award‑winning band, strong JROTC, career/technical electives and near‑whole‑school participation ('club for almost everything', championship band, DECA, vocational pathways), while square reviews rarely list comparable breadth or vocational offerings and often note cuts or limited student life.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Multiple circle reviews recount robberies, near‑daily fights, gang pressure, bathroom/after‑school assaults, rampant bullying, racism and homophobia, and failures to control or appropriately adjudicate incidents—sometimes alongside ad‑hoc security (metal detectors, multiple officers); square reviews note disorder but contain fewer or less severe accounts of violent crime or tolerated hate incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers allege administrators manipulating course placements/AP credit, encouraging drops/transfers to protect rankings, nepotism/donor favoritism, corruption or contract controversies, ignored IEPs, and resource misallocation (big athletic spend vs basic maintenance), whereas square reviews do not prominently document this pattern; concrete examples include administrators dropping an AP class, 'begged me to go to a class... for $4,000' enrollment motives, and 'many talented teachers have been let go.'
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger parenta: Circle reviews repeatedly mention active PTO/fundraising, sustained alumni reunions and feeder‑school pipelines, explicit faith/Bible‑based missions and visible religious activities, and a family‑like community feel—contrasting with square reviews that report weaker community fundraising, transient/critical families, or lack of school pride (e.g., 'PTO is active', 'I have attended every reunion', 'Biblical standards... the Gospel drives us').
candidate_defs.circle entries document more institution: This bucket captures reports that leadership or district governance actively mishandles complaints, conceals incidents, misallocates funds, shows nepotism/favoritism, or engages in PR/cover‑ups (e.g., a crash covered up because the parent worked at the school, allegations that the PR director solicited positive reviews, claims funds are diverted to administrators, complaint suppression and calls for new leadership). These are concrete, system‑level management failures rather than isolated classroom problems and distinguish many circle reviews from square ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries highlight a broader and d: This bucket groups claims that the school offers extensive advanced/specialized pathways (IB, VPA, many APs, AVID, career‑technical majors, dual/ concurrent enrollment, industry/college partnerships), concrete extracurricular competitive achievements, and quantifiable scholarship/college‑prep results (e.g., dual enrollment paid by school, Broadway actors teaching, ‘nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships,’ and 20+ AP classes). These items are about program breadth/depth and documented academic outcomes that circle reviews reference more than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, in: This bucket collects concrete descriptions of teacher-driven remediation and individualized help—after‑school tutoring, PLUS/remediation periods, mastery pacing, iterative writing drafts, grade‑recovery practices, and routine one‑on‑one attention (e.g., teachers staying after school, PLUS period for students who need help, structured credit recovery). These are operational instructional supports aimed at helping struggling students and appear substantially more often in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket aggregates reports of frequent physical fights, ongoing bullying and targeted exclusion, gang formation and violent threats (kill lists, bomb threats), substance use, and an everyday unsafe climate (e.g., 'fights every single day!', 'Bullying was a big issue', explicit gang and bomb‑threat reports). These are peer‑behavior and campus‑safety problems that square reviews emphasize more than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more chronic instr: This bucket covers repeated allegations of low instructional quality and unprofessional classroom behavior—teachers sleeping or wasting class time, 'teach to the test' AP instruction, heavy busywork/packets, counselors who dismiss serious concerns, and staff rudeness or refusal to intervene (e.g., teachers who just hand out packets, counselors 'rarely where they need to be'). These are classroom‑level instructional neglect and staff professionalism problems that square reviews describe more often than circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize college matricu: This bucket captures mentions that the school foregrounds college placement and academic prestige (e.g., “most every kid goes to a real college,” “really emphasizes matriculation into college,” “preparing my kids for the future”), statements that appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews which focus on electives and extracurriculars instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger student: This groups comments about in-class pedagogy where circle reviewers note teachers who ‘‘take time to explain things,’’ are ‘‘extremely helpful and genuine,’’ and ‘‘willing to make adjustments based on participation and interest,’’ a pattern reported more in circle than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more teacher admin: This bucket covers concrete incidents of teacher or grade-administration mistakes in circle reviews—e.g., teachers misplacing or failing to record handed work, unjustified grade reductions, and lost assignments—claims that contrast with square reviews stressing teacher support and real‑world preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic admi: This groups governance and operational complaints tied to the school/district (calls for board/superintendent investigation, refusal/obstruction of transfers, ESL/language-access failures such as an ESL teacher who doesn’t speak Spanish, locker/login/parent‑resource breakdowns, and families altering enrollment), a cluster appearing substantially more in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more explicit di: This bucket captures descriptions of formal discipline procedures and unequal student treatment reported in circle reviews—specific detention rituals (writing poems/scripts, copybooks) and allegations that the school ‘‘only focus[es] on the elite’’ or star athletes while average or misunderstood students are overlooked—patterns not emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: This bucket covers reviewer claims that the school offers named rigorous programs and documents measurable academic results — e.g., repeated mentions of IB/MYP, AP and Dual Credit classes, career academies, industry certifications, SAT/ACT/test-score gains, US News/WASC recognition, and concrete college admits — which appear far more often in Circle reviews than in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, named e: This groups descriptions of many specific, institutionally run extracurriculars and community linkages — marching band, top athletics and fan culture, Navy JROTC, strong Ag departments, 'over 100 clubs', formal mentorship/Alumni involvement and life‑skills activities — which Circle reviewers cite frequently compared with Square's more generic extracurricular statements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and sy: This bucket captures concrete allegations about weapons or threats, pervasive bullying, tolerated racial/homophobic/sexist slurs, gender bias, military-family prejudice, and repeated claims that administrators mishandle or ignore victims — patterns emphasized repeatedly in Circle reviews but largely absent or less severe in Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: Includes repeated, concrete operational complaints found in Circle: roaches/rats, broken toilets, poor heating/AC, outdated buses, failed card‑swipe/security rollouts, lost student records that delayed graduation, and alleged corrupt budget/contract practices — an operational cluster far more prominent in Circle than Square.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistentl: This bucket groups reviewer evidence that Square schools tend to report engaged and well‑educated teachers, counselors who are available and proactive, visible/responsive administrators, and an overall orderly/safe atmosphere — recurring positive adult‑support and safety descriptions that contrast with Circle's frequent reports of unresponsive or negligent staff and disorder.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe on-campus safety and conduct problems concentrated in circle schools—e.g., “Bullying is everywhere,” “40+ fights last year,” “huge drug problem…out of control,” metal-detector screening and an on-site cop—whereas square reviews lack comparable, repeated accounts of systemic violence or pervasive bullying.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite governance and operations failures—arbitrary firings and secrecy, favoritism/nepotism, purging failing students and ‘filling out applications’ to inflate metrics, lost/overcharged library books, late/absent bus service, sulfurous water, and questionable budget choices—while square reviews do not contain the same pattern of systemic mismanagement or metric manipulation.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, more c: Square reviews emphasize stable advanced offerings and college outcomes—multiple AP/CTE/dual-credit pathways, students placing out of core classes, college fairs where colleges 'roll out the red carpet,' and reliable AP/IB pathways—whereas circle reviews more often report uneven or cut advanced programs and mixed postsecondary results.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failures in s: Circle reviewers document IEP noncompliance, understaffed/overworked special-ed services, counseling that ‘does nothing’ or is punitive, and students asked to withdraw because mental-health needs were not accommodated—issues that are absent or less frequent in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more insular, cliq: Circle reviews frequently describe tight, sometimes exclusionary local networks—'unless you grow up here you can’t fit in,' teacher/athlete kid privilege, parents described as cliquey, and explicit faith practices/hiring biases (daily prayer, masses, denominational preference)—while square reviews do not foreground that combination of insularity and formal faith-based programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of ongoing fights, assaults (including shootings and ambulance‑level beatings), pervasive bullying, drug/substance problems, theft and vandalism, coerced or ineffective discipline (e.g., bullying ignored by staff, ineffective suspensions), punitive search practices, and restricted/restroom/tardy policies described in Circle reviews (examples: “one student was shot last year,” “fights occur almost everyday,” “Bullying is a huge issue,” locked bathrooms, nontransparent substance testing), contrasts with Square reviews that lack these concrete safety/violence claims or describe active enforcement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger and more: This bucket groups Circle claims of concentrated advanced offerings and outcomes—AP/IB participation, dual‑enrollment/running‑start, specialized STEM/engineering and CTE/JROTC programs, heavy homework and academic pressure, private tutoring dependence, and explicit graduation/college‑readiness metrics (examples: “I took 2 AP classes…5 this year,” “Dual credit…running start,” “99+% college acceptance rate,” heavy nightly homework)—whereas Square reviews rarely cite the same depth of advanced pathways or measurable outcome data.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more frequent admi: This bucket covers Circle reports of systemic governance problems—high superintendent/principal turnover, accusations of district corruption, nepotism (administrators/coaches related), erased yearbook photos, withholding graduation items tied to fundraising, punitive interrogations/fines, collusion among staff, and formal external/state interventions (examples: “Superintendent resigned due to harassment charges,” “they erased his name/photo from the yearbook,” “I eventually had to notify the state board”), while Square reviews do not repeatedly allege this constellation of governance malpractice.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a tuition‑drive: This bucket distinguishes Circle claims that the school operates with tuition/fees, recent capital investment, or state‑of‑the‑art facilities and technology (examples: “tuition is extremely high,” “new and high end school tools,” “best gymnasium, campus stadium”) from Square claims that funding shortfalls and failed levies have produced outdated textbooks, poor science labs, supply shortages, and deferred maintenance (examples: “have not passed a new school levy…cuts have been made,” “textbooks are outdated,” “science labs are so poorly funded”).
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: This bucket groups Square reviews that portray uniformly positive, approachable teachers/staff, active parental support, and community pride (examples: “The principal is very approachable,” “excellent teachers & staff,” “wonderful place to raise a family”), contrasted with Circle reviews that frequently report mixed teacher quality (some exemplary, some demoralized or protected by tenure), variable after‑school support, and split family/community narratives (examples: “There are some great teachers… and some low quality,” “Most teachers have given up hope,” mixed alumni/family endorsements).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize concrete college-prep offerings and results (AP/IB/dual-credit, honors tracks, academies) and frequent alumni scholarship/Ivy‑level placements — e.g., mentions of IB and dual credit, “my daughter accepted to 7/8 colleges,” “my sons... very successful in college,” and “myriad of AP offerings” — while square reviews lack repeated, school‑wide claims of such structured college pathways or systemic high college matriculation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reviews describing pervasive peer violence, bullying, racial slurs, drug use, overdoses, and students leaving for safety/mental‑health reasons — examples include “fights, drug deals in the hallways,” “the amount of racism...outrageous,” students transferring because “my mental health can not handle 2 more years,” and parents pulling kids out due to bullying; square entries rarely document this intensity or frequency of safety/harms.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: These reviews report low student‑teacher ratios, teachers who ‘go the extra mile,’ on‑site therapies and IEP successes, and targeted remediation that produced honors placement — e.g., “class sizes are small... get more one on one time,” “He receives speech therapy at school,” and remediation leading to advanced diplomas — whereas square reviews do not repeatedly portray this level of individualized support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This captures concrete administrative dysfunction: lost transcripts and paperwork, unreturned emails, arbitrary punishments, retaliation, inconsistent rule enforcement tied to parent wealth, and due‑process complaints — e.g., “no one was returning their calls… couldn't get my transcripts,” “administration makes most of the decisions…no say,” and “arbitrarily punished our son” — problems square reviews do not emphasize to the same extent.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater facility: These reviews note both extremes — missing basic instructional materials, sanitation/roach problems, outdated or unused classroom tech, and contested capital projects vs. staff retraining — e.g., “No textbooks,” “roaches throughout the building,” “Classrooms are not equipped with Smart Boards,” and “Millions of dollars for a building that should have been spent on retraining staff,” whereas square reviews seldom report this breadth of resource/maintenance failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a small-school,: These reviews describe concrete practices of small enrollment and continuity (small class sizes, teachers/principal who know students by name, K–12 cohesion, multigenerational alumni ties) and community-driven supports (parents relocating to enroll, local internships, staff who ‘go out of their way’), whereas square entries lack sustained claims of this tight, personalized community.
candidate_defs.square entries report higher measurable: Square reviews cite specific achievement evidence (almost entire classes scoring 5s on APs, students exempting Calc I at selective colleges, high SAT totals, National Merit recognition and strong IB/AP placement), while circle reviews more often reference alternative college pathways or mixed/qualitative college-prep claims rather than these consistent high-test metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete ad: Circle reviewers provide examples of administrators allegedly concealing problems, pocketing funds, forcing good teachers out, repeated unreturned parent contact, formal complaints to district/attorney general, and threatened legal action — patterns of operational/ethical failure that square reviews do not chronically report.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive phy: Circle reviews contain repeated, specific safety claims — unaddressed bullying up to threats to life, gang activity and drug use, frequent suspensions or arbitrary punishments, and staff protecting bullies or favoring athletes — whereas square reviews do not present this same concentrated pattern of severe, institutionally tolerated safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, better‑: Circle reviewers list extensive extracurricular breadth and success (strong music/theater programs, quiz/math teams competing nationally, internships, formal dual‑credit and associate‑degree partnerships, magnet specializations), while square reviews typically report narrower activity lists or highlight AP/honors pathways rather than this wide set of school-based experiential programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report far more student-s: This bucket groups raw terms where circle reviews describe acute safety problems (gangs running the town, shootings, frequent fights, high suicide/community mental‑health risk, pervasive bullying, teen pregnancy, substance abuse) that square reviews do not report; examples include "There is a major issue with gang problems...DO NOT send your child" and "Students would tell me to self harm and kill myself. Nothing was done about it."
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and more: This cluster captures circle reviews that enumerate magnet/CTE/STEM offerings, band, athletics, internships, 1:1 tech, dual‑enrollment/Early College and named honors tracks plus concrete college admissions success (e.g., medical magnet, robotics, internships, 'accepted into every college he applied'), whereas square typically lacks that same level of program breadth or explicit outcome lists.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more governance fa: This bucket covers circle claims about systemic leadership problems and policies—grade‑based disenrollment or kicking out low‑performing students, nepotistic hiring/favoritism, sweeping issues under the rug, calls for state complaints, and active suppression of forums—evidenced by statements like 'they do kicked out for getting below a "C"', 'all the staff is either family or friends', and 'Open forums... taken down because kids are scared.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent da: This bucket groups items where square reviews describe dependable, helpful adults and supports (strong counselors, great special‑education teachers, feeling safe, principal-led initiatives) that circle reviews contrastively lack or dispute—for example, square: 'provides great support for students who may be struggling' and 'I feel safe sending my child', versus circle accounts of little support or failed counseling.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic facil: This captures circle reports of sanitation and pest infestations, overcrowding/logistical congestion, lost records, budget cuts, material shortages, opaque finances, no buses or problematic scheduling and building deficiencies (e.g., 'flying roaches', 'no buses...every child is dropped', 'they don't have enough copies to last the year'), whereas square entries generally do not make these same operational/facility complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: This bucket captures concrete safety and behavior problems described more often in circle reviews — shootings outside campus, gang‑related lockdowns, repeated fights (some ending in hospitalization), drug sales, daily bullying and peer‑collusion — whereas square reviews largely lack gang/violent incident reports and describe fewer sustained bullying claims (examples: “locked down in class for hours” / “kids get jumped...ends up in the hospital” vs. square’s absence of gang/lockdown accounts).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, en: This groups items where circle reviewers praise principals, main office administrators, and prompt problem resolution and parent communication (e.g., “principal was very supportive,” “two men in the main office are the best,” “If there is ever a problem it is always taken care of immediately”), in contrast to square reviewers who report unresponsive or disengaged leadership (e.g., principals not answering emails, secretaries not passing messages).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger teacher: This bucket covers concrete instructional and student‑support practices more frequently reported in circle — caring teachers who provide one‑on‑one help, tutoring, effective special‑education aides/IEP supports, and successful catch‑up/remediation (examples: “teachers commit extra time,” “one of the finest special needs resource program,” “caught him up and worked one on one”), whereas square reviews more often report ignored IEPs, lack of help, or teachers who ‘gave up’.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, higher‑: This groups concrete programmatic strengths emphasized in circle reviews — award‑winning band/drama, state championship sports, specialized tracks (AICE/Cambridge/IB, CTE, JROTC, magnet programs), college‑credit opportunities and internship/travel pathways — while square reviews mention fewer high‑profile awards and less program breadth (examples: “Carnegie Hall‑quality choir,” “Cambridge Program…AICE Diploma,” “boys varsity soccer state championships”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more chronic facil: This bucket captures repeated, concrete operational complaints in circle reviews — severe overcrowding, antiquated computers/textbooks, broken HVAC/roof leaks, pest problems, withheld textbooks/transcript fines and visible budget shortfalls — which contrast with square reviews that rarely describe such pervasive facility decay or resource deprivation (examples: “no air conditioning…rooms in the 90's,” “computers out of date,” “we are over crowded,” “desperate need of new computers”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These items describe concrete safety problems (daily fights, physical assaults, police involvement, pepper‑spraying, on‑campus drug dealing, sexual/physical harm to special‑needs students) that circle reviewers name as routine or trauma‑level (e.g., “fight nearly every day,” “repetitive drug use/deals on school grounds,” ambulance called after wrestler slammed a girl), whereas square reviews lack or minimize such pervasive violent/drug incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: Circle reviewers frequently list formal college‑prep structures and quantified outcomes—AP/IB/Honors availability, dual‑enrollment and university partnerships (e.g., 60 free college hours through Morehead State, St. John’s affiliation), required senior college acceptances, scholarship totals and elite acceptances—giving specific programmatic and outcome evidence that square reviews typically do not provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible, proa: Circle content often points to named principals, district‑placed leadership turnarounds, active parent foundations, PTA/fundraising, alumni mobilization and community oversight (e.g., “new principal… one shining light,” “building tremendous parent and community involvement,” alumni calls to ‘take back our campus’), while square reviews rarely foreground sustained principal visibility or organized community governance.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more favoritism, i: Many circle reviewers document selective enforcement and exclusionary policies—athlete/donor/nepotistic favoritism, punitive dress‑code and tuition‑linked sanctions (withholding cap/gown), biased discipline against non‑athletes or poorer families, and suppression of dissent (e.g., ‘athletes are regarded highest’, ‘withholding graduation cap and gown for unpaid tuition’), issues that square reviews do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more identity‑and‑: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe a clear institutional identity or specialized program mix—faith formation and Catholic identity, fine‑arts magnet curricula, JROTC/military partnerships, agricultural/CTE shops and vocational pathways—that shape daily life and offerings (e.g., ‘ACTIVELY live their faith’, ‘Fine arts is a major concentration’, ‘almost half of the school is in JROTC’), whereas square reviews rarely present such strong single‑theme program identities.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket captures reports of on‑campus assaults, gang activity, dozens of fights, death threats and a stabbing—often paired with administrators who ignore victims, isolate bullied kids (e.g., forced independent study), or punish victims under zero‑tolerance. Representative evidence: “received serious DEATH threats from varsity football players,” “about 15 fights this year,” “i got shanked at this school,” and accounts that “administrators stood back watching” or “bullying is not addressed.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive a: This bucket groups mentions of high‑level academic offerings (IB, many AP/honors, dual‑enrollment), concrete metrics and scholarship outcomes, and organized in‑school help (math centers, mandatory tutoring windows, 1:1 device rollouts). Representative evidence: “IB Program is exceptional,” “earned nearly $1,000,000 in scholarships,” “math center…library which offers help in every subject,” “1:1 technology program…MacBooks and iPads,” and requests for AP/SAT/ACT pass‑rate statistics.
candidate_defs.square entries report more responsive, v: This bucket captures square reviews that highlight accessible principals, prompt parent communication, and teachers who provide relevant, timely feedback and meet parents’ requests—contrasting with circle complaints about non‑response. Representative evidence: Square: “Teachers are accessible… Feedback provided to parents is relevant and timely,” “Leslie Alexander is a great principal,” and “the principal is visible, approachable, and accessible,” versus circle accounts of unanswered emails and blocked communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater staff and: This bucket groups systemic personnel and governance problems described in circle entries: tenured/unaccountable teachers, alleged union/administrator collusion, nepotistic hiring, teacher misconduct and workplace bullying, frequent principal changes and mass teacher departures. Representative evidence: “most of the teachers were tenured and were unconcerned,” “the union representative…root of discord,” “Everyone's related…if one teacher doesn’t like you you’re pretty much done,” and “we've had 4 principals since I’ve been at this school…teachers do not stay there.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, better‑re: This bucket captures circle descriptions of rich non‑academic programming and infrastructure—extensive CTE/shop offerings, award‑winning performing arts, competitive athletics, specialized facilities and media/tech labs—plus community resource signals such as active alumni networks, donor influence, waitlists/selective admissions, and tuition. Representative evidence: “Students earn valuable trade knowledge…half the year split with shop,” “Vox chorus won at 2012 World Choir Games,” “three theatre spaces, two gyms, a professional dance studio and a pool,” “The Class of 2014 received more than $5 million in scholarship offers,” and “about 120 spots open each year for 1,500 applications” or explicit tuition/donor impacts on discipline/playing time.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more advanced ac: This bucket groups excerpts where circle reviews name concrete advanced offerings and outcomes (AP/dual‑enrollment, STEM/Honors diplomas, concurrent credit with a university) and cite measurable postsecondary results (students graduating with AP credit, cum laude alumni, large scholarships, accreditation/distinction). Examples: circle mentions 'many AP as well as concurrent college credit classes with Arkansas State', 'students graduate with college credit', 'graduated cum laude', and 'accredited with distinction', whereas square reviews lack such concrete program-level credit/outcome claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more individuali: This bucket captures claims of teacher‑level practices and classroom structure: one‑to‑one help, teachers staying after, daily lunch help, low student‑teacher ratios, and open-door tutoring policies that enable individualized progress. Examples: circle notes 'teachers willing to stay after just to help', 'classes are small so I can get individual help', 'continuous open door policies -- early morning, after school and weekend tutoring', while square does not report these routine individualized supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket includes reports of pervasive safety incidents and inadequate responses—student fights, in‑class drug use, thefts, gang activity, sexual harassment mishandling, and allegations that staff/administration tolerate or ignore misconduct. Examples: circle states 'kids literally did drugs in class', 'there is so many fights', 'bullying is horrible and the administration does nothing', and 'severe gang problem', whereas square reviews generally do not describe this level of chronic violence or staff inaction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups complaints about leadership and policy: frequent principal/superintendent turnover, administrators who don't return calls or lack transparency, punitive demerit systems with no appeals, SRO citations for minor infractions, nepotistic hiring, and claims administration prioritizes money/levies over student welfare. Examples: circle cites 'new superintendent, principal, everything', 'admin offices sometimes don't answer phones', 'no transparency, targeting (scapegoating)', 'most all employees and teachers are related', and 'all my school cares about is money', while square provides fewer or opposite leadership‑failure claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries mention more concrete fac: This bucket covers tangible infrastructure and operational matters—busing/transportation breakdowns, lunchroom overcrowding, lack of textbooks or lockers, distribution of laptops/SmartBoards, on‑site health clinics, new campus or performing‑arts buildings, extracurricular fees and space limits, and vocational/career academy certifications. Examples: circle reports 'on‑campus clinic run by a certified nurse', 'School of choice forms... will even bus into Hesperia', 'Every child is given a laptop... every classroom has a SmartBoard', 'no textbooks', 'new campus is beautiful', and 'basketball has $125 transportation fee', whereas square rarely provides this level of concrete operational/facility detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger, more str: This bucket captures differences where Square reviews name explicit, school-run advanced programs and demonstrable postsecondary outcomes (numerous AP courses, IB/programs, GT/Project Lead the Way, dual-enrollment credits, counselor-led college support, and US News rankings), whereas Circle reviews more often lack that programmatic breadth or outcome evidence (Circle sometimes reports limited AP/IB/dual options or poor college readiness). Examples: Square cites numerous AP/dual-credit offerings and RIT/college credits and students admitted to top colleges; Circle often reports 'only 2 classes' for gifted students or 'did not prepare me for college.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failures in s: This bucket groups reviews describing systemic denial, slow implementation, or mismanagement of special-education services (IEPs/504s not followed, long delays, inadequate special‑needs classroom supports, parents forced to fight bureaucracy or remove their children). Examples include explicit statements like 'Does not follow through with IEPs,' 'don't expect [a 504 plan] to be followed,' and 'special class is a joke,' all more frequent in Circle reviews than in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reports of recurrent fights, gang/safety warnings, homophobia/racism/sexism, abusive coaching or teacher bullying, and either neglectful or overly punitive disciplinary responses (e.g., rumor-based expulsions, harsh detentions, or administrators who ignore incidents). Illustrative Circle claims: 'vicious acts of physical violence go unchecked,' 'Being queer means constantly looking over your shoulder,' 'drama is NONSTOP,' and reports of frequent fights and abusive detention conditions — patterns less apparent in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers reviewer claims about school leadership and governance problems: principals or central office not returning calls, frequent leadership turnover, nepotistic hiring/favoritism, administration refusing to discipline staff or protecting athletes, and opaque decision‑making. Examples include 'refuse[s] to take disciplinary action against him,' 'many teachers are former graduates... hiring relatives,' 'leadership changes too frequently,' and 'no one ever returns phone calls,' all concentrated in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: This bucket groups tangible, day‑to‑day infrastructure and operational failures described in reviews: closed/unsanitary bathrooms, last-minute bus service cuts, multiple classroom trailers, outdated or missing technology, poor cafeteria food, cancelled programs, fundraising with unclear accounting, and shortened instructional days. Representative Circle items: 'bathrooms... no locks,' 'letter one day before school—bus gone,' 'students had no access to computers first semester,' and 'where has all the fundraising money gone?' — issues rarely raised in Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, in: These reviews emphasize small class sizes, routine one‑on‑one time, teachers who stay after school or tutor, active counselors/guidance that walk families through college steps, and regular school‑to‑home outreach (weekly emails, calls, online grade access). Examples include descriptions of 10‑student classes and teachers who 'go above and beyond,' guided step‑by‑step college counseling, and active principal visibility — patterns that Square reviews do not assert.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These comments call out leadership problems (nepotism, naming superintendents/principals, selective enforcement, manipulating admissions/rosters, union/board politics) and ask for board‑level personnel change; they describe opaque fee practices and threats to expel students. Square reviews may criticize management broadly but do not contain the detailed allegations of favoritism, enrollment selection, or targeted governance misconduct found in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviewers repeatedly document physical and safety incidents on campus — sustained bullying ignored by staff, constant fighting, on‑site drug dealing and overdoses, sexual activity in parking lots, theft of personal medical items, and unsecured front‑door procedures — and often claim these issues were not remedied. Square reviews mention cliques or isolated misconduct but do not present the same frequency or severity of unresolved safety threats.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete, d: Circle reviews disproportionately list tangible program offerings and outcomes — extensive AP/honors tracks, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit partnerships, CTE/FFA vocational programs with awards and scholarship dollar totals, and alumni college/career success metrics — whereas Square reviews rarely supply these concrete programmatic or long‑term outcome details. This bucket captures both vocational/CTE success stories and detailed college‑prep evidence (credits earned, scholarships, state/national competition awards) that Circle reviewers often cite.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more detailed acc: Circle reviewers give specific physical and extracurricular evidence — from large auditoriums, greenhouses/FFA farms and active band programs to complaints about expired food, rising lunch costs, broken computers, mobile classrooms by sewage ponds, overcrowded classes, and booster fundraising dynamics — and also note uneven funding priorities (athletics vs. arts). Square reviews discuss programs and spirit at a higher level but lack the same granularity about facilities, meal service, maintenance, and program funding patterns reported in Circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: This captures reviews where circle schools list concrete advanced-course programs and outcomes (AP/IB offerings, dual‑enrollment, 40+ college credits, IB diplomas, claims of high selective‑college matriculation or specific AP/engineering programs) while square reviews lack program detail or school‑level college outcome data; e.g., Circle: “There are lots of AP classes and the IB program,” “100% four‑year college matriculation to highly selective & Ivy League,” vs Square: no comparable AP/IB/programmatic evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This groups concrete safety complaints that circle reviewers raise (on‑campus drug use and smell, frequent fights, sexual assaults allegedly ignored by staff, off‑campus assaults spilling into school, gang protection claims) contrasted with square reviews that either omit such severe incidents or mention only bullying/fights without sexual assault or pervasive drug use; e.g., Circle: “There is a horrible drug problem… ignored by administration,” “Several sexual assaults… with no action from the staff.”
candidate_defs.circle entries document systemic favorit: These reviews allege structural governance problems at circle schools—blatant nepotism, political interference in hiring/selection, administrators protecting some students, unequal enforcement of rules, public humiliation over unpaid fees, withholding records or refunds—distinct from frontline teacher behavior and from isolated operational failures; e.g., Circle: “blatant nepotism, palm greasing,” “they would have withheld his records,” “people the principal and office staff like get away with things.”
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize named, attentiv: This bucket groups cases where square reviews single out individual teachers/counselors by name, describe hands‑on mentoring, effective college guidance, inclusive club access, and responsive communication (e.g., Mrs. Milburn, Mr. McComb, library support, teachers who 'go out of their way' or act as mentors), whereas circle entries more often omit these specific, named frontline endorsements or describe inconsistent teacher follow‑through; e.g., Square: “Mrs. Milburn is a great... Mrs. Morgan,” “teachers go out of their way to create a special learning environment.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: This groups concrete descriptions from circle reviews of many clubs, no‑cut athletics, extensive sports teams, strong school spirit, parent volunteerism and alumni attachment (marching band, JROTC, many sports, community uplift), contrasted with square reviews that rarely enumerate broad extracurricular offerings and instead focus on classroom/facility complaints; e.g., Circle: “many and varied extra curricular opportunities,” “golf, wrestling, marching band… MUCH more,” “very good school spirit.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This bucket groups raw terms where circle schools describe concrete advanced offerings (AP, IB, dual‑enrollment, CTE/robotics), higher rigor, and documented college placement or scholarship totals (examples: IB pathway and guaranteed scholarships, AP classes and 5 scores, dual enrollment and biomedical/Criminal Justice programs, large scholarship totals and multiple college acceptances), while square reviews lack or underreport those measurable advanced-program outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of pervasive physical violence and criminalized student behavior in circle reviews — daily fights, weapons, gang bullying, drug use/solicitations, theft and sexual harassment (examples: 'many frightening instances of drug use, gang-related bullying, and daily fights'; 'student asked my son if he knew where to get drugs'; reports of weapons and shooting history) — contrasted with square reviews that emphasize bullying or occasional safety issues but not the same level of violence or substance/gang problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize more extensive,: This bucket groups mentions of broad, competitive extracurricular infrastructure in circle reviews — top‑notch band, large theater programs, UIL/athletic championships, award‑winning CTE and robotics, state‑of‑the‑art campuses and recent renovations (examples: 'amazing theater program', 'gorgeous 100 acre campus', 'top‑notch Band', 'state of the art new Athletic Field') — whereas square reviews rarely report comparable breadth, competitive recognition, or major facility investments.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects claims of problematic governance from circle reviews — principals favoring athletes/teacher children or wealthy families, nepotistic hiring, retaliatory firings of dissenting teachers, dishonest communication, and punitive financial/privilege withholding (examples: 'Principal fired all the teachers who raised concerns', 'Unless you're a football player or a teacher's offspring you will be treated terrible', 'miss a tuition payment and privileges are withheld') — contrasted with square reviews which critique leadership but do not feature the same breadth of alleged nepotism/retaliation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failures or e: This bucket groups reports from circle reviews about inadequate IEP/SE integration, frequent restraints and behavioral crises, counselors avoiding struggling students, and lack of mental‑health supports (examples: 'emotional special needs program causing disruption', 'code greens went off almost every day', 'no support for students with Depression, Anxiety, ADD', 'counselor has not returned messages in 9 months'), while square reviews more often describe at least some individualized attention or responsive counseling.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more frequent an: This bucket covers reports of daily fights, police presence/arrests, assaults (inside and off campus), pervasive bullying (including homophobic/racist targeting), vaping/drug use, and victims being punished or pushed out — e.g., “fights everyday… police are there almost every day,” “He was beaten… at the train station,” “Homophobia and Racism is common,” and victims punished while perpetrators are not. Items here signal acute safety/discipline failures and direct student‑harm incidents that reviewers attribute to school practice or neglect.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups complaints about leadership, board-level dysfunction, cover‑ups, donor/nepotism influence, coercive fundraising, mass end‑of‑year staff firings, and front‑office inaccessibility — e.g., “school has never owned up… a 'circle the wagons' approach,” “pander[ing] to the rich families for donations,” “weak school board and weak Superintendent,” and “voice mail is always full.” These are systemic governance and culture problems distinct from classroom instruction.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete career: This bucket captures descriptions of named vocational shops, career academies, offsite tech partners, dual enrollment/college‑credit accumulation, and internships — e.g., automotive/culinary shops, 'Pickens Tech… go to Aurora for 1/2 the day,' 'graduated from Pace with 36 college credits,' 'partnered with the Cleveland Clinic,' and 'High Tech Academy.' Items here indicate explicit career-orientation and external partnership programming that reviewers can point to.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger formal: This bucket includes references to broad AP/honors offerings, high college‑matriculation rates and specific outcome metrics or rankings — e.g., 'They have great AP classes,' '95% of students who attend this school go on to college,' and 'recognized by Newsweek as the top 1000 schools.' These are structured, quantifiable academic-program and outcome claims that signal college‑prep rigor at the school/district level.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater variability: This bucket captures reports of frequent teacher turnover or inexperienced hires, tenure‑protected underperformance, last‑minute grade changes or aggressive grading policies, ineffective tutoring/college counseling, and both very small class sizes/one-on-one attention or overcrowding — e.g., 'well over half the staff has been let go,' 'aggressive grading system and more credits required,' 'This is not tutoring… just checking into a room,' and 'there are fewer kids in each class so teachers give one on one attention.' These items concern classroom staffing, pedagogy, grading practices and remedial supports rather than governance or program type.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe, varie: This bucket captures accounts of physical violence, frequent fights, drug and alcohol use, sexual exploitation, theft, weapons/arrests, pervasive bullying witnessed by adults, students roaming/secretive behavior, and claims that such incidents are ignored or mishandled (examples: “drugs, fights, smoking in bathrooms,” “students’ suicides are largely ignored,” “Theft is a major issue,” “locks kids in room with police,” and “My child was beaten up several times, teachers simply turned their backs”).
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, better-doc: This bucket groups claims of distinct magnet tracks, vocational pathways, dual‑enrollment, high‑profile arts/music/competition programs, measurable metrics and college/career outcomes (examples: “culinary, PCA (medical), Beta Tech… dual-enrollment college classes,” “students qualified for Intel ISEF,” “98% matriculation,” “graduates finishing associate degrees before high school,” and named awards/rankings), whereas square entries rarely supply these concrete program/outcome details.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more ind: This bucket covers explicit reports of teachers giving individualized attention, quick email responses, manageable homework loads, small class sizes, and proactive multi‑teacher intervention meetings (examples: “Teachers give the students a lot of individual attention,” “they always respond back quick,” “called a meeting with all his teacher… to come up with a plan”), contrasted with square entries that emphasize unprofessional or disengaged teaching, poor instruction, or lack of remediation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible admin: This bucket groups reports of principal/board unresponsiveness, censorship and punitive suppression (newspaper censorship, cancelling traditions), nepotism/favoritism (parents employed by district or athlete favoritism), repeated leadership turnover, and contested discipline policies (examples: “run off over half the teachers in three years,” “She censors the newspaper,” “The only way to get your child 'ahead' is if you work there,” and “weak board… leadership in this school is terrible”), distinguishing these governance and policy failures from square’s reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete com: This bucket collects statements about neighborhood wealth/poverty patterns, constrained school choice for low‑income families, enrollment decline/closure risk, facility quality or overcrowding, meal/food details, mandated device purchases and fees, and busing/safety complaints (examples: “an impoverished school district,” “I’m stuck… because we’re poor,” “parking is a nightmare; school too full,” “$700 for iPad… connectivity issues,” and “bus stop 2 houses away… walks 4 miles a day”), which are more frequently and concretely described in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: This bucket groups reports of physical/psychological harm, pervasive bullying, drug/fight exposure, tolerated hateful symbols, and frequent incidents where staff either fail to intervene or respond inadequately (examples: "9 girls jump my daughter… the staff did nothing," "Students are exposed to drugs and there are many fights!", "If your child is LGBTQ they will get suspended... administration is extremely homophobic", and near‑weekly lockdowns). These items describe concrete safety failures and victimization patterns inside the building rather than tone or reviewer style.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, ath: This bucket covers claims that discipline and rewards are applied unequally because of family ties, athletic status, or internal protectionism — including staff/administrator favoritism, corrupt evaluations, and selective enforcement (examples: "A student must have the correct last name or go to church… A lot of favoritism goes on", "He will let the athletes get away with murder", "administration is so corrupt that they evaluate these teachers with 100% each and every year"). These items are about biased personnel and enforcement practices distinct from isolated safety incidents or instructional quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: This bucket groups detailed programmatic evidence such as many AP/honors courses, Dual Enrollment and college credit partnerships, vocational/trade programs, ROTC/JROTC, and named college/ scholarship outcomes (examples: "offers many APs… Dual Enrollment… partnerships with Coppin", "brick laying, autobody, welding… students leave with careers", "my daughter achieved 3 APs and a place at an Ivy league school", and multiple band/JROTC state successes). These items are about explicit curricular offerings, credential pathways, and documented student outcomes rather than general academic impressions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more problems with: This bucket captures claims about inexperienced or unqualified hires, widespread poor pedagogy, grade‑manipulation or unreliable grading, teacher verbal abuse or unprofessional classroom behavior, and extreme homework/expectations (examples: "They get new teachers out of college who dont know anything at all", "Tons of the teachers have no idea what they're doing", "We know Dekalb school is known for writing false grade", and "average three hours of homework every night"). These items concern classroom instruction and assessment integrity distinct from available programs or facility issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This bucket groups tangible operational problems and resource signals such as chronic overcrowding/parking shortages, transportation/bus unreliability, mold/AC/maintenance, dated parent portals and missed emergency notifications, plus also visible capital investments (new athletic fields, 1:1 devices) described concretely (examples: "overcrowded… 110% capacity… almost 3000 students", "My bus is late 20 to 30 minutes", "the parent portal… highly dated and rarely updated", "the school has mold", and "1:1 iPad wireless learning system"). These items describe the school's physical capacity, maintenance, tech deployment, and parent‑school operational processes rather than pedagogy or interpersonal culture.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe concrete, repeated safety failures inside the building and on transport—e.g., “kids with guns…they fight almost every day,” metal detectors, active gang presence, drug distribution, death threats, wrongful arrests, and pervasive bullying—whereas square entries either omit such incidents or only mention milder discipline concerns. Inclusion in this bucket means the school narrative centers on persistent, serious threats to student physical safety and daily order rather than isolated infractions.
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger, measur: These circle reviews name specific programmatic offerings and outcomes (AP, Pre‑AP, Dual Enrollment, PSAT access), quantified scholarship or ranking claims (e.g., millions in scholarships, high SAT averages, Newsweek national rank), and concrete college/Dean’s‑list placements, while square entries lack comparable program detail or measurable student outcomes. Put another way, texts in this bucket foreground formal advanced coursework and demonstrable post‑secondary results rather than only aspirational or vague college readiness statements.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic favo: These accounts allege patterned unfairness—teachers favoring wealthy or popular students, administrators protecting ‘good old boy’ students (contracts not renewed for teachers who grade them down), selective enforcement, and claims of retaliation or hiring based on connections—while square entries do not portray such entrenched, network‑based gatekeeping. Materials in this bucket emphasize institutional bias and unequal access tied to relationships or status rather than routine individual staff mistakes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: Reviews here describe concrete shortages and hazards—no textbooks, outdated/absent lab resources, roaches and lab health hazards, denied lunches, lost attendance/IEP paperwork, bus transport failures, and broken/aging buildings—whereas square entries rarely report such pervasive material or operational breakdowns. Inclusion means the school is portrayed as constrained or unsafe because of physical, supply, or process failures that directly impair instruction and student welfare.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger extrac: These circle reviews highlight nationally or regionally distinguished extracurriculars (national marching band champions, state athletic achievements, high marching‑band participation), active PTO/parents’ associations, multi‑generational alumni ties, and parental sacrifices to remain in zone, sometimes paired with claims that athletics are prioritized over academics (e.g., labs removed for weight rooms). Texts in this bucket center programmatic prominence, participation, and community/parental engagement as defining school features rather than focusing primarily on core instructional quality.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: These entries repeatedly name concrete program breadth and outcomes—multiple AP/honors and IB references, extensive dual‑enrollment and CTE pathways, 1:1 device or Chromebook programs, high ACT/Bright Flight/first‑choice acceptances, and explicit graduation/college‑matriculation rates (e.g., AP/dual credit lists, “98% go to college,” “both my kids got above a 31 on the ACT”) that square entries do not provide or that square reviewers say are lacking.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more on‑campus saf: Many circle reviews cite vivid safety problems and responses—frequent fights, documented threats and lockdowns (with dates), pervasive drug/tobacco use, metal detectors/cameras, monthly drug‑dog searches and arrests—while square entries generally lack comparable descriptions of recurring security incidents or such intensive enforcement measures.
candidate_defs.square entries report more punitive, uns: Square entries more often describe administrators as unempathetic or punitive (e.g., principals 'unempathetic', 'admin is HORRIFIC', enforcement that denies privileges or treats students like criminals), examples of punitive grading/denial of excused absences, and staff behavior framed as disciplinarian or adversarial—patterns of leadership/discipline failure that reviewers contrast with more collaborative handling in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger parent/PT: Circle reviews frequently highlight active PTSA/PTSO involvement, visible parental boards and outreach, intergenerational alumni ties, and even successful local referenda or political backing to keep schools open—concrete community engagement signals (e.g., 'PTSO is AWESOME', 87% referendum yes, alumni returning) largely absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Many circle reviewers describe teachers who 'go the extra mile,' small class sizes, counselors who actively schedule and assist students, and an institutional emphasis on remediation/support for struggling students (examples: counseling staff 'truly cares', teachers who raise grades from C→A, explicit remediation/alternative‑placement missions) whereas square entries more often describe lack of such personalized supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger measurabl: These reviews emphasize quantifiable academic success and formal advanced pathways (AP/IB/dual‑enrollment/vocational academy) — e.g., 100% graduation claims, AP pass rates, dual‑credit transfer to Rutgers, high district/state test rankings, and named college‑prep programs — while square entries tend to lack sustained metrics or describe only anecdotal/partial AP offerings.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater teacher: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe teachers who stay after to tutor, small class ratios and personalized attention, active parent volunteers/boosters, and multi‑generational feeder ties (named beloved teachers, alumni success stories), whereas square entries more often report uneven teacher quality, higher churn, and less pervasive community/alumni continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle texts include concrete incidents of student fights, weapons, drug overdoses, staff‑on‑student bullying, victim‑blaming administrators, unequal punishments tied to donor/athlete status, and opaque/biased discipline codes, while square entries rarely document such systemic safety or favoritism failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic admi: Circle reviewers allege chronic leadership mismanagement (decades of poor culture, misused funds, union conflicts), high teacher turnover, and material shortages or facility failures (broken HVAC, overcrowded/mobile classrooms, unsanitary bathrooms, understaffed cafeterias, missing supplies), whereas square entries make fewer or less severe claims about deep, system‑level governance and resource collapse.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more effective a: Square reviews more often praise concrete supports (IEP/IEP‑like help, helpful drop‑out prevention counselors, successful IEP accommodations), recent leadership/renovation improvements, and broad elective/extracurricular options, contrasting with circle entries that frequently report lack of such reliable administrative follow‑through and accommodations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger measurabl: This bucket groups raw items in which circle reviews claim concrete academic credentials and pathways (e.g., ‘named a 4‑Star School by the DOE,’ ‘30–40 kids get into top colleges / Ivy admits,’ ‘wide variety of AP courses,’ ‘AP in junior high, dual enrollment’) and contrast them with square reviews that omit those objective outcomes or emphasize weaker college guidance; it captures claims about scholarships, top‑college matriculation, advanced‑course breadth and official awards.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket collects items where circle reviews describe pervasive safety problems and misconduct (e.g., ‘sexual assault, bullying, and racial bias are rampant and under addressed,’ ‘girls getting groped in packed hallways,’ ‘security guards injured students,’ repeated fights, racial slurs and staff inaction), contrasted with square reviews that either do not report or present far fewer such severe incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more consistent: This bucket covers raw terms where circle reviewers emphasize teacher professionalism and availability (e.g., ‘teachers hold extra tutoring after school,’ ‘teachers found to be professional and caring,’ ‘small class sizes, students known as individuals,’ ‘timely Skyward/robo‑call communication’), while square entries in the paired comparisons tend to report mixed or deteriorating staff engagement and weaker parent/admin responsiveness.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility/tech: This bucket groups items where circle reviews call out capital investments and resourcing or explicit money policies (e.g., ‘new extension/renovation and STEAM/biomedical plans,’ ‘school‑issued Chromebooks/1:1 deployment,’ ‘6000 dollar tuition and separate lunch fees with transcript‑holds for unpaid debt’) contrasted with square reviews that emphasize budget shortfalls, older campus buildings, or do not mention such investments or formal tuition‑consequence policies.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a stronger extr: This bucket captures circle claims about dominant extracurricular profiles and community identity (e.g., ‘school spirit / “Once a rebel” / tight alumni job pipelines,’ ‘athletic favoritism – athletes treated differently,’ ‘state‑level teams and powerhouse music programs,’ and many named clubs/arts trips), set against square reviews that either highlight different program mixes or lack the same level of community/athletic prioritization and legacy networks.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student-safet: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and enforcement extremes (e.g., students 'followed after school & beaten bloody,' 'drugs are running rampant,' reports of 'no security,' and '50 day suspensions for minor dress code violations') and also allege that bullying is frequently ignored or only addressed for well‑connected families — patterns not present in the Square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger selective: Many Circle reviews point to formal college‑prep offerings and outcomes (national scholarships, National Merit/strong SAT/ACT/AP performance, IB/AP pipelines, AVID, dual‑enrollment and named program partnerships) and selective admissions/lotteries, framing high academic rigor and measurable results that Square reviews do not provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviewers allege centralized, heavy‑handed leadership and dysfunctional governance (e.g., 'principal handles things "in house"', administrators 'threaten to sue parents', school board 'chose politics over CDC guidance', refusal to accept responsibility or follow confidentiality/legal requirements'), highlighting cover‑ups and legal/disciplinary mishandling absent from Square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: Circle reviews repeatedly enumerate wide extracurricular breadth and competitive achievements (marching band top rankings, strong theatre/choir, many clubs, vocational/hospital partnerships) while simultaneously accusing the school of favoring athletes (preferential grading/selection and resource allocation to sports) — contrasts that Square reviews rarely make.
candidate_defs.square entries report more teacher disen: Square reviews more often describe teachers as unresponsive or overwhelmed ('teachers are puppets', 'all the teachers I knew have left', slow grading, inconsistent help) and report instructional neglect and failure to protect students from harassment, whereas Circle reviews contain many accounts of engaged, stable, or named effective teachers and structured student supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, broader: These reviews describe concrete, school-run academic offerings and results (e.g., many AP classes, IB adoption, dual/concurrent enrollment with transferable college credit, high numbers of college acceptances and national awards) that circle reviewers cite as evidence of real college/career preparation; square reviews by contrast raise gaps in rigor or give no comparable quantified college‑credit/IB/AP success stories.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more robust extr: Circle reviewers repeatedly name strong arts and vocational programs, well‑supported athletics, recent capital projects, alumni/endowment backing, and concrete facilities/technology (gorgeous auditorium, stadium builds, K‑12 iPads), whereas square reviews rarely cite comparable resource depth and often point to program cuts or aging facilities.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize more personaliz: Circle reviews frequently highlight small class sizes, individualized placement/customized courses, approachable mentors, abundant teacher outreach (phone calls/parent meetings), and direct examples of staff helping disadvantaged students; square reviews more often report impersonal large campuses or lack of timely teacher outreach.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: Square reviewers commonly point to systemic instructional problems—teachers who 'don't teach', frequent poor substitutes, low classroom rigor, cancelled honors/SAT prep, overcrowded classes and coordination failures—painting a picture of uneven or declining instructional quality not as strongly claimed in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater administra: Many circle reviews allege concrete governance failures—administrative unresponsiveness, tenure‑protected staff, refusal to follow IEP/504s or investigate complaints, selective disciplinary practices, nepotistic hires, and board/donor politics—that produce unequal treatment or legal threats; square reviews do not center these same patterns as frequently or as explicitly.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and loss of classroom control at circle schools (e.g., 'fights almost every day', gang presence, weekly lockdowns, metal detectors, robberies, students smoking in bathrooms, 'over 40 school shooting threats'), and repeatedly tie those to ineffective disciplinary response; square reviews do not contain comparable clusters of ongoing violent/disorder incidents or frequent police lockdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, organized: Circle reviews catalogue extensive program breadth and external links—vocational shops and CTE (welding, culinary, ROTC), many clubs and arts ensembles, state athletic championships, AP/dual‑enrollment/early‑college offerings, internships and hospital/college partnerships, laptop programs, and named scholarship/college‑placement metrics—whereas square reviews seldom list that range of CTE/partnerships or concrete outcome statistics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Multiple circle reviewers cite front‑office rudeness, unanswered emails, scheduling errors, misplacement of students or classes, inconsistent attendance/grade tracking, frequent leadership turnover, coverups, and even legal escalation ('had to take the attorney general to get involved'), while square reviews rarely describe this pattern of chronic administrative breakdown and poor parent communication.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more favoritism, n: Circle reviews frequently allege explicit preferential treatment (athletes/connected families get leniency), nepotism and staff–parent conflicts of interest, selective/lottery enrollment or expulsions to manage ratings, manipulated student elections, and wealth/race‑based clique exclusion—claims that are largely absent or far less pronounced in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries depict a more punitive, r: Square reviewers emphasize a prison‑like or highly punitive atmosphere (e.g., 'going to Wilson is like going to jail', cancelled pep rallies, strict enforcement of passes/planners) combined with insufficient individualized remediation and counseling—statements like 'guidance is pretty limited', 'teachers snap if you ask for help', and 'does not prepare kids for college'—a pattern of rigid discipline plus poor student support that circle reviews do not emphasize in the same way.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more proactive, ca: These reviews describe concrete, student-facing instructional and support behaviors — e.g., teachers who stay late, provide daily progress updates, run lunch/after-school tutoring, accommodate IEPs, mentor students, and deliver small-class individualized help — contrasts Square comments that emphasize uneven or uncaring teachers. Representative lines: “administration has been very accommodating for our daughter academic needs including placing her in the advanced classes ahead of schedule in order to meet the guidelines of her IEP,” “teachers stayed late, worked through lunches and created extra help groups,” and “The majority of the teachers truly care…They go above and beyond.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more school/distri: These items focus on top‑level problems and policy failures — e.g., calls to remove superintendents/principals, accusations of reverse‑racism or politicized hires, missing student funds, cancelled capital projects, and explicit recommendations for board takeovers — patterns less evident in Square. Examples: “the School Board and principal have begun destroying everything good,” “Now if we can just get rid of the superintendent,” and “money paid by students for 'dues' vanishes into thin air.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent seve: These reviews document acute safety incidents and enforcement lapses — gang formation, pervasive physical attacks, sexual harassment and inappropriate exposure, repeated bullying that staff fail to stop, and security-staff incompetence — whereas Square contains only isolated or less severe bullying/attendance complaints. Illustrative excerpts: “the violence in this school is so high that gangs are formed,” “Bullying, sexual harassment, are rampant,” and “there is no security on campus and our level of protection is extremely low.”
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more concrete fac: These reviews include tangible, operational facts or problems — e.g., $23M upgrades and new science wings, smart boards and iPads, online grade portals, portable classrooms after a cancelled expansion, 4‑day weeks/‘9th hour’ tutoring, and concrete sanitation/transportation/cafeteria complaints — content Square rarely supplies. Examples: “the building is new, clean, and loaded with the latest and greatest technology,” “planned expansion was nixed…in favor of more mobiles,” “we have an intervention period every Wednesday,” and “Bathrooms smell like fish, and raw sewage…roaches.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete student-safety harms and daily disorder (frequent fights, weapons/bomb threats, on-campus drug/sexual activity, filmed privacy violations, suicidal crises) and allege that school responses are inadequate—e.g., “FIGHTS daily,” “police are there constantly, bomb threats,” “lots of drugs and illegal activities,” and bullying that forced students to transfer—whereas square entries do not document this level or frequency of safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: This captures claims about formal, high‑level academic offerings and outcomes (many AP/IB courses, STEM academies, early‑college/NAF IT partnerships, 100% graduation/major scholarships, conservatory/elite college placements), e.g. “With over 25 AP courses,” “opening a STEM Academy,” “full ride scholarship to OSU,” and “students attend Notre Dame and MIT,” while square entries lack comparable, concrete program metrics or elite college‑placement claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: Includes reports of low student:teacher ratios, teachers who know students personally and provide proactive mentorship/tutoring/extra help (e.g., “small school…teachers dedicate more time,” “teachers involved themselves with my education,” “tutoring, extra credit, study sessions”), in contrast to square entries which more often describe mixed or less individualized teacher attention.
candidate_defs.square entries report more systemic admi: This bucket groups concrete operational problems centered on administration and systems—e.g., office staff who 'rarely answer phones,' guidance counselors who 'refuse to sign me up' or 'give useless classes,' ignored IEP/ARD plans, vacant science/CTE teachers, chaotic scheduling, and broken tech rollouts—issues square reviewers raise more consistently than circle reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: Groups descriptions of a school climate shaped by explicit religious identity or conservative culture, deep multi‑generational alumni ties, and exclusionary practices or favoritism (e.g., 'CATHOLIC as the name states,' 'incredibly conservative Bible‑thumpers,' 'vast majority Caucasian,' 'if you’re rich/athlete you get special treatment,' boundary exceptions for athletes), whereas square entries do not foreground these identity‑driven community dynamics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit, nam: These circle reviews list concrete program offerings and outcome metrics (AP/IB/STEAM, Engineering Academy, CTE/dual-enrollment, 1:1 MacBooks) and cite scholarships/college placement (e.g., “11 AP courses…97th best high school,” “brand new engineering pathway,” “$4M in scholarships”), whereas square reviews rarely name equivalent program structures or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more strict, punit: Circle reviews repeatedly describe zero-tolerance or highly punitive practices (automatic suspensions, restricted restroom access, parking revocations, bans on devices), e.g. “Suspension is the ONLY form of discipline,” “only one bathroom was open,” while square reviews more often describe lax or inconsistent enforcement or calls for firmer discipline rather than systematic punitive policies.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more visible, re: Square reviews frequently praise principals and counselors for being accessible and proactive (named principals praised, counselors emailing instructors, admin ‘listens if you persist’, parent‑teacher meetings), e.g. “The principal, Mr. Kerr, is doing a great job,” whereas circle reviews more often report administrative unresponsiveness or the need to escalate repeatedly.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete op: Circle reviews contain administrative mishandling and operational breakdowns (refused transcripts, lost college documents, front‑office unresponsiveness, failed arrival/health screening logistics, lunch strikes, accreditation loss, counselor confidentiality issues, ignored bullying/assault), e.g. “Refusal to send my transcripts,” “drop‑off experience was a nightmare,” and “her transcript was never sent,” whereas square reviews rarely allege this level of systemic operational harm.
