candidate_defs.circle entries depict more small‑school,: Many circle reviews emphasize small class sizes, tight‑knit ‘family’ communities, extensive one‑on‑one teacher support and high participation/access (no‑cut sports, many students get roles), e.g. “small class size…each student has a myriad of opportunities,” while square reviews more often highlight large-school traditions and prominent athletics or performing‑arts facilities without the same small‑school intimacy.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger documente: These entries cite concrete college/scholarship metrics, named alumni successes, and school-run college-prep supports (e.g., scholarship totals, graduates who "went on to 4 year colleges," AP/IB offerings, guidance counselor scholarship assistance, and active Alumni Associations), showing verifiable postsecondary results and institutional programs that lead to college access compared with square entries that lack those outcome specifics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These entries recount multiple violent incidents, ongoing cyberbullying, drug-selling, gang-related assaults, frequent fights/fire-alarm pulls, and allegations that staff or administration overlook or inadequately respond (e.g., "rampant, constant and pervasive" bullying, drug dealers "supported"), indicating safety and enforcement issues not present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries depict a closer, small-sc: These reviews highlight small-district continuity, personalized teacher mentorship, strong parent volunteer programs, multigenerational attendance and alumni returning as leaders (e.g., "we are a family," parent-run breakfast programs, teachers named as mentors), emphasizing relational supports and community ties absent or weaker in square entries.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize formal, program: Square-focused entries foreground institutional programs and curricular pathways (IB/AP/honors, college-in-high-school credit, clearly sequenced math and AP expansions) and attribute success to these program structures rather than personalized staff or informal supports, contrasting with many circle entries that emphasize individual teacher-driven outcomes or extracurricular preparation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These items describe poor parent/staff communication, politicized boards, grade-tampering or donor favoritism, conditional admissions, inaccessible counselors, and heavy-handed or uneven enforcement (e.g., reversed punishments for favored students, teachers retained despite poor performance), pointing to systemic management and fairness problems that square entries do not consistently allege.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete violent incidents (fights, stabbings, guns), gang activity, widespread bullying/cyberbullying, and repeated staff/administrator failures to intervene or expel (e.g., “After the stabbing last year…”, “GANG ACTIVITY”, “Students brought guns… were not expelled”, “bullying issues that STILL haven't been addressed”). It signals schools where reviewers describe safety as a recurring, operational breakdown rather than isolated complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: This bucket captures reviews that specify structured college-prep offerings and outcomes (Running Start/associate-degree programs, dual enrollment, AP test mandates, 100% college‑bound claims, named college matriculations), for example: “Credits earned count for both highschool diploma and college degree's,” “My student earned their associates degree,” and “mandates that the student sit for the National AP Exam.” It groups schools where reviewers point to formal, trackable academic pipelines and documented alumni/postsecondary success.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more staff-level f: This bucket groups reviews alleging operational personnel problems such as favoritism toward employees’ children and athletes, reserved privileges, inappropriate teacher‑student relationships, targeted harassment by administrators, transphobia/misgendering, and recurring teacher departures (e.g., “favoritism… reserving the best seats,” “two incidents of inappropriate relationships… swept under the rug,” “most of the teachers have a very short tenure”). It identifies schools where reviewers describe systemic staff misconduct or staffing instability affecting student opportunities and safety.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent,: This bucket groups reviews that depict proactive administrators and consistently supportive teachers/counselors—named principals driving improvement, frequent teacher outreach, reliable counselor support, and constructive school reforms (e.g., “The principal is excellent… He shows up at sporting events,” “teachers and counselors seem to care,” “Vista Del Lago… improved tremendously under the leadership of Principal Dr. Bazanos”). It denotes schools reviewed as having stable leadership and staff practices that actively support students and families.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide more detailed acc: This bucket groups reviews that enumerate concrete physical resources and program variety—labs and chemistry facilities, conservatory-style arts production, competitive marching band trophies, JROTC/ROTC, student-run coffee shops, buses, new gyms or medical labs, and lists of clubs/teams (e.g., “chem labs and computer lab are top notch,” “A true artist… New World School of the Arts,” “student-run coffee shop… received a check for $500,” “tremendous FFA program, excellent music program, 8 AP courses”). It captures schools where reviewers supply granular, program‑level evidence of extracurricular and facility assets (or upgrades) rather than only high‑level claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher-pe: This bucket captures circle reviews that list many named clubs/teams (band, robotics, marching band), athletic milestones (regional semifinals, state championships), vocational shops, JTED/CNA pathways and dual‑enrollment/college‑credit counts (graduates with 50 college credits), whereas square reviews rarely cite specific competitive wins or extensive vocational/dual enrollment opportunities.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent an: Circle reviewers repeatedly report pervasive bullying, weekly physical fights, vaping and on‑campus drug use, daily food fights, overcrowded/unsafe buses and students openly breaking rules in front of staff; square reviews contain far fewer (and less severe) accounts of these supervision and safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize concrete teache: Many circle reviews praise teachers who stay after school or are available at lunch, name specific instructors and credit them with tangible gains (AP pass rates, 34 ACT, CDL, Ivy admits), and describe hands‑on mentorship and mastery‑oriented pacing—claims that square reviews rarely substantiate with named staff or numeric outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report explicit special-e: Circle contains multiple accounts of IEP/504 plans not being followed, guidance‑counselor bias toward special‑needs students, disability‑targeted bullying and refusal of requested placements, a cluster of concrete special‑education breakdowns largely absent from square.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize large-school in: Square reviewers often describe overcrowded/prison-like facilities, students feeling anonymous, teachers who are 'hit or miss' or 'mediocre,' weak discipline and a test‑score/teach‑to‑the‑test orientation—systemic, scale‑level organizational complaints that are less prominent in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pervasive s: This bucket captures reviews that describe concrete harms to student wellbeing and safety in the building (e.g., 'Bullying is a major issue,' 'Kids are high and drunk in school regularly,' 'One teacher is currently in a coma after trying to break up a fight,' PTSD and self‑harm reports, repeated sexual/predatory peer behaviors, and routine targeted searches) — contrasted with square entries which contain little or no comparable accounts of persistent violence, substance epidemics, or systemic bullying. Falling here means the school is described as an environment where student safety and mental/physical health are regularly compromised and discipline responses are inadequate or inconsistent.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews that allege operational and leadership failures: favoritism and confidentiality breaches ('teachers have favorites,' 'transcripts held hostage,' 'they change your child's grades'), authoritarian or punitive management ('run the school rather militantly,' 'suspend students 10 days to get rid of problems,' 'principal won't return phone calls'), and active cover‑ups or nepotistic hiring — whereas square reviews more often name and praise administrators and do not make the same breadth of governance abuse claims. Content in this bucket signals chronic leadership/discipline mismanagement, opaque decision‑making, or retaliation against complainants.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader and deep: This bucket collects concrete programmatic and outcome evidence (AP/IB, many specialized STEM electives, career/technical academies, dual‑enrollment and AA completion, JROTC high ranking, documented high AP/SAT/API results, students receiving full scholarships or top‑of‑class placements) that reviewers attribute to the school — whereas square reviews generally lack the same breadth of advanced/CTE course detail or measurable college‑credit claims. Falling into this bucket means the school is characterized by explicit program breadth (specialized electives, academies, dual credit) and named academic achievements.
candidate_defs.circle entries indicate greater tuition‑: This bucket covers reviews emphasizing heavy family financial burden and private‑school dynamics (high tuition and many mandatory fees, required parental service/fundraising, gated campus, affluent student body) alongside visible athlete/stadium investments and parent‑driven resource allocation ('brand new stadium', multi‑million dollar athletic projects vs neglected basic maintenance). Square entries instead focus on public‑funding/residency tensions or town budget constraints and rarely describe tuition or the same athlete‑first fundraising patterns. Inclusion here signals that school resources and access are strongly shaped by tuition/fundraising and socioeconomic status.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize more consistent: This bucket groups reviews that foreground positive, concrete staff and leadership engagement (named principals and coaches praised, counseling improvements, teachers who 'go above and beyond,' clear parental pride and community welcome) and describe fewer systemic safety or governance failures than circle reviews. Falling in this bucket means reviewers credit the school with dependable adult support, visible caring leadership, and a cohesive parent/student community rather than the chronic dysfunctions or safety problems described elsewhere.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: These reviews describe recurring, concrete safety incidents inside the building and on campus—e.g., 'lots of Bullying , fights,' 'infested with gangs, drugs, and gang violence,' 'too many code red this year,' and reports of death threats and daily racial slurs—whereas square entries rarely allege sustained violence, gang activity, or ongoing drug circulation.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more c: Multiple circle reviews enumerate programmatic college-prep offerings and outcomes—'AP and Honors classes,' 'IB program,' 'dual enrollment,' 'early college... over forty college credits,' and conservatory-style arts/music tracks—while square reviews emphasize limited AP breadth, low AP pass rates, or a lack of college-prep programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries portray broader and highe: Circle reviewers repeatedly cite robust extracurricular life—'Great fine arts program,' 'award winning debate club,' 'recording studio,' 'Sports have traditionally been a bright spot'—including both breadth and high-quality arts/athletics offerings, whereas square reviews tend not to document that same depth or accolades.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle text contains many allegations of biased enforcement and leadership failures—'favoritism based on last names,' 'administration chooses to do nothing because he/she is tenured,' 'The principle stalked me,' and 'privacy has been violated'—documenting personnel misconduct and uneven discipline practices that square reviews do not enumerate.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize more complex an: Circle reviews frequently discuss money, governance and familial continuity—e.g., mandatory tuition and fees, 'this poor little community raised over four hundred thousand dollars to save the school,' multi‑generational enrollment, and parents pulling children out or organizing PTAs—while square reviews generally lack this detailed account of funding models, alumni continuity, or community fundraising/withdrawal dynamics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reviews describing on-campus fights, gangs, regular physical violence, tolerated drug use, daily race- or homophobic slurs, student-on-student bullying, threats/retaliation after reporting, panic attacks and other mental‑health crises (e.g., “there's gangs, and fights,” “Most of the students are drug addicts,” “yell very racist and homophobic slurs with no reprocussions,” “I’ve had 6 panic attacks in school”), all of which appear far more often in circle entries than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: This bucket groups concrete programmatic evidence—AP breadth and high AP participation/rankings, dual‑enrollment/college‑credit pathways, AVID/honors tracking, high regional/national rankings, and alumni college success claims (e.g., “Ranked #139 in nation for AP participation,” “I went into college as basically a sophomore due to taking so many AP tests,” “students go to Ivy League caliber schools”)—features that reviewers attribute to circle schools noticeably more than to square schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket collects governance and policy complaints: coaches/athletes and staff‑families receiving special treatment, selective application of unwritten rules, expulsions from arts for low performers, punitive discipline (barring early grads from commencement, all‑day AC for tardies), grade‑alteration pressure, and nepotistic hiring or enrichment of administrators (e.g., “coaches will vouch for athletes,” “many of the Student of the Year winners are teachers’ children,” “principle had her sister‑in‑law… they favor any child that has a parent staff member”), patterns repeatedly attributed to circle entries more than square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater variabilit: This bucket targets staffing quality and student‑support consistency: accounts of highly engaged mentors, one‑on‑one tutoring, and counselor advocacy alongside frequent teacher burnout, uncertified or ineffective instructors, revolving door turnover, and gaps in special‑education/mental‑health supports (e.g., “teachers who worked with me every day,” versus “Too many uncertified teachers,” “constant staff changing,” “little to NO support for LD kids”), a contrast that appears as a defining theme in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more (and more var: This bucket groups concrete resource- and program‑level observations: descriptions of recent renovations, new stadiums, one‑to‑one devices and remote learning tech, large band/program sizes, extensive vocational/CTE offerings and internships, residential/tuition structures, AND frequent mentions of pay‑to‑play, mandatory fees, fundraising pressure or cuts (e.g., “lots of ongoing construction… newer facilities,” “one‑to‑one iPad program,” “we had to pay a $250 school fee,” “cut back extracurriculars or changed to ‘pay to play’”), all of which circle reviews report more often and with greater variety than square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced: These reviews frequently describe concrete college-prep infrastructure (AP/IB/DE courses, dual‑enrollment and >50 college credits, Regents/High ACT/Blue‑Ribbon recognitions) and student outcomes (students graduating with college credits, scholarship and selective‑college placements), e.g. circle notes “AP/IB/DE classes,” “nearly 100% matriculation,” and students leaving with a year of college credit — claims that square reviews do not consistently make and often describe lower expectations or limited academic rigor.
candidate_defs.circle entries report richer, better‑res: Circle reviews repeatedly cite high‑quality, well‑resourced extracurriculars (nationally ranked marching band, award‑winning choirs, extensive clubs, ROTC, state competitive teams, smartboards/classroom tech), for example “marching band is ranked nationally,” “hundreds of optional programs and clubs,” and robust arts magnet structures, whereas square reviews rarely describe that level or breadth of arts/competitive programming.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive bul: Square reviews more often document ongoing peer harassment, drugs and classroom harassment, and administrators who ignore or inconsistently enforce discipline (e.g., “Bullying is a large problem... ignored by any authority,” reports of drug activity and victim-punishing policies), signaling persistent safety/behavior problems and weak corrective response in square schools compared with circle.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more proactive,: Circle reviews give tangible examples of engaged leadership and community collaboration — principals who are accessible and personally involved, principal‑led remediation/coffee forums, active PTSA/after‑prom committees and business advisory partnerships, and project‑based community capstones — (“principal is on a first name basis,” “parent run After‑Prom Committee,” “10th grade Social Justice Symposium”), while square reviews more often report unresponsive or absentee leadership and weaker parent/industry partnership.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent spec: Many circle reviews detail IEP/504 breakdowns, missing service minutes, accommodations not followed, unhelpful guidance counseling, and ineffective on‑site tutoring (e.g., “504 plan accommodations not being followed,” “The special education in this school is a joke!... service minutes incorrect”), a pattern of individualized‑support failures that square reviews largely do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger individua: This bucket captures circle reviews that describe active academic supports (consistent after‑school teacher help, tutoring, AP/Scholars/STEM expansions, internships, college seminars and partnerships, Powerschool/ACT prep) and tangible outcomes (full scholarships, college matriculation) — e.g., “they will stay literally until 4 or 5 to help you,” additions of new AP courses, Bucknell‑hosted engineering seminars, and a son headed to Howard on a full scholarship — contrasts with square’s lack of sustained evidence for these concrete academic pipelines.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute safety: This bucket groups circle reviews documenting visible safety incidents and enforcement gaps — unlocked doors, dozens of cameras but staff failing to intervene, multiple witnessed fights, after‑school brawls, widespread drug/alcohol use, easy class‑cutting and open campus access — e.g., “I witnessed at least 6 or more fights,” “They allow bullying… kids do drugs there,” and “Its easy to cut class.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers circle reports of chronic or concrete administrative breakdowns: high turnover and firings, favoritism toward athletes or alumni, lowered academic-eligibility policies, grade/record mishandling, lost IEPs, scheduling collapses, mishandled legal documents, and allegations of intentional score inflation or cheating — e.g., “administrative team and dean have all been fired,” “LOWERED the minimum GPA for NHS,” and “he lost his IEP from a previous state.”
candidate_defs.square entries describe more accessible,: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize effective, visible principals and counselors, timely teacher‑parent communication, stable staff and organized operations, and schoolwide supports (accessible counselors, Chromebook distribution, anti‑exclusion programs) — e.g., “a really supportive principal,” “Counselors/Staffs are great,” and “Every student 5-12 has a chrome book,” in contrast to circle’s frequent administrative complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: This bucket aggregates circle claims about extracurricular prominence and community ties — athletics and coach mentorship, nationally noted music/mariachi programs, active alumni networks, small‑campus walkability and multigenerational family traditions, parental volunteer norms and community recruitment — e.g., “The network is unbelievable,” “The band has a long tradition,” “perfect school… small town,” and “Coaches have been great mentors,” which square reviews typically do not highlight.
candidate_defs.circle entries show a stronger faith/pri: These reviews emphasize an explicit religious or philosophical mission, tuition and private‑school indicators, merit/selective admissions, and community/alumni traditions — e.g., multiple Circle reviews cite a bible‑based curriculum, single‑sex alumnae reunions, tuition complaints ('Not worth the $18k'), selective admissions/interview processes, and calls for/against vouchers or eliminating school choice. Falling in this bucket means the school is described as mission‑driven or tuitioned/selective rather than a typical public neighborhood school.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete meas: Circle reviews frequently supply numeric outcomes and named pathways — e.g., scholarship totals ('$16M'/'$28M'), ACT/SAT averages, 97%+ college matriculation claims, AP exam workshops, IB/AP supports, dual‑enrollment and industry credential programs — while Square offers fewer metrics. Content in this bucket centers on explicit evidence of college readiness, test scores, and formal advanced‑course structures.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize athletics and f: Many Circle reviews describe athletics/music as institutional priorities or flagship identities and claim funding/staffing skews to sport or band — e.g., 'They bend over backwards to protect the football players,' 'too many coaches and not enough emphasis on education,' and 'marching band is top in state' or 'major funding goes to athletics.' Items here are about program prioritization, resource allocation, and favoritism toward athletic or flagship extracurricular programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stricter, more p: Circle reviewers report concrete operational policies and heavier enforcement — bag checks and pat downs, business‑casual dress code with harsh ISS for leggings, stricter ID/dress prioritization, tighter security and more rules — e.g., 'bag check and pat down each student' and 'girls would get a full day of ISS for wearing leggings.' This bucket groups accounts of surveillance, punitive enforcement, and formal behavioral rules being applied more rigorously.
candidate_defs.square entries report more instructional: Square reviews more often document teacher absenteeism or low instructional engagement, explicit staff criminal/misconduct incidents, recurring violent fights, drug problems, and administrators failing to enforce safety — e.g., 'teachers are hardly ever there to teach,' 'Mr. Story... inappropriately putting his hands on female students,' and 'There are fights everyday. No Discipline.' Items in this bucket concern operational failures that produce unsafe or educationally neglectful conditions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete and repeated safety failures (daily fights, robberies, lockdowns, gang activity, high pregnancy rates), pervasive bullying (including toward LGBTQ students and students with disabilities), and staff indifference to incidents — e.g., “lockdowns every other week,” “my niece was brutally attacked…Noone helped her,” and “parents with children with different sexual orientations should not go to this school.” Such raw items indicate that circle schools are characterized by more frequent violent/harassment incidents and systemic intolerance than square schools.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater administ: Circle reviews repeatedly cite leadership problems (frequent principal turnover, centralized decision‑making, punitive or opaque policies), ignored complaints (bullying and special‑ed denials that required legal action), and breakdowns in communication/operations (late grade reporting, unexplained fees, harmful schedule changes) — e.g., “Issues had been brought up to the principal… still nothing was done,” “we had to sue them to get services,” and “grades are submitted a week or more late.” These items show administrative unresponsiveness and instability are much more prominent in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, more n: Circle reviews name advanced and structured offerings—IB/AP/STEM, dual‑enrollment/college‑course partnerships, CTE/vocational majors, arts‑audition programs, and explicit college readiness outcomes—often citing iPads, science/STEM programs, tech centers, or college credit (e.g., “opportunities to take college level courses at nearby Lemoyne,” “dual‑enrollment with Wayne County Community College,” and many named career academies). These details indicate circle schools more often report concrete program breadth and college/career pathways than square schools.
candidate_defs.square entries report poorer instruction: Square reviews contain sustained claims about low teacher quality, laziness, and ineffective instruction (e.g., “Teachers are also lazy… Most of the teachers are awful and don't know how to teach,” “math department in particular is downright awful,” and “guidance is completely useless”), portraying systemic instructional shortfalls and low expectations that are less frequent in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize cohesive commun: Circle reviews foreground close intergenerational ties, visible alumni involvement, faith‑based identity or conservative values, strong school spirit, and social stratification (sports/status/donor influence, favoritism toward prominent families) — e.g., “I attended Spring Garden and most of my family attended as well,” “Christian education… chapel one day a week,” and “parents treat others very poorly… focused on money.” These items show circle schools are more often described as tightly knit, identity‑driven communities where social status and family legacy shape student life.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher‑: Circle reviews repeatedly name thriving arts and high‑level athletics—conservatory/one‑of‑a‑kind arts programs, award‑winning drama/band, ‘athletic powerhouse’, no‑cut sports—while square reviews rarely describe equivalent arts depth and emphasize only general activities or program gaps.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete operational complaints—unanswered district communication, scheduling/registration/credit errors, lost transcripts, covered‑up incidents, residency/lottery manipulation and hiring by relationships—plus allegations of favoritism/nepotism and leadership harassment; square reviews include fewer or different administrative breakdowns and generally less evidence of systemic operational malpractice.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety, stude: Many circle reviews document acute safety problems—numerous fights/riots, lockdowns, drug busts, gang activity, repeated bullying and victim‑blaming by authorities, and students reporting depression—whereas square reviews more often describe relative physical safety or social problems without the same scale of violence or administration‑backed victim neglect.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more systemic excl: Circle reviewers frequently allege exclusionary admissions/charter selection, refusal or poor accommodation of students with disabilities, IEP/504 noncompliance, and patterns of racism, homophobia/transphobia or religious favoritism (examples: “IEPs rare…parents must fight,” “students who are Church of Christ are favoured,” “transphobic…bullies not punished”), while square reviews contain fewer such systemic discrimination or special‑education failure claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, formal: These reviews emphasize institutional pathways and evidence of college success: frequent mentions of AP/IB integration, dual‑enrollment/academy programs, students graduating with college credits or associates degrees, high scholarship and matriculation figures (e.g. 'over 95 percent proceed to college', '18 college credits, 2 certifications'), and named academy/partnership offerings; square entries lack comparable program breadth or concrete placement evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Many circle reviews document chronic bullying, hate‑motivated attacks, gang/violence concerns, frequent fights, and administrators who do not enforce consequences or protect students (examples: multi‑year bullying, 'hate crimed multiple times', 'sent... back to their classroom with no consequence'), whereas square entries rarely describe sustained, systemic safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more abundant te: Circle reviewers frequently cite required teacher 'help nights', numerous tutoring programs, teacher‑run clubs/coaching, strong counseling and long‑term teacher–student relationships, and intentional inclusion supports (e.g., special‑needs programming, parent groups), while square entries provide far fewer accounts of organized in‑school remediation or pervasive one‑on‑one staff involvement.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete faci: Circle reviews repeatedly call out broken/unsanitary restrooms, poor food service, parking and bus overcrowding, construction/maintenance complaints, misplaced transcripts/credit losses and lunch/billing mistakes—operational failures not described in the square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries portray more pervasive in: Square reviews more often accuse teachers/leadership of disengagement ('just show up for their paycheck', 'teachers do not care'), stale curriculum and teaching‑to‑the‑test, and urge external fixes (private school, outside tutoring, even legal remedies), whereas circle reviews are less likely to recommend leaving or emphasize systemic teacher apathy.

candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit fait: Many circle reviews specify a religious mission (Bible‑based/Christian/Catholic language), single‑sex identity (all‑boys), and faith‑tied preferences in discipline, awards, or admissions (e.g., SDA favoritism, Catholic students advantaged), while square reviews are secular and make no comparable claims. Content in this bucket foregrounds institutional religion or single‑sex mission shaping daily policies and social treatment (examples: ‘Christ‑centered’, ‘Catholic students have an advantage’, ‘all‑boys model’).
candidate_defs.circle entries document more pervasive s: Circle reviews repeatedly allege chronic bullying and racial targeting, on‑site drug dealing and use, teacher‑on‑student assault, gun‑related incidents, and administrators who ignore or deny these problems; square reviews generally do not report this pattern. Items in this bucket describe concrete safety incidents and patterns plus ineffective administrative remediation (examples: ‘extremely targeted, bullied… physically hurt,’ ‘drug dealers in school,’ ‘two signs of gun shootings,’ ‘school refuses to address bullying’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These circle comments describe crony hires, protected poor performers, opaque governance and board conflict, program eliminations and staff layoffs, punitive new policies, and even claim removal of negative reviews — a pattern of unstable or politicized leadership and resource retrenchment not found in square entries. Material in this bucket focuses on leadership decisions and district governance harming programs and staff stability (examples: ‘hired her own friends to coach,’ ‘cut the band… firing half the staff,’ ‘take down negative reviews,’ ‘call for impartial investigation of superintendent’).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a small‑school,: Many circle reviews highlight small size, multi‑generational alumni ties, active PTO/volunteering, visible/principled principals, teacher–parent collaboration, and individualized care that create a family feel; square reviews more often describe a larger, less personalized public setting. Content placed here centers on community continuity and personal relationships as a principal school feature (examples: ‘small… personal feeling,’ ‘grandparents, parents, cousins all went here,’ ‘PTO is active,’ ‘teachers & parents work together’).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more physical bull: These reviews describe concrete safety failures—repeated physical assaults, gangs/territory, and staff inaction—and sometimes point readers to news coverage (e.g., “He was hit in the face with a book… nothing was done,” “Gang territory,” and references to external stories on bullying). Square entries do not raise comparable repeated safety or media‑reported incident claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize a formal Christ: Circle reviews repeatedly describe an explicitly Christ‑centered curriculum and enforced behavioral expectations (e.g., “expectation for students to live a life that exemplifies Christ… fully addressed in the student handbook and enforced by the staff”), whereas square reviews contain no mention of religion or faith‑based conduct.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an athletics‑ce: Circle reviews highlight broad sports and extracurricular offerings, coach dominance in staffing, and positive interschool sportsmanship (e.g., “tremendous amount of sports,” “half of the teachers are coaches,” and praise for coaches/administration facilitating homecoming), while square reviews only note sports more narrowly and do not depict a coach‑driven culture or community sportsmanship.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe formal specializ: Circle reviews list distinct academy structures (arts & humanities, STEM, education), reference programs like PACE and school progress reports, and sometimes express regret about college preparedness tied to the school choice (e.g., “arts and humanities academy, a STEM academy…,” “interested in learning more about the school progress report,” and “would have been more prepared for college…”); square reviews do not describe these organized academies or the same accountability/college‑readiness concerns.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more variable staf: Circle reviews contain multiple accounts of staff/leadership problems: bias in discipline (racial/sexist claims), counselor blaming of students for anxiety, and criticisms of district/board favoritism or misappropriation of funds (e.g., accusations about minority students being treated unfairly, “Our counselor will blame students with anxiety,” and “money… gets misappropriated by the county”). Square reviews do not raise comparable district‑level corruption/favoritism or discriminatory discipline claims and instead sometimes single out a school principal as a localized complaint rather than systemic district issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute physica: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and chronic disorder inside and around the school (e.g., “a riot broke out... hallways were peppersprayed,” “my students talks of high pregnancy rates, fights and gangs,” repeated lockdowns and bomb threats, reports of overcrowded buses and students assaulted on buses, and widespread vaping/substance use) that do not appear in the square texts; use this for entries documenting violent or system-level student-safety breakdowns rather than routine discipline issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive ide: These items allege repeated, identity‑targeted mistreatment and failures to address it (e.g., “racist remarks are made in front of teachers and nothing is done,” “I was hate crimed multiple times because I'm a gay trans man,” counselors ‘targeting him,’ and staff/administration turning a blind eye to bullying), and are distinct from general student misbehavior because they center on protected‑class harassment and institutional inaction.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, concret: Use this for reviews that enumerate specific programs and applied pathways or cite alumni matriculation (e.g., “vocational and technical schools... recording studio available,” “offers more dual‑credit hours than most,” “Best speech and debate program,” and concrete college placements like UConn/WPI/MIT alumni), distinguishing institutional program breadth and demonstrable outcomes from generic statements about academics.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater intensity an: These comments document active, high‑stakes parent/community behaviors—both positive (families moving to attend, parents with multiple children enrolled, strong alumni networks and parent booster involvement) and adversarial (parents encouraging harassment, cursing out administrators, PTA ignored, calls for state complaints or district takeover)—capturing the community’s outsized role in school life rather than ordinary parental contact.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more consistent: These reviews emphasize orderly, professional operations and reliable academic programming (examples: “general supportiveness of administration,” counselors ‘helping students decide classes,’ coordinated enforcement/working‑together language, and praised AP/IB/honors pathways) in contrast to the circle texts’ frequent reports of extreme variability, chaos, or administrative failure; apply this bucket to entries that highlight stable school management, consistent policy enforcement, and dependable academic supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger small‑sch: This bucket groups reviews that describe tight, personalized communities (small class sizes, principals who 'know each kid by name,' K–12 continuity), multi‑generational attendance, active PTA/parent partnership and church integration (e.g., 'partner with parents and church,' '3rd generation…'), which appear far more often in circle reviews than in square reviews that describe large, impersonal campuses.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more high‑profile,: Included here are claims of conservatory‑style arts curricula and nationally notable ensembles (e.g., 'Broadway‑quality theater,' 'Carnegie Hall choir,' award‑winning band, nationally competitive orchestra/robotics/journalism) that circle reviewers assert, whereas square reviews mention arts more modestly or not at all.
candidate_defs.square entries report more formalized ma: This bucket captures square reviews that emphasize institutionalized specialized programs (named magnets like 'Science, Mathematics, and Computer Science,' Communication Arts), structured internships and vocational pathways, and explicit AP/dual‑credit success and college‑readiness claims—features presented more clearly and repeatedly in square reviews than in circle reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more punitive, inc: This groups reports of excessive or uneven discipline that harm students (detentions 'to everyone,' withholding diplomas tied to exit tests/fundraising, denying bathroom access, encouraging failing students to drop out, many trivial rules producing sanctions) which are much more frequently described in circle reviews than in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups comments about leadership problems—favoritism to athletes/local families, cronyism, blame‑shifting, ignoring parent complaints, targeted harassment/forced exits of good teachers, and uneven resource allocation (e.g., chromebook distribution, funding sports over roofs)—a pattern emphasized by circle reviewers far more than by square reviewers.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures reviewer reports of repeated physical fights, sexual harassment, racial taunts/ostracism, gang/drug activity and victims being ignored or even punished by staff (e.g., 'the bullying at this school is out of control', 'girls getting groped in packed hallways', 'students were told to go kill themselves', 'administrators said it is not bullying unless they physically hit you'). Square entries generally lack these widespread safety allegations and rarely describe staff tolerance of or inaction on severe peer abuse.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete, o: This bucket groups descriptions of formal programs and measurable academic artifacts—dual-enrollment/college-credit, vocational academies (Allied Health, culinary, FFA), internships, STEM/IB/AP offerings, scholarship totals and college matriculation statistics (e.g., 'over $9,000,000 in scholarships', 'dual enrollment... saved thousands', 'top tier agriculture program', 'IB as the only district IB program'). Square entries tend to discuss general class variety or honors/AP in abstract but do not provide the same density of concrete program structures, internships, dual-credit particulars, or quantified college/scholarship outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries show stronger local commu: This bucket covers mentions of family-like atmospheres, active alumni reunions, regular parent volunteers/fundraising, donor-supported funds, and community loyalty (e.g., 'class of 72... classmates get together', 'wonderful donors... Annual Fund', 'small student body so it has a family atmosphere', 'we are growing every year'). Square reviews generally omit sustained alumni/donor narratives or portray less ongoing community cohesion.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistently: This bucket identifies that square reviewers more often portray leadership and counselors as uniformly effective and communication as responsive ('The guidance counselor has been great', 'amazing and dedicated principal'), whereas circle reviews are more internally conflicted—some praise visible, transformational principals while others allege absentee, unprofessional, or retaliatory administrators—resulting in highly polarized accounts about leadership and staff.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete mate: This bucket covers facility and operational complaints and funding practices: aging/overcrowded buildings, broken HVAC/bathrooms/pests, per-event fundraising and hidden fee waivers, punitive fines for minor infractions, and claims that athletics receive disproportionate funding (e.g., 'overcrowded... need AC', 'pay $1... Fall Festival donate a cake', 'all money goes to football not education', 'temporary id $1 each... poor student paid $100'). Square entries rarely describe this constellation of infrastructure deficits, opaque fees, or athletics-over-academics funding claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer, concrete: These reviews highlight program depth and trackable outcomes in circle schools — e.g., AP/IB, dual‑credit, vocational/engineering/medical magnets, arts majors, Cambridge levels, 100% graduation or high college‑enrollment claims and specific college‑prep results — whereas square entries rarely document equivalent structured pathways or measurable postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more allegations: Many circle reviews call out punitive or secretive leadership behavior (administration bullying parents/students, firing without explanation, refusing class changes, demerit suspension policies for parent dismissals, calls for state review), while square reviews do not advance the same volume of claims about vindictive or obstructive administration.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews more often describe day‑to‑day safety problems — fights almost every day, videos/Instagram of fights, police on campus, drugs/gangs at entry, chronic bullying ignored by staff — whereas square entries generally provide fewer or less severe accounts of violence and unresolved safety incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger teache: Circle reviewers frequently describe close, family‑like communities, small class sizes, teachers who give cell numbers, active counseling and newcomer supports, parent volunteering and teachers going above and beyond; square entries more often report uneven or impersonal teacher engagement and fewer examples of systematic individualized outreach.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced fa: Circle reviews contain many concrete infrastructure and operational complaints — broken AC, outdated textbooks/15‑year‑old tech, poor Wi‑Fi, lunches running out, hazardous busing, overcrowded lunches/parking — while square reviews mention fewer or more positive facility investments.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These reviews describe concrete, extreme safety failures inside and around the school (e.g., death threats, lynching language, shootings, repeated fights, lockdowns, students telling peers to self-harm, pervasive daily bullying and unsanitary/unsafe conditions) and often document staff nonresponse; Square reviews do note bullying or isolated incidents but do not contain the same frequency or severity of violent/targeted harassment (no lynching/shooting/death‑threat accounts).
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more and more-sp: Circle reviewers repeatedly name curricular pathways and partnerships (AP, IB/pre‑AP/Pre‑AP, PACE, vocational and magnet programs, medical academy, dual‑credit/quantified university credits, explicit college partnerships and seminars, 9th‑hour remediation) and sometimes list elite matriculations; Square mentions AP/honors and some electives but far less concrete program, dual‑enrollment, or institutional partnership detail.
candidate_defs.square entries report more staff/counsel: Square reviews more often document concrete problems with adult competence and classroom accountability—counselors who 'have no clue,' teachers who 'don’t know the material,' arbitrary grading/grade inflation claims, and reliance on parents to remediate—whereas Circle contains many counter‑examples of competent or dedicated teachers and formal academic supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: Circle reviewers frequently describe hands‑on teacher attention, mentorship programs, small class sizes, formal remediation (e.g., '9th hour'), proactive college counseling, coordinated multi‑teacher intervention meetings, and staff who 'go above and beyond' for students; Square reviews emphasize some caring teachers but more often lack descriptions of systematic individualized supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete ope: Circle reviews repeatedly cite tangible operational facts or problems—budget shortfalls, fundraising/charging parents, scholarship programs, program cuts, bus service cuts, lawsuits, 1:1 device programs (iPads/netbooks), antiquated lab computers, new $75M buildings, and specific facility upgrades—while Square rarely provides this level of concrete resource/infrastructure detail and mostly focuses on programmatic or staff observations.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, broade: These reviews highlight that circle schools more often report extensive AP/honors/IB offerings, robust dual‑enrollment and vocational/CTE academies, award‑winning arts and competitive academic teams, and concrete college/scholarship/elite‑admit outcomes (examples: named AP/honors praise, dual‑enrollment paid by school, tech centers, National Merit and Ivy/T20 acceptances), while square reviews lack similarly detailed program breadth or demonstrable college/career outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more consistent te: Many circle reviews describe teachers who stay after school, provide one‑on‑one tutoring, respond by email, and are named as caring mentors (e.g., teachers 'stay late', 'willing to help', multiple named beloved teachers), whereas square reviews more frequently report limited teacher follow‑up and few consistently available supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent te: Circle reviews contain numerous concrete personnel‑issues—misassigned or unqualified hires, repeated unprofessional incidents, nepotistic hiring or parent‑based athletic favoritism, and claims that good teachers are 'run off'—a cluster distinct from mere lack of availability and not emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviewers more often allege ongoing physical and non‑physical bullying, frequent fights (sometimes requiring police), vaping/drugs and bathroom closures, and staff who tolerate or ignore harassment, while square reviews less often describe this level of safety breakdown or sustained adult inaction.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews repeatedly point to ineffective or unresponsive administration and district leadership—closed‑door policies, unanswered records/phone requests, inconsistent or punitive discipline, nepotistic politics, budget cutbacks and facility hazards (mold, broken elevators, chaotic graduations)—a set of managerial/operational problems that square reviews do not emphasize to the same degree.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete safety failures (unsupervised fights and assaults causing concussion, a bus beating, a gun on campus, repeated lockdowns, dozens of shooting threats, theft, student deaths, chronic bullying, racial and homophobic threats) and frequent adult inaction or passive supervision; Square reviews rarely report comparable violent incidents and instead contain only occasional, less-specific fight/bullying notes. Examples: Circle recounts an unstaffed hallway assault that caused a concussion, a student with a gun on campus, and “over 40 school shooting threats” left unpunished, while Square lacks such severe incident reports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive adv: Many Circle reviews name concrete advanced programs and outcomes (broad AP catalogs, IB programs, dual‑enrollment/early‑college pathways, measurable MCAS/US News rankings, high AP pass rates, scholarships and named college matriculations), whereas Square reviews tend to highlight vocational/PBIS supports or general college readiness without the same named AP/IB/dual‑enrollment evidence. Examples: Circle cites 'a LOT of AP classes,' formal IB and early‑college pathways, MCAS improvement and scholarships to top universities; Square emphasizes tech‑prep, PBIS, and fewer advanced course specifics.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more responsive,: Square reviews frequently report accessible counselors and administrators who respond to parents, fix enrollment issues, provide tutoring/progress reports, and offer individualized accommodation; Circle reviews more often allege administrative nonresponse, rude/front‑office behavior, denied documents, rumor‑driven decisions, and slow or evasive handling of complaints. Examples: Square notes counselors who 'are extremely helpful' and administrators who 'made things right,' while Circle contains repeated claims that 'communication is non existent' and principals 'disregard you completely.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater variabilit: Circle reviews contain many allegations of staff problems—uncredentialed hires, high turnover, public humiliation of students, favoritism and nepotism, grade‑tampering, teacher sexual misconduct/arrests, absenteeism, and widely inconsistent pedagogy—whereas Square reviews more often describe a stable, committed teacher corps with fewer misconduct reports. Examples: Circle references a teacher arrest for sexual relations with a student, grade changes by staff relatives, 'teachers leave the classroom for the entire period,' and 'uncredentialed former students' hired as teachers; Square generally praises teachers as 'committed and passionate.'
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: Circle reviews frequently emphasize small‑town/small‑school feel, principals and teachers knowing students by name, long‑term resident/alumni endorsement, formal parent rituals (orientations, BBQs, Masses), PTSA/volunteer programs, and active alumni giving or mentorship; Square reviews more often depict a larger, impersonal environment with less multi‑generation engagement. Examples: Circle notes 'this community is one big family,' grandparents volunteering breakfast programs, multi‑decade resident satisfaction, and alumni pledges to give back, contrasted with Square's descriptions of a large school where 'students get lost in the large class sizes.'
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more concrete spec: This bucket collects reviews describing tangible programmatic offerings and measurable college‑prep outcomes at the school (e.g., IB diploma, Cambridge/AICE, SciTech, ECE/AP classes, ROTC/JROTC, career academies, dual enrollment, peer tutoring and named teacher mentors) and claims of strong college matriculation; examples include “full IB Diploma program,” “Cambridge Program/AICE diploma,” “students accepted into SciTech,” and ‘AP/ECE helped graduate early from college.’
candidate_defs.Square entries report more systemic inst: These reviews focus on weak instruction and outcomes — complaints that teachers are incompetent, students are underprepared for college, test scores are low, and advanced coursework is lacking or ineffective (e.g., “teachers largely incompetent,” “I feel so incredibly underprepared,” “the academic program and overall test scores…disappointingly low,” and calls for more AP/Honors that aren’t available).
candidate_defs.Circle entries document more acute safet: Reviews in this group name concrete safety harms or heavy enforcement practices: weapons and expulsions, students sent to the ICU, school resource officers issuing misdemeanor citations, probation officers on campus, on‑campus drug solicitations/sexual activity reports, and enforced searches or expulsions — e.g., “Multiple students were expelled due to bringing weapons,” “School resource officer freely handing out misdemeanor citations,” and “This year they sent 3 students to ICU.”
candidate_defs.Square entries describe more visible, re: This captures reviews that highlight proactive leadership and teacher accessibility — principals and administrators who are visible, communicative, available to parents, and teachers who give individualized help and quick responses (e.g., “administration is very visible…building a relationship,” “teachers always respond back quick,” and “teachers are more than willing to do what it takes”), distinguishing square reviews that report organized outreach from circle reviews that allege unprofessional or unresponsive staff.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more concrete faci: These reviews detail physical and resource conditions and finance-driven program changes: filthy facilities, bad cafeteria food, no air conditioning, overcrowded classes, weekend/program terminations, tuition hikes/donor favoritism, missing equipment or custodial neglect, or conversely specific positive tech programs (1:1 laptops) — examples include “Everything in this school is nasty…no soap,” “Tuition gets hiked up a few hundred dollars every year,” “it’s overcrowded…too many substitute teachers,” and “Each student gets a laptop.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger specializ: These reviews repeatedly describe concrete advanced-program offerings and outcomes (many AP classes and high AP/Exam results, IB/honors rigor, National Merit recognition, magnet tracks, dedicated CTE and vocational programs, university affiliations and dual‑enrollment pathways, and explicit selective/admissions gates), and cite measurable college‑prep success (100% college‑bound claims, scholarship outcomes). Examples: “The number of AP classes offered is tremendous,” “newly formed 4‑year engineering program,” “connected to St. John’s University” and “about 120 spots open each year and 1,500 applications.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report a stronger athleti: Multiple circle reviews portray athletics and related programs as institutionally central (top marching band, astro turf and routinely repaired courts/fields, ‘football is a huge money maker’) while also documenting coach favoritism, unsafe or abusive coaching, and preferential discipline for athletes. Illustrative notes: “everything revolves around athletics,” “home to the National marching band champions,” and complaints that coaches ‘give athletes more help’ or ‘make you continue running… when vomiting.’
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviewers more often recount widespread peer harassment, vaping/drug incidents, sexualized or ganglike student cultures, and explicit neglect or punitive treatment of students with disorders (IEP/504 failures, counselors who ‘won’t help much’), producing mental‑health harms and withdrawals. Representative lines: “bullying is terrible… happens every second of the day,” “Kids vape everywhere,” and “If your child has a disorder… do not send your kid there… they will be bullied.”
candidate_defs.Square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews frequently describe demoralized or unmotivated faculty, passive classroom instruction, poor teaching outcomes (students ‘hardly learn anything’), and communication breakdowns with teachers and counselors. Examples: “A majority of the teachers here do not want to be there,” “they give you a worksheet and text,” and “teachers do not respond to conferences / unanswered messages.”
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more visible admin: Circle reviews contain many concrete administrative actions or disputes (leadership turnover and unilateral policy changes, strict uniform/dress and disciplinary rules, metal detectors, canceled trips, wellness center or new facilities, 1:1 laptop rollouts, levy failures and accusations of misallocated capital vs staff spending, and calls for legal accountability), whereas square mentions fewer concrete policy or capital dynamics. Examples: “new director… changed the focus,” “they took away our senior prom,” “1‑1 computing for three years,” and “seems to waste money on the football team and gates at the front entrance.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews describe leadership problems inside the building—absent or rude administrators, administrators who lie or protect problem students, TA/clerical substitution for administrators, withheld transcripts, and bureaucratic obstacles to parent access (e.g., needing superintendent sign‑off). Examples: 'Administration is absent and having TA do their work', 'Administrators lied straight to my face', 'holding his transcripts hostage because I refuse to pay', and allegations that admins protected gang members—contrasted with square entries that emphasize more collaborative external relationships or at least identifiable corrective actions.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ad: Many circle reviews enumerate named curricular assets and pathways—AP counts, PLTW/TRANSTEM/FAA/aviation or cosmetology licensure, dual‑enrollment, strong marching band/arts, robotics/3D‑printing labs, and 1:1 iPad/laptop programs—presenting clear programmatic breadth and college/industry links. Examples: '8 AP courses, PLTW program, 3D printing lab, every student has an iPad', 'TRANSTEM Academy and summer scholarships to aviation camps', whereas square reviews rarely list such concrete program inventories and often emphasize limited course expansion or juggling of honors/AP supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain repeated, specific accounts of student violence, pervasive bullying (including racialized/online targeting), drug use and adult involvement, thefts, and hazing, often with claims that staff failed to intervene. Examples: 'Fights occur almost everyday', 'If you are a person of color you will NOT feel safe here...multiple instances of online bullying', 'DRUGS are horrible within the schools' and reports that administrators 'do nothing', while square entries contain far fewer or different safety narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater variability: These reviews simultaneously document highly engaged, mentorship‑oriented teachers and concrete examples of poor or protected teachers, unqualified long‑term substitutes, plus explicit instructional practices (after‑school help, heavy or negligible homework, teaching‑to‑the‑test). Examples: 'teachers have gone above and beyond' and 'incredible teachers who make the difference' alongside 'tenure teachers that need to leave', 'substitute for 6–8 weeks who can't teach math', and contrasts with square where staff descriptions are more uniformly characterized (either generally supportive or consistently poor) rather than this broad internal spread.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more social strati: Reviews frequently describe explicit peer‑status systems and staff/administrative favoritism—athletes or children of staff/wealthy families get preferential treatment, racial/social segregation and socioeconomic shaming limit belonging, and entrenched parent cliques shape access. Examples: 'If you're very smart you're in the "in crowd"', 'kids who played sports were favored', 'The social aspect... is almost entirely segregated by race', and 'parents who have been here most of their life carry an arrogance', while square entries rarely foreground this combination of athletic/wealth favoritism and racially/socioeconomically patterned exclusion.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe concrete, unresolved safety problems inside and around the school — daily fights, gang presence, drug use (even in middle grades), students physically assaulted or videoed in restrooms, and repeated allegations that administration fails to address these incidents (e.g., “a lot of drugs…people get beaten up,” “There are FIGHTS daily,” and “administration does nothing to combat bullying”). Falling into this bucket means the school profile centers on persistent student-on-student violence and unmanaged peer‑risk behaviors that reviewers tie to weak incident response.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: These reviews document leadership and governance problems — frequent principal turnover, micromanagement and abuse of power, nepotistic hiring, manipulation of enrollment/funding counts, refusal or rudeness in office interactions, and parents being ignored or belittled (e.g., “changing dates on paper so they can count your child,” “blowing parents off,” “hung up the phone,” and “unstable leadership and frequent abuse of power”). Content in this bucket signals managerial malpractice, inconsistent discipline enforcement, or deliberate administrative opacity rather than merely isolated teacher issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater chronic re: These reviews emphasize material scarcity and infrastructure problems: lack of textbooks and copies, broken air conditioning during testing, outdated technology and libraries, uncomfortable or failing facilities, and pervasive underfunding (e.g., “They don't have enough copies to last the year,” “It seriously needs air conditioning,” and “school's technology and library is outdated”). Items here indicate concrete resource deficits that interfere with instruction and daily comfort, not just pedagogical critiques.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an athletics‑do: These comments point to sports‑first priorities and unequal treatment — football or varsity athletics treated as the institutional priority, budgets and attention diverted to sports, and preferential treatment for athletes or children of influential parents (e.g., “Football is VERY important,” “sports teams get practically all the money,” and “The wealthy and connected parents make sure their kids get everything”). Belonging to this bucket means reviewers portray extracurricular and funding priorities that privilege athletic status or parental influence over broad academic equity.
candidate_defs.square entries report stronger organized: Square reviews frequently highlight formal academic and arts programs, clear college‑prep routes (AP/Honors, dual/college credit, rigorous curriculum), strong performing-arts offerings, and effective counselor/parent communication (e.g., praise for band and Broadway‑quality musicals, honors/AP coursework, National Honor Society, and counselors who assist families). Content in this bucket characterizes schools as offering coherent programmatic pathways and demonstrable postsecondary preparation with organized teacher–parent channels rather than systemic resource or safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize an explicit fai: These reviews repeatedly describe organized religious programming (weekly Mass/chapel, required religion classes, chaplains, worship teams), single-sex or faith missions (all‑boys, Catholic identity), and long family/alumni pipelines or legacy pride (multi‑child attendance, alumni engagement, ‘#Aztecforlife’) that square entries do not mention; examples include reports of spirituality driving school life and families sending several generations through the school.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader, formali: Circle reviews enumerate concrete advanced‑academic and career pathways (AP, IB, Dual Enrollment, college credits, AICE, CTE/technical academies, certifications, associate degrees), plus named outcomes/rankings and specific college matriculations and test‑score claims (700 API, national rankings, Ivy/Top‑20 placements), whereas square reviews rarely list this depth or quantification.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more accessible,: These entries highlight small class sizes, sustained teacher mentorship, tutors/after‑school/weekend tutoring, proactive teacher‑to‑parent communication, and principal‑led outreach (coffee hours, individualized interventions), with multiple reviewers saying teachers are available during lunch or stay late to help — features that square entries mention far less.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent conc: Circle reviews contain many specific allegations of ongoing bullying, physical fights, gang/robbery rumors, sexual and racist/homophobic harassment, cyberbullying, and students smoking/roaming, often coupled with claims that enforcement or protection fails (victimization, inadequate IEP protection), while square entries rarely raise this cluster of safety/harassment problems.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete adm: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe administrative mismanagement (nonresponsive communication, concealment of program info, nepotism/favoritism, retaliation/firings, politicized school boards), plus specific operational policies and facility details (locked bathrooms, three‑minute passing, shortened lunches, security hardware, technology programs, renovations or severe decay) — granular, actionable operational claims that are largely absent from square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket groups reviews that document concrete safety incidents and uncontrolled student behavior (fights, gang activity, death threats, sexual harassment, on‑campus drug use, routine alarm‑pulling and loitering) as problems the school does not contain or resolve — e.g. “students have taken and bought marijuana at school,” “I even got death threats,” “There is a lot of gang activity… safety is ALWAYS an issue,” and “All the student do is pull the fire alarm and fight outside.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures descriptions of governance and operational breakdowns such as poor communication, repeated leadership turnover, withheld records/grade penalties, counselor scheduling errors, retained criminal incidents, donor‑based favoritism, and IEP/IEP‑removal abuses — e.g. “The communication level is ZERO… not ONE SINGLE time did I ever receive a call back,” “they would not release our student’s records… grades reduced by 20%,” “Superintendent… should be fired,” and “they kicked my son out of school because he had an IEP.”
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize more formal, st: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete, organized college‑prep and career pathways (IB academies, honors/AP/academies, STEM academies, dual enrollment/Running Start, vocational trades, industry certifications, NAVY JROTC) and named outcome evidence like scholarships and college acceptances — e.g. “The IB Program is exceptional,” “Running Start and Sno‑Isle technical programs,” “Most of their courses are actual certification courses,” and “accepted into every college he applied including top schools.”
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent, c: This bucket covers reviews that portray the school as having reliable teacher availability, extra help, caring staff, fair/strict discipline, organized counseling/credit recovery, and principals who communicate and engage with families — e.g. “They are there early, they stay late and help any student,” “The principal keeps you very informed,” “the staff are caring and helpful,” and “New Principal… has done an amazing job.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: This bucket groups accounts that simultaneously praise wide extracurricular breadth and specialized facilities (over 100 clubs, multiple theatre spaces, world‑class athletic fields, robotics and band championships) while documenting conflicts tied to athletics/ donors (boundary exceptions, pay‑to‑play, donor influence on playing time, club defunding for football) — e.g. “plenty of clubs and sports… three theatre spaces,” “more than one hundred state championships,” and “sports teams… arranged by who your parents are” or “robotics club’s funding was cut to get more money for football.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket groups reviews that describe routine peer abuse (e.g., reports of sexual assault, urination in girls’ locker room, death threats from varsity players), measurable dropouts or withdrawals for safety, and administrators who dismiss or fail to intervene (e.g., dean who laughed at anti-bullying programs, parents pulled kids out). These items signal systemic student-safety failures and staff inaction in circle schools that are not present in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more robust, high-: This captures mentions of strong, visible programs—state/nationally recognized athletics and marching band, IB and specialized magnet tracks, dual-enrollment/running-start partnerships, career academies and advanced STEM electives—and concrete alumni success claims (NFL players, Fortune 500 leaders, high college matriculation). These circle reviews emphasize breadth, prestige, and concrete programmatic pathways that square reviews typically do not describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: These items describe small class sizes, routine one-on-one tutoring and remediation, personalized senior schedules, fast parent communication and a ‘village’/multi‑generational community feel—parents praising same‑day callbacks, teachers working before/after school, and strong volunteer engagement—which contrast with square reviews that report more uneven support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more nepotism, sta: This bucket covers operational and governance complaints tied to fairness and due process—allegations that teacher/coach relatives or church families get preferential recognition, athletes get grade leniency or bribery, and the school uses punitive, opaque systems (substance‑testing used coercively, confiscation/social‑media eavesdropping, no‑appeal demerit policies). These are concrete procedural and ethical problems emphasized in many circle reviews but absent from square.
candidate_defs.square entries report more consistent ad: This bucket groups square reviews that highlight stable, improvement-oriented leadership, effective anti-bullying enforcement and security response, consistent teacher quality, and documented college-readiness outcomes (AP/honors pathways with graduates going to top universities), marking square schools as comparatively organized and outcome-focused relative to circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more safety incide: These reviews describe concrete safety failures and widespread student misbehavior at the schools in circle — e.g., off‑campus assault causing concussion/brain bleed, weapons/chemicals sightings, frequent fights, gang claims, substance use, rampant bullying and Snapchat humiliation, and police reports left ‘under investigation’ — contrasts with square reviews that emphasize cameras, a sense of safety, or do not report comparable violence or chronic bullying.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failure/negle: Circle reviews recount systemic special‑education breakdowns and formal escalation (failed 504s, lawsuits to obtain services, parents 'fighting a losing battle', ignored accommodations), whereas square reviews more often report functioning special‑education progress or do not document chronic denial of disability supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater prioritiza: Many circle reviews say resources, scholarships, and administrative attention flow to athletes (e.g., ‘only football players get support’, grade/favoritism for athletes, athletics‑first identity, coaches protected, mandatory athletic-related cancellations), and claim arts/programs are cut or deprioritized; square reviews either highlight balanced extracurriculars/arts or do not document such athletic favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more advanced coll: Circle reviews frequently describe strong AP/IB/dual‑enrollment offerings, guaranteed college pathways (CUNY/Hunter), high ACT/OGT results, alumni college acceptances, or top‑in‑state claims — concrete programmatic breadth and outcomes that square reviews generally lack or criticize as insufficient (missing basic math, poor college readiness).
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle reviews contain concrete allegations of administrative failures — discipline quotas, grade‑alteration pressure, record/credit mishandling, billing and lunch‑program errors, unresponsive or rude administrators, favoritism and corruption in budgeting/awards — a pattern of governance/operational breakdowns contrasted with square reviews that more often describe responsive staff or fewer systemic administrative abuses.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe richer specializ: These circle reviews emphasize concrete advanced-program availability and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑credit, selective enrollment, vocational/aviation/ROTC pathways, adjunct-taught dual-enrollment) and cite metrics/placements (scholarship totals, 100% graduation, Ivy/competitive admits) as evidence; e.g. “abundance of AP and dual credit classes,” “WMST recently became an International Baccalaureate school,” and “THIS YEAR’S... seniors accumulated over $16 million in scholarships,” while square reviews lack equivalent program depth or measurable college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, higher‑pa: Circle reviews repeatedly name extensive arts, band/choir, theater, competitive teams and high extracurricular participation, plus multigenerational alumni ties and active parent involvement (e.g. “choir program is huge,” “one band, one family,” “Many of the teachers are Cedar Grove Alumni,” and “Fantastic parent involvement”), whereas square reviews rarely describe this breadth or deep community continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more explicit ad: Circle reviewers frequently reference recent leadership change, capital projects, facility upgrades, and quantified improvement efforts—LEED‑platinum building, superintendent-driven literacy committees, CCRPI score gains, solved mass‑retirement financial issues—(e.g. “new Administration is a positive improvement,” “increase their CCRPI score by over 10 points,” “a new edifice...platinum”) while square reviews offer few examples of such concrete district-led reforms or measurable investment narratives.
candidate_defs.square entries describe poorer day‑to‑da: Square reviews disproportionately report disengaged or incompetent teachers, weak lesson delivery, failing classroom management and low academic expectations—examples include “teachers are outrageously snotty,” “they are lazy,” “teachers are unresponsive to phone calls and emails,” and complaints about no remediation or ineffective guidance—whereas circle reviews more often describe proactive teacher help, tutoring, and high expectations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more failures or g: Many circle reviews document concrete special‑education implementation failures, overloaded or ineffective counselors, refusals to address student mental health, wrongful suspension processes, and selective enforcement or athlete/affluent favoritism (e.g. “The special education in this school is a joke,” “They refused to help with my depression,” “suspended...on a Sunday,” and “laxity increases with the wealth of the parent”), while square reviews seldom raise the same cluster of individualized‑support or procedural‑fairness allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: These reviews describe frequent physical fights, daily threats, pepper‑spraying, sexual harassment episodes, and race/sexuality‑based hostility often coupled with staff inaction or administration siding with bullies (e.g., “we have a couple of fights every week,” “teachers just turn their heads,” “Being queer… constantly looking over your shoulder”), whereas square entries rarely report routine violence and more often note active safety measures and minimal bullying.
candidate_defs.square entries describe stronger, consis: Square reviews cite high AP performance, National Merit recognition, named scholarships and steady state/ranking metrics and describe a clear college-prep culture (e.g., “Baldwin students score consistently well on AP tests,” “students admitted to some of the most competitive schools”), while circle reviews contain more mixed or uneven claims about AP pass rates, remedial college courses, and variable program completion.
