candidate_defs.circle entries evidence more administrat: Many circle reviews report poor principal/superintendent responsiveness, financial opacity, inconsistent policy enforcement, nepotism, and district-level failures (e.g., “Where does the bingo money go?”, “The principal is not present,” calls to remove the superintendent), in contrast to square reviews that more often describe engaged leadership, clear communication systems, and accountable practices.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more personalize: Numerous circle reviews highlight teachers who give extra time, after‑school tutoring, hands‑on mentorship, college trips, small-class attention and concrete IEP supports (e.g., “teachers will stay after school to help,” “Dr. Fields… takes the kids on college tours,” “IEP program is really strong”), whereas square reviews more often report uneven teacher responsiveness or that only a few teachers provide such individualized support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater material r: Circle reviews record mold, broken HVAC, outdated/limited computer labs, required expensive uniform/fees, cuts to aides/specialized learning and funds funneled to athletics at the expense of arts (e.g., “saw mold on the ceiling,” “1 computer lab… not allowed to use,” “all of the funding goes to the dance teams/football”), while square entries less frequently document such systemic facility/technology deficits or regressive fee burdens.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: This bucket captures reports of on-campus fights, gang presence, drug use, theft/robbery, public shaming on social media, chronic bullying and attendant student mental‑health harms (depression, paranoia) that appear repeatedly in circle reviews (e.g., “Fights everyday,” “Nearly everyone smokes…,” “2 of their prized cheerleaders shaming a homeless woman,” “i am depressed”), while square reviews rarely describe comparable incident-level violence, drug allegations, or sustained bullying corroboration.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger formal: This groups circle statements that name concrete high‑rigor programs and articulated career pathways (AP/IB/STEM, dual credit, vocational/shop/CTE, internships), formal grade transparency and tutoring systems, and cited college matriculation/graduation evidence (e.g., “AP, accelerated, dual credit,” “100% of seniors graduate and 98% go to college,” “excellent science program”), whereas square reviews typically note general course variety or missing advanced offerings without the same named programs or consistent outcome metrics.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more systemic admi: This bucket groups circle claims about entrenched corruption and governance manipulation—named administrators, nepotism, pushing out low performers to protect rankings, enrollment gatekeeping, committee bullying, erased yearbook entries and punitive retaliation—(e.g., “blatant nepotism,” “encourage the student to drop out…to keep the ranking up,” “they erased his name/photo”), while square reviews do not center district‑level corruption or comparable political favoritism.
candidate_defs.circle entries report superior physical: This captures circle reviewers' repeated praise of new buildings, state‑of‑the‑art fields, auditoriums, pools, and high‑tech classrooms and investments (“new high school… new everything,” “Gorgeous High School…state of the art”), contrasted with square reviewers who more often report overcrowded portables, outdated technology, missing supplies and public budget shortfalls (“AP Calculus 45 students stuffed into a portable,” “not enough money for paper,” “underfunded”).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader, award‑: This bucket groups circle claims of extensive extracurricular breadth and success—award‑winning band/choir/robotics/athletics, high participation rates, mandatory or celebrated sports traditions, active PTSA/booster support and community fundraising (e.g., “top notch Band program,” “state champs,” “The PTSA and the booster club really care”), whereas square reviews either omit such program breadth or mention far fewer/less‑celebrated extracurricular offerings and parent organization activity.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger special: These circle reviews repeatedly name selective or magnet structures, concentrated AP/IB/honors offerings, specialty centers or academy tracks and give concrete college‑placement metrics (e.g., magnet majors like Engineering/Computer Science, IB program, “99–100% college placement,” admits to MIT/Harvard/Yale), whereas square reviews emphasize general AP/college prep without the same track-based selectivity or named top-college outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader, award‑win: Circle reviews emphasize extensive, high‑participation extracurricular breadth and recognized extracurricular excellence (e.g., nationally known madrigals, award‑winning drama and sports state championships, conservatory-style arts programs, dozens of clubs and no‑cut athletics), while square reviews rarely document comparable award-level arts/sports achievements or such pervasive student participation.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent bu: Circle reviews more often describe tangible safety problems and contested discipline (media‑covered bullying, frequent fights, police presence, students leaving short-term due to bullying) plus discriminatory/punitive enforcement (gendered dress‑code shaming, detention for body modification, racialized avoidance advisories), whereas square reviews contain little or no reporting of this cluster of severe safety/discipline incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: Circle entries repeatedly allege governance and personnel abuses (grade changes, targeted harassment/expulsions, nepotistic hiring, bribery/collusion, rude/intimidating front office, calls for district investigations) and inconsistent enforcement across staff roles, while square entries do not raise these systemic favoritism/nepotism and corruption claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries provide richer operationa: Circle reviews supply numerous concrete operational observations—both positive and negative—such as intervention periods, mandatory tutoring/study tables, one‑on‑one math help, but also textbook shortages, cafeteria meal deficits/no spoons, severe overcrowding/long commutes, and IEP/ELL implementation gaps; square reviews rarely document this level of granular service or logistics detail.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: These circle reviews repeatedly describe unresolved bullying, frequent fights, drug and gang involvement, sexual relationships between staff/students, and staff/administration ignoring or minimizing incidents (e.g., “My kid has been bullied and it was never addressed,” “Too many drugs go around,” “chants… 'Black Lives Don’t Matter'… staff would turn the other way,” and allegations of teachers having relations with students). By contrast square reviews typically frame student behavior as more supported or describe fewer safety incidents, making safety and staff inaction a distinguishing feature of circle texts.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more formalized: Many circle reviews enumerate concrete program infrastructure—academies (STEM, arts, culinary), dual enrollment/college-credit opportunities, AVID/AP offerings, 1:1 device deployment, extensive arts/music programs, internships and career certifications (e.g., “Biomedical Sciences program… opportunities for college credit,” “Chromebooks available in every classroom,” and extensive arts/music listings). Square reviews rarely list that breadth of structured pathways or concrete dual-credit programs, instead focusing on operational or staffing concerns.
candidate_defs.circle entries flag more systemic admini: Circle reviewers frequently blame district/school leadership or governance for problems—accusing corruption, naming superintendent/principal misconduct, citing misdirected persistent phone messages, zoning/transportation mistakes, and nonresponsive staff (e.g., “for over two years I have had to complain about messages left…,” “This school district is absolutely horrible; it's very corrupt,” and “they turn the other way when issues arise”). Square reviews tend to focus critiques at classroom or policy levels rather than alleging widespread administrative malfeasance.
candidate_defs.circle entries show greater within-schoo: Many circle texts contain sharply divergent accounts from the same school—high praise for named teachers, elite college placements, and standout departments coexisting with reports of failing academics, sanitation, or safety (e.g., “Mr. Moss… amazing” alongside “the school is doing so poorly… test scores steadily declining,” and ‘standout band/theater but other programs tanked’). Square reviews are comparatively more uniform in their narratives, so internal inconsistency and program-by-program contrast is a signature of circle entries.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive ins: Square reviews more often allege that teachers don’t teach or are unqualified, guidance is unreliable, programs struggle to survive (e.g., taped-together band instruments), and students leave behind academically (e.g., “He was so far behind… poor college readiness,” “subs unequipped to be teaching that subject,” and “TSA program… literally struggle to survive”). These recurring claims about instructional weakness, poor counseling, and program instability distinguish square entries from circle ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, docume: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete advanced-academic pathways and results—multiple circle reviewers cite abundant AP/IB/Honors offerings, high AP/ACT/SAT performance, millions in scholarships, and admissions to selective colleges (e.g., “My son took many AP classes… scored very high on the ACT,” “brought in almost 5 million in scholarship funds,” “acceptances to Duke, UNC, Columbia”), while square reviews lack comparable measurable college-prep outcomes and instead focus on vocational tracks or generalized academic complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe greater personal: This bucket groups accounts emphasizing low student:teacher ratios, sustained teacher availability/tutoring, wide & named clubs, and easy multi‑sport participation (examples: “small classroom sizes,” “teachers stayed after school as long as you need them,” “Dance, robotics, DECA…,” “easy to play multiple sports guaranteed”), whereas square reviews more often report larger classes, limited individualized attention, or fewer enumerated extracurricular options.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket covers systemic operational breakdowns and adversarial bureaucracy found mainly in circle reviews—lost doctor notes and attendance errors, unanswered emails and application non‑response, accusations of nepotistic hiring and misdirected spending, and allegations that administrators threatened legal action (e.g., “They lost doctor notes… tried to give Saturday school,” “No one returns your emails,” “Good Ol' Boy system,” “administrators that will threaten to sue you”), whereas square reviews seldom allege this pattern of institutional incompetence or legal harassment.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This bucket captures concrete safety/discipline deficits reported by circle reviewers—frequent fights, bathroom drug offers, theft of personal/medical items, bullying of minority and special‑needs students, and claims that discipline is uneven or favoritist (e.g., “lot of drugs, fights and everyone do what they want,” “my inhaler was stolen,” “Not a good school for African American children… Administration was not much help,” “they pick and choose who they want to discipline”), while square reviews less often describe this combination of high violence/substance incidents and selective enforcement.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more visible par: This bucket covers reviews where the dominant issue is overt community conflict and episodic misconduct reported at the school—square reviewers describe polarized parental complaints about leadership, explicit front‑office insensitivity, staff physical grabbing/arrests, surveillance or heavy policing at events (examples: “polarized parental/staff conflict and complaints,” “the main office lady... ‘I don't think family emergency cuts it,’” reports of staff arrests and surveillance), a pattern less prevalent in circle reviews which focus more on systemic bureaucracy or academic/programmatic strengths.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, exp: These reviews describe concrete safety incidents and weak physical safeguards (fights, stabbings, overdoses, drug deals in halls, working security cameras/doors left unlocked, food‑safety/poisoning), e.g., circle notes “fights at least once a week,” “After the stabbing last year…,” visible drug deals and smells, and broken/insufficient cameras or unlocked doors, whereas square reviews mostly allege generalized lack of discipline rather than named violent incidents or specific security failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete adva: These reviews cite explicit college-prep programs and outcomes (AP credits, early college/dual-enrollment, named AP/STEM teachers, students admitted to selective universities, SAT/ACT scores), e.g., circle lists AP Computer Science, early college/associate-degree options, and alumni at Stanford/Georgia Tech, while square tends to describe program-level rigor or IB/AP presence more abstractly and without the same concrete matriculation evidence.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, higher-: Circle reviews frequently enumerate rich arts and sports offerings plus recent capital improvements (award‑winning music/forensics, robust marching band, favoritism toward football, new stadiums, solar/energy upgrades, brand‑new buildings), e.g., “amazing marching band program,” “brand new state‑of‑the‑art stadium,” whereas square mentions clubs/activities or limited athletics but lacks the same breadth of thriving programs and facility modernization claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more individualize: These reviews emphasize personalized supports—teachers who call/meet parents, invite students to lunch, Campus Portal communication, Math/English Resource Centers, peer tutoring or credit‑recovery options—e.g., circle: “teachers go out of their way…always communicating,” “Math Science Resource Center,” while square reviews more often report inconsistent or spotty academic help and limited individualized follow‑through.
candidate_defs.square entries report more administrativ: Square reviews repeatedly call out leadership inaction and guidance-office unwillingness to help—examples include “principal or teachers did nothing” about bullying, “the principal's lack of a spinal cord… Administrators just didn’t care,” and guidance that won’t change schedules—whereas circle reviews contain more examples of active/principal‑led initiatives or organized outreach alongside other patterns.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger, organi: These reviews emphasize concrete, school‑level college‑prep systems: required senior college acceptance rules, dual‑credit partnerships, AVID and full‑time college counselors, expanded AP/honors pathways and alumni matriculation data (e.g., 'all seniors are required to be accepted by a 4 year college,' '4 full time college counselors,' '99% of Servite grads go on to college'). Square entries rarely document that level of organized, measurable college‑prep structure or outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and fr: Many circle reviews catalog repeated, acute safety incidents and on‑campus threats—weekly fights, gang presence, visible drug/tobacco use, K9 searches, even clusters of student suicides and theft—often coupled with students leaving or families relocating ('every other day there is a fight,' 'Gang violence... do not send your child,' 'drugs in this school'). Square entries, by contrast, more often describe limited past incidents or a caring/safe environment rather than chronic, townwide safety failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent teac: Circle reviews contain repeated, concrete allegations about low instructional competence, punitive teacher behavior (yelling, belittling), poor substitute management, and contested rigor/grade‑inflation—examples include 'teachers are incompetent,' 'substitute... sits on his phone,' and alumni needing remediation in college. Square reviews mention some teacher burnout or gaps but lack the same breadth of classroom‑level incompetence and punitive conduct claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance, f: These reviews point to governance problems—secret or unresponsive boards, donor‑driven favoritism, nepotism, inconsistent discipline enforcement, and district deflection of parent concerns (e.g., 'the school is now run by a secret board,' 'pander to the rich families,' 'district just says contact the principal'). Square entries seldom allege systemic board secrecy or donor favoritism and more often describe specific staffing or program complaints instead.
candidate_defs.circle entries document greater variety: Circle reviews frequently inventory concrete campus amenities and program breadth—new baseball/turf fields, huge theater, CTE and magnet academies, international travel, and assorted fee/tuition policies ('first 3 things you'll see... new baseball field... huge theater,' 'Vo‑Tech, AOC internships,' 'pay to play for sports,' 'tuition raised to $11,900'). Square entries rarely list that same diversity or visible capital investment and instead focus on curricular or staffing matters.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger special: This bucket captures reviews that report concrete, school‑level academic assets and outcomes found more often in circle entries — e.g., named AP/IB/biomedical/academy programs, Running Start/dual‑enrollment and associate‑degree pathways, high national rankings, Ivy League acceptances, Mu Alpha Theta placements, and explicit test‑score percentiles — contrasted with square entries that lack such programs or report weak college preparedness and remedial needs.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader extracurri: This groups reports where circle reviewers list many clubs/teams, award‑winning arts and championship athletic records, community internships, international exchange programs and donor‑funded facility upgrades (e.g., state football titles, band awards, international MUN wins), while square reviews tend to describe limited or narrowly funded extracurriculars.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more organized s: This bucket covers descriptions of concrete student supports more commonly noted in circle entries — graduation coaches, formal mentoring K–12, strong special‑education accommodations, structured tutoring and summer/Saturday programs, effective ADHD accommodations, and active parent‑partnership programs — contrasted with square entries that report weak/unhelpful counselors, missing college advising, and scarce targeted supports.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: This groups reviews that document frequent, incident‑level safety and conduct problems in circle entries — repeated physical assaults, rampant bullying and cyber‑bullying, everyday drug/alcohol use, fights during unstructured times, and sexual/peer‑health concerns — whereas square entries typically include fewer or different accounts of these pervasive safety issues.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more governance, a: This bucket captures structural and policy problems emphasized in circle reviews: school‑board or superintendent failures, administrators 'making up rules', nepotism/donor/varsity favoritism, racial/exclusionary traditions or religious enrollment criteria, opaque discipline/lockdown of parent access, and misuse of surveillance — contrasted with square entries that do not foreground these systemic governance or favoritism claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more student safet: These reviews describe concrete safety problems—widespread drug/vaping use, on‑campus dealers, frequent fights/threats, property theft, racial harassment, staff inaction, unsecured entrances, and even alleged physical/sexual abuse—occurring inside or around the school; example evidence includes warnings about buying drugs during the school day, assertions that 'there is so much bullying... staff do NOTHING,' reports of unlocked front doors and negligent guards, and an account of student physical abuse by aides.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger formal co: Many circle reviews cite specific academic programs and outcomes—robust AP success rates, honors/IB/academy offerings, dual‑credit/AA pathways, vocational credentialing, and high graduation/college‑acceptance statistics—claiming the school prepares students for college and yields alumni success; illustrative notes include 'great AP program and high passing rates,' 'academies that count as college credit,' and '99+% graduation and college acceptance rates.'
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive adm: Square reviews disproportionately describe systemic leadership problems—unresponsive or absent principals, poor district governance, politicized favoritism, bungled administrative processes, and organizational decline—that reviewers link to poor outcomes; concrete examples include reports that attempts to contact principals were ignored, claims the school 'is terribly mismanaged' and warnings about district‑level cover‑ups or leadership scandals.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: Circle reviews frequently document a wide array of clubs, competitive band/choir/athletic achievements, JROTC/ROTC and camps, parent‑run safety/volunteer programs, fundraising and alumni reinvestment, and local traditions—often noting athletic prestige or a lively arts culture; examples include nationally ranked teams, respected choir/band accolades, parent‑run designated‑driver and fundraising efforts, and statements about strong alumni support and community camaraderie.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete op: Circle reviews contain many specific, operational details about how services are delivered or fail: explicit praise for IEP adherence or free transit, but also reports of SPED noncompliance, lost transcripts, late grade reporting, counselor insufficiency, busing problems, pest infestations, cafeteria issues, and technology investments/shortcomings; representative items include 'my son has an IEP and the principal makes certain it is adhered to,' 'we don't have books / only two counselors,' 'lost my transcript over the summer,' and Title I tech updates.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more con: These reviews emphasize explicit AP/IB/dual-enrollment counts, SAT/graduation metrics, scholarship totals, documented Ivy/top‑college matriculations, and structured college-prep requirements (e.g., 14 AP classes, $28M scholarships, 1124 SAT average, dual enrollment/ROTC pathways, mandatory college applications), whereas square reviews tend to describe program-level aspirations or isolated enrichment without the same volume of quantifiable outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent alle: Many circle reviews allege racism/colorism, sexuality- and religion‑based shaming, grooming/hairstyle bans, refusal to admit or accommodate 'behavior' or disabled students, IEP noncompliance, and explicit narratives of minority-targeted mistreatment—claims that are largely absent from square entries (examples: bans on braids/locs, "beyond racist and homophobic," IEP coverups and denial of services).
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe thriving band/choir/theatre programs, sports championships and new athletic facilities, many clubs, community rescue fundraising and strong alumni ties (e.g., new stadium, World Choir Games win, community raised $400k), while square reviews focus more narrowly on curricular features and rarely cite the same range of sustained community/extra‑curricular investments.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: Concrete operational complaints recur in circle reviews—running out of lunches, locked/unsanitary bathrooms, unreliable buses, overcrowded halls/ trailers, scheduling burdens and broken tech rollouts—which are described as affecting daily student life and family logistics; square entries rarely name this cluster of recurring facility/operational breakdowns.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive on‑: Square reviews more often spotlight active drug problems, frequent fights, pervasive student disrespect, and perceptions that administration or staff ignore reports (e.g., 'Huge Drug problem', students laughing at principal, staff who 'don't care'), framing an on‑campus behavioral/safety crisis and weak follow‑through that circle entries less consistently portray.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, more for: Reviews in Circle repeatedly name structured college-prep offerings and outcomes (IB diploma programs, AP/Dual Credit, integrated ACT prep, high ACT averages and scholarship wins) and describe a high‑pressure, rigorous workload—e.g., “The IB program is really taking off,” “average ACT score of 23,” and “VERY academically rigorous” — whereas Square reviews more often complain of poor college preparation and grading practices rather than listing programmatic supports or measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report exceptional/select: Circle reviewers frequently cite elite arts/band performance, statewide/national wins, JROTC/ROTC, auditioned ensembles, and selective admissions/tryouts (e.g., “performing arts and music programs here are astounding,” “you have to try out,” “the band… one of the best in the state”), while Square tends to note general activity breadth without the same level of competitive excellence or selection.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe tighter parent/c: Many Circle reviews describe low student–teacher ratios, teachers knowing families, high parent involvement and alumni engagement, and explicit local choice decisions (e.g., “smaller size allows us to get to know parents & their kids,” “The parent involvement is great,” and parents choosing between nearby schools), whereas Square reviews do not emphasize sustained small‑school personalization or strong alumni/parent continuity.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews contain repeated claims about teachers not teaching, staff acting like bullies, credential/competence issues and classroom neglect (e.g., “most teachers do not teach,” “teachers themselves act like bullies,” “could not speak the foreign language she was teaching”), whereas Circle reviews far more often praise teacher quality or describe structured remediation and one‑on‑one support.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent acut: Circle reviewers repeatedly allege daily fights, gang presence, drugs/vaping, thefts and institution of strict security (metal detectors, monthly lockdowns, drug‑dog searches) and even weapons incidents (e.g., “there are fights almost daily,” “kids with guns,” “We have to go through the metal detectors every morning”), while Square reviews emphasize rule enforcement or isolated bullying but do not report this same level of chronic, weaponized or drug‑related safety breakdowns.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report stronger, organize: This bucket groups items where circle reviews cite concrete academic programs and outcomes (AP/IB/dual‑credit, average ACTs, honors tracks, CTE credentialing, early-college credit and high graduation/college‑placement rates) that square reviews do not — e.g., “South Warren offers more AP and Dual Credit Classes,” “average ACT scores of 21,” “students graduated with associate degrees,” and sustained CTE/health‑technologies pathways and college‑prep mentoring programs.
candidate_defs.Circle entries report broader, higher‑pr: Includes mentions of wide extracurricular breadth, named academies, award‑winning arts/music/FFA/ag programs, internships/fellowships, upgraded facilities and capital projects that circle reviewers highlight but square largely omits — e.g., “chorus, band, orchestra, drama… top‑notch,” “award winning Agriculture department,” “new library, new stadium, field house,” and music trips to Carnegie Hall/Rome.
candidate_defs.Circle entries describe more consistent,: Covers reports of teacher qualifications, in‑class innovation, routine before/after‑school tutoring, professional development and specific emotional support examples that appear in circle reviews more often than square — e.g., “several with doctorates, most with masters,” teachers who ‘sing theorems,’ ‘Teachers take extra steps to tutor before and after school,’ and students saying teachers ‘cheered you up’ or ‘helped me improve 100%.’
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more frequent stud: Groups accounts of student violence, pervasive bullying/cliques, gang activity, repeated lunch‑time fights, unsafe or overcrowded buses, bathroom closures causing health incidents, and refusal to close for extreme weather which circle reviews document more often — e.g., ‘about 15 fights this year,’ ‘Cellphone use runs rampant,’ ‘Most of them are closed during the day…UTI infections,’ and ‘WE DONT CLOSE SCHOOL EVEN IF ITS -50 DEGREES.’
candidate_defs.Circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures allegations of poor front‑office communication, lost transcripts/medical records, selective enforcement/favoritism, unqualified or departing principals, fabricated or contested data and opaque athletic/discipline policies that circle reviewers frequently cite — e.g., ‘No phone calls back from Principal,’ ‘they lost my son's medical documents three times,’ ‘administration chooses which families they want to interact with,’ and ‘one of the principals does not even have an administrative certificate.’
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe and fr: This bucket captures concrete accounts of campus violence and safety breakdowns that appear far more often in circle reviews — e.g., explicit claims of ‘GANG ACTIVITY’, students ‘being assaulted’, ‘way too many fights’, drug problems, thefts, and an author saying ‘I had my life threatened and they didn't do ANYTHING about it.’ Square entries rarely describe violent incidents and instead note only occasional non-violent bullying.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more explicit adva: This bucket groups concrete programmatic and outcome evidence emphasized in circle reviews: listings of AP/IB/honors options, dual‑enrollment/college credits, high ACT/SAT averages and scholarship totals, one-to-one device rollouts, and named career/internship outcomes (e.g., ‘both my sons... are now college graduates’, ‘graduated with 50 credits’). Square reviews rarely claim comparable breadth/scale of advanced coursework or documented measurable outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: This bucket captures recurring operational teaching failures described more often in square reviews — teachers ‘give up almost entirely’ in on‑level classes, counselors ignoring students, IEPs being neglected, and claims that ‘the faculty doesn't care about the students’ education.’ While circle reviews also show teacher variability, square entries disproportionately describe instructional apathy, low expectations, and failure to support struggling students.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more visible, name: This bucket captures circle reviewers’ frequent references to named principals and leadership-driven change (positive turnarounds: ‘When Mr. McDonald came over everything turned around’), active discipline/enforcement (‘bullying is actually dealt with’), or explicit administrative responsiveness — even when that same school also receives some administrative criticism; square reviews, by contrast, more often portray administrators as disengaged or the source of decline without those named turnaround narratives.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more community-enr: This bucket groups content about how the school is embedded in its community and who is included or excluded: circle reviews repeatedly mention lotteries/waitlists/boarding, faith or doctrinal curriculum, generational alumni pride, parents withdrawing children or moving districts, and explicit claims of racial/wealth-based favoritism or exclusion (e.g., ‘Please don't come to this school if you are not a Christian, white, and rich’). Square entries seldom contain this mixture of enrollment‑model, religious identity, legacy, and explicit discrimination/selection dynamics.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute student: These reviews describe concrete safety problems inside the building and on campus — e.g., “Bullying in this school is out of control,” “Fights on campus almost daily… a staff member was hospitalized,” “kids bring weapons to school,” rampant vaping, cutting class and graffiti — complaints that are far more frequent in circle than in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries document broader and stro: Circle reviews repeatedly cite structured college-prep and enrichment programs (many AP/DE classes, Cyber Security and programming teams, FFA/mariachi/award-winning bands, state championships, multi‑million dollar scholarship totals), giving concrete course counts and outcome metrics that square reviews do not.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more hands-on, i: Examples include claims that “EVERY teacher has after school extra help hours,” a morning academic lab, counselors who ‘bent over backwards’ to save a student, and well‑documented in‑school therapists and success coordinators — operational supports emphasized in circle but absent or weaker in square.
candidate_defs.square entries report weaker instruction: Square reviews emphasize problems with classroom management and instruction (teachers ‘cruise the internet,’ using movies as facts), low expectations in regular classes, limited AP/dual enrollment access, and guidance-department failures for college-bound seniors — concrete gaps in curriculum alignment and college counseling more prominent in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more distinctive g: Circle reviewers call out board-level political favoritism, family/name-based advantages, Catholic/faith identity and tuition/mandatory fees, reports of both recent renovations and simultaneous basic facility failures (broken toilets, rotten food, textbook shortages), and transportation or budget cuts — community/governance dynamics and operational extremes that are far more visible in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more on-campus vio: These reviews describe concrete student-safety problems (mass fights, 17 fights in one day, shootings/bomb threats, sexual misconduct on campus), pervasive bullying and racialized harassment, and prevalent substance use (vaping, chewing tobacco, drugs) that square reviews do not report; examples include accounts of students 'looking for drugs,' organized social-media glorification of fights, and students leaving campus unmonitored, all indicating systemic safety failures rather than isolated complaints.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ad: Many circle reviews enumerate formal rigorous offerings and results—AP/IB coursework, partnerships with colleges and hospitals, JROTC national rankings, 1:1 device rollouts, and explicit outcome metrics (ACT scores, selective‑college matriculation, remediation rates)—whereas square reviews rarely cite such measurable programmatic partnerships or quantified postsecondary outcomes; examples include named college-credit programs, '100% four‑year college matriculation' claims, and specific AP/IB participation notes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more facility, sta: Circle reviews frequently document infrastructural and operational breakdowns—overcrowding and mobile classrooms, unsanitary cafeteria/food-safety issues, water quality problems, custodial understaffing, missing teachers, disrupted schedules, and technology or e‑text outages that harmed grades—whereas square reviews seldom cite this combination of chronic physical‑resource and staffing failures; cited incidents include 'over 110% capacity,' 'worms falling from the ceiling,' 'over half of the students don't get a lunch,' and an e-book outage that caused mass course failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: These reviews highlight leadership problems and policy/discipline misapplications—unreturned counselor messages, misapplied handbook rules, misuse or overreach of Zero‑Tolerance, inconsistent enforcement (appearance punished while harassment ignored), administrative denial of gang/drug problems, and poor central‑office responsiveness—where square reviews tend not to document this pattern of procedural breakdown; concrete examples include a counselor who 'has not returned any messages in 9 months,' hand‑book timing conflicts, and suspensions applied without explanation.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pronounced lo: Circle reviews repeatedly reference multigenerational alumni and family‑like communities, explicit faith/single‑sex school identities, and also social stratification and favoritism (athlete favoritism, nepotism in hiring, elitist cultures) as well as PTO/parent engagement—dimensions of local community and social ordering that square reviews rarely emphasize; examples include multiple generations attending the same school, stated Catholic/Jesuit identity, parents 'sacrificed financially' to attend, and accusations that 'teachers favor athletes' or that 'nepotism is tolerated.'
candidate_defs.circle entries document stronger formal: These reviews highlight organized college-prep pathways and measurable alumni success (growing AP/honors offerings, dual‑credit partnerships with community colleges, Ivy Tech/Ivy League acceptances, claims like “99% of students go to college” and parents reporting their children were “fully prepared for college”), whereas square reviews lack comparable claims of systematized college-prep or consistent, quantified postsecondary outcomes.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Many circle reviews recount concrete safety breaches—assaults in front of security, daily harassment, repeated physical fights, alcohol/drug use at events, car break‑ins—and describe school leaders as ignoring or mishandling those threats (e.g., assaulted child not held accountable, bullying 'swept under the rug'), a pattern largely absent or weaker in square reviews.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more administrat: Circle entries frequently allege governance problems—refusal to provide transcripts, procedural violations in special education, formal complaints filed with districts/attorney general, contested tuition/fee enforcement, misallocated spending or marketing priorities, restrictive volunteer policies and punitive graduation/attendance rules—indicating breakdowns in leadership, transparency and policy implementation not emphasized in square reviews.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: Square reviews repeatedly describe instructional problems tied to staff behavior—teachers who play videos, are frequently absent, allow late submissions with no penalty, grade very slowly, or otherwise provide uneven pedagogy—whereas circle reviews more often document structured tutoring, teacher‑run clubs, or named teachers who provide individualized support.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize stronger commun: Circle reviewers commonly note multigenerational loyalty, tight family networks, faith‑centered identity, small‑school personalization, and an abundance of extracurriculars (robust fine arts, competitive clubs, athletics traditions, teacher‑run clubs and volunteerism), features that square reviews either omit or report far less consistently.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: This bucket captures reviews that detail pervasive peer violence, vaping/drug problems, racial/homophobic slurs, daily fights, gang activity, suicides and physical assaults—and explicit accounts that staff/administration failed to stop or retaliated against complainants (e.g., “My child was beaten up several times, teachers simply turned their backs,” “There is a huge vaping, drug, and bulling problem,” “Between the middle school and high school there seems to be a fight nearly every day”). These are concrete safety/fidelity-of-response complaints that occur far more often in circle reviews than in square ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups accounts of leadership and HR problems—principals abusing staff, administrators who hide problems or lie, nepotistic hiring and surname-based favoritism, punitive discipline and staff harassment (e.g., “the principals at BSGS abuse their power,” “superintend who only cares about hiding problems,” “They hire ex-students… good old boy attitude,” and “They give me suspends for no reason”). These describe top-down misconduct, cover-ups, and relationship‑based access that reviewers attribute to the school’s leadership and governance.
candidate_defs.square entries emphasize a high-pressure: This bucket collects reviews that portray an academically intense, selective culture with emphasis on AP/IB rigor, competitiveness and associated student stress (e.g., “AP courses are so beneficial,” “stress, insomnia, anxiety,” and sustained references to IB/AP workloads). These are concrete descriptions of instructional intensity and normative pressure that appear more often in square reviews than in circle ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more concrete co: This bucket groups reviews citing measurable postsecondary results and formal advanced pathways—dual enrollment completions, scholarship totals, high matriculation/graduation rates, AP/Honors rigor and structured honors tracking (e.g., “graduated with four college classes completed through Dual Enrollment,” “over $9 million in scholarships offered,” “SHC slots kids pretty effectively into honors programs,” and “Almost 98%… go on to advanced education”). These are outcome- and program-focused claims that circle reviewers mention more often.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger community: This bucket covers concrete descriptions of active parent/PTA/booster support, abundant extracurricular and competitive programs (sports, band, FFA, robotics), and superior on-site facilities/technology provisioning (new buildings, laptops, SmartBoards) reported in circle reviews (e.g., “The PTO is active… we now have soccer and baseball thanks to booster clubs,” “Every child is given a lap top… every classroom has a SmartBoard,” and multiple competitive program wins). These elements emphasize community engagement and material resources for non-classroom programs and appear more frequently in circle entries than square ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger advance: These reviews emphasize formal advanced curricula and measurable student success (IB, AP, honors, dual-enrollment, CTE pathways) and concrete admissions/scholarship outcomes (Ivy admits, National Merit, full scholarships), e.g. “IB program… top 20 go to Ivy’s,” “AP program is great,” and “my son… headed to Howard on a full academic scholarship,” whereas square lacks comparable programmatic depth or documented matriculation claims.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent stud: Many circle reviews detail fights, daily food‑throwing incidents, thefts, severe bullying (including racially‑motivated and homophobic harassment), on‑campus drug use, and security lapses or evacuation concerns—examples include “fights in class,” “so many food fights like once per day,” “SEVERE drug problem… faculty choose to ignore,” and “security are worthless,” while square reviews generally do not describe this level of violent or illicit behavior.
candidate_defs.circle entries allege more administrativ: Circle reviewers repeatedly accuse leadership of nepotism/favoritism, grade manipulation, privacy breaches, financial/legal misconduct, ‘who you know’ admissions, and punitive enforcement (e.g., 50% grading policy, exam bans tied to payments), with quotes like “nepotism and favoritism are beyond belief,” “50% policy,” and “privacy issues abound,” whereas square contains few or no such governance or legal‑misconduct allegations.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more operational: Numerous circle reviews call out overcrowded classrooms and high student–teacher ratios, decade‑old computers and slow login times, late busses and slow lunch service, missing supplies, facility decay or consolidation, and failures to implement 504/IEP accommodations or provide effective counseling—e.g. “student/teacher ratio 27/1,” “computers… AMD CPUs a decade old,” “no supplies! No books!” and “504 Plan… never happened”—problems that square’s reviews rarely describe at the same scale.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe stronger extracu: Circle reviews repeatedly celebrate high participation rates, state/regional athletic championships, award‑winning arts and strong JROTC programs, plus active alumni and community volunteerism (e.g. “Participation in athletics… about 95%,” “national award‑winning chorus,” “JROTC… top notch,” and “great alumni support”), while square does not report the same consistent breadth of extracurricular achievements or alumni/community mobilization.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe substantially st: These reviews emphasize concrete advanced offerings at circle schools—multiple AP/IB/dual-enrollment classes, on‑campus college credits, CTE/Academy pathways, industry certifications and measurable outcomes (e.g., 40+ college credits, state/national CTE awards, scholarship totals)—while square reviews rarely document comparable volume of college-credit, certification, or organized career-academy programming.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews contain detailed accounts of violence, fights, gang activity, drug use/on‑campus selling, pervasive bullying, threatened/intimidatory vandalism and even sexual-staff allegations, and also note tightened security (alarms, new security) — whereas square reviews lack these sustained, concrete safety/bullying crises.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Many circle comments call out principal bias, nepotism/‘hiring from within’, athletic favoritism, staff enabling bullying, failure to honor IEP/504 directives, counselor inaccessibility, exam sabotage, and even alleged sexual relationships and intimidation—systemic leadership and policy failures that square reviews do not repeatedly describe.
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete, va: Circle reviewers supply detailed infrastructure accounts ranging from recent renovations, new science wings, MacBook/iPad 1:1 programs and modern classrooms to severe HVAC failures, filthy buildings, crowded lunchrooms, and dated parent portals—showing both tangible investments and acute operational breakdowns that square entries mention far less.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize broader extracu: Circle reviews repeatedly catalog many clubs, award‑winning music/theater, extensive sports, traditions (powderpuff, marching band wins), small‑town or tight‑knit pride and multigenerational enrollment—painting a robust extracurricular/community life that square reviews rarely describe with the same scope or continuity.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more explicit sp: These reviews name concrete curricular offerings and measurable academic outcomes (IB, AP, dual enrollment, on‑site college classes, new STEM programs, scholarship totals, AP/college placement data) and list vocational/CTE pathways and industry certifications (construction, culinary, OSHA, SkillsUSA), whereas square reviews offer more generic claims about college readiness without program-level detail. Examples: “new STEM program,” “85 seniors won $7.5 million,” “third most dual enrollment courses,” and multiple CTE pathway descriptions.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe studen: Many circle reviews recount specific, high‑risk safety failures and student harm—stalking with no protection, being told to carry a pocketknife, students bringing weapons, in‑class drug use, daily fights, suicidal behavior and panic disorders—details that square reviews largely do not provide. Illustrative items: “When a stalker was reported, nothing was done… carry a pocket knife,” “students literally did drugs in class,” and “Fights everyday…teachers cuss at the kids.”
candidate_defs.circle entries document more administrat: Circle reviewers repeatedly describe concrete organizational breakdowns and problematic staff behavior—lost paperwork and records, counselors ignoring students, administrators protecting favorites, grade entry errors, political protection of poor teachers, rude office staff, PTA/finance disputes—whereas square reviews rarely list this level of operational dysfunction. Representative examples: “the doctor's note that I turned in was lost,” “principle and most teachers show favouritism,” “they refused to fill out a form I needed,” and “grade entry errors/incorrect Fs.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more acute facilit: Circle reviews frequently cite tangible infrastructure and operational resource shortfalls—roaches and rodent odors, bathrooms smelling of sewage, no air conditioning or heat, overcrowded classrooms and shortened passing periods, bus no‑shows and poor cafeteria food—conditions largely absent from square’s accounts. Examples include: “Roaches are all over campus,” “lacks air conditioning… lacks heat,” “your child's bus will just not show up,” and “Lunches are unspeakable… pizza is Walmart $1 pizza.”
candidate_defs.circle entries describe larger‑scale, be: Circle reviews emphasize broad, organized extracurricular ecosystems and high competitive achievement (large JROTC, state‑championship teams, award‑winning band/choir, extensive clubs, funded arts and fundraising) and document strong local political backing (referendum victories), while square reviews tend to mention activities more modestly. Examples: “thriving JROTC which involves about 300 students,” “great success in soccer (state champs),” “choir went to State Contest and received a Superior Rating,” and “87% of voters… decided that it was important to keep our doors open.”
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive adv: These reviews emphasize concrete program breadth and outcomes (AP/IB/Early College, dual enrollment, National Merit/High SATs, 1:1 laptops, vocational certifications and measurable test/GPA statistics), e.g. ‘Advanced placement classes are great,’ ‘IB classes available,’ ‘full ride to a private jesuit college,’ and ‘most graduate with 3.0+ GPAs,’ while square reviews rarely cite comparable advanced-program availability or systemic outcome data.
candidate_defs.square entries report more frequent and: Square reviews repeatedly document fights, gang/drug activity, lockdowns, sexual/physical assaults, and bullying tolerated or ignored by staff (e.g. ‘constant fights,’ ‘bullying is rampant,’ ‘police intervention required,’ ‘no one helped her’), whereas circle reviews much less often describe ongoing violent incidents or chronic staff non‑intervention.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger, better‑r: Circle reviewers highlight championship athletics, high‑quality band/conservatory arts, film/media programs, and named caring leaders (e.g. ‘state‑winning teams,’ ‘the band director is fabulous,’ ‘conservatory-style arts tracks’), portraying sustained program excellence and staffing that square reviews generally do not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more cohesive fa: Many circle reviews emphasize small‑town fit, multi‑child family continuity, active PTO/PARENT groups, alumni networking and local pride (e.g. ‘one big family,’ ‘we sent 4 of our 5 children,’ ‘PTO is very involved,’ ‘alumni come back for career day’), while square reviews more often report weak parent involvement or fragmented community sentiment.
candidate_defs.square entries report greater instructio: Square reviewers frequently call out unresponsive administration and office miscommunication, ineffective guidance counselors, inconsistent or punitive discipline, favoritism, and staff churn (e.g. ‘the administration never does anything,’ ‘GUIDANCE DEPT. severely lacking,’ ‘teachers come and go,’ ‘refuse to take disciplinary action’), patterns that are much more prominent in square reviews than in circle ones.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more severe safety: This bucket captures reviews that describe life‑threatening incidents, gang formation, on‑campus weapons/shooting signs, drug use, sexual/romantic staff–student misconduct, pervasive physical bullying, or students traumatized by the environment — and where reviewers say administration ignores, minimizes, or fails to investigate those complaints (examples: “One teacher is currently in a coma…”, “the violence… gangs are formed”, “they fired the Physical Therapist… didn’t contact authorities”, and “Bullying is a major problem here. If a student tries to get help they are blown off by administrators”). Square entries lack comparable reports of systemic, high‑severity safety failures and administrative dismissal of safety concerns, instead mentioning isolated fights or better-managed incidents.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket groups reviews alleging leadership problems that go beyond ordinary complaints — principal apathy or hostility, refusal to respond to parents, punitive blanket punishments, claims of record‑manipulation, nepotistic hires or board conflicts of interest, improper fee handling, and assertions of constitutional or legal violations (examples: “Administration is unavailable and incompetent,” “they make up stories to cover up their mistakes,” “Board President’s live‑in boyfriend is the chef paid $95K,” and “applying the 4.0 GPA scale retroactively”). Square entries do not make these kinds of systemic governance/misconduct allegations and often describe at least some accessible, compromising administrators.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more concrete, for: This bucket covers reviews that describe explicit programmatic investments in rigorous curricula and credit pathways — many AP/IB classes, new IB adoption, distance learning to access AP, dual enrollment/college credit outcomes, formal career/technical programs, or named college‑preparation initiatives (examples: “about 20 AP classes and a new IB program,” “they orchestrated distance learning for AP classes,” and “Both daughters walked into college with 12 credit hours”). Square entries more often complain of lack of challenge, limited AP offerings, or focus problems rather than detailing institution‑level college‑prep program breadth or measurable credit outcomes.
candidate_defs.square entries report more pervasive tea: This bucket groups reviews that focus on instructional and day‑to‑day classroom failings attributed to teachers as a system — widespread apathy, refusal to teach effectively, slow/absent grading practices, teachers not managing student behavior, and a 9–5 mentality (examples from square: “the teachers and staff do not care about students,” “Teachers do not care… they see the bullying and do nothing,” and “faculty literally treats it as a 9-5 job”). Circle reviews contain many contrasting accounts of engaged, sacrificial, or consistently supportive teachers and so are less represented in this negative, teacher‑quality cluster.
candidate_defs.circle entries report greater concrete f: This bucket captures reviews emphasizing physical investments and activity breadth — new buildings/renovations, phenomenal athletic or band facilities, robust arts/music/club offerings, one‑to‑one iPads or technology programs, active booster and parent fundraising, and organized family services (examples: “NEW Belleville High School… athletic facilities are phenomenal,” “each having their own Apple iPad,” “arts program in this district is amazing,” and “PARENTS CLUB is INCREDIBLE!”). Square entries more often report limited facilities, fewer extracurriculars, missing athletic fields, or funding shortfalls without the same catalogue of recent capital upgrades and broad extracurricular infrastructure.
candidate_defs.circle entries report broader and deeper: This bucket groups reviews that describe concrete, high‑value program offerings and student outcomes (IB, AP, dual‑enrollment, honors, STEAM, award‑winning CTE/robotics, extensive clubs/band/FFA, students graduating with 40+ college credits or large scholarship totals) — e.g., multiple circle items cite IB pathways, AP/dual enrollment, CTE, full scholarships and measurable college placement that square reviews do not.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent, sev: This bucket covers reviewers describing pervasive bullying, fights, drug problems, weapon/security incidents, meal‑denial or harsh attendance enforcement, frequent suspensions, and an overall carceral or punitive atmosphere — for example multiple circle reports of bullying 'very high', drugs ignored by staff, a gun taken from a locker, denial of lunches, and constant suspensions which are not present in square.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more administrativ: This bucket captures accounts of principals/administrators who use fear or threats, protect relatives/athletes, practice opaque targeting/scapegoating, resist transparency or complaints, and create a climate where staff fear speaking up — e.g., circle claims of administrators 'using fear', '98% related so they won't address issues', threats to call CPS, and removal/targeting of critics, contrasts absent from square.
candidate_defs.circle entries mention special‑education: This bucket groups reviews that explicitly discuss IEP teams, social‑work supports, inclusion practices, dyslexia/ autism/ADHD accommodations (both success stories and concrete failures), plus racial/religious inclusion or exclusion — for instance circle contains detailed IEP/social‑work praise, dyslexia remediation failures, racial safety worries and faith‑based exclusion that square does not emphasize.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational a: This bucket covers concrete, day‑to‑day operational issues (late/changed bus routes, meal program policies, cafeteria food, bathroom sanitation, overcrowding, registration/scheduling failures, uniform/fundraising costs) as well as major capital contrasts (new construction or big athletic stadium investments), for example circle reports late buses, denied lunches, mice and shooting outside, plus community bonds/new school builds — topics square reviews lack or treat differently.
candidate_defs.circle entries report stronger advanced-: These entries emphasize concrete advanced offerings and outcomes—AP/Honors tracks, dual-enrollment/IB/CTE academies, documented AP pass rates, college matriculation, and vocational-to-job pipelines (examples: “lots of honor classes…AP,” “prepared them well to compete and succeed in being admitted to selective collegiate programs,” “CTE academies that lead to job offers”), so a school whose reviews fall here will be described as having substantive advanced coursework and tracked college/career results.
candidate_defs.circle entries document more frequent an: This grouping covers reports of ongoing fights, pervasive bullying, sexual-assault allegations, daily physical danger, on-campus vaping/drug sales, and inconsistent/biased discipline (examples: “Too much bullying and fights happen every other day,” “Sexual assault, bullying, and racial bias are rampant and under addressed,” “they let kids vape anywhere”), so content in this bucket signals schools with recurring safety/behavior incidents and enforcement failures.
candidate_defs.circle entries emphasize close-knit comm: These reviews highlight interpersonal community features—small‑town or family atmosphere, alumni-dominated staffing and social hierarchies, faith-based curricula/chapels, boarding/dorm issues, and intergenerational enrollment (examples: “a very close knit community…many teachers are former students,” “CATHOLIC…faith based first,” “the barracks are DEPLORABLE”), indicating the school’s culture is organized around tight community, religious identity, or residential life.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more extensive a: This bucket groups mentions of broad, award‑winning extracurriculars (music, choir, band, debate, FFA), athletic dominance and many competitive teams, facility renovations/technology, and also program-fee complaints or coach behavior concerns (examples: “Best Athletics in the Area,” “award‑winning fine arts program,” “Recently renovated building…lots of technology,” “they Charge way the Heck too much…do something about the coaches”), meaning reviews here point to robust extracurricular infrastructures often accompanied by cost or coaching controversies.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more operational,: This category captures concrete administrative and governance problems—unresponsive counselors, lost transcripts, IEP and special‑education placement breakdowns, attendance/credit mishandling, favoritism/nepotism, and contentious school-board/staff relationships (examples: “The counseling department is useless…transcript was never sent,” “IEP area handled very poorly,” “coaches son as a math teacher,” “ask why other school districts have recently withdrawn from this collective”), so entries here indicate systemic operational dysfunctions that impede students’ progress or equity.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more extensive adv: These reviews describe concrete, high‑level academic offerings at circle schools (many AP courses, IB programs, Early College/dual‑enrollment, quantified college credit and awards, National Merit and high ACT scores) while square reviews lack equivalent program breadth or outcome metrics; examples include circle claims of ‘‘over 25 AP courses,’’ IB diploma recipients, ‘‘excess of 40 hours of college credit,’’ and named college matriculations that square does not provide.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more pervasive stu: Circle reviews recount specific violent incidents, daily targeted bullying, gang/drug activity, drug busts and students hospitalized — often paired with ineffective administrative follow‑through — whereas square reviews typically mention only occasional or general bullying; concrete items include assaults with minimal suspension, repeated bullying of an autistic student, gang threats, and multiple recent drug busts reported only in circle entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe broader, better‑: Many circle reviews enumerate extensive extracurricular offerings (theater, award‑winning bands/choir, culinary programs, NJROTC, robotics clubs, extensive sports), vocational/IT certification and hands‑on media labs, and modern campus/tech (state‑of‑the‑art buildings, smart boards, school laptops, high‑end cameras) that square reviews do not describe; examples include named culinary chefs, media equipment lists (Adobe, 3D cameras), JROTC awards, and museums/library art displays.
candidate_defs.circle entries document systemic adminis: Circle reviews frequently allege entrenched favoritism or family control, hiring based on connections, mis‑registration/scheduling errors, missing report cards, fake credentials, budget/levy funding problems and calls for public investigations — operational and governance problems absent from square; illustrative claims include ‘‘husbands and wives run the school,’’ students ‘‘bumped’’ from classes for money, district noncompliance requiring state intervention, and persistent communication failures.
candidate_defs.square entries describe more accessible,: Square reviews more often highlight helpful, available principals and staff, active parent groups, one‑on‑one registration counseling, in‑school tutoring and targeted counselor support for struggling students, whereas circle entries more often report lacking or uneven individualized supports; examples include square statements that ‘‘school leadership is excellent,’’ ‘‘personal, one‑on‑one counseling when registering’’ and readily available staff tutoring/support programs.
candidate_defs.circle entries describe more concrete ad: These reviews name specific rigorous pathways and documented student outcomes (AP course lists, IB/Cambridge claims, dual‑enrollment partnerships, college credits, alumni degrees and scholarships) that square reviews do not. Examples: circle reviewers cite AP/IB/Cambridge equivalency, Dual Enrollment with Valencia/Valencia Community College credits, students transferring into Georgia Tech after remediation, and alumni Masters degrees or scholarship offers — concrete program and outcome evidence absent or less specific in square entries.
candidate_defs.circle entries report more frequent and: Circle reviews more often recount on‑campus violence, pervasive bullying (including staff‑on‑student bullying), drug and alcohol use, and alleged mishandling of sexual‑assault reports, whereas square reviews largely omit or downplay these systemic safety failures. Illustrative mentions include 'kids are high and drunk in school regularly,' 'vicious acts of physical violence go unchecked,' multiple allegations that sexual‑assault reports were ignored, and calls for drug prevention.
candidate_defs.square entries present more consistently: Square reviews are characteristically uniform in praising caring, well‑qualified teachers, steady college‑prep programs, and strong extracurriculars/community support, while circle reviews show far more polarized experiences. Examples: square statements like 'incredible -- so passionate, well‑educated, caring' and 'a solid 8 out of 10' contrast with circle's mixed accounts (some parents cite 'amazing' teachers and state championships, others describe incompetence and bullying).
candidate_defs.circle entries contain more concrete ope: Circle reviews frequently document procedural breakdowns and frontline service failures — e.g., offices not returning calls, counselors who mess up profiles or encourage dropout, transcripts withheld, 504/IEP accommodations not followed, late buses, unacceptable food items — problems that square entries rarely enumerate with such operational detail. Sample claims include 'no one was returning their calls… couldn't get my transcripts,' '504 plan failing every subject,' and 'Chromebooks are always broke.'
candidate_defs.circle entries discuss facilities, techn: Circle reviews are much more likely to name explicit physical‑resource conditions — often at extremes — such as newly built million‑dollar campuses, $23M upgrades, schoolwide iPad rollouts and security camera installations, but also chronic maintenance neglect, broken bathrooms, no textbooks, and custodial problems.
